For O-GlcNAc perturbation experiments, 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 was included during labelling to maintain treatment conditions. Where indicated, SiR-tetrazine (Spirochrome, SC008) or JF646-tetrazine (Tocris, 7279) was used following the same protocol. After labelling, cells were washed with 1× PBS and imaged immediately in FluoroBrite Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (Thermo Fisher, A1896701) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, 1% l-glutamine, 1% sodium pyruvate and 10 mM HEPES. Imaging was performed at room temperature with the dish sealed to ensure stable conditions during the roughly 2-h acquisition period.

COS-7 cells labelled with HD653 were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS for 10 min, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 min and blocked with 3% bovine serum albumin in PBS for 90 min. According to recent reports, to estimate the local concentration of importin-β at the nuclear pore, solutions containing free Alexa Fluor 488 at known concentrations (1 μm–1 mM) were added to immunostained cells. Nuclear pore fluorescence remained distinguishable from the background in the presence of up to 100 μM free dye but became indistinguishable at 1 mM (Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that the effective local concentration of importin-β at the nuclear pore is in the millimolar range.

The doxycycline-inducible U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cell line described above was treated with doxycycline (0.5 μg ml−1) for 0, 6, 10, 15 or 24 h. Non-transduced U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells without doxycycline treatment were used as a parental control. Cell lysates were collected at the indicated time points and analysed by immunoblotting using an anti-FLAG antibody (Proteintech, 66008-4-Ig; 1:1,000 dilution) to detect exogenous importin-β and an anti-KPNB1 antibody (1:2,500 dilution) to detect both endogenous and exogenous importin-β. α-Tubulin detected with an anti-α-Tubulin antibody (ABclonal, AC012; 1:5,000 dilution) was used as a loading control. Doxycycline induction resulted in detectable FLAG-tagged importin-β expression, whereas the total KPNB1 signal highlighted no substantial increase compared with the parental control, consistent with near-endogenous expression of the exogenous protein (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20).

In a recent development, to verify modulation of cellular O-GlcNAcylation, COS-7 cells were treated with 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 as described above and lysed directly in Laemmli sample buffer. Proteins were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS–PAGE), transferred to nitrocellulose membranes and probed with the anti-O-GlcNAc antibody RL2 (Invitrogen, MA1-072; 1:1,000 dilution). Bound antibody was detected using an IRDye 800CW goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (LI-COR Biosciences, 926-32210; 1:10,000 dilution) and visualized using an Odyssey imaging system (Fig. 4b).

Live-cell nuclear-import assays were performed as described previously49 with minor modifications. COS-7 cells expressing NES–mCherry–LINuS were treated with 10 μM Thiamet-G or 10 μM OSMI-4 and imaged 24 h after transfection following Hoechst 33342 staining (10 μg ml−1, 10 min). Imaging was performed on a Zeiss LSM 980 confocal microscope. Nuclear import was induced by 488-nm illumination and monitored by mCherry fluorescence using 561-nm excitation. Images were acquired every 10 s for 820 s. Nuclear regions were segmented using Hoechst fluorescence, and nuclear mCherry intensity was quantified over time and normalized to the pre-activation signal. Apparent nuclear-import rate constants were obtained by fitting fluorescence accumulation curves to y = 1 + (b − 1)(1 − e−kt), where b is the plateau fluorescence intensity and k is the apparent nuclear-import rate constant.

The human NUP98 FG domain (residues 1–505) was cloned into a pQE-14his-TEV vector. As described previously26,59, the GLEBS domain (residues 157–213) was excluded to avoid misfolding of this structured region on rapid dilution from denaturant during phase separation (see ‘In vitro phase separation assay’ below); intrinsically disordered FG regions, by contrast, readily regain their dynamic ensemble under native buffer conditions. The construct was transformed into Escherichia coli BL21-AI cells and grown in terrific broth supplemented with kanamycin (50 µg ml−1) at 37 °C with shaking at 200 rpm. Protein expression was induced when optical density at 600 nm (OD600) ≈ 0.6 with 0.02% (w/v) arabinose and 1 mM iIsopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside, followed by incubation for 16 h at 18 °C.

It has been revealed that cells were collected and lysed using a high-pressure cell disruptor (CF1, Constant Systems) in lysis buffer containing 6 M guanidine hydrochloride (GdmCl), 0.2 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), 20 mM imidazole and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Following clarification by centrifugation (12,000g, 1 h, 4 °C), lysates were incubated with nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) resin for 2 h at 4 °C. Bound protein was washed with 2 M GdmCl buffer and eluted with 500 mM imidazole in 2 M GdmCl and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). After dialysis into 0.5 M GdmCl and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), the N-terminal His-tag was removed by overnight TEV protease digestion. The cleaved protein was separated from uncleaved protein and TEV protease by a second Ni-NTA purification step and further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL, Cytiva, 28990944) in 2 M GdmCl, 0.2 mM TCEP and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0). Purity was confirmed by SDS–PAGE and Coomassie staining. Protein fractions were concentrated to about 15 mg ml−1, quantified using a bicinchoninic acid assay and stored at −80 °C.

Industry observers note that the purified NUP98 FG domain was enzymatically glycosylated using recombinant OGT1 and UDP-GlcNAc (Sigma, U4375). The reaction mixture contained 10 µM NUP98 FG domain, 1 µM OGT1 and 1 mM UDP-GlcNAc in glycosylation buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 200 mM NaCl, 20 mM MgCl2, 0.2 mM TCEP and 1% Tween-20). Samples were incubated for 16 h at room temperature with gentle rotation. Following O-GlcNAcylation, His-tagged OGT1 was removed using Ni-NTA resin. O-GlcNAcylated NUP98 FG domain was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200) in 2 M GdmCl, 0.2 mM TCEP and 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and concentrated to about 40 mg ml−1. O-GlcNAcylation efficiency was assessed by mass spectrometry, confirming successful modification of the NUP98 FG domain (Extended Data Fig. 8c).

According to recent reports, for experiments requiring higher levels of O-GlcNAc modification, the purified glycosylated protein was subjected to a second round of enzymatic O-GlcNAcylation under identical reaction conditions. Unless otherwise stated, all experiments were performed using NUP98 FG domains that had undergone a single round of O-GlcNAcylation. Proteins subjected to two rounds of O-GlcNAcylation were used only for the experiments shown in Supplementary Fig. 18.

Excess dye was quenched with 10 mM dithiothreitol and removed by ultrafiltration (3 kDa molecular-weight cutoff), followed by size-exclusion chromatography (Superdex 200). Protein concentrations and labelling efficiencies were determined spectroscopically using a Duetta fluorometer (Horiba). Labelled proteins were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C.

Industry observers note that the human importin-β coding sequence was cloned into a pTXB3-intein-CBD-12His vector and transformed into E. coli BL21-AI cells. Cultures were grown in terrific broth supplemented with kanamycin (50 μg ml−1) at 37 °C with shaking (200 rpm). Industry observers note that purified NUP98 FG domains stored in 2 M GdmCl were induced to phase separate by rapid dilution into transport buffer (20 mM HEPES, 110 mM KOAc, 5 mM NaOAc, 2 mM Mg(OAc)2, 1 mM EGTA and 2 mM dithiothreitol, pH 7.3). Unless otherwise indicated, 1 μl protein solution was mixed with 24 μl transport buffer on a chambered coverslip (ibidi, 81507) immediately before imaging. The residual GdmCl concentration after dilution was about 80 mM and did not interfere with condensate formation.

Recent findings suggest that because O-GlcNAcylated FG domains exhibited reduced phase-separation propensity, a final concentration of 25 μM was used for the experiments in Fig. 4g–i to generate condensates of comparable size and morphology to those formed by wild-type FG domains.

For cophase separation assays, importin-β was diluted into transport buffer to the desired concentration before mixing with FG domains. Wild-type FG domains were used at 10 μM unless otherwise indicated. Glycosylated FG–importin-β condensates were prepared from 25 μM glycosylated FG domains and 10 μM importin-β to obtain condensates comparable to those formed by wild-type FG domains. The final concentration of GdmCl was maintained at 80 mM across all conditions.

Recent findings suggest that dense- and dilute-phase concentrations of NUP98 FG condensates were determined using trace amounts of Alexa Fluor 594-labelled NUP98 FG domain. Condensates were formed from mixtures of unlabelled wild-type NUP98 FG domain and labelled tracer protein at molar ratios of 2,000:1, 5,000:1 or 10,000:1, as described above. Immediately after formation, condensates were sedimented by centrifugation at 4,300g for 5 min.

Dense-phase fluorescence was measured on a custom-built confocal microscope equipped with a 560-nm pulsed laser. Dense-phase regions were identified from their high fluorescence intensity and characteristic condensate morphology. Fluorescence intensities were converted to protein concentrations using calibration curves generated from known concentrations of free Alexa Fluor 594 measured under matched buffer conditions. Differences in fluorescence quantum yield between free dye and dye-conjugated protein were measured independently using a Duetta fluorometer and used to correct the calculated protein concentrations.

Industry observers note that dilute-phase concentrations were measured by focusing well above the condensate layer and applying the same calibration and quantum-yield correction. An unlabelled/labelled protein ratio of 20:1 was used to increase dilute-phase signal while minimizing perturbation of phase behaviour. Small dynamic nanoclusters were occasionally observed in the dilute phase of wild-type NUP98 FG condensates in the absence of importin-β (Extended Data Fig. 3d).

It has been revealed that the experimentally determined dense- and dilute-phase concentrations were used to constrain FG–importin-β interaction strengths in the coarse-grained molecular-dynamics simulations (Extended Data Fig. 3e).

Industry observers note that to examine the effect of O-GlcNAcylation on FG-domain partitioning, NUP98 FG domains containing a cysteine substitution at residue 221 were site-specifically labelled with fluorescent maleimide dyes. Unglycosylated NUP98 FG domains were labelled with Alexa Fluor 488 maleimide, whereas unglycosylated, modestly O-GlcNAcylated (single-round glycosylation) and highly O-GlcNAcylated (two-round glycosylation) NUP98 FG domains used as probe molecules were labelled with LD655 maleimide.

Preformed condensates were generated from unglycosylated NUP98 FG domains (final concentration roughly 10 μM supplemented with 4 nM Alexa Fluor 488-labelled protein) as described above. Samples were incubated for 30 min at room temperature to allow condensate maturation before probe addition. LD655-labelled probe proteins (unglycosylated, modestly glycosylated or highly glycosylated NUP98 FG domains) were then added to the chamber at a 1:1 volume ratio, yielding a final probe concentration of 20 nM. The incorporation of probe molecules into preformed condensates was monitored by time-lapse confocal microscopy using a Zeiss LSM 980 microscope (Supplementary Fig. 18).

According to recent reports, TRFA measurements were conducted on a custom-built confocal microscope equipped with picosecond pulsed laser diodes (560 nm: LDH-D-TA-560, PicoQuant; 660 nm: LDH-D-C-660, PicoQuant) controlled by a Sepia II PDL 828 multichannel laser driver26. The excitation beam was delivered through a single-mode polarization-maintaining optical fibre (KineFLEX-P-2-S-405/640-2.5-2.5-p2), passed through a Glan-laser polariser (Thorlabs), directed through a FLIMbee laser scanning system (PicoQuant) and focused onto the sample through a ×60 water immersion objective lens (SR Proposal Apo IR, 1.27 NA, Nikon). Fluorescence emission was collected through the same objective, spatially filtered using a pinhole (100 μm for live-cell measurements and 50 μm for in vitro measurements) and separated into parallel and perpendicular polarization components using a polarizing beam splitter. Each component was further separated spectrally by dichroic filters (ZT561 RDC and T647 LPXR, Chroma), passed through bandpass filters (Cy3B: 612/69 BrightLine HC, Semrock; HD653: ET700/75m, Chroma) and detected with hybrid photon-counting detectors (PMA Hybrid 40, PicoQuant). Photon arrival times were recorded with a HydraHarp 400 time-correlated single-photon-counting module at 16-ps resolution. Data were acquired using SymPhoTime 64 software (v.2.6, PicoQuant).

Instrument response functions (IRFs) were measured daily using Erythrosine B in saturated potassium iodide solution and used for reconvolution analysis. Detection channels were aligned using the measured IRFs. We note that a small discontinuity around 4 ns is observed in the raw anisotropy-decay curves; this arises from weak optical reflections in the time-correlated single-photon-counting setup and is accounted for in the analysis by reconvolution with the measured IRFs.

It has been revealed that HD653 fluorescence intensity at the nuclear rim was first verified under 660-nm laser excitation (optimized to 50 μW average power at 40 MHz) to assess the expression level, ensuring comparable expression levels and avoiding overexpression artefacts. Data acquisition was performed using T3 mode, with fluorescence photons collected separately by parallel and perpendicular detectors. Imaging parameters included a pixel size of 100 nm, an image size of 256 pixels × 256 pixels, a pixel dwell time of 150 µs and an imaging time of 5 min. Regions of interest corresponding to the nuclear rim were selected, where thresholding algorithms were applied to identify regions of interest on the basis of pixel intensity and average fluorescence lifetime. The time-resolved intensity curves for parallel and perpendicular channels were extracted for further analysis.

Condensates were imaged immediately after formation as described above. Fluorescence photons were collected in T3 mode using 560-nm excitation (40 MHz repetition rate). To minimize photobleaching and ensure representative sampling, the imaging field was changed every 5 min to examine different condensates throughout the measurement period. Imaging parameters included a pixel size of 150 nm, an image size of 256 pixels × 256 pixels, a pixel dwell time of 203 μs and a time resolution of 16 ps. Condensates were identified on the basis of fluorescence intensity and morphology, and time-resolved intensity curves were extracted from condensate regions using SymPhoTime 64 software.

Industry observers note that for measurements of individual FG chains in solution, purified and labelled FG domains were diluted in transport buffer to a final concentration of 10 nM. Data acquisition and analysis were performed as described above for condensate measurements.

where L1 and L2 are polarization mixing factors caused by the high numerical aperture of the objective lens and G accounts for the differential detection efficiencies between the parallel and perpendicular polarization components:.

To determine L1 and L2, the fluorescence decays of a reference sample, yellow fluorescent protein (YFP), were measured. YFP has a known fluorescence rotational relaxation time (ρ = 16 ns) (ref. 61). The fluorescence decays for the parallel and perpendicular components of YFP were globally fitted using the following equations61:.

Recent findings suggest that where I0 is the initial fluorescence intensity, τ is the fluorescence lifetime and ρ is the rotational correlation time of YFP. The G factor was determined by measuring the ratio of the average intensities in the perpendicular and parallel channels using a solution of tris(2,2’-bipyridyl)dichlororuthenium(II) chloride ([Ru(bpy)3]Cl2), which exhibits isotropic rotational motion.

For IDPs, r(t) can be modelled using a double-exponential decay32:.

where r0 is the fundamental anisotropy of the fluorophore, ρfast is the fitted rotational correlation time associated primarily with local dye/linker motion, rp is the residual anisotropy remaining after fast local motion and reflecting slower, larger-scale chain motions and ρslow is the fitted slow-component timescale used here as an apparent segmental-motion parameter. Values approaching the upper fitting bound of 1,000 ns were interpreted as indicating very slow apparent segmental motion and were not considered well resolved.

When ρfast is much smaller than ρslow, equation (5) can be approximated and simplified to.

where βfast = 1 − rp/r0 and βslow = rp/r0 represent relative amplitudes of the fast (local) and slow (segmental) components, respectively.

Sources indicate that the fluorescence lifetime (τ) was first determined by fitting the total fluorescence decay obtained from the parallel and perpendicular emission channels. The resulting τ value was then fixed during the subsequent global fitting of the parallel and perpendicular fluorescence decays using the 2_exp_rot model implemented in TauFit in the PAM package62, where IRFs were included through reconvolution analysis. Here we interpret ρslow primarily as an apparent segmental-motion parameter for relative comparisons rather than as a precise absolute rotational correlation time. Rotational components slower than the fluorescence lifetime can nevertheless influence the measured anisotropy decay and be estimated by model-based fitting, with precision depending strongly on photon statistics and decreasing as the correlation time increasingly exceeds the fluorescence lifetime63,64. Although three-exponential models were also evaluated, the additional component was consistently negligible or degenerate with existing components and therefore did not improve the fits.

Sources indicate that to calculate steady-state anisotropy (rss), the integrated intensities of the fluorescence emissions collected in the parallel (\({I}_{\parallel }\)) and perpendicular \(({I}_{\perp }\)) channels were used. The steady-state anisotropy was computed using the equation.

The steady-state anisotropy value provides a single, time-averaged measurement of the overall fluorescence anisotropy, which complements the dynamic information obtained from TRFA decay analysis.

For live-cell measurements, single-cell anisotropy-decay traces were used for subsequent analysis. In Fig. 1i, the fitted slow-component parameter (ρslow) was calculated on a per-cell basis to capture relative temporal trends in apparent segmental motion. For all other experiments, a non-parametric bootstrap strategy was applied to improve signal-to-noise and ensure robust curve fitting.

For each condition, 200 bootstrap replicates were generated by resampling single-cell decay traces with replacement, summing photon counts and fitting the resulting decays in TauFit62. Bootstrap depth was selected on the basis of convergence analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2). Differences between conditions were assessed using two-sided bootstrap tests. P values were calculated as the proportion of null resamples with absolute differences greater than or equal to the observed effect. Percentile confidence intervals were derived from the empirical distribution of independent bootstrap differences.

Sources indicate that for in vitro measurements, anisotropy decays were analysed every 5 min and fitted individually. Reported values represent the mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments.

To assess the suitability of HD653 as a probe for TRFA, control experiments were performed using a globular protein with known rotational properties. Purified EGFP containing a single BCN at residue 39 was site-specifically labelled with either HD653 or the rigid, well-characterized anisotropy dye Cy3B30,31. TRFA measurements were conducted on both unlabelled and labelled EGFP at 10 nM in 1× PBS. The rotational correlation times were obtained by fitting TRFA decay curves using the 2_exp_rot model function in TauFit62. For globular EGFP, the fitted slow component, ρslow, corresponds to its overall rotational correlation time and was used to determine the hydrodynamic radius:.

where kB is the Boltzmann constant, T is the absolute temperature and \(\eta \) is the solvent viscosity. Hydrodynamic radii determined for labelled EGFP were consistent with wild-type EGFP and previously reported values65,66, confirming HD653 as a reliable anisotropy probe and supporting its use for segmental dynamics measurements in live-cell and in vitro assays.

Doxycycline-induced U-2 OS-CRISPR-NUP96-mEGFP cells expressing importin-β-3×FLAG-ALFA were prepared as described above. Cells were fixed with 4% PFA for 10 min, washed three times with 1× PBS containing 100 mM glycine and permeabilized and blocked for at least 30 min at room temperature in blocking buffer consisting of 3% bovine serum albumin, 10% donkey serum and 0.3% Triton X-100 in 1× PBS.

DNA docking strand-conjugated anti-GFP and anti-ALFA nanobodies (Massive Photonics) were diluted 1:200 in antibody incubation buffer (Massive Photonics) and incubated with cells for 1 h at room temperature. Samples were washed three times with washing buffer (Massive Photonics) and post-fixed with 2.4% PFA for 8 min. Gold nanoparticles (250 nm diameter; BBI Solutions) were then added for 10 min as fiducial markers for active drift correction, followed by extensive washing with 1× PBS.

It has been revealed that cy3B-labelled DNA-PAINT imager strands (Massive Photonics) were diluted in imaging buffer (Massive Photonics) to a final concentration of 200–500 pM. Samples were mounted in custom imaging chambers, and imager solution was added immediately before imaging. All MINFLUX measurements were completed within 2 days of sample preparation.

In a recent development, two-colour DNA-PAINT MINFLUX measurements were performed on a commercial MINFLUX microscope (Abberior Instruments) based on an Olympus IX83 inverted microscope equipped with a ×100 UPlanXApo objective and controlled by Imspector software. The excitation beam pattern and pinhole position were calibrated daily using fluorescent calibration nanoparticles (Gold 150 nm and 2C Fluor 120 nm; Abberior Instruments).

It has been revealed that cells expressing the inducible importin-β construct were identified by tagBFP fluorescence. Imaging was performed at the basal surface of the nucleus adjacent to the coverslip. Transient DNA-PAINT binding events were verified by rapid confocal imaging before MINFLUX acquisition. At least three gold fiducials were present in each field of view and were used by the active stabilization system to correct real-time drift, maintaining subnanometre lateral stability throughout acquisition.

In a recent development, regions of interest were imaged using the standard two-dimensional MINFLUX acquisition sequence with a pinhole diameter of 0.83 Airy units. Following acquisition of the first target, imager strands were exchanged using a custom perfusion system while maintaining uninterrupted MINFLUX acquisition and active stabilization. Buffer exchange was performed at about 10 μl s−1 until DNA-PAINT binding events were no longer detected, indicating complete removal of the first imager strand. The second imager strand was subsequently introduced and imaging resumed. Sequential two-colour imaging and strand exchange typically required roughly 4 h.

Industry observers note that NPCs were analysed using custom MATLAB routines adapted from the published MINFLUX_NPC_Tracking workflow14. Candidate NPCs were selected from the NUP96 channel and filtered using geometry-based quality-control criteria to exclude incomplete or poorly resolved pores.

In a recent development, for each NPC, the pore centre was determined from NUP96 localizations and used for spatial registration. The eightfold rotational phase was estimated from the angular distribution of NUP96 localizations using the complex order parameter \({z}_{8}=\langle {e}^{i8\theta }\rangle \). Individual NPCs were rotated into a common eightfold reference frame, and the same rigid-body transformation was applied to the corresponding importin-β localizations. Aligned NUP96 coordinates were rendered directly to preserve the native octagonal architecture of the NPC scaffold.

According to recent reports, because importin-β localizations did not exhibit a robust eightfold angular organization, their spatial distribution was quantified using radial density analysis relative to the NUP96-defined pore centre. Localizations were binned by radial distance, corrected for annular area, normalized in each NPC and averaged across pores. Individual radial profiles were smoothed before calculation of the population mean and s.e.m. The resulting mean radial density profile was rotationally symmetrized to generate the final importin-β density map. To assess the contribution of radial geometry, a uniform random two-dimensional distribution was generated in the analysed pore radius and processed using the same radial binning, annular-area correction, normalization, smoothing and symmetrisation as the experimental localizations (Fig. 3g).

According to recent reports, we adapted a previously established coarse-grained model of the NPC26 to incorporate importin-β proteins. In this model, each amino acid (p) of NPC and importin-β proteins is represented by a single bead, the nuclear envelope is modelled using fixed membrane particles (m), and the solvent is treated implicitly. Protein residues are divided into three sub-categories: scaffold residues (sc) and FG residues (FG) of NPC proteins and importin-β residues. The potential energy of the system is given by.

Sources indicate that non-bonded interactions between particles i and j are described by Lennard–Jones potentials, whose strength \({\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{ij}}\), length σij and cutoff values \({r}_{{\rm{c}}}^{{\rm{\alpha }}}\) are provided in Supplementary Table 2. The Lennard–Jones potentials were shifted by their values at the corresponding cutoff radii: that is, \({U}_{{\rm{LJ}}}({r}_{c}^{\alpha })\). The bond potential between adjacent beads of the FG-protein was modelled using the finitely extensible nonlinear elastic potential67 with kFE = 30kBT and RFE = 1.5σ. The radiall positions of importin-β were confined by a half-harmonic potential with stiffness kc = 100kBT/σ2, limiting their radial distance to r ≲ Rc = 81σ ≡ 48.6 nm.

Simulations were performed in LAMMPS (Release Sept. 2021)68,69. Time is reported in units of \(\tau =\sqrt{m{\sigma }^{2}/{k}_{{\rm{B}}}T}\), where m is the bead mass (identical for all bead types). Following earlier work26, we determined the reduced length scale of Lennard–Jones potential obtained as σ ≡ 0.6 nm by matching the root-mean-square inter-residue distance (RE) of a single NUP98 FG chain (amino acids 1–499) in both the homopolymer model and the corresponding Martini representation in the weakly interacting regime70. We found that \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5 reproduces the RE of a single NUP98 FG chain measured by single-molecule FRET, whereas \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.42 best matches in situ FLIM–FRET for the NUP98 FG domain in the NPC26, reflecting in particular the effects of PTMs.

The membrane particles representing the nuclear envelope were constructed from a 100 × 100 nm2 coarse-grained POPC bilayer using the Python script insane.py71,72, with a reduced area per lipid (0.3 nm2) to prevent solvent permeation (command: insane.py -l POPC -x 100 -y 100 -z 100 -a 0.3 -o bilayer.gro). A half-toroidal pore was then generated using BUMPy71 (command: bumpy.py -s double_bilayer_cylinder -f bilayer.gro -z 10 -g l_cylinder:10 r_cylinder:430 r_junction:120 l_flat:1920). To reduce computational cost, only phosphate beads were retained. NPC scaffold and membrane particles were fixed throughout the simulations. To prevent FG domains and importin-β molecules from crossing the membrane, a Lennard–Jones potential with a large repulsive range was applied (Supplementary Table 2).

We used the constricted NPC model II26 including the following FG-NUPs: NUP54, NUP58, NUP62, NUP98, POM121, NUP214, NUP153 and NUP358. Importin-β was modelled using PDB ID 3W5K (ligand Snail1 removed)73. Importin-β molecules were treated as rigid bodies using a rigid-body integrator with a Langevin thermostat and a damping coefficient 10τ (LAMMPS command: fix rigid langevin molecule). FG beads were integrated using the Verlet algorithm74. NUP98 FG chains were thermalized using Langevin thermostats with damping coefficient 10τ (ref. 75).

It has been revealed that importin-β molecules were added to systems of size 320σ × 320σ × 400σ. FG-NUPs were first equilibrated at \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5 for 106τ, during which they formed a surface condensate on the NPC scaffold. These compact conformations allowed us to efficiently introduce NImp-β = 100 importin-β molecules76 with random initial positions and orientations around the NPC. With FG-NUPs frozen and weak interactions (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.1), importin-β molecules were allowed to diffuse for 3.4 × 104τ with thermostat damping coefficient 1,000τ. Subsequently, the full system was equilibrated with \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.42 and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.1 for 105τ using a time step δt = 10−3τ and thermostat damping coefficient 10τ. Production conditions were then applied by setting \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β to their target values, followed by simulations of at least 106τ. Three independent configurations from the equilibration phase were selected as starting points for independent production runs. Structural visualization was performed using VMD77.

To examine how O-GlcNAcylation affects FG-NUP dynamics, we performed molecular-dynamics simulations of the human NPC using the Martini 2.2 coarse-graining scheme. We used the constricted NPC structure (PDB ID: 7R5K, ref. 39). NUPs were grouped into scaffold proteins and disordered FG-NUPs and converted to Martini CG models using the martinize.py script50,78. FG-NUPs included NUP54, NUP58, NUP62, NUP98, POM121, NUP214 and NUP358 (Supplementary Table 3). All scaffold proteins and grafting-anchored ordered domains of FG-NUPs were restrained with a harmonic spring (1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−2).

Recent findings suggest that we generated O-GlcNAcylated NPC models at three modification levels (fgly = 0.18, 0.3 and 0.6), where fgly denotes the fraction of O-GlcNAcylated Ser/Thr sites (Supplementary Fig. 11). Potential O-GlcNAcylation sites were predicted using YinOYang79, which assigns each residue a probability p ∈ [0,1]. Residues with p ≥ pth were considered glycosylated. The resulting number of modified sites Ngly determined fgly = Ngly/Ntotal, where Ntotal = 58,768 is the total number of Ser/Thr residues across all FG-NUPs.

Simulations were performed using GROMACS (v.2020.6 and v.2025.2)80,81. Interaction strengths for protein–protein, protein–sugar and sugar–sugar interactions were rescaled by parameters α, λ and γ, respectively70,82. The optimal α = 0.78 was determined by matching RE of an untreated NUP98 FG chain to single-molecule FRET measurements (Supplementary Fig. 12) and the dense-phase density of FG condensates (Supplementary Fig. 14 and Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). For O-glycosylated FG-NUPs, interactions involving sugars used λ = 0.15 and γ = 0.5, consistent with experimental osmotic second virial coefficients of aqueous sugars and protein–sugar mixtures83,84.

In a recent development, A cubic box (170 nm per side) was constructed to accommodate the NPC. Secondary-structure restraints were assigned using DSSP85. Elastic networks in ordered domains were generated using Elastic Network in Dynamics86 (default parameters; a distance range of 0.9 nm; force constant 500 kJ mol−1 nm−2). All FG domains were modelled as coils except for locally ordered regions in NUP358 (Supplementary Table 3). The system was solvated with Martini water containing 10% antifreeze beads87 and neutralized with NaCl to 150 mM. The total number of solvent particles was about 4 × 107.

Industry observers note that initial energy minimization used steepest descent with maximum step size 0.01 nm and force tolerance 1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−1. During this step, position restraints (1,000 kJ mol−1 nm−2) were temporarily removed to allow global relaxation. Lennard–Jones and Coulomb potentials were first softened using the GROMACS free-energy framework (parameters: couple-lambda0=vdw-q; sc-alpha = 0.1; sc-coul= yes; sc-power = 2; sc-sigma = 0.3), followed by a second minimization using full potentials.

In a recent development, equilibration proceeded as follows. First, NVT simulations at 310 K were performed for 100 ns (velocity-rescaling thermostat88, time constant 1 ps, time step δt = 0.015 ps) using reduced interaction scaling (α = γ = λ = 0.3) to relax chains into coil-like conformations. Next, NPT equilibration at 310 K and 1 bar was performed for 100 ns (velocity-rescaling thermostat88, semi-isotropic Berendsen barostat89, time constant 12 ps, compressibility 3 × 10−4 bar−1). Interaction parameters were then gradually increased. For untreated NPCs, α was raised from 0.3 to 0.5 and then 0.6. For O-glycosylated NPCs, α was increased from 0.3 to 0.6 and then 0.7, with γ = 0.5 and λ = 0.15. This stage lasted 1.5 μs. Production simulations were conducted for at least 2 μs at target α values, using the same thermostat and barostat parameters as in the final equilibration step and a time step δt = 0.02 ps.

Sample sizes were not determined by formal statistical power calculations but were based on previous experience with the respective imaging and biophysical assays26, practical considerations and the requirements for robust and reproducible measurements. For molecular-dynamics simulations, replicate numbers and trajectory blocks were selected on the basis of convergence and reproducibility criteria. Exact sample sizes, numbers of independent experiments and independent sample preparations are reported in the corresponding figure legends.

For experiments in which representative images are shown, including those in Figs. 1b, 2a, 3e and 4b, Extended Data Figs. 1a,b, 2a and 8e and Supplementary Figs. 18–20, experiments were independently repeated at least three times and yielded similar results. Representative images were selected from these independent experiments. Randomization was not applicable because treatments were applied to entire cell cultures or biochemical samples. Experimental variability was minimized by using matched culture, sample-preparation and acquisition conditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daniele Massaro has spoken about how much Franco Baresi meant to him, and how much he now misses the AC Milan icon.

The incredibly sad news broke over the summer that Baresi had passed away following a battle with illness. Thousands of fans lined the streets to pay tribute at his funeral, while the club have honoured him in several ways, including in the first home game against Venezia.

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Given his importance to Milan both as a player and then as an ambassador, it has left a huge hole in the hearts of many, above all his former team-mates and colleagues who shared a dressing room and/or an office with him for many years.

Industry observers note that at the presentation of Mauro Suma’s book ‘Il Milan nel Mondo’ many former players spoke, including Daniele Massaro. He was visibly emotional during his speech, admitting it is actually getting harder to arrive at work each day and not have Baresi there.

Sources indicate that “It was something rare in football. For me every day it’s harder and harder to walk into the office where he used to sit, I miss him. Franco will always be a part of me,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that “I was lucky enough to meet him as an opponent one of the few times we played against each other in Serie B with Monza, then in ’82 we played in the World Cup together. At Milanello I would get changed in front of him, it seemed unreal.”.

A post shared by Milan Press (@milanpress.it).

Scott Parker’s ‘training session reveal’ indicates clean break with Nuno’s strategy | West Ham United

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (339 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With key players absent on international duty, these mid-international break training sessions are challenging for coaching staff who are keen to improve the team but of course don’t get to drill the whole squad.
  • West Ham United, though, with their reduced circumstances this season, have fewer players away than in the ‘old days’ of the Premier League thanks to player departures and others – like skipper Jarrod Bowen – simply being overlooked by their national coaches.
  • Yesterdays ‘inside training’ video demonstrates clear blue water between the old days of Nuno Espírito Santo and the new-era Scott Parker training session.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With key players absent on international duty, these mid-international break training sessions are challenging for coaching staff who are keen to improve the team but of course don’t get to drill the whole squad.

West Ham United, though, with their reduced circumstances this season, have fewer players away than in the ‘old days’ of the Premier League thanks to player departures and others – like skipper Jarrod Bowen – simply being overlooked by their national coaches.

Yesterdays ‘inside training’ video demonstrates clear blue water between the old days of Nuno Espírito Santo and the new-era Scott Parker training session. The very public participation of former ‘discards’ Edson Alvarez and Soungoutou Magassa – both featured from the outset along with perennial discard Maxi Cornet – shows Parker’s pledge to wipe the slate clean has being carried out.

Integrated and back in full training along with Edson Alvarez: Soungoutou Magassa.

There’s been much written about either one of Alvarez or Magassa being the solution to West Ham’s defensive frailties – with a defensive midfielder sitting in front of the back four being suggested by footballleagueworld.co.uk who claim ‘Parker will be reversing the decision which angered West Ham’s bosses’ – that decision being Nuno’s refusal to play either of the midfielders and leaving them to languish outside the match day squad.

From the video evidence yesterday I’d say it is clear those days are long gone. Magassa has already started one game – hooked at half time – but I’d wager either the Frenchman or his Mexican midfield colleague, once upto speed, will be putting in an appearance in a reshaped Parker side this autumn: as the FLW article concludes:.

“Hammers fans have long been calling for Alvarez and Magassa to be given a chance to solve their side’s midfield problems, and with the club’s hierarchy seemingly sharing that view, Parker should focus on reintegrating the duo over the international break.”.

Industry observers note that looks like that’s another box ticked then: Job done. Now get them playing.

Manchester United endured another embarrassing draw against 10-man Tottenham after failing to register their second win despite bringing in a plethora of players.

Manchester United invested heavily last season in their attacking options, bringing in Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha.

Industry observers note that this season, they overhauled their midfield. United spent massively on Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos. Despite spending massively, they have failed to produce the control they would have expected in the midfield. The lack of control was evident in the recent Tottenham game, where Mainoo-Tielemans partnership failed to control the game collectively.

The midfield question was covered in our recent report as well, highlighting a lack of control and carried comments from Gary Neville and Jamie Redknapp.

Industry observers note that the bigger question is when United will strengthen their defence. As per our previous report as well, Manchester United are planning to overhaul their defence in the upcoming transfer windows.

According to recent reports, united were heavily linked with several left backs but eventually failed to bring any one. The situation left Luke Shaw as the only senior option in the position, while Patrick Dorgu is used upfront by Michael Carrick.

Harry Amass is another option for Michael Carrick, but he is only here because of a failed transfer move. He has been rarely used at left back as Dalot and Mazraoui get the nod in the position ahead of him.

The situation at right-back isn’t all good either. Diogo Dalot is the first option there, but he rarely provides the assurance that puts Michael Carrick at ease. Noussair Mazraoui is the second choice at right-back, but his attacking numbers aren’t great either.

Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez form up United’s centre-back pairing while Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven are used all over the defensive line in rotation when needed. Yoro was used at right-back against Tottenham while Heaven arrived as left-back towards the end of the game.

Recent findings suggest that manchester United’s season hasn’t been defensively strong or anywhere near being good. They have conceded goals in all Premier League games and only kept one clean sheet against Sabah in the Champions League.

Lisandro Martinez has come under scrutiny after errors on four occasions. Against Ipswich Town, Manchester United won 5-2, but his error resulted in Ipswich’s second goal.

Industry observers note that his own goal against Fulham gave away two points at Craven Cottage in the 1-1 draw. Another error led to Solanke’s goal against Tottenham, when he took his eyes off the ball.

His injury concerns are another aspect, and maybe Michael Carrick needs to make a decision.

It has been revealed that manchester United’s success depended heavily on youth over the years. When pundits questioned them, Sir Alex Ferguson gave them the chance to prove them wrong. Alan Hansen made the famous quote “You can’t win anything with kids” on the BBC’s Match of the Day on August 19, 1995. United did exactly that, played youth and went on to win everything.

Michael Carrick needs to do exactly that. He needs to trust youth and allow them to make mistakes. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven arrived as massive potentials, but they haven’t been given the license to express themselves, without fearing for their places. Both the youngsters have rarely started together or in a stretch of games. It is maybe time for them to take their chances.

Sources indicate that michael Carrick needs to keep Harry Maguire as a senior experienced figure around them. There is no doubt over Martinez’s ability, but he is not the answer to United’s long-term problem. United need to blend youth with experience as their identity moving forward. Lisandro Martinez perhaps isn’t the answer to United’s problem.

A defensive revival expected in the upcoming transfer windows needs to happen now. It must happen with chances to the Youth. Michael Carrick needs to be brave enough and throw the youngsters in the mix. What it will bring is a long-term solution. They need to experience the errors and pressures that will shape them in football.

Industry observers note that the Glazers took control of Manchester United in 2005. That takeover has since caused so many disruptions and protests by the fans over massive debts and insufficient backing of the team in the transfer market, despite successful periods in the Premier League and Europe.

Recent findings suggest that now Manchester United need to think about who should control the club in the future. Laurie Whitwell has now shared his views on why Manchester United need an ownership change. He simply wants the Glazers gone from Old Trafford. However, he also recognizes that replacing the current ownership doesn’t automatically mean things will improve for United.

Sources indicate that the journalist believes the change in ownership has had a lasting effect on United, with the club still feeling its consequences today. A fresh start might be welcome, but the identity of the next owners would matter just as much as the departure of the existing ones.

“Personally, I would like to see the Glazers gone from Manchester United,” Laurie Whitwell said on The Rest is Football podcast with Gary Lineker.

“That change, you know, just really affected and still impacts United now.”.

The desire for different ownership is one thing, but finding people capable of taking the club forward is another.

Whitwell admitted there is no perfect answer when it comes to who should take charge.

That leaves United facing a difficult choice. A sale could offer the chance to change how the club is run, but simply bringing in a new owner would not guarantee better decisions or a brighter future.

According to recent reports, whitwell also raised the idea of United supporters having a greater say in the club’s ownership and decisions, much like the Barcelona model where fans own the club itself. However, he highlighted that the Barcelona model isn’t ideal either and has its own shortcomings.

Changing the names at the top would only be one part of the change. The club would also need an ownership structure capable of making sound decisions and providing a direction.

Industry observers note that the issue of ownership goes beyond whether the Glazers should stay or leave. Manchester United needs to find the right people and the right model to secure the club’s future. Getting that decision wrong could leave them facing the same circus the fans are enduring under the Glazers.

The Argentinian defender has also apologized to the United higher ups as well over his comments, as shared by Fabrizio Romano.

Lisandro Martinez has held discussions with Jason Wilcox and Michael Carrick after speaking out following United’s 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid.

Martinez had questioned whether Carrick was backed enough in the summer and suggested the club needed changes.

Fabrizio Romano has now confirmed that United consider the matter resolved for now and expect Martinez to remain available for selection.

Speaking about the situation on his YouTube channel, as quoted by Football 365, Romano explained why Martinez’s comments caused concern inside the club.

Industry observers note that “He spoke very strongly after the game against Atletico Madrid, which Man Utd lost. It was a very negative moment for the Red Devils. Romano added that Martinez had spoken directly to those at the club after the incident.

Sources indicate that “Licha apologised to Man Utd as a club. He spoke to the directors, he spoke to Jason Wilcox, and he spoke to Michael Carrick, who was also involved in this conversation.”.

“So, the underlying message remains the same. Lisandro is apologising for the way he expressed himself after a game during a difficult moment for Man Utd, but there was a discussion about the substance of what he remarked.”.

Romano also revealed that United had imposed a financial penalty on the centre-back. However, the punishment does not appear to involve removing him from the squad.

“According to the information available tonight, Lisandro Martinez has been fined.”.

He added that Martinez is expected to return to the squad as normal, with the fine considered sufficient punishment for the incident.

Recent findings suggest that “The internal discussion also helped to resolve all the challenges. For Man Utd, the case is closed.”.

That should bring some immediate clarity to the situation, although questions remain about how the episode could affect Martinez’s longer-term position at Old Trafford.

Romano also pointed towards Martinez’s contract, which expires next summer, with United holding an option to extend it.

“So, let’s see what is going to happen there. For sure, this is the kind of situation that will have an impact on the situation surrounding Lisandro, but we have to see what happens next in terms of future transfers and everything else.”.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader concern was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

It has been revealed that enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

Published: 18:44 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 19:02 EST, 13 November 2026.

Scotland boss Sebastien Pocognoli admitted his side were far from perfect in their Nations League win over North Macedonia – but he believes they ARE moving in the right direction under his stewardship.

The victory puts the Scots one point behind second-placed Slovenia in Group B1, ahead of Monday’s trip to runaway leaders Switzerland.

John McGinn notched a second-half double to secure a hard-earned second win of this campaign and Pocognoli’s first in front of the Hampden crowd.

It has been revealed that ‘We knew before the game that it [a win] will help to build a winning culture,’ he said. ‘And would make the work through the week end with a good feeling.

Recent findings suggest that ‘In terms of what we produced on the pitch, I know exactly what we worked on this week. I’m quite satisfied about what I see in some moments of the game, about the work on the ball and off the ball.

‘It was not always perfect but we created a lot of chances that we should score and maybe have a better feeling of the game.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his Hampden win as Scots boss after a 2-1 win over North Macedonia.

Stalwarts John McGinn (left) and Andy Robertson applaud the Hampden crowd at full-time.

‘Off the ball, I think we were quite aggressive. We recover a number of balls that we managed well in some moments of transition.

‘We created a substantial chance for Billy [Gilmour] from this also. So that’s a fresh approach of the game.

Industry observers note that ‘We created chances and we had a lot of pressure in the side of Macedonia. After the first goal I think we need to learn not to drop the intensity. Because after the first goal for five minutes I really feel like we dropped the intensity and the focus. So, it’s something that we need to fix.’.

According to recent reports, asked whether his side need to be more clinical, Pocognoli added: ‘Yes, probably. But I prefer to talk about this with creating a lot of chances. We should score two or three. And probably we should have kept a clean sheet. So that’s really the critical aspect and the demanding aspect.

‘But it’s part of the challenge and we are early in the challenge to try to fix this for the future.’.

Talisman McGinn put the Scots ahead on 54 minutes before Elmin Rastoder headed the visitors level against the run of play shortly after, with McGinn then stepping up to convert what turned out to be the winning penalty after a foul on Ben Gannon-Doak with 16 to play.

The Aston Villa midfielder has now taken his tally to 24 for the international team – just six behind legends Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law.

His manager is confident that it is only a matter of time before the 32-year-old is standing alone as his nation’s top scorer, and believes McGinn will have plenty of opportunities to smash the record playing in his team.

John McGinn scored from the penalty spot to clinch an unconvincing victory.

It has been revealed that he remarked: ‘I’m more focused on the collective challenge and goals. And I believe if we can build something nice around the collective, then John will one day break the record.

‘We created a lot of chances through these five [Nations League] games together. The individual record is crucial, but I always focus on the collective package.’.

McGinn admitted that chasing the record is in the back of his mind and stressed his relief that he’s back among the goals after a lean spell at international level.

‘It’s been something that’s been in the back of my head, but obviously the results haven’t been the way we’ve wanted,’ mentioned McGinn.

‘The team come first, but whether it’s myself, Scottie (McTominay), Che (Adams), anyone that’s going on the scoresheet at the minute, we’ll take it.

‘It’s been a bit of a dry patch for me over the past year or two on the goal front, so I’m delighted to get back on that trail and hopefully the same again Monday.

Industry observers note that ‘I feel good. I’ve still got many years to go, but the first priority is getting Scotland back to another major tournament and we’ll take it from there.’.

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

It has been revealed that chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

Industry observers note that that matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

According to recent reports, 🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F.

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Industry observers note that gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Sources indicate that alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

It has been revealed that that is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

Industry observers note that one is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

Industry observers note that the complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness challenges, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.

Sources indicate that chelsea have spent heavily on attacking upside. Olise’s rise is a reminder that the real separator is not potential, but repeatable elite production.

Bayern’s own season review underlines why the conversation has accelerated.

Recent findings suggest that the German champions confirmed Olise finished 2025/26 with 25 goals and 28 assists from 57 competitive appearances. He was also named Bayern’s Player of the Season for a second straight year, finishing ahead of Harry Kane and Luis Diaz in the fan vote.

That is elite production from a wide creator who does not play like a chalk-on-boots winger.

According to recent reports, olise can receive wide, drift inside, manipulate the half-space and still deliver the last pass at match-winning speed. Chelsea have bought attackers with pieces of that profile, but few have joined the dots with that level of consistency.

There is an obvious recruitment lesson here.

The market will now price that blend of creativity, ball security and goal threat close to superstar territory. If Chelsea want an Alonso attack that controls games rather than simply runs through them, the next winger decision cannot be judged on pace or upside alone.

It has to be judged on game control, final-third calm and repeat output.

The World Cup has sharpened the comparison.

That same analysis highlighted the tactical adjustment that moved Olise closer to Kylian Mbappe after half-time. His passing range then became the lever that changed the game.

Industry observers note that that matters for Chelsea because Alonso’s best Bayer Leverkusen sides were built around players who could receive between lines without killing the tempo. Cole Palmer already gives Chelsea one version of that.

The wider question is whether the squad has another attacker who can bend matches from the opposite side without turning every possession into a one-v-one.

Olise’s Chelsea connection can easily become sentimental. The sharper editorial point is structural.

This is the calibre of player who once passed through the academy pathway and later became a global-level attacker elsewhere. Chelsea cannot change that history, but they can use it to stress-test the next wave of decisions.

That matters for Tyrique George, Kendry Paez, Estevao and any latest wide signing.

Sources indicate that readChelsea has already looked at how Tyrique George’s likely Everton return gives Alonso a fresh winger audit. Olise’s current standing raises the standard of that discussion.

He is no longer just a former academy name or a missed Premier League target. He is evidence of what happens when technical security, role clarity and patience meet elite coaching.

For Alonso, that is the real value of the Olise noise.

Chelsea do not need to turn every academy exit into regret. They do need to recognise the standard now being set by one of Cobham’s former pupils.

The next wide forward who gets serious minutes at Stamford Bridge has to be assessed against that ceiling, not against the safer language of potential.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea fans have followed Manchester City’s financial rules case for years. Everyone at Stamford Bridge knows a guilty verdict could cost City serious money, and much of it could end up with rivals lower down the table.

Reports now suggest an independent panel has reached a decision. If that holds up, the scale of any Chelsea Manchester City compensation payout could run into tens of millions of pounds for the Blues alone.

The Premier League charged Manchester City with 115 alleged breaches of financial regulations in February 2023. That followed a four-year investigation into the club’s accounts. The case has hung over the competition ever since. Every top-flight club knows the outcome could change how recent Premier League seasons are remembered.

According to recent reports, this matters directly to Chelsea. If City are found to have broken spending and disclosure rules, clubs who finished below them could argue they lost out on prize money and European qualification. Chelsea have competed directly with City for top four places and cup competitions throughout that period.

According to The Athletic, Manchester City were found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges by the independent panel. The Premier League has not confirmed the verdict or issued a statement.

Sources indicate that manchester City have not accepted any suggestion of guilt. The club released a statement addressing the ongoing process directly.

According to recent reports, “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023. ‘The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'”.

According to recent reports, that statement makes clear the club does not see the case as settled. Until the Premier League confirms a result, the reported verdict will linger on for official sentencing.

Data specialists at OLBG have estimated the potential Chelsea Manchester City compensation windfall if City are found guilty. They believe City could owe domestic rivals well over £500m in lost Premier League prize money if the charges are proven.

Within that total, London clubs are said to be due around £164m between them. Chelsea, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur are among the clubs who could be entitled to a share. Other Premier League sides could benefit too, depending on where they finished compared with City in the seasons in question.

Prize money in the Premier League is tied closely to league position. If City gained points unfairly, that would have pushed a rival down the table and cost them money too. That is the basis for the OLBG figures, and it explains why the sums involved are so large.

For Chelsea, even a share of that £164m pot would be a massive boost. It could help fund newly introduced signings, or simply ease the pressure around the kind of transfer valuations at Stamford Bridge the club faces every window.

Sources indicate that city chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak has already made clear the case is far from finished. He described the process as having “a long way to run.” That points to appeals and further legal steps, whatever the panel has decided.

Industry observers note that chelsea, for their part, carry on with life under Xabi Alonso regardless of how the case unfolds. Attention stays on squad rotation and Xabi Alonso’s squad management strategy, not on any potential windfall. The financial case will not change anything on the pitch in the short term.

According to recent reports, the Premier League has stayed silent on the reported verdict, and confidentiality remains strict around the process, according to reports from Football.London. Chelsea fans should expect a long wait before any compensation, if it comes at all, reaches the club’s accounts.

#2433. Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer

Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 96 min read (19209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~96 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2.
  • Recent findings suggest that aberrant enhancer-driven transcription sustains many cancers, including metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)3,4.
  • Recent findings suggest that chemically induced proximity (CIP) reprograms protein–protein interactions to manipulate cellular functions14,15.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2. Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.

Recent findings suggest that aberrant enhancer-driven transcription sustains many cancers, including metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)3,4. AR, a central driver of mCRPC, undergoes ligand-induced activation and dimerization upon binding to androgen response element (ARE)-enriched enhancers and assembling cancer-specific neo-enhanceosomes4,5,6. These complexes depend on the paralogous acetyltransferases p300 and CBP7. p300 has been identified as the predominant paralogue supporting AR-positive (AR+) prostate cancer growth, and the p300/CBP-dependent enhancer mark H2B N-terminal acetylation (H2BNTac) and AR–p300 co-bound enhancer activity are increased in prostate tumours8. Previous studies indicated that the N-terminal domain (NTD) of AR interacts with p3002, and this interaction stimulates the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity of p300, leading to enhancer remodelling and transcriptional activation by establishing a permissive chromatin environment9,10. Although p300/CBP-targeted therapies have been developed for castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC)11,12, global p300/CBP inhibition may cause toxicity in normal tissues13.

Recent findings suggest that chemically induced proximity (CIP) reprograms protein–protein interactions to manipulate cellular functions14,15. Established CIP modalities include proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), which promote target protein degradation via E3 ligase recruitment16; regulated induced proximity targeting chimeras (RIPTACs), which couple disease-associated proteins to essential effectors17,18; transcriptional/epigenetic chemical inducers of proximity (TCIPs), which redirect transcriptional coactivators19,20,21; and targeted relocalization activating molecules (TRAMs), which alter protein localization22. These approaches predominantly connect non-native partners. Here we introduce DALTACs, which enforce neomorphic domain interactions between physiological partners to disable endogenous oncogenic complexes. DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) connects the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR to the bromodomain (BRD) of p300/CBP, reprogramming substrate engagement, eliminating H2BNTac and suppressing AR–p300/CBP-dependent transcription. DALTAC-1 outperforms combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition, selectively targets AR-dependent prostate cancer, and induces tumour regression without overt toxicity, establishing domain-level rewiring as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Previous studies established that AR physically interacts with the coactivator p300 through its NTD2, and that dimerized transcription factors can stimulate p300 HAT activity9. To reprogram this native interaction, we designed heterobifunctional molecules that tether an AR-LBD binder to a p300/CBP-BRD binder through an appropriate linker. We reasoned that these molecules would induce non-native AR–p300/CBP interactions and thereby inhibit the growth of AR+ cancer cells by concurrently inhibiting both AR and p300/CBP functions (Fig. 1a).

It has been revealed that a, Schematic showing how DALTAC-1 rewires domain–domain interactions of the native AR–p300/CBP complex. Created in BioRender; Young, E. https://BioRender.com/ehpy9qp (2026). b, Structure of DALTAC-1 (JZY3032), comprising AR and p300/CBP binders connected by a linker. c, Cellular thermal shift assay of VCaP cells treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (100 nM, 4 h). Left, immunoblots showing stabilization of p300, CBP and AR, but not BRD4. Right, protein levels normalized to the lowest temperature condition (three independent experiments). d, Dose–response curves and IC50 values of AR+ VCaP and LNCaP cells treated with DALTAC-1, CBPD-409 or p300/CBPi plus ARi for five days. Data are mean ± s.d.; n = 3 replicated wells; three independent experiments. e, Ranked IC50 values for DALTAC-1 and CBPD-409 across different human cell lines after five-day treatments. Colours indicate specific cell types. PCa, prostate cancer.

According to recent reports, to test this premise, we designed and synthesized a series of heterobifunctional molecules using a potent p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor (GNE-04912) and a selective AR-LBD binder23 tethered through a linker (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We selected the tethering site in the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor based upon the co-crystal structure with GNE-049 and its analogues, which highlighted that our selected tethering site was exposed to the solvent environment24. Similarly, we chose the tethering site in the AR binder on the basis of our modelled complex structure with AR and extensive structure–activity relationships reported for this class of AR inhibitors23,25. We evaluated our synthesized compounds with proliferation assays in AR+ LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, which were shown to be responsive to p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors and PROTAC degraders11,26. GNE-049, the AR binder JZY3221, and their combination were included as controls. Treatment with GNE-049, JZY3221 or their combination showed limited inhibitory activity, particularly in 22Rv1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Recent findings suggest that to optimize these heterobifunctional molecules, we replaced the tetrahydropyran group of GNE-049 with a piperidinyl group that preserves p300 binding24 and systematically varied linker composition, length and rigidity (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Note 1). Several compounds demonstrated substantially greater anti-proliferative activity than the parent-inhibitor combination. Compound 7 (JZY3031) emerged as a lead, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 1.9 nM and 2.6 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

According to recent reports, replacing an oxygen atom in the AR-binding moiety of compound 7 with an N-methyl group, a modification previously shown to improve oral bioavailability25, generated JZY3032 (Fig. 1b). JZY3032 achieved IC50 values of 0.26 nM and 1.0 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the parent-inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b). JZY3032 also showed improved systemic exposure and 18.5% oral bioavailability in mice, despite its high molecular mass of 975 Da (Extended Data Fig. 1c).

In an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) measuring induced AR–p300 complex formation, compound 7 and JZY3032 were the most potent and effective compounds that we tested. JZY3032 also produced the strongest inhibition of AR transcriptional activity in HEK293 ARE–GFP reporter cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b). By contrast, three enzalutamide-based bifunctional molecules were substantially less active in VCaP, LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, demonstrating the importance of the AR-binding moiety (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e).

Sources indicate that based on its cellular, biochemical and pharmacokinetic properties, we designated JZY3032 as DALTAC-1. We also generated Neg-1, with reduced p300/CBP binding24, and Neg-2, with reduced AR binding27 (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Fluorescence polarization assays confirmed their intended binding profiles (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). Cellular thermal shift assays further demonstrated that DALTAC-1 stabilized AR, p300 and CBP, but not BRD4, supporting selective engagement of its intended targets (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1j).

It has been revealed that to assess the activity and selectivity of DALTAC-1, we compared its anti-proliferative activity with the p300/CBP dual degrader CBPD-4098 and the combined treatment with the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor GNE-049 (p300/CBPi) and AR-LBD binder JZY3221 (ARi). DALTAC-1 potently inhibited growth across all tested AR+ prostate cancer cell lines, with activity comparable or superior to CBPD-409 and consistently greater than p300/CBPi plus ARi in CellTiter-Glo (CTG) and colony-formation assays (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This superiority suggests a gain-of-function mechanism arising from enforced miswiring of AR–p300 domain interactions. DALTAC-1 also retained potent activity in the AR-V7-high, p300/CBP-dependent 22Rv1 and CWR-R1 models (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) and outperformed enzalutamide, darolutamide28,29, the AR PROTAC degrader ARV-76630 and the recently reported AR–BRD4 RIPTAC-131 (Extended Data Fig. 2c). By contrast, the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 revealed substantially reduced activity, and excess p300/CBPi or ARi competitively attenuated DALTAC-1 activity, demonstrating that engagement of both targets is required (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e).

Sources indicate that compared with CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 exhibited markedly reduced cytotoxicity in AR-negative yet p300-dependent Kelly and NCI-H211 cells8 (Extended Data Fig. 2f). It remained highly active in AR+ MDA-MB-453 cells32, which depend on both AR and p300/CBP, but showed minimal activity in AR+ U-87 MG cells33, which were less sensitive to CBPD-409 and ARV-766 (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Across a broader cancer cell line panel, CBPD-409 displayed activity across multiple lineages, whereas DALTAC-1 selectively inhibited AR+ prostate cancer cells (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2h). Moreover, a 4-h DALTAC-1 pulse followed by washout produced inhibition comparable to continuous exposure, whereas CBPD-409 or p300/CBPi plus ARi activity was substantially diminished after washout (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j). Collectively, these findings establish DALTAC-1 as a potent, durable and lineage-selective heterobifunctional compound whose activity depends on dual AR and p300/CBP engagement.

In a recent development, ternary complex formation is central to the CIP strategy34. Using purified proteins, DALTAC-1 induced AR–p300 association in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas the combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors and the binding-deficient analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 did not induce association (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) further demonstrated DALTAC-1-dependent complex formation. In the presence of 10 μM DALTAC-1, titration of GST–AR-LBD produced concentration-dependent binding to p300, with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 333.1 nM, whereas minimal interaction between GST–AR-LBD and p300 was detected under the DMSO control condition (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Reciprocally, titration of DALTAC-1 at a fixed GST–AR-LBD concentration (1 μM) progressively increased the binding response, yielding an apparent Kd of approximately 4.3 μM (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Neither DALTAC-1, GST–AR-LBD, nor their combination produced significant binding to immobilized Flag–FOXA1 (residues 1–268), excluding nonspecific association with the immobilized protein or sensor (Extended Data Fig. 3d). Moreover, the individual AR-LBD and p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors, alone or combined, did not induce complex formation, whereas excess p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor markedly attenuated the DALTAC-1-induced BLI signal (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f). Together, these results demonstrate that DALTAC-1 specifically recruits the AR-LBD to p300 to promote concentration-dependent formation of the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300 ternary complex.
