Intracellular ternary complex formation was confirmed by ELISA, which showed that DALTAC-1, but not Neg-1 or Neg-2, enhanced AR–p300 association in VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Co-immunoprecipitation similarly demonstrated that DALTAC-1 enhanced the interaction between AR and p300/CBP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i). Consistently, reciprocal immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry analyses identified AR as strongly enriched in p300 immunoprecipitates, and p300/CBP were among the most enriched AR-associated proteins following DALTAC-1 treatment (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3j,k). Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) further showed DALTAC-1 increased AR–p300 proximity, which was competitively blocked by either p300/CBPi or ARi (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m). Sequential co-immunoprecipitation of co-expressed Flag–AR, haemagglutinin (HA)–AR, and V5-p300 showed that DALTAC-1 maintained the interaction of HA–AR with Flag–AR from p300-containing complexes, indicating the incorporation of multiple AR molecules into the DALTAC-1-induced complex and supporting AR dimerization within the complex (Extended Data Fig. 3n). In 22Rv1 cells, DALTAC-1 enhanced p300 association with full-length AR but not the LBD-deficient AR-V7 variant, demonstrating the LBD dependence of the association (Extended Data Fig. 3o). DALTAC-1 also promoted p300 association with the DNA-binding-deficient AR-C619Y mutant35 (Extended Data Fig. 3p), indicating that complex formation does not require AR binding to DNA. Together, these findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 induces the formation of a LBD-dependent AR–p300 complex.

In a recent development, domain-resolved interaction mapping in HEK293 cells demonstrated minimal basal association between AR and the p300 core region, comprising the BRD, RING/PHD and HAT domains, yet DALTAC-1 strongly enhanced this interaction (Extended Data Fig. 3q). Reciprocal domain mapping demonstrated that DALTAC-1 selectively recruited the AR-LBD, but not the AR-NTD, to p300 (Extended Data Fig. 3r). Accordingly, co-expressed AR-LBD and p300 core region showed minimal basal association but robust complex formation following DALTAC-1 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 3s), establishing a non-native AR-LBD–p300 core interaction.

To investigate its structural basis, we modelled the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300-BRD ternary complex and the corresponding binary complexes, followed by 1-µs molecular dynamics simulations. The top-scoring ternary model predicted an AR–p300 interface stabilized by polar and hydrophobic interactions (Extended Data Fig. 3t). Key contacts included salt bridges between Asp1088 of p300 and Arg871 of AR and between Arg1133 of p300 and Glu872 of AR; hydrogen bonds involving AR Arg871–p300 Gly1085 and AR Ile816–p300 Leu1083; hydrophobic packing between Ile816 of AR and Leu1083 of p300; and a cation–π interaction between His874 of AR and the piperazine moiety of DALTAC-1. Molecular mechanics-generalized born surface area (MM-GBSA) analysis yielded a more favourable model-dependent interaction-energy estimate for the ternary complex (−161.8 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) than for the DALTAC-1–AR (−81.4 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) or DALTAC-1–p300 (−90.3 ± 0.4 kcal mol−1) binary complexes (Extended Data Fig. 3u,v). Computational removal of DALTAC−1 yielded an AR–p300 interface energy of −53.5 ± 1.1 kcal mol−1, consistent with favourable protein complementarity (Extended Data Fig. 3v).

Industry observers note that experimentally, mutation of the predicted interface residues in AR(R871A/E872A) and p300(D1088A/R1133A) substantially impaired DALTAC-1-induced complex formation (Extended Data Fig. 3w). Together, these findings establish that DALTAC-1 rewires AR–p300 domain interactions to form a stable ternary complex, providing a mechanistic basis for its downstream epigenetic and transcriptional effects.

In a recent development, in contrast to the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 did not reduce p300/CBP protein abundance but rapidly suppressed H3K27ac and H2BK20ac, two histone marks associated with active enhancers (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). H2BNTac is deposited exclusively by p300/CBP and marks active enhancers in prostate cancer8. Our data demonstrate that DALTAC-1 exerts a de novo heterobifunctional effect by potently suppressing this critical histone mark without degrading p300/CBP. This level of H2BNTac suppression was not observed with the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 or with the combination of AR and p300/CBP inhibitors (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). DALTAC-1 also highlighted limited activity in AR-negative Kelly cells, supporting its AR-dependent selectivity (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Furthermore, in HEK293 cells, DALTAC-1-driven loss of H2BNTac increased in direct proportion to the amount of ectopically expressed AR, underscoring that both AR and p300 are required for DALTAC activity (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Moreover, a 2-h DALTAC-1 pulse caused sustained suppression of histone acetylation and MYC expression after washout, whereas the effects of combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors were markedly reduced (Extended Data Fig. 4f).

Industry observers note that beyond histone substrates, p300/CBP acetylate non-histone regulators of transcription and signal transduction36. Whereas p300/CBP HAT inhibitors and degraders broadly suppress histone and non-histone acetylation7,8, acetyl-lysine profiling in VCaP cells revealed a distinct acetylation signature induced by DALTAC-1. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed global histone acetylation, particularly enhancer-associated H2BNTac, more potently than combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g–i). Consistently, immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry identified H2B as the most significantly displaced p300 interactor, indicating disruption of p300 engagement with its canonical histone substrate (Extended Data Fig. 3j).

It has been revealed that concurrently, DALTAC-1, but not combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition, increased acetylation of AR and its cofactors SRC2 and SRC337 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h,j,k). AR acetylation occurred in the NTD, suggesting that DALTAC-1-induced ternary complex formation redirects p300 catalytic activity towards the N terminus of AR as well as its associated cofactors. In an ARE reporter assay, glutamine substitution of the five SRC2 lysines most strongly acetylated by DALTAC-1 (multi-K-Q) modestly increased AR activity relative to wild-type SRC2, whereas alanine substitution (multi-K-A) modestly reduced it, indicating that acetylation at these sites has limited effects on SRC2 coactivator function (Extended Data Fig. 4l,m). Thus, DALTAC-1 suppresses enhancer-linked histone acetylation while selectively increasing acetylation of AR and its associated cofactors.

Sources indicate that we next examined how DALTAC-1-mediated reprogramming of p300 substrate engagement affects transcription. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed AR activity in an ARE–GFP reporter assay and repressed canonical AR target genes, whereas Neg-1, Neg-2 or combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition exhibited weaker effects (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) in VCaP cells revealed downregulation of androgen response, p300/CBP target, MYC target and MTORC1 signalling pathways (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5d–f). Chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) further revealed rapid RNA polymerase II (Pol II) displacement from AR and p300 target loci (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Together, unlike the transcriptional activation mechanism of TCIPs19,20, DALTAC-1 represses AR–p300/CBP-driven oncogenic transcription.

Consistently, DALTAC-1 and the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409 markedly reduced prostate-specific antigen (PSA), CCND1 and NKX3-1 protein levels, whereas combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition had modest effects on these proteins (Fig. 2g). Quantitative proteomics confirmed selective depletion of AR- and MYC-regulated proteins without reducing AR or p300/CBP abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these results show that DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate utilization to broadly suppress AR-driven oncogenic transcription.

We next tested whether this activity requires an antagonist-derived AR binder. We replaced the AR moiety of DALTAC-1 with enobosarm38, a non-steroidal AR agonist, to generate JZY4055 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). JZY4055 potently inhibited growth of AR+ VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Whereas enobosarm activated canonical AR target genes, JZY4055 repressed these genes and reduced p300/CBP-dependent H2BK20ac and H3K27ac, as well as the expression of AR- and p300/CBP-regulated proteins NKX3-1 and MYC (Extended Data Fig. 5k,l). These data demonstrate that AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-mediated transcriptional repression does not require an antagonist-derived AR binder.

According to recent reports, p300/CBP are central AR coactivators that sustain oncogenic transcription through enhancer-associated histone acetylation8. To investigate how DALTAC-1 modulates p300 chromatin occupancy, we performed p300 ChIP–seq in VCaP cells. DALTAC-1 markedly expanded and redistributed p300 binding genome-wide (Fig. 3a). Approximately 40% of DALTAC-1-depleted peaks were promoter-proximal, whereas gained peaks occurred predominantly in intronic and distal intergenic regions, with only approximately 10% being located near promoters, indicating increased enhancer engagement (Fig. 3b). At AR-binding enhancer sites identified under DMSO (control) conditions, DALTAC-1 proportionally increased AR and p300/CBP occupancy (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Motif analysis revealed that gained p300 and CBP peaks were strongly enriched for canonical palindromic AREs and closely related nuclear receptor motifs, including progesterone- and glucocorticoid-response elements (PRE and GRE)39 (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). These findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 redistributes p300/CBP through AR-dependent recruitment and stabilizes neomorphic AR–p300/CBP complexes on enhancer chromatin.

UTR, untranslated region. c, ChIP–seq read-density heat maps of AR and p300 at AR-bound enhancer sites in VCaP cells treated with DMSO or 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 3 h (n = 1). d, HOMER analysis showing the fold enrichment and statistical significance of sequence motifs at non-promoter p300-binding sites in VCaP cells treated with DMSO or 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 3 h. DALTAC-1 also significantly reshaped the AR cistrome (Fig. 3e). DALTAC-1 treatment increased AR occupancy at palindromic AREs while reducing binding at FOXA1–AR chimeric motifs associated with oncogenic AR neo-enhanceosomes40 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). Thus, rather than uniformly increasing AR binding, DALTAC-1 redirected AR away from oncogenic enhancers and concentrated it at canonical nuclear receptor response elements. Because AREs share substantial sequence similarity with PREs39, we examined whether their enrichment reflected progesterone receptor (PR) activation. DALTAC-1 instead reduced PR occupancy genome-wide while increasing AR occupancy at PR-binding sites (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i), indicating that these shared motifs were predominantly engaged by AR. Despite increased AR and p300/CBP binding, DALTAC-1 markedly decreased coactivator (BRD4 and ERG) recruitment, Pol II loading, and histone acetylation (H3K27ac and H2BK20ac) at AR/p300 co-bound enhancers (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). DALTAC-1 therefore stabilized AR–p300/CBP chromatin binding while functionally decommissioning the associated transcriptional complexes.

Recent findings suggest that oncogenic transcription factors such as ERG and FOXA1 mutants are known to redirect AR to non-canonical AREs, thereby forming cancer-specific AR neo-enhanceosomes that drive lineage-dependent oncogene programs8,41. In TMPRSS2–ERG fusion-positive VCaP cells42, DALTAC-1 globally reduced ERG occupancy, although a subset of latest ERG peaks emerged in intronic and distal intergenic regions (Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). Motif analysis revealed that DALTAC-1 depleted ERG binding at canonical ETS motifs and redistributed ERG towards palindromic AREs (Extended Data Fig. 7e). At non-promoter AR–ERG co-bound regions, DALTAC-1 increased AR and p300 occupancy, modestly increased SRC2 binding, and minimally altered FOXA1 occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Nonetheless, ERG and BRD4 binding declined, whereas Pol II occupancy and enhancer-associated histone acetylation were almost completely lost (Extended Data Fig. 7i). Thus, DALTAC-1 collapses AR–ERG neo-enhancers into a transcriptionally inactive state despite increased AR–p300 occupancy, dismantling the oncogenic output of the AR–ERG neo-enhanceosome (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 7j).

According to recent reports, to assess DALTAC-1 efficacy across prostate cancer subtypes, we tested organoids derived from genetically engineered mouse models. We treated organoids derived from wild-type, Rosa26ERG/Pten−/−, Pten−/−, FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− and Trp53−/− mouse prostates with DALTAC-141,43. DALTAC-1 preferentially reduced the number and size of Rosa26ERG/Pten−/− and FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− organoids and suppressed MYC and CCND1 relative to wild-type, Pten−/− and Trp53−/− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Given that ERG and mutant FOXA1 enhance AR activity and sustain the AR neo-enhanceosome5,41,43,44, these findings suggest that DALTAC-1 effectively suppresses AR-driven prostate cancer. Furthermore, we evaluated DALTAC-1 efficacy across organoids derived from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumours45,46. Consistently, DALTAC-1 potently inhibited AR+ organoids, particularly AR+/ERG+ models (Fig. 4a). Thus, DALTAC-1 exhibits potent, lineage-selective activity across mouse and human organoid models.

Industry observers note that to evaluate in vivo activity of DALTAC-1, we first examined VCaP castration-resistant prostate cancer (VCaP-CRPC) xenografts established in castrated male severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) mice (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Mice were randomized to DALTAC-1 administered intraperitoneally (30 mg kg−1) or orally (60 mg kg−1), or an equipotent combination of p300/CBPi and ARi. Intraperitoneal DALTAC-1 induced tumour regression in 75% (12 out of 16) of tumours, whereas oral dosing also robustly suppressed tumour growth and outperformed the combined inhibitors (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d). In vivo PLA confirmed increased AR–p300 proximity in treated tumours (Fig. 4c). COMET multiplex immunofluorescence (COMET-mIF) analyses revealed that DALTAC-1 reduced ERG, PSA, MYC, Ki-67, H3K27ac and H2BK20ac without decreasing AR, p300 or CBP abundance, consistent with non-degradative AR–p300/CBP rewiring (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 9e,f).

In a recent development, we next assessed the efficacy of DALTAC-1 in two prostate cancer PDX models, MDA-PCa-146-12 and MDA-PCa-18345,47. DALTAC-1 significantly inhibited MDA-PCa-146-12 growth (Extended Data Fig. 9g) and induced rapid, sustained regression of TMPRSS2–ERG-positive, PTEN-deficient MDA-PCa-183 tumours, with no progression observed during the 35-day treatment period (Extended Data Fig. 9h–k). In the MDA-PCa-183 model, DALTAC-1 induced marked tumour regression throughout the 50-day treatment period, whereas enzalutamide produced only modest tumour growth inhibition and ARV-766 was less effective than DALTAC-1 (Fig. 4e,f). Following treatment withdrawal, DALTAC-1-treated tumours showed no evident recurrence for 16 days, whereas ARV-766-treated tumours regrew (Fig. 4e,f). DALTAC-1 was well tolerated, with no significant changes in body weight, liver or kidney function, or haematological parameters (Extended Data Fig. 10a–e). Together, DALTAC-1 produces potent and durable antitumour responses across prostate cancer models through selective, non-degradative reprogramming of AR–p300/CBP complexes.

Sources indicate that recent advances in CIP have led to the development of a diverse array of compounds capable of modulating protein functions through enforced protein–protein interactions14. RIPTACs induce proximity between a target protein and a pan-essential effector that disrupts the function of the essential effector, leading to selective cancer cell death while sparing healthy cells17. By contrast, TCIPs recruit transcriptional coactivators to specific genomic loci, paradoxically activating the target pathway by enhancing transcription of pro-apoptotic genes that are normally repressed by corepressors such as BCL619,20. The emerging clinical activity of daraxonrasib (RMC-6236), which forms a ternary complex with cyclophilin A and active RAS, further supports the translational potential of proximity-induced pharmacology48. Recent molecular glue degraders further demonstrate that small molecules can stabilize pre-existing or newly enabled protein interfaces and alter target organization to promote E3 ligase-dependent degradation49. Complementary studies targeting FOXA1, SWI/SNF and p300 establish that DNA-binding specificity, ATPase cycling and chromatin engagement are also pharmacologically actionable50,51,52. DALTACs build on these principles but produce a distinct pharmacological outcome: rather than recruiting an E3 ligase, degrading a complex component or modulating an individual regulator, a DALTAC bifunctional molecule imposes an additional domain-selective interaction between two members within an existing transcriptional complex, converting the complex into a non-productive state. Our proof-of-concept compound, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1, targets the AR–p300/CBP complex by repurposing the natural interfaces to block activation of the AR oncogenic enhanceosome. Mechanistically, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 potently suppresses AR transactivation by disrupting the chromatin landscape at AR-bound enhancer sites, particularly AR/ERG co-bound neo-enhancer sites, as evidenced by reduced cofactor recruitment, loss of histone acetylation marks, and displacement of Pol II. Functionally, this shutdown of AR neo-enhanceosome activity translates into strong antitumour efficacy in AR+ prostate cancer models, underscoring the translational potential of DALTAC-1 as a precision therapeutic agent.

In a recent development, the activity of CIP molecules is founded on formation of a ternary complex between the recruited proteins. Using purified full-length proteins, we demonstrated that DALTAC-1 directly enhances AR–p300 complex formation in the absence of DNA or accessory factors. This association requires simultaneous engagement of both proteins by the intact bifunctional molecule and cannot be reproduced by unlinked ligands or control compounds lacking either AR- or p300-binding activity. The activities of multi-protein transcriptional complexes are governed by finely tuned protein–protein interactions at the sub-domain level53. AR normally recruits transcriptional coactivators primarily through its intrinsically disordered NTD, whereas transcription factors engage distinct regions of p300, including its N- and C-terminal regions, to support histone acetylation and transcriptional activation2,9. Our domain-mapping and interface-mutagenesis studies support a refined model in which DALTAC-1 does not necessarily abolish these native contacts. Rather, it imposes an additional, neomorphic interaction between the AR-LBD and the p300 core region containing the BRD and HAT domain, thereby reorganizing the domain-level engagement within the retained AR–p300 complex. Although the atomic architecture of the ternary complex remains unresolved, owing in part to the large size, conformational flexibility and extensive intrinsically disordered regions of full-length AR and p300, our orthogonal biochemical and cellular data demonstrate a DALTAC-induced binding pattern that is distinct from the basal complex and functionally alters AR–p300/CBP activity. This interaction reprogramming markedly suppresses histone acetylation, including H2BNTac, despite the inability of the p300-binding moiety alone to directly inhibit this modification8. In parallel, DALTAC-1 induces acetylation of the AR-NTD and core components of the AR complex, including SRC2/3 and ARID1A/B4,37,54. Because p300 has previously been shown to acetylate AR primarily within the hinge region under androgen stimulation55, the emergence of AR-NTD acetylation suggests that DALTAC-1 redirects p300 substrate engagement, potentially by bringing the AR-NTD into altered proximity to the p300 HAT domain. This substrate reprogramming distinguishes DALTAC-1 from conventional p300/CBP inhibitors and degraders: unlike BRD inhibitors, it extinguishes enhancer-associated H2BNT acetylation and broadly represses transcription, and unlike PROTAC degraders, it acts independently of ubiquitin–proteasome-mediated target depletion.

It has been revealed that because many oncogenes also have essential roles in normal physiology, their pan-inhibition often causes severe side effects. For example, systemic inhibition of p300/CBP disrupts haematopoiesis and leads to thrombocytopenia13. Thus, achieving lineage-selective targeting of oncogenic pathways is an urgent therapeutic need. Existing approaches such as antibody–drug conjugates deliver cytotoxic payloads selectively to cells that express target surface antigens56. However, their broader applicability is limited by the restricted repertoire of tumour-specific surface markers and, in many cases, by suboptimal pharmacokinetic properties57. By contrast, DALTACs offer a fundamentally distinct strategy, selectively rewiring lineage-specific protein complexes that drive oncogenic transcription. In this study, AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 specifically inhibits the growth of AR+ prostate cancer cells with potency comparable to or better than the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409 but reveals markedly reduced activity in p300/CBP-dependent, AR-negative cancers such as neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma and haematological malignancies8. Notably, in AR-negative cells, DALTAC-1 does not suppress H2BNTac, underscoring that DALTAC-1-mediated inhibition of p300/CBP histone acetylation is context-dependent and conferred by domain reprogramming within AR–p300/CBP complexes.

It has been revealed that in summary, we establish DALTACs as a latest type of chemical proximity modulators that rewire domain-specific protein interactions to selectively deactivate oncogenic complexes. DALTAC-1 induces formation of an AR–p300–DALTAC-1 ternary complex and reprograms the substrate engagement of p300/CBP, markedly suppressing global histone acetylation while enhancing the acetylation of core components within the AR complex. Consequently, DALTAC-1 reinforces AR–p300/CBP co-occupancy at palindromic ARE loci but disrupts the higher-order assembly of the AR complex and erases histone activation marks at AR neo-enhanceosomes (Fig. 5). This work expands the conceptual framework of induced-proximity therapies beyond degradation and coactivator hijacking, paving the way for the rational design of domain-alteration strategies for precise control of disease-relevant protein complexes.

In a recent development, left, endogenous AR–p300/CBP interactions recruit coactivators and promote histone acetylation at oncogenic AR-bound enhancers, sustaining oncogenic transcription. Right, DALTAC-1 induces a neomorphic interaction between AR and p300/CBP that stabilizes the ternary complex at palindromic AREs and reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, suppressing histone acetylation while increasing acetylation of core AR complex components. Consequently, DALTAC-1 disrupts productive complex assembly at AR neo-enhanceosomes, erases activating histone marks and suppresses oncogenic transcription. VCaP cells were seeded at a density of 10,000 cells per well, and all other prostate cancer cell lines were seeded at 3,000 cells per well in poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates (Corning) and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. After 24 h, cells were treated with a serial dilution of test compounds, with 6 replicate wells for each concentration. Following 120 h of incubation, cell viability was determined using the CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Luminescence was measured on an Infinite M1000 Pro plate reader (Tecan) and data were analysed using GraphPad Prism (v10; GraphPad Software).

A total of 4,000 VCaP cells or 1,500 LNCaP cells per well were seeded into poly-d-lysine-coated 96-well plates. After 24 h of incubation, cells were treated with a fixed concentration (100 nM) or serial dilutions of compounds and incubated for 4 h. The medium was then removed, and cells were washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) before fresh medium containing either vehicle or compounds was added. Phase-contrast images were collected every 4 h, and cell proliferation was quantified by measuring the percentage of confluence (phase object area).

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 1× Halt Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and denatured in NuPAGE 1× LDS sample buffer containing a reducing agent (Invitrogen) by incubation at 70 °C for 15 min. Equal amounts of protein (15–30 µg) were resolved on NuPAGE 3–8% Tris-Acetate or 4–12% Bis-Tris protein gels (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and transferred onto 0.45-µm nitrocellulose membranes (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using the iBlot 3 Dry Blotting System (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Membranes were blocked in TBS-T (Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20) containing 5% non-fat dry milk for 1 h at room temperature and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies and imaged using an Odyssey CLx Imager (LI-COR Biosciences). According to recent reports, the binding affinities of test compounds to AR and CBP/p300 were measured using fluorescence polarization-based competitive binding assays. AR binding was assessed using the PolarScreen Androgen Receptor Competitor Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A15880) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

Industry observers note that CBP/p300 fluorescence polarization assays were performed in 96-well plates (MTP96VPWB-EP, Eppendorf) using a CLARIOstar microplate reader (BMG Labtech). Serial dilutions of test compounds were incubated with fluorescein-labelled tracer (2 nM final) and CBP/p300 protein (20 nM final) in assay buffer (PBS pH 7.4 supplemented with 0.01% BGG, 0.01% Tween-20, and 2 mM DTT) to a final reaction volume of 100 µl per well. Plates were mixed for 15 min and incubated at room temperature for 1 h to reach equilibrium. Fluorescence polarization (mP units) was measured at 485 nm excitation and 530 nm emission.

For both AR and CBP/p300 assays, data analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 10 using nonlinear regression. IC50 values were determined by fitting competition curves, and inhibition constant (Ki) values for competitive inhibitors were derived using nonlinear regression based on the Kd of the tracer and the concentrations of tracer and protein in the reaction. All fluorescence polarization experiments were conducted in duplicates across three independent biological replicates.

VCaP or LNCaP cells were seeded in poly-d-lysine-coated 100 mm culture dishes (Corning) and incubated overnight. Cells were incubated with the DMSO control or indicated compounds for 4 h at 37 °C before being collected and washed once with PBS. The cell suspension was then distributed into PCR tubes (50 µl per tube) and exposed to a predefined temperature gradient for 3 min using a Veriti Thermal Cycler (Applied Biosystems). Following equilibration to room temperature, cells were lysed by three freeze–thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen. Insoluble protein aggregates were pelleted by centrifugation at 20,000g for 20 min at 4 °C, and the resulting supernatants containing soluble proteins were recovered for western blot analysis.

All modelling and simulations were performed with Schrödinger 2025-2 (Schrödinger). Because co-crystal structures of the LBD of AR in an open antagonist conformation were not available, we used our previously reported pseudo-open model58. The bound AR ligand was modified to generate JZY3221, the AR ligand used in our design of DALTACs. To model the p300-BRD interaction with GNE-049, we used the CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure (Protein Data Bank (PDB) 5W0E) as the starting structure59. CBP and p300 are highly homologous proteins, especially in their BRDs, which share conserved sequence and structures. Both proteins were prepared for further modelling using the Protein Preparation Wizard60.

In a recent development, we used the following structures as inputs to generate the initial AR–DALTAC-1–p300 complex: (1) AR in complex with JZY3221; (2) the p300 complex with GNE-049; and (3) JZY3032 (DALTAC-1) prepared with LigPrep module61. These inputs were submitted to Generate Degrader Complex (default settings: MCMM 10,000 steps, maximum clashes 5, maximum poses 50) to construct the ternary AR–JZY3032–p300 complex. The top 20 predicted complexes were further refined using Prime62. The top-scoring ternary complex was then selected for molecular dynamics simulations.

To perform molecular dynamics simulations, the predicted ternary complex was solvated in an explicit water box with periodic boundary conditions. A cubic box was constructed with a 10 Å buffer between solute and box edge and filled with TIP4P water63. The OPLS4 force field was used for all components. Production dynamics used a RESPA integrator with a 2 fs time step. Temperature was maintained at 300 K with a Nosé–Hoover chain thermostat64 (relaxation time 1.0 ps). Pressure was controlled at 1 atm with a Martyna–Tobias–Klein barostat65 (relaxation time 2.0 ps). Long-range electrostatics used a 9 Å real-space cutoff with particle–mesh Ewald for reciprocal space66. One continuous 1-µs simulation was performed without restraints.

In a recent development, root-mean-square deviation analysis of protein backbones and ligand position indicated that the system equilibrated after approximately 750 ns. Accordingly, trajectory analysis focused on the last 250 ns. Protein–protein interface features were defined as minimum heavy-atom distances between AR and p300. Contacts shorter than 0.5 nm (5 Å) were retained. Principal component analysis was applied to these interface distances, and components explaining 95% of the variance were kept. The reduced data were clustered with HDBSCAN (min_cluster_size 25, centroids enabled)67. For each cluster, the frame closest to the centroid in principal component analysis space was saved as a representative PDB. Cluster occupancies are reported as percentages of frames per cluster. Protein–protein interaction fingerprints were computed with Schrödinger’s analyze_trajectory_ppi.py. Clustering in this reduced dimensional space revealed two dominant populations, with the most prevalent state comprising nearly 80% of the ensemble. The interaction analysis was performed on snapshots representative of this dominant state.

Industry observers note that MM-GBSA binding energies were estimated using Prime MM-GBSA (Schrödinger Release 2025-2; thermal_mmgbsa protocol) with the OPLS4 force field and the VSGB 2.0 implicit-solvent model68,69,70. Snapshots were sampled evenly from the final 250 ns of each trajectory, after which water molecules and ions were removed and each complex, receptor, and ligand were locally energy-minimized. The MM-GBSA binding energy was calculated as ΔGbind = Ecomplex − Ereceptor − Eligand, where ΔGbind is the estimated MM-GBSA binding energy and Ecomplex, Ereceptor and Eligand are the calculated MM-GBSA energies of the complex, receptor and ligand, respectively. For compound binding, DALTAC-1 was defined as the ligand and AR, p300, or AR + p300 as the receptor. For p300 association with the ternary complex, p300 (residues 1049–1160) was defined as the ligand and AR + DALTAC-1 as the receptor. To isolate the direct AR–p300 contribution in the induced geometry, DALTAC-1 was deleted from the same ternary snapshots, with p300 defined as the ligand and AR as the receptor. MM-GBSA values were used as model-dependent interaction-energy estimates to compare the relative stability of the modelled complexes and were not interpreted as experimental binding affinities.

AR protein was expressed according to the manufacturer’s protocol for the Expi293 PRO Expression System Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A40003643). In brief, Expi293 PRO cells were transfected with the HA–AR expression plasmid and cultured for 24 h before the addition of 1 μM R1881. The cultures were then incubated for an additional 24 h, and cells were collected 48 h post-transfection. Cell pellets were washed and collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The cells were resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.5% NP-40, supplemented with cOmplete EDTA-free Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (Roche, 4693159001). Cells were lysed by sonication, and the lysates were clarified by centrifugation at 15,000 rpm for 40 min at 4 °C. The clarified lysate was incubated with anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific, 88837) for 3 h at 4 °C. After binding, the beads were washed three times with wash buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, and 0.05% NP-40. Bound AR protein was eluted twice using elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881 and 0.05% NP-40) supplemented with 2 mg ml−1 HA peptide (Thermo Scientific, 26184). The eluted protein was further purified by size-exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) pre-equilibrated with gel filtration buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 100 nM R1881, and 0.05% NP-40. Peak fractions containing purified AR protein were pooled to a final concentration of approximately 0.5 mg ml−1 and used for all subsequent studies.

Recent findings suggest that for each reaction, 15 μl of anti-HA magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88837) was blocked with 0.3% BSA in PBS for 1 h at 4 °C and washed three times with AR protein buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0; 150 mM NaCl; 0.05% NP-40) for 5 min per wash. Purified HA-tagged full-length AR (1 μg) was incubated with the blocked beads for at least 4 h at 4 °C. The beads were then washed three times with p300 protein buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP) for 10 min per wash and incubated overnight at 4 °C with purified Flag-tagged p300 (Active motif, 81858) (200 ng or 1 μg) in 350 μl of p300 protein buffer containing the indicated compounds or an equivalent volume of DMSO. Beads were subsequently washed at least three times with p300 protein buffer containing the corresponding compounds for 10 min per wash. Bound proteins were eluted in SDS–PAGE loading buffer and analysed by immunoblotting.

Anti-Flag IgG biosensors (Sartorius, 18-5187) were pre-equilibrated in assay buffer containing 25 mM HEPES-NaOH (pH 7.5), 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 0.04% Triton X-100, and 0.5 mM TCEP. N-terminal Flag-tagged full-length recombinant p300 protein (1 μg; Active Motif, 81858) was immobilized onto the biosensors at 25 °C until the binding signal reached a plateau. After immobilization, the biosensors were washed in assay buffer to remove unbound protein and minimize nonspecific binding.

Sources indicate that the biosensors were then incubated with recombinant GST–His-tagged AR-LBD protein (Invitrogen, A15675) at varying concentrations in assay buffer containing either 10 μM DALTAC-1 or an equivalent volume of DMSO. The association phase was monitored, followed by transfer of the biosensors into assay buffer to measure dissociation. Binding data were analysed using Octet Analysis Studio 13.0 (Sartorius). Sensorgrams obtained in the presence of DMSO were used as reference controls and subtracted from those obtained with DALTAC-1. The reference-subtracted data were globally fitted to a 1:1 binding model to determine the equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd).

VCaP cells were plated in 96-well plates (50,000 cells per well) and cultured for 3 days in medium containing 5% charcoal-stripped FBS. Nuclei were collected by centrifugation at 2,000g for 5 min at 4 °C, the supernatant (cytoplasmic fraction) was discarded, and nuclei were washed once with hypotonic buffer.

Sources indicate that the nuclear pellet was lysed in 1 ml nuclear lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 10 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, 0.5% Triton X-100, 15 mM β-mercaptoethanol) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors and rotated for 1 h at 4 °C. It has been revealed that total RNA was isolated using QIAzol Lysis Reagent (QIAGEN). In brief, 1 × 106 cells were lysed in 700 µl QIAzol and incubated for 5 min at room temperature to allow for complete dissociation of nucleoprotein complexes. Tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomic analysis was performed as previously described8, with minor modifications. VCaP cells were treated with DMSO or DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) in three independent biological replicates. Cell lysates were prepared, and protein concentrations were determined. For each sample, 75 µg of protein was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol, alkylated with 15 mM 2-chloroacetamide, precipitated with ice-cold acetone, and digested overnight with a trypsin/Lys-C mixture at a 1:50 protease-to-protein ratio. Peptides were labelled with TMTpro 16-plex reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A44521), with DMSO replicates assigned to channels 126, 127N and 128N and JZY3032 replicates assigned to channels 130C, 131C and 132C. Labelled peptides were pooled and separated into 12 fractions by high-pH reversed-phase chromatography.

In a recent development, fractions were analysed at the University of Michigan Proteomics Resource Facility using an Orbitrap Ascend Tribrid mass spectrometer equipped with a FAIMS source and coupled to a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system. Peptides were separated on an Easy-Spray PepMap Neo C18 column, and data were acquired using two FAIMS compensation voltages (−45 and −65 V) and a MultiNotch MS3 method to minimize reporter-ion ratio distortion. Data were processed using Proteome Discoverer v3.0 and searched against the Swiss-Prot Homo sapiens protein database (TaxID 9606; version 5 February 2025). Peptide-spectrum matches and proteins were filtered to a false-discovery rate of ≤1%. TMT quantification was based on high-quality MS3 spectra with an average signal-to-noise ratio of ≥10 and isolation interference of <50%.

It has been revealed that VCaP cells were treated with DMSO, 100 nM DALTAC-1 for 4 or 12 h, or a combination of p300/CBPi and ARi for 12 h, each in three biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to acetyl-lysine proteomics analysis as previously described8. In brief, total proteins were extracted, digested with trypsin, and acetylated peptides were enriched using anti–acetyl-lysine antibody–conjugated beads. Enriched peptides were analysed by nano-liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (nanoLC–MS/MS) on a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and raw data were processed using MaxQuant (v2.3.0.0) with acetyl-lysine and protein N-terminal acetylation set as variable modifications.

In-solution digestion: VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) or DMSO for 4 h. Co-immunoprecipitation assays were performed as described above. The beads were resuspended in 50 µl of 0.1 M ammonium bicarbonate buffer (pH ~8). Cysteines were reduced by adding 50 µl of 10 mM DTT and incubating at 45 °C for 30 min. Samples were cooled to room temperature and alkylation of cysteines was achieved by incubating with 65 mM 2-chloroacetamide, under darkness, for 30 min at room temperature. An overnight (~16 h) digestion with 1 µg sequencing grade, modified trypsin was carried out at 37 °C with constant shaking in a Thermomixer. Digestion was stopped by acidification and peptides were desalted using SepPak C18 cartridges using the manufacturer’s protocol (Waters). Samples were completely dried using a vacufuge. The resulting peptides were dissolved in 8 µl of 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile solution, and 2 µl of the peptide solution was resolved on a nano-capillary reverse phase column (Acclaim PepMap C18, 2 µm, 50 cm, Thermo Scientific) using a 0.1% formic acid/2% acetonitrile (buffer A) and 0.1% formic acid/95% acetonitrile (buffer B) gradient at 300 nl min−1 over a period of 180 min (2–22% buffer B in 110 min, 22–40% in 25 min, 40–90% in 5 min followed by holding at 90% buffer B for 5 min and requilibration with buffer A for 25 min). The eluent was directly introduced into the Orbitrap Fusion tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) using an Easy-Spray source. MS1 scans were acquired at 120K resolution (AGC target = 106; max IT = 50 ms). Data-dependent collision induced dissociation MS/MS spectra were acquired using the Top speed method (3 s) following each MS1 scan (NCE ≈ 32%; AGC target = 105; max IT 45 ms).

Proteins were identified by searching the MS/MS data against the UniProt human database (sp_canonical TaxID=9606, v2025-02-05) using Proteome Discoverer (v3, Thermo Scientific). Search parameters included MS1 mass tolerance of 10 ppm and fragment tolerance of 0.2 Da; two missed cleavages were allowed. Carbamidomethylation of cysteine was considered a fixed modification and oxidation of methionine, deamidation of asparagine and glutamine were considered as potential modifications. The false-discovery rate (FDR) was determined using Percolator, and proteins or peptides with a FDR of ≤1% were retained for further analysis.

VCaP cells were treated with 100 nM DALTAC-1 or a combination of 100 nM p300/CBPi and ARi for 4, 12 or 24 h, each in two biological replicates. The cells were then subjected to RNA-seq as previously described8. In brief, total RNA was extracted, and ribosomal RNA was removed using the RiboErase module of the KAPA RNA HyperPrep Kit (Roche). rRNA-depleted RNA was used for library preparation following the manufacturer’s protocol, and libraries were quality-checked on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer before sequencing on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform (paired-end, 2× 100 bp). Sequencing reads were quantified with Kallisto (v0.50.1), normalized with edgeR (v3.34.1), and analysed for differential expression using limma-voom (v3.58.1). GSEA was performed using fgsea (v1.28.0), and data visualization employed tidyverse, gplots, ggplot2, gtable (v0.3.0), and EnhancedVolcano (v1.15.0) packages in R.

ChIP–seq was performed as previously described8. In brief, cells were cross-linked in 1% formaldehyde, quenched with glycine, and lysed for chromatin extraction. Chromatin was sheared to 200–600 bp fragments using a Bioruptor (Diagenode) and subjected to immunoprecipitation with antibodies against transcription factors (AR, FOXA1, p300, ERG and BRD4) or histone marks (H3K27ac, H2BK20ac and RNA Pol II) using the iDeal ChIP–seq Kit (Diagenode). Drosophila spike-in chromatin (Active Motif, 53083) and spike-in antibody (Active Motif, 61686) were added during the overnight incubation. After reverse cross-linking and DNA purification, sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform. For PR, SRC2, and CBP ChIP–seq, we performed double-cross-linking. In brief, 10 million cells were cross-linked with 250 μl of 200 mM DSP (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 22585) for 30 min at room temperature. PBS was then added to a final volume of 9 ml, followed by 40 μl of 0.5 M EDTA. Formaldehyde (250 μl, 37%) was added, and the cells were incubated for an additional 10 min at room temperature. Cross-linking was quenched by adding 1 ml of 1.25 M glycine and 200 μl of 10% Tween-20, followed by incubation for 5 min. Samples were then processed according to the ChIP–seq protocol described previously.

According to recent reports, chIP–seq reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic (v0.39). Alignment was then performed separately to both the human genome (hg38) and the Drosophila genome (dm6) using BWA (v0.7.17-r1198-dirty). Low-quality and duplicate reads were filtered with SAMtools and Picard, respectively. Normalization ratios were calculated based on the lowest amount of uniquely aligned reads per ChIP target to each genome as recommended on the vendor’s website. Reads were then downsampled per the normalization ratios. Peak calling was then performed with MACS2 (v2.1.1.20160309) using narrow or broad settings depending on the target, and blacklisted genomic regions were removed using BEDTools with the ENCODE exclusion list. Motif enrichment analysis was performed using HOMER (v4.10). Processed data were converted to BigWig format using UCSC wigToBigWig for visualization.

Sources indicate that read density heat maps and average enrichment profiles were generated using deepTools. For histone marks, signals were plotted within ±2.5 kb of the reference point, and for transcription factors within ±1 kb. The parameters --skipZeros, --averageType mean, and --plotType se were applied. ENCODE blacklist regions (ENCFF356LFX) were excluded from analysis. Genomic interval operations were performed using the IRanges Bioconductor package (v2.36.0), and non-promoter regions were defined using the ChIPseeker R package tool annotatePeak excluding ±1 kb windows surrounding annotated gene transcription start site regions. Peak overlap and annotation analyses were additionally performed using the ChIPpeakAnno R package (v3.6.5).

It has been revealed that mouse prostate organoids and patient-derived xenograft organoids were established and maintained following previously described protocols41,71. In brief, organoids were cultured in 50 µl Matrigel domes and overlaid with prostate organoid medium, with media changed every 2–3 days and passaging performed weekly. For growth and drug-response assays, organoid fragments were dissociated into single cells and used to generate new organoids (1,000 cells per dome for standard viability assays) in complete organoid medium. Cell viability was measured using the CellTiter-Glo 3D assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

It has been revealed that all animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol PRO0001291) and performed in accordance with institutional guidelines. Male CB17 SCID mice, 4–6 weeks old, were procured from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions on a 12 h light:12 h dark cycle, with ambient temperature maintained at 18–23 °C and relative humidity maintained at 40–60%. Only male mice were used, as prostate cancer is specific to males.

In a recent development, sample sizes for efficacy studies (n = 7–20 tumours per group) were chosen prospectively based on a power calculation: with >7 tumours per group, the study had an estimated 92.3% power to detect a 50% decrease in mean tumour volume or metastatic burden, assuming a coefficient of variation of 40%. No animals or data points were excluded from analysis. Mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups prior to dosing. Histopathological evaluation and immunohistochemistry-based scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; blinding was applied to other end-points (for example, tumour volume measurement). Per IACUC protocol PRO0001291, tumour burden was not permitted to exceed 4,186 mm3, and this limit was not exceeded in any experiment reported here.

Sources indicate that male SCID mice (6–8 weeks old) were obtained from the breeding colony at the University of Michigan and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions. All animal procedures were approved by the University of Michigan IACUC (protocol PRO0001291). Subcutaneous xenograft tumours were established by injecting 3 × 106 VCaP cells suspended in serum-free medium mixed 1:1 with Matrigel (BD Biosciences) into both dorsal flanks. Tumour growth was monitored weekly using digital calipers, and volumes were calculated as (π/6) × (length × width2). At study end-points, mice were euthanized, and tumours were excised and weighed.

According to recent reports, the castration-resistant VCaP model was generated as previously described8. In brief, mice were castrated once tumours reached 150–200 mm³, and treatment with DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1 intraperitoneally or 60 mg kg−1 orally), combination of p300/CBPi (30 mg kg−1 orally) and ARi (10 mg kg−1 orally), or vehicle was initiated after tumour regrowth to baseline size for 24 days.

A tissue microarray (TMA) was created according to a design involving 8 unique cases from 4 different subgroups: vehicle (n = 2), p300/CBPi + ARi (n = 2), DALTAC-1 intraperitoneal (n = 2) and DALTAC-1 oral administration (n = 2). Two independent samples were selected from each subgroup. To ensure data reliability and representativeness, a replicate core from each sample was included in the TMA, resulting in a focused 16-core TMA. Technical details are as follows: in brief, FFPE donor blocks for the selected samples were chosen by two study pathologists (R.M. and S.M.) after reviewing the haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The pathologists then annotated the H&E slides to identify the most representative tumour area of interest (AOI) on the surface of each donor block. The Semiautomatic tissue arrayer from Beecher Instruments (Sun Prairie) was used to punch 1 mm-diameter cores from each marked region. These cores were carefully transferred into a recipient acrylic block in a grid-like pattern. Once transferred, the recipient block was incubated at 37 °C for 30 min to ensure proper fusion of the cores within the paraffin. The prepared TMA block was then sectioned at 4-μm thickness and stained with H&E to assess the quality of the final TMA.

According to recent reports, four-micrometre-thick sections from the PDX TMA, mounted on positively charged slides, were cut and prepared according to the guidelines and recommendations. Subsequently, the slides were deparaffinized using a standard xylene and graded ethanol series, followed by heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER) as per the Lunaphore COMET protocol to unmask target epitopes72. Automated sequential immunofluorescence (seqIF) staining was performed on the COMET instrument (Lunaphore) to enable highly multiplexed protein detection with the target primary antibodies. This process involved cycles of staining, imaging, and elution managed by the COMET Control software through controlled temperature and microfluidic reagent delivery. Each cycle included incubation with unconjugated primary antibodies, followed by species-specific fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies (for example, Alexa Fluor 555 and 647), automated image acquisition including DAPI counterstaining, and complete antibody removal via elution. After the final staining cycle, the COMET Control software (v1.5.0.0) automatically stitched, aligned, and stacked images to produce a single OME-TIFF file for each sample. During post-processing, autofluorescence background was systematically subtracted using reference images acquired from unstained tissue sections at the beginning of the protocol.

Recent findings suggest that the raw prostate TMA data included single-cell measurements across multiple markers along with their spatial locations. Markers were grouped into two panels based on biological relevance, as shown in the plots. To normalize marker expression and reduce skewness, a log1p transformation (log1p(expression)) was applied. Outliers were identified and removed separately for each marker within each group. Outliers were defined as values exceeding ±5 median absolute deviations from the group-specific median. The median absolute deviation is a robust measure of statistical dispersion that calculates the median of the absolute deviations from the median, making it less sensitive to extreme outliers than standard deviation. This approach preserves most of the data while minimizing the impact of extreme values.

In a recent development, the prostate cancer PDX models MDA-PCa-146-12 and MDA-PCa-183 were established and maintained as previously described8. MDA-PCa-146-12 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from the adenocarcinoma region of a primary prostate tumour with mixed adenocarcinoma–neuroendocrine morphology. MDA-PCa-183 is an AR+ and ERG+ adenocarcinoma PDX derived from a bone marrow aspirate of a treatment-naive patient with metastatic prostate cancer. Both models harbour PTEN loss and TP53 loss-of-function alterations. In brief, tumour fragments (~2 mm3) were implanted subcutaneously into the dorsal flanks of six- to eight-week-old male SCID mice bred in-house and propagated by serial passage. Once tumours reached approximately 200 mm3 using the formula (π/6) × (length × width²), mice were randomized into treatment groups. Mice bearing MDA-PCa-146-12 tumours received vehicle or DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week). Mice bearing MDA-PCa-183 tumours received vehicle, DALTAC-1 (30 mg kg−1, intraperitoneally three times per week), ARV-766 (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week), or enzalutamide (10 mg kg−1, orally, 5 times per week). Tumour volumes were measured weekly, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with protocols approved by the University of Michigan Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC, protocol PRO0001291).

In a recent development, all experimental procedures and statistical analyses were performed as previously described8. In brief, key experiments were independently repeated at least three times, with most quantitative assays carried out in biological replicates as noted. Representative images and immunoblots reflect reproducible results, and the number of biological replicates is provided in the figure legends. No data were excluded from analysis. For in vitro experiments, sample sizes were not predetermined by a statistical method and randomization was not applicable, as cells were allocated to experimental conditions under homogeneous culture conditions. For animal studies, sample sizes were determined prospectively (see Methods), and mice were randomly assigned to treatment groups. Histopathological and immunohistochemical scoring for drug toxicity studies were performed in a blinded manner by two independent pathologists; all other data collection and quantification relied on automated instruments or standardized computational pipelines and were therefore not blinded. Two-sided statistical tests were used unless otherwise stated. Comparisons between two groups used unpaired t-tests or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, and multiple comparisons were corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. Exact P values are reported in the figure legends.

Industry observers note that all data are available in the manuscript and Supplementary information. Raw sequencing data (RNA-seq and ChIP–seq) have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) under accession numbers GSE310948 and GSE310949. This study used the following public databases and reference datasets: human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38), used for ChIP–seq read alignment (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001405.26/). Drosophila melanogaster reference genome (dm6), used for ChIP–seq spike-in normalization (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/assembly/GCF_000001215.4/). The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifiers PXD084247, PXD084250 and PXD084305. Protein Data Bank (PDB) entry 5W0E (CBP-BRD–GNE-781 co-crystal structure) was used as the structural template for computational modelling of the p300-BRD–GNE-049 interaction. No restrictions apply to the availability of these data. Source data are provided with this paper.

No custom code or software was used in this study. All computational analyses were performed using publicly available software and code, which are described in Methods.

J.L., J.Y., S.W. and A.M.C. conceived and designed the studies. J.L. performed all of the in vitro and functional genomics experiments with assistance from S.D., J.C., Y.L., X.J., X.W., K.G., S.E. and M.W. Y.Q., J.C.Y.-T. and J.L. performed all of the organoid and animal efficacy studies with assistance from S.E., Y.Y. and A.J.T. E.Y. and S.L. carried out all of the bioinformatics analyses with assistance from A.P. J.T. and J.Y. performed the computational modelling of the AR–p300–DALTAC-1 complex. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the histopathological evaluations of drug toxicity as well as quantified all of the histology-based data. R.M. and S.M. carried out all of the immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence staining. R.S. and A.R. conducted quantification of sequential multiplex immunofluorescence datasets. X.C. and F.S. performed sequencing. J.Y., W.X., M.W., S.J. and S.W. designed, synthesized and performed initial evaluations of a large number of DALTAC molecules, leading to the discovery of DALTAC-1, as well as Neg-1 and Neg-2 control compounds. J.L., J.Y., S.J.M., J.C.Y.-T., S.W. and A.M.C. wrote the manuscript and organized the final figures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is not often that West Ham fans appear unified over anything, after recent seasons of strife, division, disagreement and dispute with the Sullivan and Brady leadership, it feels as if ‘disharmony’ has been the default setting.

Not, it seems, about everything. There is one hot topic on which a huge majority of West Ham fans are in almost total agreement.

According to the NY Times’ fan survey, the biggest consensus was not for the approval of the new manager – although there is a pretty strong 77% majority of fans who responded who give the appointment of Scott Parker the thumbs up.

The biggest single factor on which most West Ham supporters agree is the choice of goalkeeper. According to the survey:.

“Of the fans surveyed, an overwhelming 85.4 per cent believe Alphonse Areola should reclaim the No 1 jersey from Mads Hermansen.

Likeable yes, dependable no: 85% of West Ham fans want Hermansen out of the team.

Interestingly, though, a sizeable 62 per cent of supporters believe the travelling contingent at Ewood Park were not right to boo Hermansen.”.

Eighty five percent of fans have had enough of the Dane’s inept performances in between the sticks, with one fan driven to comment that West Ham’s goal would be better defended simply by hanging a green jersey on the cross bar rather than continuing to select the out of form Hermansen.

Of course the fly in the ointment is that Areola has been reported as ‘unfit’ – whether that means third choice Finlay Herrick comes into consideration – who can say- but it’d be a brave selection for Parker to leave his number one on the bench if Areola isn’t ready for the Preston North End fixture next weekend, however much it seems supporters want to see Hermansen out of the team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that jamie Gittens has withdrawn from the England Under-21 squad. He suffered an ankle injury during Tuesday’s qualifier against Kazakhstan at Molineux. The Chelsea winger left the ground on crutches. He has returned to Stamford Bridge, where the Jamie Gittens injury will now be assessed by the club’s medical staff.

Recent findings suggest that gittens picked up the knock after a challenge during the second half of England’s win over Kazakhstan. He was withdrawn as a precaution. He did not take any further part in the match. England have been careful not to overstate the matter and no further reports have come out further.

The 21-year-old struggled to put weight on the affected ankle and was seen limping around Molineux after full time. That prompted an immediate release back to his club, rather than any attempt to assess him further in camp.

England Under-21 boss Lee Carsley addressed the injury directly after the game. He confirmed the nature of the knock and the decision to send Gittens home.

It has been revealed that “Jamie got a kick on his ankle,” Carsley noted after the match. “We never take any risks. With the age of these players, we don’t ever keep them in camp to see how they are. He will go back.”.

England’s statement on the squad changes, detailed in a report from Football.London, confirmed the wider fallout from the fixture.

“Mukasa’s call-up follows the withdrawal of Chelsea’s Jamie Gittens and Norwich City pair Kellen Fisher and Ben Chrisene through injury,” the statement read. West Ham midfielder Divine Mukasa has been called up as cover for all three.

Industry observers note that gittens has been an unused substitute in every Premier League fixture Chelsea have played this season, with his only two appearances under Xabi Alonso coming in the Carabao Cup. Those minutes have offered him little platform after his massive summer move.

In a recent development, alonso’s squad selection has been a talking point since he took charge. Our earlier look at Xabi Alonso’s squad choices at Stamford Bridge covered how competitive things have become. An ankle injury will not change his pecking order in the short term. It does, though, remove any chance of him pushing his case this week.

Sources indicate that chelsea’s break has brought other headlines too. Cole Palmer also withdrew, for entirely different reasons, after his recall by senior boss Thomas Tuchel to the full England squad. Chelsea will be watching both returns closely before domestic football resumes.

Chelsea have not yet issued a formal revision on the severity of the injury. Any recovery timeline will depend on an assessment by the club’s medical team once Gittens is back at Cobham. Nothing beyond the crutches seen at Molineux has been confirmed.

It has been revealed that given his limited game time this season, the immediate concern is less about missed fixtures than a setback to his integration under Alonso. Fans can follow how the squad shapes up before the next fixtures through our recent line-up updates. Further news on Gittens is expected once Chelsea’s medical staff finish their evaluation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United had a difficult evening once again as they were held to a 1-1 draw at Leeds United. Pressure mounts on Michael Carrick as United have just 7 points from 7 games.

Manchester United took the lead through Bryan Mbeumo in the first half, with the forward finishing Youri Tielemans’ excellent cross from the right. However, the visitors couldn’t hold on to their advantage as Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised for Leeds United from a corner.

The draw extended United’s frustrating run of results, leaving Michael Carrick still searching for the consistency his side need.

Carragher, though, believes there were positives to take from the trip, particularly one performance at the back.

Jamie Carragher has singled out Harry Maguire for praise after Manchester United drew 1-1 with Leeds United at Elland Road on Sunday.

Speaking on Sky Sports, the former Liverpool defender admitted that picking up a point at Elland Road was not necessarily a bad result in isolation, even if United’s recent form made it feel like a missed opportunity.

“Going away to Leeds is going to be tricky for any team except for Manchester City and Arsenal at the moment,” Carragher said.

“A lot of teams will take a point at Leeds this season but the problem for Manchester United is the results have been so poor that they need to start winning games so it almost feels like two points dropped.”.

Carragher then turned his attention to Maguire, who he felt played a major role in keeping United in the game when Leeds began to push for a winner.

In a recent development, “But in isolation, getting a point at Leeds is a decent result. I thought Harry Maguire was fantastic, especially in the second half.”.

Recent findings suggest that leeds United grew into the contest after Calvert-Lewin brought them level, putting United under pressure during the closing stages. Carragher felt Maguire’s efforts in defence helped prevent the visitors from falling apart.

“After Leeds got that goal back there was a stage of the game where it felt like Man United could go under, but Maguire at the back held it together for them. He was fantastic.”.

The result may feel like another opportunity missed for Carrick, but Maguire’s performance gave United something positive to take away from Elland Road.

Breaking: Manu Koné: Roma slap £86m price tag on Chelsea target

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readchelsea

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Roma have put an £86m (€100m) price tag on Manu Koné, according to Gazzetta dello Sport, reviving the Manu Koné Chelsea transfer link that first emerged over the summer.
  • Koné remains under contract at the Stadio Olimpico, and he has become a key part of Roma’s midfield since his move from Borussia Mönchengladbach.
  • Roma sporting director Tony D’Amico has confirmed Chelsea made contact late in the summer window, though he was quick to draw a clear line under how far things went.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roma have put an £86m (€100m) price tag on Manu Koné, according to Gazzetta dello Sport, reviving the Manu Koné Chelsea transfer link that first emerged over the summer. Roma want any interested club, including Chelsea, to know the price before serious talks can even begin.

Koné remains under contract at the Stadio Olimpico, and he has become a key part of Roma’s midfield since his move from Borussia Mönchengladbach. The Gazzetta report reads like a warning to potential buyers rather than proof of any talks between the two clubs.

Roma sporting director Tony D’Amico has confirmed Chelsea made contact late in the summer window, though he was quick to draw a clear line under how far things went.

According to recent reports, “There was an inquiry and some preliminary contact with Chelsea on the final day of the transfer window. No official offers arrived that would allow us to approach the player. Something was imagined that simply didn’t happen. There was no official offer; the final day of the transfer window got everyone a little worked up.”.

Recent findings suggest that D’Amico’s comments confirm Chelsea looked at signing Koné before the deadline, but they stop well short of showing an official bid was ever made. He also explained why Roma had no wish to sell a key player so close to the window closing.

Industry observers note that “Before the match against Fiorentina (on 24 August), I said it would be difficult for us to deprive ourselves of key players so near to the end of the transfer session, and so it proved. Kone is an important player, we’re happy he stayed with us, and we’re confident he’ll give his contribution during the season.”.

Chelsea’s midfield has changed shape under Xabi Alonso since the summer, with Morgan Rogers arriving to add depth and competition for places. That signing came during a window that also saw exits acceleration under Xabi Alonso, as the head coach reshaped his squad around his own style.

Recent findings suggest that koné’s ball winning and his range of progressive passing would suit Alonso well, should Chelsea ever revisit their interest. Supporters have already seen how Alonso rotates his midfield for the biggest games, including the recent derby line-up selections against Brentford.

For now, Rogers and Chelsea’s existing central options give Alonso enough cover without needing an immediate signing. Roma’s reluctance to sell also means any deal would need patience rather than a quick resolution.

Nothing in D’Amico’s comments suggests Roma are open to a sale in the near term, and Koné has given no sign that he wants to leave. The £86m valuation, reported by Football London, stands as Roma’s marker rather than an asking price involved with Chelsea.

Recent findings suggest that will Chelsea return with a more formal approach in a future window? D’Amico’s comments give no hint either way. The Manu Koné Chelsea transfer link is unlikely to fade given Chelsea’s history of scouting France’s leading midfielders, but any fresh move will have to wait for Roma’s stance to soften.

Strip away the headlines and the numbers alone tell an uncomfortable story. Drinkwater spent five years on Chelsea’s books. In that time he made just 23 appearances, according to the original interview report.

Do the maths and it barely comes to five games a year. That is a thin return for a central midfielder signed to compete for a first-team place. It is also the kind of record that rarely sits well at a club of Chelsea’s size and ambition.

According to recent reports, chelsea’s best attacking spells over a similar stretch of seasons look far more productive, as our striker rankings show. Set next to those numbers, Drinkwater’s five quiet years stand out even more starkly.

Five years. Twenty three games. These numbers alone explains why this transfer still gets talked about by Drinkwater, long after the headlines faded.

The numbers only tell part of the story. A string of incidents turned a quiet, underwhelming spell into something far more pointed.

Drinkwater had a training-ground bust-up while out on loan. He was also involved in an on-pitch brawl with Chelsea’s own under-23s side. Flashpoints between a first-team player and a development squad are rare at any club, let alone one with Chelsea’s standards.

In a recent development, taken alone, either incident might have passed as a bad day. Taken together, it became harder to see Drinkwater simply as an unlucky squad player who could not catch a break.

The most serious moment came during his time at Aston Villa. Drinkwater headbutted team-mate Jota and was fined two weeks’ wages for it. He indicates the consequences at Chelsea did not stop there.

“They didn’t formally ban me, but I got removed from the first team building after the incident at Villa,” Drinkwater stated.

One off-field incident, at another club, pushed him out of the manager’s day-to-day looks back home. No formal punishment at Chelsea followed. The effect was much the same.

According to recent reports, chelsea fans saw a similar breakdown of trust play out when Graham Potter struggled to win over the dressing room during another difficult Chelsea transition. Trust can break down fast once results or behaviour turn against the person at the centre of it.

Drinkwater’s comments matter beyond his own career. They are a reminder that saying yes to a major move does not guarantee it will work once a player walks through the door.

That tension has not gone away. Chelsea’s current transfer business, covered in our transfer watch, shows the club still weighing major calls on players whose futures depend on more than form alone.

Recent findings suggest that squad management under Xabi Alonso, assessed in our bomb squad verdict, raises a familiar glitch. Players who fall outside a manager’s intends rarely find a quick way back in, whether the exile is formal or not.

Drinkwater never found his way back into Chelsea’s plans after the Villa incident. His account of the Danny Drinkwater Chelsea years stands as a blunt warning. A move that looks impossible to refuse can still become one of the hardest spells of a career.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michael Carrick has come under immense pressure as a disjointed Manchester United sit just two places above the relegation places.
  • Despite the scrutiny and the news of a possible sacking, Michael Carrick has been given another chance at Manchester United.
  • Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their Premier League trip to Chelsea on Saturday after the club decided to give their under-pressure head coach another opportunity to turn things around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Carrick has come under immense pressure as a disjointed Manchester United sit just two places above the relegation places.

Despite the scrutiny and the news of a possible sacking, Michael Carrick has been given another chance at Manchester United.

Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their Premier League trip to Chelsea on Saturday after the club decided to give their under-pressure head coach another opportunity to turn things around.

United have gone eight games without a win in all competitions, with Sunday’s humiliating 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth leaving them 16th in the Premier League table, just one point above the relegation zone.

Carrick’s position looked increasingly uncertain after the Bournemouth loss. As a result, United chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox were at Carrington on Monday to discuss the situation.

It has been reported by Sky Sports that United have considered other options internally as well to replace Micahel Carrick but for the weekend, they are sticking with Michael Carrick.

Carrick took training on Tuesday and the decision means he has at least one more match to convince the club’s hierarchy that he can get United back on track.

Gary Neville admitted he was surprised that Carrick had survived the immediate threat of losing his job, although he welcomed the decision.

“I am surprised, but I am happy because I was absolutely certain that what I witnessed on Sunday would be the end of Michael,” Neville noted in Sky Sports.

The former United captain explained that Carrick’s actions after the Bournemouth defeat had made him think the manager was preparing to say goodbye to the supporters.

“It looked like he was walking round at the end on his own with the players behind him, like it was almost a goodbye lap,” Neville added.

Fans continued singing the manager’s name after the final whistle, while the rest of the team drew boos.

Despite his surprise, Gary Neville hopes Micahel Carrick can use the extra time to get a response from his squad.

“I hope he can somehow get those players to start playing for him again because they haven’t played for him in the last few weeks,” he noted.

The trip to Chelsea now becomes a crucial test for Micahel Carrick but United need a result and a far better performance to ease the pressure at Old Trafford.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pierre Sage felt Crystal Palace were “really far off” his expectations after suffering a 3-2 away Europa League defeat by his former side Lyon.

Corentin Tolisso opened the scoring for the hosts and Ernest Nuamah doubled Lyon’s advantage late in a first half devoid of any shots on target for the visitors.

Yéremy Pino halved the deficit five minutes after the break, before Pavel Sulc restored the two-goal lead, and substitute Daichi Kamada’s late goal proved a mere consolation.

“At the end, we were frustrated by the result, but in the first half we have to be frustrated in the way we play,” said Sage, speaking to PalaceTV.

Industry observers note that “I think we didn’t play this first half. We are really far off our standards in the mental side of the play, in the tactical side of the play, because the players are too high between our lines and we really struggled a lot with that.

According to recent reports, “When you give back the ball to your opponent, you suffer a lot and we were better in the second half. You cannot win this kind of game by playing only one half.”.

Sage’s side got the better of his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, after they bounced back to beat Nottingham Forest 3-1 at Selhurst Park on Sunday.

After that victory, the Frenchman called for more consistency from his team, but on Thursday night was left ruing missed opportunities and goals conceded too easily by last season’s Conference League winners.

Sources indicate that sage was sacked by Lyon in January 2025 after a 14-month spell with the Ligue 1 outfit. Like Glasner’s, his own reunion ended in disappointment.

He told Uefa: “It’s a very disappointing return because we lost. I can’t take satisfaction from coming back home or seeing familiar faces when the result isn’t there.

“The scoreline may have been close, but there was a big difference in the way the two teams played.

“We improved considerably after the break and gave ourselves a chance, but conceding that third goal made things difficult.

“I think our second-half efforts deserved an equaliser, although winning would have been a generous reward given that we only really played [to our level] for one half.”.

In a recent development, the veteran captain said: “It has been a long time coming. The fans were up for it, the players were up for it so we’re very happy with the performance.”.

When asked about Evanilson’s header, which Smith supplied the assist for, he replied: “It wasn’t my best cross but I put it in an area, what a finish from him and I think we deserved that little bit of luck.

“From there on we went on to win the game but in the second half we got a little bit tired but the quality that came off the bench is great and we look forward to Sunday now.

“It’s a great header, he deserved it because he has worked very hard this season and many more to come from him.”.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Thursday night’s European football with Crystal Palace, Sunderland and Bournemouth in Europa League action, and Brighton hosting Kauno Zalgiris in the Uefa Conference League.

Palace manager Pierre Sage managed Lyon between November 2023 and January 2025, and another sub-plot is American businessman John Textor’s involvement with the French club. The former Palace shareholder was the reason the club missed out on Europa League participation last season because Lyon were in the same competition and thus Palace were considered in breach of multi-club ownership rules. Textor sold his stake in Palace, but despite the club’s best efforts they had to settle for the Conference League, a competition they subsequently won.

Palace could have been three or four down against Nottingham Forest at the weekend but fought back for a much-needed Premier League victory. They made a winning start in Europe, beating Lech Poznan 4-0 at Selhurst Park in their opening Europa League game.

Sources indicate that bournemouth and Sunderland also made winning starts, despite both teams’ poor form domestically. Sunderland travel to Portuguese side Torreense, while Sturm Graz are the opposition for Bournemouth’s first ever European game at the Vitality Stadium (or Dean Court if you prefer). Bournemouth continue to be without Justin Kluivert, Eli Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott because of injury.

It has been revealed that brighton are favourites to win the Conference League and play their first game in the competition against Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris. Lifting the trophy in Istanbul at the end of the season would assure Brighton of a place in next season’s Europa League, though given their Premier League form and Manchester City’s predicament, Champions League qualification could be a realistic aspiration. Brighton won with 10 men at Sunderland on Saturday, and were successful in their appeal against Pascal Struijk’s red card.
