There’ll be some relief amongst the West Ham medical staff at Rush Green tonight knowing that Manor Solomon was left out of Israel’s match altogether after the winger could not train owing to the pain of an ongoing injury.

However there will be concern that this same concern which dogged Solomon through September might yet prevent him playing his full part in the busy run up to Christmas  – with its demanding schedule of nine games in a little over a month.

Solomon came back from the last international break in September looking washed out, and in truth, his performances since have been a disappointment after his early season impact and man-of-the-match award.

Solomon – early season form has fallen away as his back injury has made itself known.

Sources indicate that there’s been a sneaking suspicion that Solomon has been playing with an injury -and this would seem to be confirmed by his being left out of his national side. In truth he probably should not even have travelled. According to Yahoo Sports:.

“The winger missed out on the Israel squad completely for the 0-0 draw with Kosovo on Saturday.

Solomon had been suffering from back complications, and only partially trained on Wednesday.

He participated in the first session, before missing the second one and then tried to train on Friday.

However, Israeli boss Ran Ben-Shimon confirmed that he was in too much pain, and ultimately left him out of the contest.”.

From a purely selfish club vs country perspective, West Ham could really do with the winger sitting out Israel’s next fixture against Austria on Tuesday evening.

Whilst Edvin Austbø has pulled ahead of Solomon in the pecking order, I shouldn’t wonder if Solomon’s back problems have been affecting him ever since he arrived at London Stadium and as the hours on the pitch have racked up, his high-energy output has nose dived.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, more information about the structure and cost of Goncalo Ramos’ move to AC Milan has been revealed.

It’s fair to say that Ramos’ start to life with Milan has been poor. The Portuguese striker has not scored (or assisted) as many as had been hoped from a player worth a substantial amount and it’s fair to suggest that some have been disappointed with his time at San Siro so far.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

However, the club will not be giving up on him anytime soon, considering he is their record arrival.

This evening, Calcio e Finanza have looked at the fee paid for Ramos – as they did for Diego Moreira recently – and picked apart both the fee, the bonuses and the structure of the payment, as MilanNews relays.

In terms of the fixed fee, the Rossoneri agreed on a deal worth €70 million, with an extra €3.1m in additional costs. This figure will be paid over the course of four years, with yearly payments scheduled on July 15 on each year – ending in July 2029 – and each payment will be worth €17.5m.

Then, there is €16m in bonuses that can be achieved, taking the total fee to almost €90m if all bonuses are achieved.

Sources indicate that if Milan win the Scudetto, €2m will be owed; then there are several Champions League bonuses, which could be worth up to €5.2m if the Diavolo win the competition. Finally, if he is the top goalscorer in Serie A, another €2m will be owed to PSG.

These bonuses are capped at €16m and are repeatable, but they’ll only be redeemable if the Portuguese plays 60% of games in that season, unless he is the top scorer, where only the €2m will be owed.

The international break has rolled back around and with it a chance to take stock of the Premier League season so far.

The first ten games of the new campaign have thrown up a few surprises – none of three  promoted teams find themselves in the drop zone at this stage and the race for Europe is wide open with teams such as Brighton and Everton excelling.

Here is a look at the players who have defined the opening weeks as Daily Mail Sport, in collaboration with stats gurus Sofascore, compile our team of the season so far...

Many will be surprised to see the Argentine's name here instead of Arsenal's David Raya or Brighton's Bart Verbruggen, but despite Chelsea's defensive woes it is their £7million summer signing that makes the cut.

Martinez has been out for the last three games after sustaining a nasty head injury away at Everton but his average match rating remains the highest out of all the division's shot-stoppers.

Industry observers note that A look at the stats tells you why. Despite only keeping one clean sheet so far, Chelsea's upcoming No1 has prevented 1.64 goals, had 13 high claims and 0 errors leading to goals.

The massive man has also looked extremely competent with the ball at his feet, something that Blues keepers have struggled with in previous years, and has even created three chances from his own box so far this season.

Emiliano Martinez has been out for three weeks with a head injury he sustained at Everton but has still done enough to make our team.

Industry observers note that there was always going to have to be at least one of this Brighton team in our XI. We all knew they were an excellent outfit coming into the season but perhaps even Fabian Hurzeler  may not have envisaged his side sitting second after ten games.

The linchpin of this side has of course been their skipper, Lewis Dunk. A local boy who came through the ranks at Brighton and has spent virtually his entire career at the club, he continues to impress at 34 years of age.

Sources indicate that dunk has played in nine of Brighton's ten games this season looking solid in each, leading his side to six wins and keeping a clean sheet in each victory. And his personal defensive stats make for excellent reading as well – he has won 22 aerial duels and registered 31 recoveries already this season.

But there are some things that can't be quantified, such as Dunk's impact on the  Brighton dressing room and the guidance he gives such a young squad which must be immense – after all, he is a year older than his own manager.

Next up is another old school English centre-half who has captained his team to an excellent start to the season.

The big man is rolling back the years as the Toffees look to push for Europe.

In recent years the Toffees have become far more familiar with the bottom of the table than the top but at present are making a serious push for the European places and are at the moment in sixth place, level on points with fifth.

And the 33-year-old has been vital to David Moyes's upcoming system, providing stability and strength to a defence that has conceded just ten goals – with only Arsenal (five), Brighton (seven) and Leeds (eight) conceding fewer.

Again similar to Dunk, Tarkowski's stats show the veteran's ability to adapt to the demands of the modern game, having 108 line-breaking passes, creating four chances and one big chance so far this season.

The skipper has also come up trumps in close games, bagging a crucial goal in a 1-1 draw at Bournemouth and getting an assist in the 1-0 win over Ipswich.

Completing the back three is the only one out under 30, but is also the man with the highest average match rating in this team.

Considering Tottenham's defensive record this season, one of their defenders making it in may come as a bit of a shock but anyone that has watched the north Londoners this season will know that 26-year-old Van Hecke is hardly the reason for their woes.

The Dutchman has been magnificent since moving from Brighton and reuniting with his old boss Roberto De Zerbi, playing every single minute of the Premier League season so far.

Van Hecke epitomises the modern centre-half, having the second most one-line breaking passes (162), the most two-line breaking passes (37) and the most passes into the final third (138) out of any player in the league – and has even bagged two goals for Spurs as they have started to pick up some form.

Despite Sunderland's poor start, the Black Cats' skipper anchors our midfield with the highest average match rating in his position this campaign. Most would have been expecting Pascal Gross to take this position in an XI such as this considering his eight goals and assists and all-round stellar showing this season.

Xhaka is a surprise entry considering Sunderland's form but the stats tell us that the skipper is still performing.

But the boffins have Xhaka here instead and the numbers show why. The Swiss international has excelled in a number of areas despite Sunderland's faltering start having the second-most passes into the final third (132) and the joint most line-breaking passes into the box (21).

Moving onto the midfield, we have perhaps the most electrifying winger in the league  this season.

Manchester City have tailed off with three defeats on the spin but Jeremy Doku still remains a major source of headaches for the league's full-backs and a full-time entertainer for us viewers.

In a recent development, when he first joined the league the Belgian was criticised for a lack of consistency but recently he appears to have put that all behind him. Doku does only have one goal and one assist this season, but that does not tell the full story.

He has completed the most dribbles in the league this season (27), won nearly 60 per cent of his duels and has created 4.25xG while on the pitch.

He also provided us with arguably the performance of the season so far when he changed the game off the bench away at Liverpool, scoring a goal-of-the-season contender to down the Reds.

The first and only man from the champions and league leaders to get into our team is Bukayo Saka.

Saka appears to be getting back to his best as the champions get off to an excellent start in their title defence.

It was always going to be hard for the man the fans call 'Starboy' to keep up his form from last season but in actual fact his desire to bring more silverware to the Emirates appears more prevalent than ever.

We all know what he can do going forward and the Englishman has netted three goals in the league, but this year he has improved his defensive game massively, winning 43 duels, 11 tackles and registering 23 recoveries already.

Saka has struggled with his fitness for the past year or so and although he has played their first seven Premier League games, has been on the sidelines since mid-October with a thigh injury.

Despite a testing start to the season, Chelsea are the team with the most players to make the list – though few will quibble with this man's inclusion.

Morgan Rogers proved himself to be a special talent at Aston Villa and there won't be many Chelsea fans doubting the wisdom of paying £117million for his services after his flying start.

Morgan Rogers has been a revelation at the bridge thus far, scoring six goals in all competitions and assisting five more.

The Englishman has lit up Stamford Bridge with six goals and five assists in all competitions and has instantly formed a deadly front three with best friend Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro.

The Blues have struggled for form under fresh manager Xabi Alonso but no criticism can be laid at the feet of Rogers who will hope his goals can bring some much-needed consistency to west London.

Sources indicate that completing the midfield is a man who is finally getting his flowers after months of quality and consistency. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall is one of the many reasons Everton fans are excited for the first time in a while.

The Englishman became an instant fan favourite at the Hill Dickinson after moving from Chelsea last year but this season has gone up a gear in every way, running  games from start to finish with surgical passing, clever dribbling and an incredible work rate.

Only seven players have covered more ground in the league than his 101km (63 miles), and he has also contributed three goals and an assist – as well as delivering a magnificent 79 defensive contributions. His spot in this team could not be more deserved.

Going into the strike-force these next two names are simply must haves, and the first of the two is the mercurial Joao Pedro.

Joao Pedro has the best goals and assists ratio to games in the league with eight in six games.

After an excellent debut season in blue the Brazilian took the risk of taking on the infamously cursed Chelsea No9 shirt. But it appears to have only spurred him on further as he has enjoyed a  stellar start to the campaign in front of goal.

It only took him two minutes to get on the score sheet this season in Chelsea's opening game away to Fulham and he just hasn't stopped scoring since.

Pedro has five goals and three assists in just six Premier League games and has become a menace for opposition defences. Unfortunately for gaffer Xabi Alonso his side have been unable to match that consistency, having won five, drawn one and lost four in the league.

But the Spaniard will hope to have his star man back soon – in the six games Pedro has managed to play this season the Blues have lost just one.

It would not be an elite Premier League XI without this man in it.

Even with all the controversy surrounding Manchester City, Erling Haaland manages to roar on and continue scoring at an alarming rate. It is yet another season where he props up the Premier League goal scoring table with nine in ten games.

For a  City side in transition away from a decade under Pep Guardiola Haaland's goals this season have been so crucial in smoothing the process and getting notable wins.

Industry observers note that the significant Norwegian has bagged winners against rivals Manchester United, Ipswich and Coventry as well as netting the vital opener in their 3-0 win at Anfield. Yet again,  he is proving he is the ultimate goal machine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend with a growing treatment table and a lot of questions for Xabi Alonso to answer before Saturday’s visit of Bournemouth.

According to recent reports, the main concern revolves around Joao Pedro. Chelsea’s current player of the season rescued a point against newly promoted Hull, but he suffered a knock and sat out the damaging 3-0 defeat at Brentford. The problem also prompted his removal from Brazil’s squad shortly after he had returned to it.

Industry observers note that it is understood that he is undergoing specialist knee treatment in an attempt to expedite his recovery, although reports in Brazil suggest that he could be out for up to four weeks. No date has yet been set, but a return later in October looks most likely.

It has been revealed that there is more good news elsewhere. Cole Palmer was among the players called up to the latest England squad, which did not go down too well with Thomas Tuchel.

Recent findings suggest that the midfielder has been recovering from a persistent groin injury and has been working with a rehab coach. He is likely to be fit this weekend.

Moises Caicedo has also struggled with an injury this season, playing just 14 minutes across the campaign. He’s spent the majority of time on the bench recovering from a bad calf injury, which ruled him out for most of the season.

He made his only appearance as a substitute against his former club Brighton, but the game was red-flagged for Ecuador’s friendlies, so he did not play.

It has been revealed that alonso noted before the Brentford match that the player would be ready to return. It seems to be the case, unless something went wrong.

Industry observers note that captain Reece James missed the Brentford game with yet another hamstring problem. Alonso said he only just missed out, so a return seems likely.

In a recent development, there may also be debuts. Marco Palestra, the £27m signing from Atalanta, has been sidelined since a training injury just before the opening match against Fulham. He is back in full training and was expected to feature in a behind-closed-doors friendly with Portsmouth. Chelsea lost 2-0. Emmanuel Emegha, injured after scoring against Bromley in July, is also pushing for involvement.

It has been revealed that less clear is the position of Jamie Gittens. He limped off with an ankle injury playing for England Under-21s against Kazakhstan and was seen on crutches. Mike Penders is fine after a quad scare on Belgium duty. Returning to the bench against Turkey.

Chelsea badly need a lift. Defeat at Brentford before the break left Alonso’s side looking shaky, and a squad stretched by injuries has not helped.

It has been revealed that saturday brings a chance to steady things. If Palmer, James and Caicedo are available, with Palestra and Emegha potentially adding fresh options, the picture will look much brighter at Stamford Bridge. Joao Pedro’s absence will still sting. However, a strong response against Bournemouth would go a long way towards easing the pressure and restoring belief.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United will use the November international break to decide whether Michael Carrick stays on as head coach, after a three-game reprieve that delivered only one win.

According to The Guardian, Carrick came close to being sacked after the 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth on 25 October.

Director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada discussed his position at the training ground the following day and agreed to give him three matches to turn things around before the break.

Those games brought a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea, a 3-2 win over Roma and a chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa at Old Trafford on Sunday. United conceded eight goals across the three fixtures, and defensive frailty remains the biggest worry.

Recent findings suggest that wilcox is now leading a review of Carrick’s position. He will consult Berrada before making a recommendation to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who oversees the club’s sporting operations. Talks are expected to begin on Monday and continue through the break.

The league table makes grim reading. United sit in the Premier League relegation zone with just one league win in their last 10 matches.

If he does win a stay of execution, results will need to follow. Manchester United cannot be languishing in 17th place.

Recent findings suggest that carrick remains defiant. Speaking to Sky Sports News after the Villa draw, he admitted his side “haven’t won enough games” but insisted he expects to move forward.

“I’m quite clear with what direction the club needs to go in, and it’s got to win games, said Carrick after the late Villa draw.

“I think there’s more than enough [to turn things around].”.

If United do make a change, former Newcastle manager Eddie Howe is reported to be Wilcox’s preferred candidate. Howe has been out of work since leaving St James’ Park during pre-season, after four and a half years in charge.

In the meantime, there are no intends to strengthen Carrick’s coaching staff.

For now, Carrick is expected to be in charge for United’s next match, against Liverpool. Whether three games were enough to convince the hierarchy should become clear before then.

The trip to Anfield could be do or die for the decorated former United midfielder.

He’s not likely to survive a heavy defeat at the home of the club’s fierce rivals, but a galvanising win would surely buy him time and goodwill.

In a recent development, that’s if he makes it through the next fortnight before then. A decision or indication could be two days or two weeks away.

The only certainty at Old Trafford is uncertainty.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Laurence Stewart is set to leave Chelsea by mutual consent after almost four years at Stamford Bridge, with the club opting to redistribute his responsibilities rather than appoint a direct replacement.

In a recent development, the departure is understood to be amicable and won’t take immediate effect. Stewart could continue attending matches before formally leaving, following discussions with co-owner Behdad Eghbali over the club’s evolving sporting structure.

The story was first reported by Matt Law of The Telegraph and Nizaar Kinsella of BBC Sport, with Ben Jacobs subsequently providing further details about how Chelsea intend to operate.

Stewart arrived from Monaco in October 2022 as technical director before becoming co-sporting director alongside Paul Winstanley in February 2023.

Chelsea’s day-to-day sporting leadership will now be shared between Winstanley, Sam Jewell and Joe Shields, each with defined responsibilities.

According to recent reports, winstanley will continue overseeing transfer negotiations, player contracts and several departments at Cobham, including medical and performance operations. Shields’ work centres on the academy and player pathways, while Jewell has wider responsibilities across the BlueCo operation, including Strasbourg.

According to Jacobs, discussions about restructuring began in April and accelerated following the appointment of Xabi Alonso as head coach.

Stewart had overseen investment in Chelsea’s data analysis operation, although Jewell and Shields have increasingly taken responsibility for using that information in recruitment and talent identification.

Dave Fallows will remain involved in an advisory capacity, rather than taking on a fixed day-to-day portfolio.

It has been revealed that the changes are being described as a natural evolution of Chelsea’s sporting model. There is no suggestion that Stewart’s departure followed a breakdown in relations, and the club are not at the moment planning to recruit a replacement.

There’s been another twist in the chaotic career of one of West Ham’s standout signings of the Tim Steidten era.

It would be fair to say that Jean Clair Todibo was largely unknown to Hammers fans when Tim Stediten whisked the former Barca defender to east London in his private jet for a VIP welcome in the summer of 2024.

Sadly its would also be fair to say that the defender has been part of a chaotic two and a half years during which he’s seen three West Ham managers – and fallen out with all of them – and declared himself unwilling to play for the club again.

Todibo – dressing room chaos never seems far away.

Chaos appears to have followed Todibo to France when West Ham finally – gratefully – found a loan destination for their unhappy defender in the summer as Todibo was sent to Lens owing to his desire (apparently) to work with manager Dino Toppmoller.

No sooner had the wayward West Ham defender landed than Toppmoller was fired – and his successor Yannick Cahuzac fared little better, lasting just two months.

Todibo is surely the only player in the Lens dressing room who will have played under six managers in side three years, as his newly introduced head coach is revealed as Didier Digard.

Scott Parker can’t have missed the fact that Todibo is due to return to east London at the end of the season – putting the defender on course to test Parker’s own managerial credentials when his loan ends next May. And few West Ham fans will welcome him back after his turbulent and truculent career in Claret and Blue.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have confirmed an agreement with Mauricio Pochettino to become their next head coach, with the Argentine set to take charge after the international break.

The 54-year-old will replace Michael Carrick, who was dismissed on Thursday following United’s disastrous start to the Premier League season. Pochettino is set to sign a two-and-a-half-year contract that will keep him at Old Trafford until the summer of 2029.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss is presently managing the United States national team but is expected to fly straight to Manchester after completing his USA international games.

According to recent reports, pochettino will first oversee the USA’s CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final ties against Haiti on Saturday and next Tuesday. He is expected to arrive in Manchester on Wednesday before taking charge of the club on Thursday.

Pochettino’s first taste of action as a United manager will be against Liverpool at Anfield on November 22.

Industry observers note that pochettino brings considerable Premier League experience after previous spells with Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. He has also managed Paris Saint-Germain before the USA job.

His appointment makes him Manchester United’s eighth permanent manager since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Carrick’s departure came less than six months after he signed a two-year contract. His second spell in charge ended after United managed just one win in their opening 10 league matches, leaving them in the relegation zone.

Carrick’s coaching staff, including Jonny Evans, Jonathan Woodgate, Steve Holland, Travis Binnion and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson, have all left alongside Carrick.

#2401. The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 95m • 📚 Deep Dive (18921 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 95 min read (18921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~95 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication.
  • Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6.
  • The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eukaryotic genomes are exposed to numerous sources of DNA damage that impede replication. Only a decade ago, repriming by the primase–polymerase PRIMPOL was identified as a pathway that enables cells to tolerate DNA damage1,2,3,4. However, the molecular mechanism that underlies repriming remains poorly understood, and it is unclear how PRIMPOL is precisely targeted to stalled forks, where along single-stranded DNA PRIMPOL binds and how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize error-prone DNA synthesis. Here, to dissect the molecular basis of repriming, we perform real-time single-molecule imaging in nuclear extracts that recapitulate genome maintenance. We directly visualize how stalled forks restart through repriming. We show that PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS (CMG). This facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. At near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL reprimes leading strands in a CMG-dependent manner and polymerase ε extends those primers. This primary mode of repriming does not require DNA damage checkpoint signalling. PRIMPOL overexpression and checkpoint activation promote a secondary mode of repriming, whereby PRIMPOL restarts DNA synthesis far from CMG and polymerase δ extends those primers. Our data reveal a simple yet effective mechanism that directs PRIMPOL’s activity to stalled forks awaiting restart, and suggest a strategy to inhibit the repriming pathway.

Multiple pathways maintain genome stability during replication stress (RS)5, including fork reversal and translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)6. In 2013, a new RS response pathway called repriming was identified in eukaryotes1,2,3,4. PRIMPOL performs repriming and enables cells to tolerate diverse DNA lesions1,2,3,4,7,8. As it lacks proofreading, PRIMPOL has an error rate comparable to that of TLS polymerases (10−2−10−4)9,10. PRIMPOL-deficient cells and mice are hypersensitive to several DNA-damaging agents8,11,12,13, underscoring its role in genome maintenance. While repriming enables cancer cells to tolerate RS induced by oncogenes14 and chemotherapy15, PRIMPOL generates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) gaps16,17 that sensitize cells to PARP inhibitors18,19,20. Blocking fork reversal enhances repriming, suggesting that cells favour high-fidelity pathways to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis7,21,22.

The replicative helicase CMG unwinds parental DNA23 and is functionally coupled to polymerase ε (Pol ε)24, which synthesizes the leading strand. The lagging strand is primed and extended by primase–polymerase α (Pol α) and polymerase δ (Pol δ), respectively24. Damage on the lagging strand is readily bypassed due to the discontinuous nature of Okazaki fragment synthesis25,26. This is not the case for leading strand DNA lesions, which stall Pol ε while CMG continues to unwind DNA25,26,27. This CMG uncoupling exposes ssDNA that is rapidly coated by replication protein A (RPA)28. The notion that PRIMPOL may reprime leading strand synthesis was hypothesized at the time of its discovery2, and discussed in later work7,16,29, but there is no direct evidence for this idea.

Industry observers note that although repriming is a major RS response pathway and PRIMPOL is an attractive therapeutic target, key mechanistic aspects of repriming remain unclear. For example, although RPA recruits PRIMPOL to ssDNA30,31, it is unclear why PRIMPOL acts at stalled forks, but not on ssDNA generated by other processes (transcription, recombination). One study reported that high RPA concentrations inhibit PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA in vitro30, presumably because RPA fully coats ssDNA and prevents PRIMPOL’s access to the template. Another study found that RPA stimulated PRIMPOL’s activity on ssDNA long enough to accommodate the simultaneous binding of both proteins, that Pol ε can extend PRIMPOL’s primers in vitro and that RPA stimulates PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in synergy with Pol ε31. It remains unclear how repriming occurs in the nucleus, where RPA is abundant and rapidly coats exposed ssDNA. Although PRIMPOL is a known target of checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1)22, how the DNA damage checkpoint regulates repriming remains poorly understood. Finally, it is unclear how PRIMPOL is regulated to minimize mutagenic DNA synthesis during repriming.

Recent findings suggest that to address these questions, we used single-molecule imaging to directly visualize PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in Xenopus egg extracts. We found that PRIMPOL preferentially binds near stalled forks, suggesting that it interacts with fork-associated proteins. We identified an interaction between PRIMPOL and CMG that is required for targeting PRIMPOL to stalled forks and for efficient fork restart in nuclear extract and in human cells. Our data indicate that the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction facilitates primer handover from PRIMPOL to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, therefore minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis. Finally, in conditions that mimic PRIMPOL overexpression, we found that PRIMPOL can reprime DNA synthesis far from the replicative helicase, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our findings support a simple-yet-elegant mechanism that targets PRIMPOL’s activity specifically to stalled forks and suggest a strategy to inhibit repriming.

To investigate the mechanism of PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we used nuclear extract prepared from Xenopus laevis eggs32. This extract contains all soluble nuclear proteins, supports efficient DNA replication and recapitulates several RS response pathways33. We could not detect frog PRIMPOL in egg extract using mass spectrometry (MS) or western blotting (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Table 1). To reconstitute repriming, we supplemented nuclear extract with recombinant human PRIMPOL, which displayed robust enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d).

To visualize PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart in real-time, we adapted a single-molecule assay called kinetics of eukaryotic replication via molecular imaging and tracking (KERMIT)25,34. A biotinylated linear DNA template was double-tethered onto a streptavidin-coated coverslip in a microfluidic flow-cell (Fig. 1a). DNA was incubated with high-speed supernatant—an extract that supports origin licensing but not origin firing, mimicking G1 (ref. 32) (Fig. 1a). The flow-cell was washed with buffer to remove any soluble proteins while retaining DNA-bound MCM2–7. Licensed DNA was incubated with nucleoplasmic extract—an extract that supports origin firing, elongation and RS response, mimicking S phase32 (Fig. 1a). Replication was monitored in real-time using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy.

Sources indicate that a, The single-molecule imaging workflow. b, Kymograms showing CMG dynamics at unperturbed forks. GINS–LD655 (orange) tracks the CMG helicase, and FEN1–KikG (blue) serves as a nascent DNA marker. c, CMG dynamics in aphidicolin-treated extract. d, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract. e, CMG dynamics in Pol-α-depleted extract with 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows denote PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart events. f, Fork restart efficiency: the fraction of uncoupled CMGs that resumed fast translocation. Data are mean ± 95% confidence interval (CI) estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of forks. g, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in undepleted extract. The yellow arrows indicate fork stalling at the lesion. h, CMG speeds measured in different experiments. The blue lines indicate medians, shaded areas represent 95% CI estimated by bootstrapping. n values denote the number of CMG molecules. Ctrl, control. i, CMG dynamics at DNA lesions in extract + 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL. The white arrows indicate PRIMPOL-mediated restart events. The experiments shown in b–h were repeated twice with different extract preparations. j, Autoradiogram of plasmid replication assay in mock-depleted (i) versus Pol-α-depleted extract + buffer (ii), +3 nM WT PRIMPOL (iii), +10 nM WT PRIMPOL (iv), +30 nM WT PRIMPOL (v), +30 nM PRIMPOL(AxA) (vi) or +30 nM PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (vii). The cartoons illustrate replication intermediates corresponding to bands on the gel (blue indicates nascent DNA). k, Quantification of the plasmid replication assay shown in j from three independent repeats. Total DNA synthesis (dark grey) or supercoiled DNA (light grey) signal was measured at 90 min and normalized to the total signal of the 30 nM WT PRIMPOL reaction. Data are mean ± s.d. from three independent experiments. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (f and h) and two-tailed two-sided Student’s t-tests (k); NS, not significant (P > 0.05); *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001.

In a recent development, to visualize CMG, we used GINS-depleted extract supplemented with fluorescently labelled GINS (GINS–LD655). To monitor DNA synthesis, we supplemented extract with FEN1–KikG (flap endonuclease 1 fused to the fluorescent protein KikG)35. FEN1 is recruited to chromatin through its interaction with PCNA36, and was previously validated as a marker of nascent DNA37, which does not require FEN1’s enzymatic activity37.

In a recent development, in mock-depleted extract, origin firing generated two diverging CMGs travelling at around 300 nucleotides per min with FEN1–KikG signal accumulating behind each helicase (Fig. 1b). To induce RS, the extract was supplemented with 15 µM aphidicolin (APH)—an inhibitor of B-family polymerases (including α, ε and δ) that does not inhibit PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In APH-treated extract, CMG travelled around 10× slower than in mock without any accompanying FEN1–KikG signal, indicating a failure to synthesize DNA (Fig. 1c). This substantial CMG slowing during RS (reported by us25 and others38) is a hallmark of CMG uncoupling28 (Fig. 1b,c). Adding 30 nM of wild-type (WT) PRIMPOL to APH-treated extract did not support fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1e), reflecting the fact that APH inhibits Pol ε and δ and prevents them from extending PRIMPOL’s primers.

Recent findings suggest that to recapitulate RS without inhibiting Pol ε/δ, we devised two independent strategies. First, we immunodepleted Pol α from nuclear extract (depleting or inhibiting Pol α was previously used to induce RS in cells22,39,40,41). In Pol-α-depleted extract, CMGs travelled very slowly (around 30 nucleotides per min) without any accompanying FEN1 accumulation (Fig. 1d). This is indicative of helicase uncoupling and is consistent with reports that Pol α is required for establishing leading strand synthesis42,43. When Pol-α-depleted extract was supplemented with recombinant WT PRIMPOL, we routinely observed that slow/uncoupled CMGs suddenly sped up to around 300 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1e (white arrows)). We interpret this switch to fast CMG progression as fork restart. Around 75% of stalled forks restarted in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 30 nM WT PRIMPOL, versus only around 5% restart efficiency in reactions supplemented with buffer (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Importantly, the sudden switch from slow to fast CMG progression was accompanied by FEN1–KikG accumulation behind the fork, indicative of DNA synthesis (Fig. 1e). To corroborate the idea that fast CMG progression corresponds to DNA synthesis, we repeated these experiments with fluorescently labelled PCNA (PCNA–LD655)—an established marker of nascent DNA44,45. Like FEN1–KikG, PCNA–LD655 accumulated behind restarted forks (Extended Data Fig. 1g). Disrupting FEN1’s interaction with PCNA eliminated FEN1–KikG binding (Extended Data Fig. 1h) without impacting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1i). We conclude that FEN1–KikG is recruited to nascent DNA by PCNA, and that the sudden speed-up of CMG represents fork restart. We subsequently used FEN1–KikG as a DNA synthesis marker because it provided better signal-to-noise than PCNA–LD655 (Methods).

Second, we designed a DNA substrate with site-specific DNA lesions on the leading strand template, each consisting of a small (around 4 amino acids) peptide adduct (Extended Data Fig. 2a). This lesion should easily fit through CMG’s central channel46, and should induce helicase uncoupling. After encountering the lesion, CMG instantly slowed down from around 300 nucleotides per min to 30 nucleotides per min (Fig. 1g,h), indicative of uncoupling. In the absence of PRIMPOL, forks stalled at the lesion restarted very inefficiently (around 7%) (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 1f), probably through TLS as shown previously47,48. In extract containing 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL, around 50% of forks stalled at the lesion restarted (Fig. 1i,f), causing CMG to speed up from around 30 nucleotides per min to 300 nucleotides per min—matching the speed of unperturbed forks (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 2b). Importantly, lesion-stalled forks restarted in a PRIMPOL-dependent manner in extract containing endogenous levels of Pol α.

We conclude that recombinant human WT PRIMPOL supports robust fork restart in our single-molecule assay using two orthogonal sources of RS (Fig. 1f). We subsequently used the Pol α depletion method because it provided a higher throughput, and was easily adapted for ensemble assays (see below).

To establish an ensemble assay for PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we replicated a 3 kb plasmid in Pol-α-depleted extract, which strongly suppressed DNA synthesis in comparison to the mock-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (compare i and ii)). The low levels of DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (ii)) are probably caused by trace amounts of Pol α that evaded the immunodepletion (Extended Data Fig. 2c).

Recent findings suggest that supplementing Pol-α-depleted extract with 3–30 nM of WT PRIMPOL led to a significant increase in DNA synthesis, in a PRIMPOL-concentration-dependent manner (Fig. 1j,k). As human cells contain around 17 nM of PRIMPOL49, the concentrations used here are near physiological. Notably, 30 nM of WT PRIMPOL did not fully rescue DNA synthesis (Fig. 1j (v versus i)). We attribute this to the fact that depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint (Extended Data Fig. 2c), which partially inhibits origin firing and results in fewer forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 blot)). We revisit CHK1’s role in Fig. 4.

Recent findings suggest that to verify that PRIMPOL is responsible for the partial rescue of DNA synthesis in the biochemical assay, we tested two previously characterized mutants: (1) PRIMPOL D114A/E116A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(AxA)), which lacks primase and polymerase activity2,3; and (2) PRIMPOL D519R/F522A/D551R/I554A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)), which cannot interact with RPA30 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The in vitro primase–polymerase assay showed that PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) (but not PRIMPOL(AxA)) exhibits catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 1d). Chromatin fractionation experiments indicate that WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (but not PRIMPOL(ΔRPA)) are recruited to DNA in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 2d) and in APH-treated extract (Extended Data Fig. 2e). In contrast to WT PRIMPOL, neither PRIMPOL(AxA) nor PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) rescued DNA synthesis in Pol-α-depleted extract (Fig. 1j (v–vii)), corroborating reports that repriming requires both PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity1,4 and its interaction with RPA30,31. These data indicate that Pol-α-depleted extract recapitulates PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, providing a powerful model system to dissect the molecular mechanism of repriming.

Recent findings suggest that it was previously proposed that RPA recruits PRIMPOL to stalled forks4,30. As uncoupled CMGs generate long tracts of RPA-coated ssDNA, it remained unclear where exactly PRIMPOL binds along ssDNA. To address this question, we visualized AlexaFluor647-labelled WT PRIMPOL (PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647) in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with FEN1–KikG, and RPA fused to mCherry-XL50,51 (hereafter, RPA–mCherryXL) (Extended Data Fig. 3a). This enabled us to simultaneously monitor PRIMPOL binding and dissociation, DNA synthesis and the extent of RPA–ssDNA. Importantly, fluorescent labelling did not impair PRIMPOL’s fork restart activity (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c).

At 30 nM of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647, there were too many PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA, making it impossible to resolve individual molecules (Extended Data Fig. 3d). To distinguish each PRIMPOL binding event, we visualized 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 at 15 s per frame (Fig. 2a). Initially, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew bidirectionally very slowly (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3e)—consistent with uncoupled helicases (Fig. 1h). After PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart, RPA–ssDNA tracts grew rapidly, but the RPA signal intensity decreased around twofold (Fig. 2a (bottom)). This suggests that PRIMPOL reprimes synthesis only on one strand (the leading strand, as shown in Fig. 4).

For clarity, the RPA kymogram is shown separately from FEN1 + PRIMPOL. The grey lines mark the boundary of the RPA signal: the dotted lines denote uncoupled CMGs and the dashed lines mark restarted forks. The white arrows indicate fork restart. Data in a–f are from experiments imaged at 15 s per frame. g, Kymograms showing fork restart in Pol-α-depleted extract with 3 nM PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 (magenta) imaged at 3 s per frame. h, Cumulative probability plot of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding event duration in Pol-α-depleted extract imaged at 3 s per frame (at this temporal resolution, short-lived events dominate both fork-distal and fork-proximal subpopulations). n values denote the number of binding events analysed. P values were computed using two-sample two-sided Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests (c–f and h); ***P < 0.001. All experiments were performed twice, with different extract preparations.

It has been revealed that we detected numerous short-lived PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding events far from replication forks (Fig. 2a (orange triangles)), which we call fork-distal. Most fork-distal PRIMPOL binding events (~84%) lasted one frame (15 s) or less (Fig. 2c) and were randomly distributed along RPA–ssDNA. We also detected fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events close to the fork (within 1 pixel = 160 nm), which tended to be longer than fork-distal binding events (Fig. 2c). Notably, long-lived fork-proximal PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 binding (Fig. 2a,b (curly brackets)) preceded most (~70 ± 10%) fork restart events (Fig. 2a,b (white arrows)).

To gain further insights, we quantified the frequency of fork-proximal (Fig. 2d) and fork-distal (Fig. 2e) binding events in Pol-α-depleted extract supplemented with 3 nM of fluorescently labelled WT PRIMPOL, PRIMPOL(AxA) or PRIMPOL(ΔRPA). As expected, PRIMPOL(ΔRPA) exhibited very little fork-proximal or fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, indistinguishable from the negative control, for which we measured the frequency of non-specific binding using free AF647 dye (Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Both WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited high levels of fork-proximal and fork-distal binding in Pol-α-depleted extract, consistent with chromatin fractionation experiments (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). Notably, PRIMPOL(AxA) exhibited the most fork-proximal binding (Fig. 2d), probably because it can repeatedly bind to stalled forks without restarting them (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, WT PRIMPOL promotes fork restart, after which it no longer binds to the unstressed fork (the mock-depleted control is shown in Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3h). Notably, there was no statistical difference between binding event durations for WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(AxA) (Fig. 2f), even though only WT PRIMPOL supported fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 2i).

We also observed long-lived fork-proximal WT PRIMPOL binding events before fork restart on the template with a site-specific lesion (Extended Data Fig. 3j). These productive WT PRIMPOL binding events lasted around 3 min, similar to those measured in Pol-α-depleted extract (Extended Data Fig. 3j). Notably, there was a delay of 3–5 min between the dissociation of PRIMPOL(WT)–AF647 from the fork, and fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 3j). This delay probably reflects the time needed for a replicative polymerase to capture the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL, and for the reassembly of an active replisome.

Occasionally, we observed PRIMPOL binding in consecutive movie frames at nearby positions on DNA (Fig. 2b (light blue ovals)). This could represent a PRIMPOL molecule diffusing along ssDNA, or may represent different molecules binding at slightly different positions along ssDNA. To distinguish between these scenarios, we repeated the experiment at 3 s per frame (Fig. 2g, five times faster than in Fig. 2a–f). At this higher frame rate, we frequently observed different PRIMPOL molecules briefly binding to ssDNA in non-consecutive video frames (Fig. 2g (white ovals)). Such binding sequences could be misinterpreted as diffusion of a single PRIMPOL molecule if imaged at lower framerates. This experiment also revealed that the vast majority of PRIMPOL binding events are very short-lived, lasting 3 s or less (Fig. 2h). We still observed long-lived fork-proximal binding events that preceded fork restart (Fig. 2g (white curly brackets)). In summary, although we cannot rule out PRIMPOL diffusion across short distances, our data argue against long-range PRIMPOL diffusion on ssDNA.

Recent findings suggest that although PRIMPOL can transiently bind anywhere along ssDNA–RPA (Fig. 2a,b), the vast majority (over 99%) of binding events are non-productive—that is, they do not lead to fork restart. Productive PRIMPOL binding events occur predominantly near stalled forks and tend to be long-lived (~3 min; Extended Data Fig. 3j), raising the question of why fork-proximal binding events are longer. We hypothesized that PRIMPOL’s binding at the fork may be stabilized by yet unknown interactions with fork-associated proteins. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that several replisome subunits may interact with PRIMPOL52. By cross-referencing AlphaFold predictions for human and frog proteins, we singled out PRIMPOL’s putative interaction with MCM4—a CMG subunit (Fig. 3a). Positively charged residues in human PRIMPOL (Arg29, Arg31, Lys34) are predicted to form salt bridges with MCM4 residues (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To test this prediction, we generated three mutants: PRIMPOL R29A/R31A/K34A (hereafter, PRIMPOL(3A)), PRIMPOL R29D/R31E/K34D (hereafter, PRIMPOL(DED)) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) (in which residues 29–35 were replaced with the linker GGGSGGGS) (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

First, we measured the duration of fork-proximal PRIMPOL binding events in APH-treated extract. APH does not alter the duration of PRIMPOL-binding events (Fig. 2c) but allows PRIMPOL to repeatedly bind without promoting fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 4e). All three PRIMPOL mutants exhibited significantly reduced fork-proximal binding times compared with WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 3c), suggesting that disrupting the predicted PRIMPOL–MCM4 impairs PRIMPOL recruitment to stalled forks.

In a recent development, second, we co-immunoprecipitated MCM2–7 from extract using PRIMPOL residues 1–60 as bait. We compared the WT bait versus the 3A, DED and 29-35:linker mutants (Extended Data Fig. 4f). All three mutant bait proteins co-immunoprecipitated with MCM2–7 less efficiently than the WT PRIMPOL(1–60) bait (Fig. 3d,e), corroborating AlphaFold’s prediction.

Sources indicate that third, we examined whether the three full-length PRIMPOL mutants can reprime stalled forks in Pol-α-depleted extract. PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants exhibited significant defects in DNA synthesis while PRIMPOL(3A) indicated a more subtle defect (Fig. 3f,g). Notably, all three mutants exhibited similar enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), consistent with the fact that residues 29–35 are in a disordered region distant from the catalytic core. Notably, AlphaFold3 predicted that PRIMPOL may also interact with MCM753, which is located next to MCM4 within CMG (Extended Data Fig. 4b). These additional interactions with MCM7 may explain the modest defect of PRIMPOL(3A) in the biochemical fork restart assay (Fig. 3f,g). To disrupt PRIMPOL’s interaction with both MCM4 and MCM7, we prepared the mutant PRIMPOL K8E/E13R/R15E/R29D/R31E/K34D (PRIMPOL(EREDED)). Unfortunately, PRIMPOL(EREDED) exhibited diminished enzymatic activity in vitro (Extended Data Fig. 4d), so we did not investigate it further.

Finally, we examined whether the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction is key for fork restart in human cells, using an established DNA fibre assay1 (Fig. 3h). Plasmids encoding WT or mutant PRIMPOL were transiently transfected into PRIMPOL-deficient HCT116 cells. Both PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(3A) mutants were expressed at levels similar to WT PRIMPOL, while PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) was expressed at lower levels that were similar to endogenous PRIMPOL (Extended Data Fig. 4g). To measure the fork-restart efficiency, ongoing forks were pulse-labelled with 5-chloro-2′-deoxyuridine (CldU) for 20 min and cells were irradiated with UV-C light (30 J m−2) to arrest fork progression. Cells were allowed to recover for 30 min and were pulse-labelled with 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine (IdU) for 20 min to label only forks that restarted (Fig. 3h). DNA fibre analysis revealed that the PRIMPOL(DED) and PRIMPOL(29–35:Linker) mutants significantly impaired fork restart compared with the WT control (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 4h). While the PRIMPOL(3A) mutant also impaired fork restart, it exhibited more variability between experimental repeats, rendering the difference between WT PRIMPOL and PRIMPOL(3A) not statistically significant (Fig. 3i). The findings presented in Fig. 3 indicate that the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction helps target PRIMPOL to stalled forks, and is required for efficient fork restart.

Recent findings suggest that we found that WT PRIMPOL promotes efficient fork restart at concentrations as low as 3 nM (Fig. 2a,b). In the low PRIMPOL concentration regime, restart involves long-lived PRIMPOL binding to the fork through MCM4. Consequently, we refer to these events as CMG-dependent restart. Notably, at higher concentrations of WT PRIMPOL (>10 nM), we observed a distinct subpopulation of restart events that occurred far behind the fork (Fig. 4a (white asterisks)). The frequency of these fork-distal restart events increased proportionally to WT PRIMPOL concentration (Fig. 4b (grey bars)), indicating that they also represent repriming.

Sources indicate that we repeated experiments with PRIMPOL(DED) and observed a substantial decrease in CMG-dependent restarts (Fig. 4b (green bars)), but not in fork-distal restarts (Fig. 4b (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b). This suggests that the latter represent a distinct type of restart event, which we call CMG independent. Notably, the FEN1-labelled nascent DNA tracts grew significantly faster during CMG-independent restart (~700 nucleotides per min) than during CMG-dependent restart (~300 nucleotides per min) (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 5c), corroborating our hypothesis that CMG-dependent and CMG-independent restarts are mechanistically distinct (see below).

We conclude that PRIMPOL supports two distinct types of restart event: (1) CMG-dependent restart that requires the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction and is efficient at limiting PRIMPOL concentrations; and (2) CMG-independent restart that does not require the PRIMPOL–CMG interaction and becomes efficient only at high PRIMPOL concentrations that mimic overexpression15.

The PRIMPOL–CMG interaction raises the possibility that PRIMPOL’s primer could be handed directly to the leading strand polymerase Pol ε, which is physically tethered to CMG54,55,56 in a manner that should not prevent PRIMPOL from binding to MCM4 (Fig. 3a). If so, Pol ε could capture PRIMPOL’s primer and extend it to restart leading strand synthesis. Alternatively, PRIMPOL’s primer could be extended by Pol δ first, and then handed to Pol ε, reminiscent of how leading strand synthesis is established during replication initiation42,57.

To test these hypotheses, we performed experiments in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol δ, or in extract depleted of Pol α and Pol ε (Fig. 4d). Depleting Pol δ caused only a minor reduction in CMG-dependent fork restart efficiency, whereas depleting Pol ε ablated CMG-dependent restart events (Fig. 4d (green bars) and Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). Importantly, CMG-dependent fork restart was fully rescued by adding 100 nM (Pol ε concentration in human cells49) of recombinant Pol ε to Pol-ε-depleted extract (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 6d). These data support the hypothesis that CMG-dependent restart entails the primer handover from PRIMPOL to Pol ε, which subsequently performs long-range DNA synthesis.

It has been revealed that notably, depleting Pol δ (but not Pol ε) eliminated CMG-independent restart events (Fig. 4d (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 6a). Supplementing Pol-δ-depleted extract with 400 nM (Pol δ concentration in human cells)49 of recombinant Pol δ fully rescued CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). These findings suggest that CMG-independent restart entails the primer handover from PRIMPOL to Pol δ, which subsequently performs long-range DNA synthesis.

We conclude that PRIMPOL primarily acts as a leading-strand primase by synthesizing primers immediately behind CMG, and those primers are extended by Pol ε. However, at higher concentrations, PRIMPOL can also reprime DNA synthesis in a CMG-independent manner, and those primers are extended by Pol δ. Our observation that DNA synthesis proceeds faster during CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4c) may reflect the fact that this process does not require template unwinding, or may point to Pol δ being able to synthesize DNA faster than Pol ε.

It has been revealed that it was previously reported that CHK1 phosphorylates human PRIMPOL at Ser255, which promotes more repriming and RS tolerance in human cells22. The same study proposed that a disordered loop in human PRIMPOL (residues 201–260) autoinhibits repriming, but that Ser255 phosphorylation by CHK1 relieves this autoinhibition22. We examined whether CHK1 modulates PRIMPOL’s activity in our biochemical fork restart assay. We supplemented Pol-α-depleted extract with an ATR inhibitor (AZD6738) that blocked CHK1 phosphorylation (Extended Data Fig. 7a (lane iii versus iv)). Notably, inhibiting ATR in Pol-α-depleted extract enhanced the amount of PRIMPOL-dependent DNA synthesis (Extended Data Fig. 7b (v versus vi) and 7c). This indicates that checkpoint activation is not required for PRIMPOL to restart stalled forks. This finding also explains the low levels of DNA synthesis reported in Fig. 1j: depleting Pol α activates the DNA damage checkpoint, which suppresses origin firing, resulting in fewer replication forks (Extended Data Fig. 2d (CDC45 immunoblot)). Thus, although PRIMPOL can restart most stalled forks in Pol-α-depleted extract, the overall amount of DNA synthesis is expected to be lower than in the mock control (Fig. 1j (i versus v)).

Sources indicate that immunoblotting of phosphorylated CHK1 in Pol-α-depleted extract collected from the flow cell revealed that the checkpoint is not active in our single-molecule experiments. This is because the DNA template concentration in the flow-cell is very low (10−3−10−2 ng μl−1) while checkpoint activation requires at least around 1 ng μl−1 (ref. 58) of DNA template. The fact that we observe robust PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart in the single-molecule assay (Fig. 1f) in the absence of CHK1 activation (Extended Data Fig. 7a (flow-cell lane)) supports our conclusion that checkpoint activation is not required for repriming.

Sources indicate that given the report that CHK1 stimulates PRIMPOL activity in human cells22, we hypothesized that CHK1 may regulate another aspect of PRIMPOL’s function. To test this idea, we performed single-molecule fork restart experiments with four previously characterized PRIMPOL phospho-mutants22 (Extended Data Fig. 7d,e): phospho-dead PRIMPOL(S255A), phosphomimetic PRIMPOL(S255E) and PRIMPOL(S255D), and a mutant that phenocopies the phosphomimetic mutants—PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) (in which residues 201–260 were replaced by a flexible linker). At a near-physiological concentration (30 nM), all four mutants supported similar levels (80–90%) of CMG-dependent fork restart to WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 4e (green bars) and Extended Data Fig. 7f). However, the mutants supported different levels of CMG-independent restart (Fig. 4e (grey bars)): PRIMPOL WT and PRIMPOL(S255A) exhibited the lowest efficiency (~25%); PRIMPOL(S255E) and PRIMPOL(S255D) supported intermediate efficiency (~40%); while PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) displayed the highest efficiency (~70%).

We further examined PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) across a wide range of concentrations (Fig. 4f). At near-physiological concentrations (10 nM and 30 nM), PRIMPOL(Δ201–260) supported significantly more CMG-independent restart than WT PRIMPOL (Fig. 4f (grey bars) and Extended Data Fig. 7g). We conclude that CHK1 phosphorylation of Ser255 does not affect PRIMPOL’s primary mode of repriming (CMG dependent), but significantly enhances PRIMPOL’s secondary repriming mode (CMG independent). Consistent with our conclusion, the stimulatory effect of CHK1 phosphorylation on PRIMPOL’s activity was previously observed in cells treated with a Pol α inhibitor22—which exposes large tracts of ssDNA behind the fork, generating the ideal substrate for CMG-independent repriming.

In a recent development, our experiments revealed several mechanistic insights into PRIMPOL function, dynamics and regulation, supporting a upcoming model of PRIMPOL-mediated fork restart (Fig. 5). First, PRIMPOL can briefly bind anywhere along RPA–ssDNA (Fig. 5a–c), but such binding events are very short-lived (Fig. 5c) and rarely cause fork restart. Second, PRIMPOL can reside on RPA–ssDNA much longer near uncoupled CMGs (Fig. 5d–f), and such long-lived binding events frequently lead to fork restart. Third, the PRIMPOL–MCM4 interaction is required for efficient fork restart (Fig. 5e) in nuclear extract and in human cells. Finally, our data indicate that, at near-physiological concentrations, PRIMPOL primarily acts as a leading-strand primase, and that PRIMPOL’s primers are directly handed to Pol ε (Fig. 5f–h). Notably, PRIMPOL-driven restart can also occur far behind stalled forks (Fig. 5i–l), but only at high PRIMPOL concentrations (mimicking overexpression), or after ATR/CHK1 activation. It is tempting to speculate that chemotherapy-induced PRIMPOL overexpression observed in cancer cells14,15 may unlock this alternative CMG-independent restart mechanism. As PRIMPOL cannot prime on ssDNA fully coated with RPA30, CMG-independent repriming events may occur only when a RPA molecule transiently dissociates from ssDNA in PRIMPOL’s immediate vicinity (Fig. 5i,j). Notably, RPA can spontaneously dissociate from ssDNA in vitro59, albeit slowly (koff = 0.006 s−1).

a, During unperturbed replication, Pol ε and Pol δ synthesize the leading and lagging strands, respectively, minimizing the accumulation of RPA-coated ssDNA. b, During RS, CMG becomes uncoupled from DNA synthesis and continues to unwind DNA, generating RPA-coated ssDNA. c, PRIMPOL transiently binds to RPA far from CMG, but such fork-distal binding events are short-lived and rarely lead to repriming. d, PRIMPOL binds to RPA near CMG. e, PRIMPOL simultaneously interacts with both RPA and MCM4, which prolongs PRIMPOL’s residence at the stalled fork. f, Long-lived fork-proximal binding enables PRIMPOL to synthesize a short primer behind CMG. g, After PRIMPOL dissociates, Pol ε captures the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL. h, Pol ε elongates the primer and restarts leading-strand synthesis. i, At high PRIMPOL concentrations, there are many short-lived PRIMPOL binding events on RPA–ssDNA. j, Infrequent RPA dissociation generates exposed ssDNA near PRIMPOL. k, PRIMPOL synthesizes a primer far behind CMG. l, Pol δ captures the primer synthesized by PRIMPOL and elongates it, restarting DNA synthesis independently of CMG. b–h, (blue-shaded panels) CMG-dependent fork restart is efficient at low PRIMPOL concentrations and occurs independently of CHK1 signalling. i–l, (red-shaded panels) CMG-independent fork restart becomes more frequent at higher PRIMPOL concentrations (which mimic overexpression) and depends on CHK1 phosphorylation of PRIMPOL at Ser255.

We show that efficient repriming requires both PRIMPOL–RPA and PRIMPOL–MCM4 interactions. As RPA binds to PRIMPOL’s C terminus30 and MCM4 binds to PRIMPOL’s N terminus (Fig. 3), we propose that PRIMPOL simultaneously interacts with both RPA and MCM4 during repriming (Fig. 5e). This model provides simple-yet-elegant answers to three long-standing questions. First, PRIMPOL can interact with both RPA and MCM4 only behind uncoupled CMGs, explaining how PRIMPOL is targeted specifically to stalled forks (Fig. 5e). Second, the simultaneous interaction with both RPA and MCM4 positions PRIMPOL near CMG’s exit channel (Fig. 3a). This enables PRIMPOL to engage the leading-strand template before it is coated by RPA (Fig. 5f), explaining how repriming can occur in the nucleus where RPA is very abundant. Third, PRIMPOL’s binding to CMG facilitates rapid primer handover to Pol ε (Fig. 5g), minimizing error-prone DNA synthesis during repriming. It is unclear what causes PRIMPOL’s dissociation after primer synthesis but before fork restart (Fig. 2b). It is possible that PRIMPOL disengages RPA once the primer becomes too long (Fig. 5f), which could promote PRIMPOL’s dissociation from DNA. Alternatively, PRIMPOL may transiently dissociate from MCM4 while CMG recruits replication factors that prevent PRIMPOL from re-binding the helicase.

Notably, we observed a negligible amount of PRIMPOL binding to unperturbed forks (mock in Fig. 2d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3h). This could be because, during normal replication, there is no RPA-coated ssDNA immediately behind CMG (Fig. 5a). Alternatively, during unperturbed replication, PRIMPOL’s docking site on CMG may be sterically occluded by a replication elongation factor. For example, CTF18 binds to the C terminus of MCM7 (ref. 45) (next to MCM4), which may prevent PRIMPOL binding to CMG during replication elongation.

During the preparation of this manuscript, we became aware of a similar study60 from the Yeeles group (MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, UK), which reconstituted PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart using purified human proteins and obtained a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of the CMG–PRIMPOL complex that is highly similar to the AlphaFold prediction (personal communication).

In a recent development, there are a few notable similarities between PRIMPOL’s role in the nucleus and mitochondria. First, PRIMPOL interacts with the mitochondrial replicative helicase Twinkle61 and the ssDNA-binding protein mtSSB9, reminiscent of its interactions with CMG and RPA. Notably, PRIMPOL also interacts with the mitochondrial DNA polymerase γ61, but there is no evidence of PRIMPOL interacting with Pol ε/δ. Second, PRIMPOL is required to restart replication after mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) damage61, similar to its role in restarting forks in the nucleus. Notably, Twinkle can stimulate PRIMPOL’s enzymatic activity in vitro62, but it remains unclear how this regulates repriming in mitochondria. Third, PRIMPOL overexpression leads to increased levels of lagging strand priming during mtDNA replication, reminiscent of CMG-independent restart events observed by us at high PRIMPOL concentrations (Fig. 4b (grey bars)). The ability of PRIMPOL to restart DNA synthesis far behind CMG may reflect a vestigial or primordial role of PRIMPOL to prime mtDNA lagging strand synthesis. This activity is normally suppressed by ssDNA-binding proteins (RPA or mtSSB), but becomes possible after PRIMPOL overexpression. Notably, DNA damage checkpoint activation and the subsequent phosphorylation of PRIMPOL by CHK1 (ref. 22) further upregulate CMG-independent repriming (Fig. 4e,f).

Although PRIMPOL is regarded as an attractive therapeutic target17,63, currently there are no small-molecule PRIMPOL inhibitors. Our findings suggest an alternative strategy to inhibit repriming—namely, to prevent PRIMPOL binding to CMG. This could be accomplished using peptides or molecules that bind to PRIMPOL’s N terminus, which normally interacts with MCM4–CMG.

Testes from adult laboratory-bred male X. laevis frogs (Xenopus 1, 4293) were used to prepare sperm chromatin. All human cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination and consistently tested negative throughout the course of the study.

To prepare the PRIMPOL(S255E), PRIMPOL(S255D) and PRIMPOL(S255A) mutants, primers oJP022 (for S255E), oJP023 (for S255D) and oJP024 (for S255A) were ordered from IDT and PCR-amplified with oJP021 using pJP012 as the template. To prepare human mutant His6–Flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL1-60 variants (3A, DED and 29-35:Linker), the same cloning strategy described above was used, yielding plasmid pJP095, pJP085 and pJP097, respectively.

Previously published protocols were used to purify recombinant GINS25. FEN1–KikG, RPA–mCherry, RPA–mKikGR, human SNAP–PRIMPOL (WT and mutants) and X. laevis s6–PCNA were purified using the following protocols. Rosetta (DE3) pLysS cells overexpressing each protein were collected and the cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (500 mM NaCl, 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 30 mM imidazole, 10% glycerol, 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol and 1 mM PMSF). Cells were lysed by sonication, and the lysates were cleared by ultracentrifugation at 35,000 rpm for 1 h at 4 °C using the Beckman Type 70 Ti rotor. The cleared lysates were incubated with 0.5 ml of Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at 4 °C. Bound protein was eluted with elution buffer identical to the lysis buffer except containing 400 mM imidazole.

Recent findings suggest that for FEN1–KikG, the imidazole eluate was sufficiently pure and was therefore dialysed into storage buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) and 10% glycerol), flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C. s6–PCNA was further purified by FPLC using the HiTrap Heparin HP affinity column (Cytiva, 17040701), followed by a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 28990944). The Ni–NTA eluate containing 500 mM NaCl was diluted with buffer A (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 0.5 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT, and 10% glycerol) to a final salt concentration of 150 mM and loaded onto the heparin column. Bound proteins were eluted over a 150–750 mM KCl gradient using a mixture of buffer A and buffer B (buffer A supplemented with 1 M KCl). The fractions corresponding to the protein peak (typically eluting at ~30% buffer B, ~300 mM KCl) were collected and concentrated for subsequent size-exclusion chromatography. Heparin-purified proteins were further purified and buffer-exchanged into storage buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 1 mM DTT and 10% glycerol) by size-exclusion chromatography on the Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column. Peak fractions were pooled, concentrated (Amicon Ultra Centrifugal Filter, 3 kDa MWCO, Millipore, UFC800324), flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C. For other proteins, the Ni-NTA eluate was further purified by FPLC using a HiTrap Heparin HP affinity column (Cytiva, 17040701), followed by a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 28990944). The Ni–NTA eluate containing 500 mM NaCl was diluted with buffer A (20 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 0.5 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT and 10% glycerol) to a final salt concentration of 150 mM and loaded onto the heparin column. Bound proteins were eluted over a 150–750 mM KCl gradient using a mixture of buffer A and buffer B (buffer A supplemented with 1 M KCl). Fractions corresponding to the protein peak (typically eluting at ~30% buffer B, ~300 mM KCl) were collected and concentrated for subsequent size-exclusion chromatography. Heparin-purified proteins were further purified and buffer-exchanged into storage buffer (150 mM NaCl, 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 1 mM DTT and 10% glycerol) by size-exclusion chromatography on the Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column. The peak fractions were pooled, concentrated (Amicon Ultra Centrifugal Filter, 3 kDa MWCO, Millipore, UFC800324), flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C. For s6–PCNA, the HiTrap Q HP affinity column (Cytiva, 17115301) was used, followed by the Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 29091596) after fluorescent labelling. The buffer conditions were the same.

Industry observers note that flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL(1–60) proteins (WT and mutants) used for co-IP assays were purified exactly same as described above using the same buffers. The Ni-NTA eluate was further purified by FPLC using a HiTrap Heparin HP affinity column using the same procedure. The fractions corresponding to the Flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL(1–60) peak were collected and concentrated, flash-frozen and stored at −80 °C.

Sources indicate that full-length X. laevis Pol δ was purified as follows. A bacmid was generated by transforming DH10EMBacY cells with [pLDL158] pBiG_TwinStrep-HRV3C-S6-Pol δ, and the resulting bacmid was purified using the ZR BAC DNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, D4049). Baculovirus was amplified in three 72 h stages (P1, P2, P3) in Sf9 cells. We initially attempted to express Pol δ in Tni Cells; however, the POLD3 subunit was not recovered (presumably due to proteolysis). Instead, TwinStrep-HRV3C-S6-Pol δ was expressed in 2 l of Sf9 suspension culture by infection with 4 ml of P3 baculovirus for 65 h. Cells were collected, pelleted by centrifugation and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Cell pellets were thawed and resuspended in 200 ml of lysis buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT—bubbled with argon gas to remove dissolved oxygen) supplemented with 1× Pierce Protease Inhibitor EDTA-free (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A32965) and lysed by dounce homogenization. The lysates were cleared by ultracentrifugation at 35,000 rpm for 45 min at 4 °C in a Beckman Type 70 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter). Cleared lysates were incubated with 1 ml of Strep-Tactin XT 4 Flow resin (IBA Lifesciences, 2-5010-010) for 1 h at 4 °C. The resin was washed three times with 10 ml lysis buffer. The protein was eluted from the resin using 4 ml buffer N supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 HRV3C protease for 2 h at 4 °C on a rotator, and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. The eluent was thawed and then diluted with 2 ml of no-salt buffer (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) to reduce the NaCl concentration to 200 mM, and loaded onto the Mono Q 5/50 GL column (Cytiva, 17516601). The protein was eluted in 20 column volumes (CVs) from the MonoQ column with a linear gradient of 200 mM–1,000 mM NaCl and eluted around 350 mM NaCl. The peak fractions were pooled, spin-concentrated to about 0.5 ml using the Amicon Ultra-4-10K column (Merck Millipore, UFC801024) and loaded onto a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 gel-filtration column (Cytiva, 28-9909-44) equilibrated in 25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT and 150 mM NaCl. The peak fractions were pooled, spin-concentrated to about 4 µM using the Amicon Ultra-4-10K column (Merck Millipore, UFC801024), and frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Approximately 50 µg total protein was obtained from 2 l of Sf9 cells.

Industry observers note that full-length X. laevis Pol ε was purified as follows. A bacmid was generated by transforming DH10EMBacY cells with [pLDL158] pBiG_TwinStrep-HRV3C-S6-Pol ε, and the resulting bacmid was purified using the ZR BAC DNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, D4049). Baculovirus was amplified in three 72 h stages (P1, P2, P3) in Sf9 cells. TwinStrep-HRV3C-S6-Pol ε was expressed in 1 l of Tni suspension culture by infection with 2 ml of P3 baculovirus for 48 h. Cells were collected, pelleted by centrifugation and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Cell pellets were thawed and resuspended in 100 ml of buffer N (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT, bubbled with argon gas to remove dissolved oxygen) supplemented with 1× Pierce Protease Inhibitor EDTA-free (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A32965) and lysed by dounce homogenization. The protein was eluted from the resin using 4 ml buffer N supplemented with 50 μg ml−1 HRV3C protease for 2 h at 4 °C on a rotator, and flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Eluent was thawed and diluted with buffer A (25 mM HEPES-NaOH pH 7.5, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) to reduce the NaCl concentration to 200 mM, and loaded onto the Mono Q 5/50 GL column (Cytiva, 17516601).
