Recent findings suggest that the denaturing purification of antigens was performed as follows. The Rosetta (DE3) pLysS cell pellet overexpressing His6-tagged antigen was thawed in denaturing lysis buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 30 mM imidazole, 6 M urea) and sonicated. The lysates were cleared by ultracentrifugation at 35,000 rpm for 1 h at room temperature in the Beckman Type 70 Ti rotor. The cleared lysates were then incubated with 0.5 ml of Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at room temperature. The protein was eluted with 400 mM imidazole in denaturing elution buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 6 M urea).

Custom polyclonal antibodies were generated as previously described34. Most home-made antibodies used in this study were raised by Cocalico Biologicals using a protocol approved by the Institute Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC-33724). Antibodies were affinity purified from sera in the lab, except for Xenopus PRIMPOL antibody 2 (amino acids 662–674; L3754/3755), which was raised and affinity-purified by Biosynth. All antibodies used in this study were affinity purified. In total, 1–5 mg of purified antigen was cross-linked to 1 ml of AminoLink Plus Coupling Resin (Thermo Fisher Scientific, PI20501) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Then, 10–30 ml of serum was incubated with the affinity resin for 30 min at room temperature. The resin was washed twice with 10 ml of 1× PBS + 500 mM NaCl, and twice again with 10 ml of 1× PBS. Next, antibodies bound to the affinity resin were eluted 5–6 times with 1.0 ml of 200 mM glycine-HCl pH 2.5. Each elution was collected into a tube containing 0.1 ml of 1 M Tris-HCl pH 9.0, which immediately neutralized the glycine. Eluted fractions were pooled and dialysed against 1 l of 1× PBS + 10% (w/v) sucrose. The IgG concentration was measured using the Thermo Fisher Scientific NanoDrop UltraC (Thermo Fisher Scientific), normalized to 1 mg ml−1 through dilution or spin-concentration, aliquots were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Human PRIMPOL monoclonal antibodies (mouse MAb 106E and rat MAb 71D), were raised in the Méndez laboratory and the CNIO monoclonal antibody facility13. All commercially available antibodies were validated by the manufacturers. Non-commercially available antibodies were generated and validated by the indicated laboratories. For example, antibodies used for western blotting were validated using the corresponding recombinant proteins as positive controls. Antibodies used for immunodepletion were validated by IP followed by western blot analysis of the supernatant and bead-bound fractions. The specificity of immunodepletion was further assessed by add-back of the corresponding recombinant protein to the immunodepleted extract. Detailed information on the antibodies used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 3.

Sources indicate that for ensemble DNA replication assays, 3 kb pBlueScript II SK(+) plasmid DNA was purified using the QIAprep Spin Miniprep Kit (Qiagen, 27106) and used as the replication templates. All single-molecule experiments used doubly tethered λ phage DNA, except for the experiments shown in Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 2d, which used DNA templates containing two site-specific leading strand lesions (small peptide adducts). The detailed protocol for the preparation of biotinylated λ DNA is described in our recent methods paper34. Preparation of DNA templates containing two site-specific leading strand lesions (DNA–protein cross-links, DPCs) has been described previously25. To generate small peptide adducts rather than bulky DPCs, DPC-containing DNA templates were treated with 1 µL of 120 U ml−1 thermolabile proteinase K (NEB, P8111) at room temperature for 15 min, followed by heat inactivation at 55 °C for 10 min before use.

It has been revealed that all single-molecule experiments were conducted according to a previously published protocol34 at temporal resolutions of 3, 15, 30 or 60 s per frame. During the λ DNA tethering step, 20 pM of Streptavidin–AF647 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, S21374) was added to the streptavidin solution. Streptavidin–AF647 spots were used as a fiducial marker for focusing immediately before starting imaging. After λ DNA tethering, DNA was licensed in undepleted high-speed supernatant (HSS) containing 26 ng µl−1 of 30 bp carrier oligonucleotide and ATP regeneration system (ARS) for 3 min. After licensing, DNA was washed with 1× ELB-sucrose, and a replication mix containing of 33% NPE, 33% HSS, 20 ng µl−1 pBlueScript carrier plasmid DNA, ARS, and unlabelled or fluorescently labelled proteins (typically, 20 nM GINS–LD655, 200 or 830 nM FEN1–KikG, 300 nM RPA–mCherry, 3–100 nM PRIMPOL or PRIMPOL–AF647, 100 nM Pol ε, 400 nM Pol δ and 300 nM PCNA–LD655) was flowed into the microfluidic chamber. When using Pol-α-depleted extract, 10 µM of CD437 was also added to the reaction mixture to suppress the activity of trace amounts of endogenous Pol α that evaded the immunodepletion (we used the ensemble plasmid replication assay to verify that this concentration of CD437 does not impair PRIMPOL’s activity).

The OpenCell database estimates that human cells contain around 17 nM of PRIMPOL49. However, a substantial portion of PRIMPOL is in mitochondria, and there are no reliable estimates of PRIMPOL’s concentration in the nucleus. Moreover, the exact concentration of nuclear PRIMPOL is likely to vary between cell types. For this reason, we sampled a wide range of PRIMPOL concentrations (3–100 nM), but we refer to concentrations of 10–30 nM as near-physiological based on OpenCell estimates.

It has been revealed that to visualize fluorescently labelled PCNA–LD655 during fork restart (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h), we immunodepleted >95% of endogenous PCNA from extract and supplemented this depleted extract with 500 nM of PCNA–LD655. We estimate that NPE and HSS contain ~30 µM and ~1 µM of PCNA, respectively, corresponding to ~10 µM PCNA in the final replication reaction (consisting of 33% NPE, 33% HSS and 33% buffer). After immunodepletion, around 300 nM of endogenous PCNA remained in the final reaction mixture (ensemble plasmid replication assay confirmed that this residual PCNA concentration was sufficient to support normal DNA replication). Supplementation with 300 nM PCNA–LD655 therefore resulted in an approximately 1:1 ratio of fluorescently labelled to endogenous PCNA in the experiments shown in Extended Data Fig. 1g,h. However, imaging fluorescently labelled PCNA in this system is technically challenging because PCNA is highly abundant in egg extracts and these experiments require simultaneous immunodepletion of Pol α (to induce RS) and PCNA (to reduce the concentration of endogenous/unlabelled PCNA). Without PCNA depletion, addition of 300 nM PCNA–LD655 to extracts containing ~10 µM endogenous PCNA in the final reaction would result in only a small fraction of the total PCNA being fluorescently labelled, substantially reducing the signal-to-noise ratio. For this reason, we used PCNA–LD655 imaging as an orthogonal validation of FEN1–KikG as a marker of nascent DNA rather than as the primary marker of DNA synthesis throughout this study.

GINS–LD655 was imaged using the following settings: total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) arm set to 9,000 (~67°), 1 s exposure, 10% 640 nm laser power (~150 µW power out of the objective, ~1.5 W cm−2 power density), 150 EM gain. PRIMPOL–AF647 was imaged using the following settings: TIRF arm set to 9,000 (~67°), 500 ms exposure, 25% 640 nm laser power (~380 µW power out of the objective, ~3.8 W cm−2 power density), 150 EM gain. FEN1–KikG was imaged using the following settings: TIRF arm set to 9,000 (~67°), 500 ms exposure, 8% 488 nm laser power (~70 µW power out of the objective, ~0.7 W cm−2 power density), 150 EM gain. RPAmCherry was imaged using the following settings: TIRF arm set to 9,000 (~67°), 1 s exposure, 10% 561 nm laser power (~70 µW power out of the objective, ~0.7 W cm−2 power density), 150 EM gain. PCNA–LD655 was imaged using the following settings: TIRF arm set to 9,000 (~67°), 1 s exposure, 20% 640 nm laser power (~300 µW power out of the objective, ~3.0 W cm−2 power density), 150 EM gain. Given these exposure durations, 4–10 fields of view (FOVs) could be sequentially imaged during the 15–60 s per frame. A suite of MATLAB scripts written in house was used to select and analyse data as described in our recent methods article34. Below we summarize the data analysis pipeline specific for the single-molecule experiments analysed in this study.

Ensemble DNA replication experiments were performed following a detailed protocol described in a recent methods article34. In brief, licensing mixtures contained mock- or Pol-α-depleted HSS, ARS, pBlueScript plasmid DNA and α-32P-dCTP. Replication reactions were initiated by addition of mock- or Pol-α-depleted NPE supplemented with ARS and PRIMPOL proteins (WT or mutants). We chose to use human PRIMPOL because: (1) PRIMPOL is highly conserved across vertebrates2; (2) we could easily interrogate mutants that were previously characterized in human PRIMPOL; and (3) human PRIMPOL expresses well in bacteria3. Reactions were quenched at the indicated timepoints by addition of 1× stop buffer (10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 1% SDS, 30 mM EDTA, 10% glycerol and 0.1% (w/v) bromophenol blue) containing proteinase K (1 mg ml−1 final concentration). The samples were analysed by 0.8% native agarose gel electrophoresis. After electrophoresis, gels were dried, exposed to a phosphor screen and analysed by phosphor imaging using the Azure Sapphire Gel Imaging System (Azure Biosystems).

According to recent reports, all of the samples were boiled in 1× SDS–PAGE sample buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 2% SDS, 10% glycerol and 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue) and run on 4–15% Mini-PROTEAN TGX Precast Protein Gels (Bio-Rad, 4561086) using Tris-glycine-SDS running buffer (Boston BioProducts BP-150). Colour Prestained Protein Standard Broad Range (NEB, P7719) was run alongside samples to infer protein band sizes. For Coomassie staining, protein gels were incubated with Optiblot Blue InstantBlue Coomassie Protein Stain (Abcam, ab119211) for at least 1 h at room temperature with gentle shaking. For immunoblotting, proteins were transferred from the gel onto a PVDF membrane (VWR, 10061-492) in transfer buffer (Boston BioProducts, BM190). Membranes were blocked in 1× PBST (1× PBS (Boston BioProducts, BM220), 0.05% Tween-20) containing 5% (w/v) non-fat milk for 1 h at room temperature with gentle shaking. After a wash in 1× PBST, the membrane was incubated with primary antibodies diluted in 1× PBST containing 1% (w/v) BSA overnight at 4 °C with gentle shaking. The membranes were washed three times with 1× PBST and incubated with secondary antibody diluted in 1× PBST + 5% non-fat milk for 1 h at room temperature with gentle shaking. For immunoblotting of Ser345-phosphorylated CHK1, 1× TBST (1× Tris-buffered saline (TBS) Boston BioProducts, BM301, 0.05% Tween-20 for immunoblotting) was used instead of PBST and the membrane was blocked in 1× TBST containing 10% (w/v) BSA. The membranes were washed three times with 1× PBST (or TBST), developed using SuperSignal West Pico PLUS Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, PI34577) and imaged using ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad).

Industry observers note that the in vitro PRIMPOL primase–polymerase assay was performed according to a previously published protocol68. In brief, a 5′-T36CCTGT20-3′ ssDNA was used as the template. The reactions were carried out in buffer containing 50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 1 mM MnCl2, 10 μM dNTP and SYBR Green I at a dilution of 1:20,000. Reaction mixtures contained 30 nM ssDNA template and PRIMPOL (WT and mutants) at concentrations ranging from 1 nM to 100 nM. Reactions were incubated in Corning 96-well plates (Corning, 3904) for 1 h at room temperature with moderate agitation. Fluorescence was measured using SpectraMax M2 Microplate Readers (Molecular Devices) with excitation at 497 nm and emission at 520 nm.

Industry observers note that for the chromatin fractionation assay, sperm chromatin was used at a final concentration of 1,000 sperm per µl in the reaction mixture. Sperm chromatin was licensed with mock- or Pol-α-depleted HSS (or undepleted HSS for experiments using APH as a source of RS) for 30 min at room temperature. Replication reactions were initiated by addition of mock- or Pol-α-depleted NPE (or DMSO- or APH-treated NPE for APH experiments) supplemented with recombinant PRIMPOL (WT or mutants), followed by incubation for 45 min at room temperature. The reactions were quenched by addition of ice-cold 1× ELB-sucrose (0.25 M) containing 0.2% Triton X-100 and immediately layered onto a 1× ELB-sucrose (0.5 M) cushion. The samples were centrifuged at 15,000g for 1 min at 4 °C to pellet chromatin. The supernatants were carefully aspirated, leaving 15 µl above the pellet. Chromatin pellets were washed twice with ice-cold 1× ELB-sucrose (0.25 M). After washing, chromatin pellets were resuspended in SDS loading buffer containing β-mercaptoethanol and boiled. Samples were resolved by SDS–PAGE, transferred to PVDF membranes and analysed by western blotting using the indicated primary antibodies.

It has been revealed that IP for MS analysis was performed using Protein A Dynabeads (Invitrogen, 10002D). Dynabeads were incubated with the indicated antibodies (mock control or Xenopus PRIMPOL antibodies 1 or 2) and washed with PBS containing 0.02% Tween-20 to remove unbound antibody. Clarified HSS extract was added to the antibody-bound beads and incubated for 1 h at room temperature with rotation to allow IP. After incubation, beads were washed with ELB-sucrose buffer containing 0.02% NP-40 and subsequently washed with PBS.

Sources indicate that samples were trypsin-digested on magnetic beads. The embedded proteins were exchanged into 200 μl of 100 mM triethyl ammonium bicarbonate and reduced with 500 mM of DTT, added to a final concentration of 10 mM. After incubation for 5 min at 55 °C, the beads were mixed head-over-head at room temperature for 25 min on the Barnstead Thermolyne Labquake rotisserie shaker. They were then alkylated with 1 M acrylamide (30 mM final concentration) at room temperature for 30 min. The reduced and alkylated proteins were digested overnight at 37 °C, using 500 ng of MS-grade trypsin/LysC mix (Promega). After digestion, the samples were quenched with formic acid (adjusted to a pH of around 3), eluted from the beads and desalted using the MonoSpin C18 Solid-Phase Extraction (SPE) columns (GL Sciences). Finally, the samples were dried in a SpeedVac SPD 130 DLX vacuum concentrator (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and exchanged into liquid chromatography (LC)–MS reconstitution buffer (2% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid in water) for instrumental analysis.

Industry observers note that proteolytically digested peptides were separated using an in-house pulled and packed reverse-phase analytical column (~25 cm length, 100 μm inner diameter), with Dr. Maisch 1.9 μm C18 beads as the stationary phase. Separation was performed with an 80 min reverse-phase gradient (2–45% B, followed by a high-B wash) on the Acquity M-Class UPLC system (Waters) at a flow rate of 300 nl min−1. Mobile phase A was 0.2% formic acid in water, while mobile phase B was 0.2% formic acid in acetonitrile. Ions were formed by electrospray ionization and analysed on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), operated in a data-dependent mode using HCD fragmentation.

Industry observers note that the .raw data were analysed using Byonic v.5.1.1 (Protein Metrics) to identify peptides and infer proteins. A concatenated FASTA file containing UniProt X. Laevis proteins, bait sequences and other likely contaminants and impurities was used to generate an in silico peptide library. Proteolysis with trypsin/LysC was assumed to be fully specific. The precursor and fragment ion tolerances were set to 12 ppm. Cysteine alkylated with propionamide was set as a fixed modification in the search. Variable modifications included oxidation on methionine, dioxidation on tryptophan, N-terminal acetylation, and cyclization of glutamine and glutamic acid. Proteins were held to a false-discovery rate of 1% using the standard reverse-decoy technique69.

It has been revealed that xenopus adult tissues were dissected on ice and washed thoroughly with ice-cold 1× PBS. Tissues collected from female animals included heart, liver, spleen and lung. Ice-cold RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitor was added at a ratio of 50 mg tissue per ml of lysis buffer. Tissues were finely minced using scissors and incubated at 4 °C for 1 h with vigorous vortexing every 10 min. After lysis, the samples were centrifuged at 16,000g for 20 min at 4 °C. The clarified supernatants were collected, and total protein concentrations were determined using a BCA assay. Equal amounts of protein were resolved by SDS–PAGE and analysed by western blotting using a Xenopus PRIMPOL antibody.

Labelling of purified human His6–SNAP–PRIMPOL was performed using SNAP-Surface Alexa Fluor 647 (NEB, S9136S). A 1.5-fold molar excess of dye relative to the protein was added and incubated overnight at 4 °C with gentle end-over-end rotation. The reaction mixture was aliquoted, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C. Labelled PRIMPOL was used directly in single-molecule assays without further purification.

Recent findings suggest that purified X. laevis His6–s6–PCNA was fluorescently labelled using in-house purified SFP synthase (surfactin phosphopantetheinyl transferase) and LD655–CoA (purchased from Lumidyne Technologies). S6–PCNA, SFP synthase and LD655–CoA were mixed at a molar ratio of 1:2:10 and incubated at room temperature for 1 h in reaction buffer containing 25 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 60 mM NaCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 10% glycerol. The reaction mixture was further purified using the FPLC-Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 29091596) to separate unreacted fluorophore and SFP from PCNA–LD655. The peak fractions containing PCNA–LD655 were pooled and concentrated.

Sources indicate that protein co-IP assays were performed using anti-Flag M2 Magnetic Beads (Millipore, M8823). Flag-tagged SNAP–hPRIMPOL(1–60) proteins (WT or mutants) were purified as described above and immobilized on Flag beads before incubation with Xenopus egg extracts. For each reaction, 3 µl of beads (binding capacity of around 20 pmol Flag peptide) was incubated with 200 pmol of Flag–SNAP–PRIMPOL(1–60) protein (tenfold molar excess relative to bead capacity). Xenopus egg extracts were prepared by mixing NPE and HSS at a 1:1 ratio and diluting fivefold in 1× ELB-sucrose buffer. Beads were then incubated with Xenopus extract for 1 h at room temperature with gentle rotation to allow co-IP of interacting proteins. After incubation, beads were washed with 1× ELB-sucrose containing 0.05% NP-40. Bound proteins were eluted by resuspending beads in SDS sample buffer and boiled at 98 °C for 5 min. Beads were pelleted by brief centrifugation, and only the supernatants were collected for analysis. Eluted proteins and input samples were resolved by SDS–PAGE and analysed by western blotting with the indicated antibodies.

To measure fork restart after replicative stress, cells were first pulsed with 50 μM 5-chloro-2′-deoxyuridine (CldU; Sigma-Aldrich, C6891) for 20 min, irradiated with UV-C (30 J m−2) and, after a 30 min recovery time, pulse-labelled with 250 μM 5-iodo-2′-deoxyuridine (IdU; Sigma-Aldrich, I7125) for 20 min. Cells were collected in ice-cold PBS, resuspended at 0.3 × 106 cells per ml and lysed on microscope slides with spreading buffer (0.2 M Tris pH 7.4, 50 mM EDTA, 0.5% SDS; 6 min at room temperature). DNA fibre spreads were prepared by tilting the slides 15° after cell lysis. The slides were air-dried and fixed in cold methanol:acetic acid (3:1) for 2 min, and incubated in 3 M HCl (30 min at room temperature) to denature DNA. CldU and IdU tracks were detected by immunofluorescence using anti-BrdU monoclonal antibodies with different specificity (rat monoclonal antibody, Abcam, ab6326, for CldU; BD Biosciences mouse monoclonal antibody, 347580, for IdU). The DNA fibre integrity was assessed using a mouse monoclonal anti-ssDNA antibody (DSHB, AB10805144); all incubations were for 1 h at room temperature in a humidity chamber. Standard secondary antibodies were used (anti-mouse IgG1 AF-488, Invitrogen, A21121; anti-rat IgG AF-594, Invitrogen, A11007; anti-mouse IgG2a AF-647, Invitrogen, A21241; all incubations were 30 min at room temperature). The slides were mounted with ProLong Gold antifade reagent (Invitrogen, P36930). Images were acquired on the DM6000B Leica microscope with an HCX PL APO ×40/0.75 NA objective and analysed with ImageJ. For functional complementation assays, HCT116 PRIMPOL-KO cells were transfected with pcDNA3.1/V5-PRIMPOL plasmids expressing the WT form or the indicated mutant derivative (DED, 3A and 29-35:Linker), using Lipofectamine 2000. n = 4 replicates (WT, PRIMPOL KO, PRIMPOL KO + WT) or n = 3 replicates (PRIMPOL KO + DED, PRIMPOL KO + 3A, PRIMPOL KO + 29-35:Linker). 500 replicative structures were counted in each condition and replicate.

Nikon Elements AR (v.5.20.02) was used to acquire raw microscopy data. ImageJ Fiji (v.2.1.0) was used to stabilize the raw microscopy videos and to quantify signals from autoradiographs and western blots. MATLAB (R2023b) and Origin (2023b) were used to analyse the data. All figures (including cartoons) were created and laid out in Microsoft PowerPoint for Mac (v.16.113.2).

In a recent development, details of the statistical analyses performed are indicated in the figure legends. As some quantities measured in this study did not have symmetric distributions, we reported the median of the distribution. Unless otherwise specified in the figure captions, error bars represent the 95% CIs for the median. This was calculated using MATLAB’s built in bootstrapping function. The exact meaning of the number ‘n’ reported in each figure is indicated in the figure captions, it usually refers to the number of the number of replication forks or the number of binding events. For single-molecule experiments, we typically used n ≈ 100 events to report. No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample size. No data blinding or randomization was used. P values were computed using the two-sample two-tailed Kolmogorov–Smirnov test function built into MATLAB, and all experiments were repeated at least twice, with independent extract preparations. For the ensemble DNA replication assay, co-IP assays and cell-based fibre assays, we carried out 3 or 4 independent replicates. P values were computed using the two-sample two-tailed Student t-test function built into MATLAB. The data presented in the Figures are derived from one of the replicates. The exact P values for all data presented in the Figures and the Extended Data Figures are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

In a recent development, each replication initiation experiment imaged 4–10 FOVs over the course of 60–90 min with a resolution of 15, 30 or 60 s per frame. Each FOV typically contained 50–200 DNA molecules stretched to 80–90% of their contour length. A suite of MATLAB scripts written in house were used to select and analyse data as described in our recent methods article70. Below we summarize the data analysis pipeline specific for the single-molecule experiments analysed in this study.

Industry observers note that regions of interest corresponding to individual DNA molecules were selected manually based on the previews of DNA stained with SYTOX Orange (these were acquired before the start of the experiment). Only well-separated DNA molecules were used in the analysis.

In a recent development, to measure fork speed before/after the PRIMPOL-dependent fork restart, we fit the GINS (Fig. 1) or RPA (Fig. 2 and Fig. 4) signals with a linear model (mock + buffer, mock + 10 µM APH, ∆Polα + buffer conditions), a bilinear model (∆Pol α + PRIMPOL, leading-strand DNA lesion + buffer) or a trilinear model (leading-strand DNA lesion + PRIMPOL) in MATLAB and extracted the slope of each linear fit (this has units of pixels per frame). To calculate the fork speed, we multiplied the slope of each linear fit segment to 160 nm per pixel (the size of our camera’s pixel), and divided it by 0.34 nm per bp (to convert nanometres into base pairs), and further divided it by 0.85 (to account for the fact that the DNA template is stretched to around 85% of its contour length).

In Fig. 4, PRIMPOL-mediated CMG-independent fork restart was monitored by FEN1–KikG signal. To measure the speed of DNA synthesis during CMG-independent restart, the raw FEN1 signal was automatically thresholded using OTSU’s method using a built-in MATLAB function. The OTSU threshold binary image was used to fit straight lines to the edges of the growing FEN1 signal, and the fork speed value was extracted from the slope of the line (accounting for pixel size, the time resolution of the experiment and the extent to which DNA was stretched). Note that the efficiency of CMG-dependent and CMG-independent restart can add up to more than 1. This is illustrated in Fig. 4a, which contains two replication forks: both forks restarted in a CMG-dependent manner (white arrows), and there were two additional CMG-independent restart events (white asterisks).

According to recent reports, to analyse the binding and dissociation (Δt1) of PRIMPOL–AF647, we used the generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) as described in our previously study71. Specifically, we used GLRT to convert single-molecule images into binary images, which were subsequently segmented into binding events. The GLRT algorithm accounts for the intrinsic properties of noise in each experiment—a sliding window (we used a five-pixel window) is used to determine whether the signal at any pixel represents noise or signal. Using GLRT, we determined the time of PRIMPOL binding and PRIMPOL dissociation (and therefore Δt1) before a fork-restart event. To calculate the time delay between PRIMPOL–AF647 dissociation and fork restart (Δt2), we first measured the time of PRIMPOL–AF647 dissociation (as described above for Δt1), and the time of fork restart. The time of fork restart was extracted from the bilinear fit to the edge of the RPA signal (Fig. 2a): fork restart corresponds to the changepoint when the fork suddenly speeds up.

To measure the location and duration of PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events, we used the GLRT method as described above. To determine whether any given PRIMPOL–AF647 binding event is fork-proximal or fork distal, we compared the position of the binding event along the DNA molecule with the position of the replication fork measured by fitting the fluorescent RPA tract (as illustrated in Fig. 2a). Any PRIMPOL–AF647 binding event within 1 pixel of the replication fork was classified as fork-proximal, and all other binding events were classified as fork-distal.

To quantify the frequency of fork-proximal binding events across different conditions (no RS and RS), or for different PRIMPOL constructs (WT, AxA mutant or RPA-interaction mutant), we measured (1) Nproximal, the number of fork-proximal PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events for each fork; and (2) Tfork, the total duration that we observed that replication fork. We divided Nproximal by Tfork to obtain the normalized quantity shown in Fig. 2d.

We chose a different normalization strategy for fork-distal PRIMPOL–AF647 binding events because they can occur anywhere along RPA-coated ssDNA. To this end, for each replication fork we measured (1) Ndistal, the number of fork-distal binding events; (2) LRPA–ssDNA, the extent of the RPA-coated ssDNA; and (3) Tfork, the total duration of time that the fork was monitored. We divided Ndistal by LRPA–ssDNA and Tfork to obtain the normalized quantity shown in Fig. 2e.

According to recent reports, (a) Diagram of single-molecule experiments with site-specific leading-strand DNA lesions. Top: a 30-kb DNA molecule containing DNA-Protein Crosslinks (DPCs) positioned ~10 kb away from each end was digested with ProteinaseK, leaving behind small (~4 aa) peptide adducts. If a replication origin fires in the middle of this DNA substrate, both replication forks will encounter the peptide adduct on the leading-strand template, resulting in CMG uncoupling. Bottom: a representative kymogram illustrating CMG uncoupling from both peptide adducts. This experiment was performed in extract supplemented with 30 nM PRIMPOLWT, which promoted fork restart at ~50% of uncoupled CMGs. Chelsea’s interest in Alex Scott remains despite Bournemouth transfer stance

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (372 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Readchelsea

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bournemouth’s determination to keep Alex Scott has done little to discourage Chelsea, who remain among the leading contenders to sign the England midfielder.
  • The Blues had a £64m bid rejected during the summer, but their interest has continued into the fresh season.
  • Bournemouth, however, have no intention of allowing Scott to leave in January.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bournemouth’s determination to keep Alex Scott has done little to discourage Chelsea, who remain among the leading contenders to sign the England midfielder.

The Blues had a £64m bid rejected during the summer, but their interest has continued into the fresh season. According to Matt Law of The Telegraph, Chelsea are at the front of the queue of clubs monitoring the 23-year-old.

Bournemouth, however, have no intention of allowing Scott to leave in January. talkSPORT reported this week that the south coast club remain determined to retain him, despite his reluctance to sign a contract extension.

Scott’s current deal runs until 2028, leaving Bournemouth with time to negotiate, although their position could become more complicated if no agreement is reached before next summer.

Industry observers note that the midfielder’s immediate priority is recovering from a thigh injury sustained while representing England. He impressed during the 7-0 Nations League victory over Croatia but was withdrawn after 70 minutes. Subsequent examinations revealed a quadriceps problem, with BBC Sport reporting that he could miss six to eight weeks.

Recent findings suggest that his absence is a setback for Bournemouth, who have relied heavily on the former Bristol City midfielder this season. It also introduces another consideration for clubs monitoring his progress ahead of the January window.

Industry observers note that chelsea are not alone in their admiration. Arsenal and Liverpool have also been linked with Scott, whose performances have attracted attention beyond the Premier League.

Suggestions circulating on social media that Bournemouth have already agreed to let him leave in January remain unsubstantiated. There has been no reliable confirmation of such an arrangement, and the club’s reported position is firmly against a winter sale.

For Chelsea, the more realistic opportunity may come next summer, particularly if Scott continues to resist signing a latest contract.

#2399. Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (587 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Claretandhugh ↗ Open Full Page

Championship data highlights exactly what West Ham’s midfield is still missing

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.
  • The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes.
  • The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fascinating piece of Championship analysis from Loft Insights on X may provide an uncomfortable reminder of where West Ham’s midfield falls short.

The graphic plots central midfielders based on two key metrics: line-breaking passes per 90 minutes and ball-winning actions per 90 minutes. Put simply, it measures which players are able to progress the ball through opposition lines while also contributing defensively.

The most interesting takeaway for me was not necessarily which players stand out, but where West Ham’s own midfield profiles sit on the chart.

The Championship’s elite midfielders increasingly occupy the top-right quadrant, combining progression and defensive intensity. That is why the chart identifies Norwich City’s Kenny McLean as one of the Championship’s most complete midfielders, posting outstanding line-breaking numbers while maintaining strong defensive output, despite only featuring for ten games out of fifteen due to an ankle injury.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Portsmouth’s Ebou Adams is highlighted as a “defensive monster”, producing exceptional ball-winning statistics while still offering significant progression. Sheffield United’s Kalvin Phillips (yes the same player that flopped on loan at West Ham!), Queens Park Rangers’ Jonathan Varane and Norwich’s Jacob Wright also occupy impressive positions, demonstrating the ability to impact both sides of the game.

Mohamadou Kanté is viewed as a dynamic ball-carrying midfielder with strong physical attributes, but his game is built more around energy and transition play than elite progression metrics. Arne Engels offers technical quality and creativity, yet is generally more comfortable operating higher up the pitch than acting as a defensive controller.

Recent findings suggest that the data is only based on players who have played an average of 540 mins so one omission is Tomas Souček, whose strengths have always been obvious. The Czech international on paper would arguably be the Championships most effective midfield goalscorer (3 in 7 appearances so far) and I’d expect him to feature highly for aerial presence. However, if plotted on a graph measuring line-breaking passes and ball-winning volume, he would likely owe more to his physicality and attacking threat than his ability to dictate possession through midfield.

That perhaps explains why West Ham can sometimes appear disconnected between defence and attack.

Sources indicate that too often there is a reliance on direct balls into attacking areas rather than building through the centre of the pitch. Equally, when possession is lost, the midfield does not always possess the combination of mobility and defensive output needed to regain control quickly.

West Ham arguably have midfielders who can create and win duels. What they appear to lack is a genuine “two-way” midfielder capable of consistently ranking highly in both categories.

Sources indicate that that was precisely what Declan Rice offered during his time at the club. His ability to recover possession and immediately progress the ball remains incredibly difficult to replace.

The reality is Rice was never truly replaced, although finding a like-for-like successor was always going to be a near-impossible task.

Sources indicate that former West Ham midfielder James Ward-Prowse’s position on the chart is also interesting. A casualty of Nuno’s reign, he ranks among the highest players for line-breaking passes but has one of the lowest ball-winning outputs. Ward-Prowse excels at progressing possession but offers relatively little defensive contribution compared to the league’s most complete midfielders.

Above all the data serves as a reminder that Koppen’s recruitment and Parker’s existing choices for midfield should focus less on individual statistics and more on complete profiles.

Because the numbers suggest that is where Championship matches are increasingly won.

Chelsea make early move for Palmeiras teenager Eduardo Conceicao

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chelsea have reportedly made contact with Palmeiras as they attempt to gain an early advantage in the race to sign Brazilian teenager Eduardo Conceicao.
  • The 16-year-old forward has attracted attention from several leading European clubs, but Chelsea are understood to be among the first to establish direct contact with Palmeiras over a potential future transfer.
  • According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, the London club have held a series of discussions as they seek to position themselves ahead of their rivals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea have reportedly made contact with Palmeiras as they attempt to gain an early advantage in the race to sign Brazilian teenager Eduardo Conceicao.

The 16-year-old forward has attracted attention from several leading European clubs, but Chelsea are understood to be among the first to establish direct contact with Palmeiras over a potential future transfer.

According to Mark Brus of CaughtOffside, the London club have held a series of discussions as they seek to position themselves ahead of their rivals.

Palmeiras are reportedly preparing for substantial offers, with some figures at the Brazilian club discussing a valuation as high as €100m (£85m).

That figure has not been established as a firm asking price, however, and Brus reports that industry sources expect the eventual cost to be lower. Chelsea’s previous investment of approximately £51m in Estevao is regarded as a possible benchmark.

Manchester City’s ownership group have also made contact regarding Conceicao, while Arsenal, Manchester United, Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain are among the clubs reported to have watched him.

Chelsea’s existing relationship with Palmeiras could help their efforts, although the level of competition means there is no guarantee that their early interest will lead to a deal.

The player’s age is another consideration. Conceicao cannot complete an international transfer to England until he turns 18, leaving interested clubs facing a potentially lengthy wait before he can join their squads.

Chelsea have already demonstrated their willingness to agree deals for young players well before they are eligible to arrive, with Estevao providing a particularly relevant example.

It has been revealed that no formal bid or agreement has been reported for Conceicao. Nevertheless, the latest claims suggest Chelsea are prepared to explore another long-term investment in Brazilian talent rather than wait until the player becomes available for an immediate move.

Why Bukayo Saka's England spot is suddenly under threat: Clocking up the miles has made Arsenal star a fitness concern - while his rival Morgan Rogers is hitting top gear: CRAIG HOPE

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 08:57 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:21 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Five seasons ago, Bukayo Saka clocked up 3,000 Premier League minutes for Arsenal.
  • It has been revealed that in the same week that Rogers, a Manchester City junior, made his only league start during an unhappy loan season on the south coast - in a goalless draw at Peterborough - Saka was scoring in a 3-1 win in the North London derby.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CRAIG HOPE, CHIEF FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 08:57 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:21 EST, 14 November 2026.

Five seasons ago, Bukayo Saka clocked up 3,000 Premier League minutes for Arsenal. Morgan Rogers appeared in just 217 for Bournemouth, then of the Championship. The pair are the same school age. Yet, back then, one was a young man at the very top of the game, the other was a boy wondering where, and how, he would ever get a game.

It has been revealed that in the same week that Rogers, a Manchester City junior, made his only league start during an unhappy loan season on the south coast - in a goalless draw at Peterborough - Saka was scoring in a 3-1 win in the North London derby. They were on very different flight paths.

According to recent reports, today, the ascent of Rogers compares with, dare we say it, the gradual descent of Saka. His supporters will contest that trajectory. They can point to his two goals for England in Croatia last month, his hat-trick in the 6-4 World Cup bronze-medal victory over France and, of course, his Premier League winner’s medal. Their argument has merit, as does any that defends a player of such talent.

Industry observers note that except, this is not about ability. It is about durability. It is about mileage and the fear that, at 25 years old, a near 400 career games are weighing heavy. Rogers, quite remarkably, has played 10,000 fewer Premier League minutes. He is, to borrow horse-racing parlance, unexposed and open to improvement.

Industry observers note that until three years ago, this was Saka. He started 87 consecutive Premier League games for Arsenal, a club record, and was getting better season on season - seven, 12, 15 and 20 were his goals tallies from 2021 to 2024. He was both the present and future of the England team.

Bukayo Saka's starting spot in the England XI is now under serious threat ahead of Euro 2028.

England are flourishing with Chelsea's Morgan Rogers (right) occupying the right-hand side.

According to recent reports, and yet now, increasingly among those who obverse and are close to the England camp - including, you suspect, Thomas Tuchel - there is a feeling of Saka’s presumed starting jersey being under serious threat. In fact, you wonder if the threat has already passed. Does the position on the right of England’s forward line, with a view to Euro 2028, now belong to Rogers?

Sources indicate that this, it should be mentioned, is as much about the exceptional development of Rogers, who will again start on the right here in Spain on Sunday night. But there is another, more uncomfortable possibility, and that is of Saka’s very best days belonging to those North London derbies of yesterday, not tomorrow. He is currently injured with a thigh strain and faces several more weeks on the sidelines.

I was in the room with Tuchel at the World Cup pre-camp in Florida when he revealed, to some surprise, ’Bukayo is just not there yet. Some things are missing’. We had assumed Saka was fit after arranging private sessions in the wake of the Champions League final. The head coach, however, said it would be ‘very unlikely’ that Saka, nursing Achilles discomfort, would be able to start and finish all of England’s matches, and so it proved. He did not start and finish any before the France kick-about, a match that should have been played at Miami Beach, not Miami Stadium.

In a recent development, in the days prior to the semi-final against Argentina, Saka told Tuchel and medical staff he was ready to start. Tuchel went with Rogers on the right and Saka was an unused substitute. After his treble three days later, Saka spoke of his frustration with his playing time in North America.

Throughout the tournament, Tuchel rejected the idea of the Arsenal man being ‘the saviour’, as it was put to him by one colleague following the group-stage goalless draw with Ghana.

According to recent reports, ‘I’m not engaging in that,’ he told us. ‘It’s not like Bukayo comes back and everything is solved.’.

And Tuchel was right. Saka did a lot of good - three assists in the tournament proper - but it felt like he was existing in moments, much like at Euro 2024. Gone was that whiplash speed taking him through defensive lines, the drag and dribble that defenders knew was coming but could do little about. Club-mate Noni Madueke had that explosion, just not Saka’s end product. Combine the two and we had a player. It was why, come the semis, Tuchel went with Rogers.

Recurring injuries and setbacks have plagued the Arsenal winger over the past few seasons.

He was once viewed as England's present and future - but has suffered from a gradual decline.

In a recent development, to revisit our Daily Mail Sport tournament ratings, in which Saka scored 6/10, we recorded: ‘Fitness complications should offer some context, but this was a version of Saka unrecognisable from the player we thought was up there with Kane and Bellingham when it came to being a game-changer. He did provide three assists, including a lovely cross for the opener in Mexico, but never appeared to fully trust his body. Has a bit to prove when back to full fitness.’.

Will he ever, though, regain a consistent level of fitness, strength and sharpness that allows him to impact - again, consistently - like he once did? Just last week, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta admitted the club were struggling to identify the underlying reason for injuries which total double figures in three years.

‘We have openly discussed a lot of things with him to understand what could possibly have gone wrong,’ stated Arteta. ‘But the reality probably is that unfortunately we don’t know.’.

According to recent reports, saka, to return to horse racing, has the form in the book, but that is the concern. There is, perhaps, too much form at too young an age, especially when coupled with a game reliant on acceleration and intensity.

Rogers himself still has a lot to prove, not least because of his £117million transfer from Aston Villa to Chelsea in the summer. With that, though, he has grown. That much was evident by him taking centre stage against Croatia on Thursday night despite the presence of Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham. Previously, you suspected Rogers was waiting for the leading men to hand him his script.

According to recent reports, his tendency to come infield will suit Tuchel, too. Kane the quarterback, as we saw at Wembley, leaves a space to populate and exploit. Rogers had more touches in the penalty area than any other player, including the one for his opening goal. And if Anthony Gordon, on the opposite flank, is the one with chalk on his boots, Rogers muddying his in the goalmouth is what the team needs.

Meanwhile, Rogers has hit top gear at Chelsea and become a key man under Thomas Tuchel.

In a recent development, this debate, Saka versus Rogers, is not one that should keep Tuchel awake at night. It is a nice problem to have - the hope that Saka will return to his best, the expectation that Rogers is still to realise his.

On Sunday, at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid, Rogers has another opportunity to further his claims. He has come a long way since a drab Wednesday night at Peterborough’s London Road in 2021. It is, though, the distance yet travelled that is most exciting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal’s controversial penalty claim against Hull City has raised newly introduced questions about how the offside rule is interpreted in football.
  • Former Premier League official Dermot Gallagher believes that whilst he understands why the officials made the decision, the result would have been different under the current rules.
  • Speaking on Ref Watch on Sky Sports, Gallagher said that the holding should have been the main focus of the incident involving Kai Havertz and Hull defender Nobel Mendy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal’s controversial penalty claim against Hull City has raised newly introduced questions about how the offside rule is interpreted in football.

Former Premier League official Dermot Gallagher believes that whilst he understands why the officials made the decision, the result would have been different under the current rules.

Speaking on Ref Watch on Sky Sports, Gallagher said that the holding should have been the main focus of the incident involving Kai Havertz and Hull defender Nobel Mendy.

In a recent development, his comments have increased criticism of referee Farai Hallam and VAR official Michael Oliver. However, Gallagher also feels that the language used in the laws needs to be addressed to avoid this glitch in the future.

The incident happened shortly before half-time during Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Hull at the Emirates Stadium.

Mendy pulled Havertz’s shirt inside the penalty area, prompting VAR to recommend an on-field review. Hallam subsequently confirmed that the Hull defender had committed a holding offence.

However, he ruled that Havertz was in an offside position and awarded Hull a free-kick.

Gallagher believes that was incorrect under the laws of the game. He explained that being in an offside position does not automatically constitute an offence.

Sources indicate that the player must be involved in play before the referee can give a penalty. In this instance, Havertz had not tried to play the ball or challenge an opponent before being pulled back by Mendy.

This means that the player was held first, so a penalty should have been given to Arsenal.

Gallagher said that the AR had first raised their flag for offside. He said that it was a great process with VAR, but the initial decision could have affected the outcome.

He recognised why the decision was made even though he felt Arsenal should have been awarded the penalty.

In terms of common sense, he remarked it does not look right to award the penalty, as Havertz was in an offside position and couldn’t legally contest for the ball.

Recent findings suggest that but he emphasised that the officials must strictly enforce the laws of the game. Gallagher thinks there is some grey space here which can be addressed by having more specific wording.

This could be crucial in these types of situations as the difference between being in an offside position and committing an offside offence can have a big effect on whether a penalty is awarded.

It’s a small comfort for Arsenal after missing the chance to take the lead from the spot. But Martin Odegaard did eventually score the winner in the 72nd minute to give Mikel Arteta’s men three points.

Sources indicate that the incident has exposed a wider problem for referees. Until the laws provide clearer guidance, similar decisions could continue to generate controversy.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recently, it’s felt like AC Milan have been set on signing Nicolo Tresoldi in the winter.
  • Industry observers note that at a time when Milan are doing the PR side of things almost perfectly, Tresoldi feels like another easy win.
  • Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recently, it’s felt like AC Milan have been set on signing Nicolo Tresoldi in the winter. It may be the easy option, but is it the right one?

Industry observers note that at a time when Milan are doing the PR side of things almost perfectly, Tresoldi feels like another easy win. It seems increasingly likely that Francesco Camarda departs in the winter mercato, so why not replace him with another Milanista?

Recent findings suggest that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Replace the boy who was destined to become king with another who seems further down the career line. He’s already scored a senior goal – or three – at San Siro and he’s got attention from all of Europe’s best clubs. However, if the Rossoneri came knocking, would he be able to say no to his boyhood club?

Well, here is the alternative view: maybe they shouldn’t knock at all.

Sources indicate that now, it’s unpopular to suggest that Tresoldi isn’t the right man, but stick with us here, especially after reports today. If you’ve not seen, Club Brugge have made a statement in the Belgian outlet Het Laatste Nieuws that they won’t be selling him in January.

It’s a ‘club policy’ and even for €60-70 million, he won’t be leaving Belgium. We’ve seen these kinds of statements become pointless in the past and this could become one of them. However, that’s not really the key thing here.

Instead, it’s that Tresoldi has now entered a latest bracket. €50m in January is steep, but it’s workable. Ultimately, we’re not in record-breaking territory. Taking that €10-20m step upwards, though, that’s where we enter that territory. There’s also a possibility that more would be needed, too.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a figure that Gerry Cardinale may not be afraid to spend. In fact, reports would have you believe that he really loves Tresoldi and sees him as a perfect addition to a strong frontline roster. However, that’s a lot of money on two strikers in one season.

Industry observers note that then, you’ve also got negotiations with Brugge to deal with. Historically, the Diavolo have found it difficult to close deals with them and with Tresoldi, it’ll be harder than ever, especially after the Ardon Jashari situation.

With the figures being discussed too, you can only imagine how small the margins will be.

Then, you have maybe the most difficult factor. Tresoldi, taking romanticism out of it, has only performed in, with respect, sub-tier leagues. Now, that’s not to take away from his records; scoring-wise, he’s been phenomenal and he’s matched it in the Champions League.

However – and it’s a massive however – we’ve already seen that it doesn’t always translate. For example, look at Charles De Ketelaere, but that’s not the real parallel here.

Recent findings suggest that here, we head to the parallel. In the summer just gone, Milan hired a new Portuguese coach, who initially faced a few questions. After an up-and-down first half of the season, they find themselves in need of a statement January window and stumble upon a boyhood fan of the Rossoneri.

Said fan is banging goals in for fun in a league outside of Europe’s top five, but there’s no need to panic as he’s performing in the Champions League, even against the biggest teams. So, the Rossoneri make the plunge.

It has been revealed that six months later, they try to sell him and a year after that, he’s on loan at Porto, with an €18m buy clause sitting in his deal, unlikely to be touched. Of course, that’s Santiago Gimenez.

There are differences between them, of course, but the formula has already been tried and the results speak for themselves. Trying it again, whilst enticing for the same romantic reasons as Gimenez’s arrival, may not be the answer.

Yes, Gimenez had issues with selection and injuries and eventually, both together. Nevertheless, even without these problems, it was a rushed deal and the Diavolo are going to be the ones paying for that rush next season.

The point here isn’t to discredit the Mexican, but rather suggest that rushing to sign a romantic connection isn’t always the best way to spend big money. It’s about balance, which is why another striker signing like Nicolas Füllkrug wouldn’t be ideal.

Recent findings suggest that denying that Tresoldi could become a great would be naive, but it would also be as bad to ignore the reasons why the deal is becoming more of a gamble. At €50m, it makes sense, but we’re entering an echelon of deals that requires serious consideration.

In January, Milan would probably have to spend upwards of €70m and that wouldn’t guarantee them Champions League football. Nothing really will offer complete assurances in football; few things – if anything – are guaranteed. Yet, for that fee, it would be expected and you’re still not really addressing the problems within the squad completely.

To do that, Cardinale would have to spend at least another €30-40m to satisfy the fanbase and that’s unreasonable halfway through a season.

In a recent development, so, diversifying the money across the team and then reassessing in the summer may be the best route forward. After all, with this increased price demand, you’re hardly going to be paying more in the summer – and if their demands reach that amount, you’re voicing fresh questions.

With Markus Krösche also coming in, the January mercato will be one where everything has to be considered carefully and judgements will be made before February 1 rolls around. Spending so heavily on one target may also be an early and unnecessary strike on his record, if it doesn’t work.

For many, Tresoldi made sense in January because he’d be an investment at an investment price. Now, you’re looking at a major budget depletion for a striker who has yet to become a senior international and/or a regular goalscorer in one of Europe’s top five leagues.

Industry observers note that the romantic side of it is great; it’s difficult not to fall for that. Financially, though, signing Tresoldi is becoming a tougher sell and that’s where we might have to start listening to the brain rather than the heart.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

In a recent development, “Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

It has been revealed that “We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”.

Alonso is speedily shifting perceptions of this previously underperforming bunch, the Stamford Bridge culture on and off the pitch already unrecognisable from a few months ago.

It was Chelsea’s trip to Everton last season which facilitated the endgame of Liam Rosenior’s short, but generally hideous reign.

For those who tried to banish memories, it was a darkly comical period when Chelsea’s players were paying their respect to stationary footballs, seemingly finding latest ways to stand in front of travelling fans to apologise for meek and rancid performances.

How different the scenes after Pedro Neto’s double on Merseyside – a success built on those old-fashioned and too often underestimated qualities of character and application before the artists had the final say. These are the wins that build connections and trust between players and supporters, especially during the getting-to-know-you period of a managerial tenure. While neutrals mutter about a generally disappointing spectacle, the players and supporters return home clutching three points believing they have fought together in the trenches.

It cannot be overlooked how this win owed a debt to the erratic refereeing of Paul Tierney, especially the amnesty he offered to Morgan Rogers on the stroke of half-time.

Already booked, Rogers was fortunate not to receive a second caution for a lunge on James Garner which took the man after the ball. A replica challenge by Everton’s Harrison Armstrong had warranted a yellow card in Tierney’s world just 21 minutes earlier.

The home team’s argument that this was a potential game changer was supported when the England midfielder was inevitably involved in the move which led to Neto breaking through 44 seconds into the second half – a lead Chelsea never looked like surrendering as Everton’s attacking limitations were exposed.

That should not disguise how this is a different Chelsea, contrasting not just with the characterless and rudderless team of last season, but also the defensively flawed version that began this one. Mike Penders deputised for the stricken Martínez – conscious but taken to hospital as a precaution – and was well-protected.

As much as Alonso’s artistry as a midfield maestro is presumed to define him as a coach, one cannot help but believe there are many who underestimate him as a football student. He was never going to return to England clinging to one idea given his previous Premier League experience, and he intuitively knew an away game at Everton was one for foot soldiers.

According to recent reports, he signed Jordan Henderson for such a task. Just like his manager, the former Liverpool captain was primed for enemy territory.

Alonso’s anticipation of a fixture in which a battle had to be fought before there was an outbreak of football proved correct, aided by the fussy and generally terrible first-half officiating of Tierney.

Bizarrely, Alonso had as much cause to curse Tierney for the first of several contentious decisions, booking Armstrong for an aggressive but ultimately fair lunging challenge on Josh Acheampong. That enraged the home supporters to inspire Everton to their most dangerous spell, Thierno Barry coming closest to troubling Martínez before half-time.

Although Moisés Caicedo was denied a goal-of-the-season contender when a vicious 20-yard volley struck the crossbar, the scrappy, stop-start flavour of the occasion initially suited the hosts.

“They didn’t score, but did a fantastic job for the team,” Alonso pointedly mentioned of his attackers.

According to recent reports, alonso’s name has not echoed so loudly across the Mersey since he played a few miles down the road from Everton’s upcoming home. After several calamitous appointments, those fans can believe their team are in safe hands again.

Thanks for reading along this afternoon.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Everton vs Chelsea.

It has been revealed that chelsea return to Premier League action this weekend looking to harness the momentum of their emphatic 5-1 victory over Bournemouth before the international break. That Stamford Bridge masterclass ended a frustrating three-match winless streak and was built upon braces from Joao Pedro and Jordan Henderson, alongside another strike from summer signing Morgan Rogers.

Yet the true catalyst for the resurgence was the return of Moises Caicedo. Having shaken off the calf problem that hindered his early-season involvement, the midfielder anchored the side’s win. While defensive vulnerabilities persist - extending an unwanted run of league matches without a clean sheet back to January - the victory offered clear signs of progress under their head coach, Xabi Alonso.

According to recent reports, next up is a notoriously difficult trip to Merseyside to face Everton in Saturday’s lunchtime fixture. Historically, Everton have proven to be a formidable stumbling block for the capital club, particularly on home turf. Everton enter the weekend unbeaten in eight of their last nine home encounters against Chelsea, a stretch that has seen the Londoners fail to score on seven visits and suffer six defeats, including a chastening 3-0 reverse last term that spelt the end for Liam Rosenior.

David Moyes will demand a sharper defensive showing from his side this time around, following a frustrating 2-2 draw with Hull City where a 2-1 lead slipped away. Even so, Everton’s broader defensive record at home offers encouragement, having kept clean sheets in two of their opening three league fixtures at their base.

With both teams eager to build consistency, Saturday’s clash pits Chelsea’s newly found attacking spark against an opponent that traditionally relishes this fixture.

  • It has been revealed that west Ham United are facing something of a dilemma over Manor Solomon, with Israel reportedly considering bringing the winger back into the team for Tuesday’s Nations League clash against Austria.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to Sport5, Solomon could now be in contention for the Austria fixture.
  • Sources indicate that for West Ham manager Scott Parker, however, the situation presents an interesting dilemma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that west Ham United are facing something of a dilemma over Manor Solomon, with Israel reportedly considering bringing the winger back into the team for Tuesday’s Nations League clash against Austria. The 26-year-old has been struggling with back pain during the international break, although Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon has suggested that he is feeling better after returning to training.

Recent findings suggest that according to Sport5, Solomon could now be in contention for the Austria fixture. That follows comments from Ben-Shimon suggesting the player had trained and was feeling better, although his fitness would need to be reassessed.

Sources indicate that for West Ham manager Scott Parker, however, the situation presents an interesting dilemma. We desperately need the old Manor Solomon back, but I wonder whether another international appearance is really what the player needs right now.

According to recent reports, manor Solomon representing Israel during a difficult international break. The West Ham winger has been carrying a back injury since October.

Look, I’m caught between a rock and a hard place on this one.

There is part of me that hopes Solomon gets a game, so he can get back to form. Because there’s no doubt about it, West Ham have a far bigger chance of getting promoted this season if Manor Solomon is back to the sort of form he was in when he played for Leeds in the Championship.

In a recent development, clearly Scott Parker has faith in him because he has seen how destructive he can be in that division. Getting that player back would be a significant boost for the Hammers, particularly with the Championship promotion race starting to get serious.

But, and it’s a significant but, we have had complaints of back injury during the October internationals, and we’ve already had it during this international break.

As I reported earlier in October, a West Ham source confirmed that Solomon was in considerable pain after an exhausting international schedule. More recently, we reported on his latest back problem, which restricted his training with Israel.

There is also part of me that wonders whether we would not have been better served, and the player himself, actually resting up, getting some medical treatment, or even being given ten days off completely to recuperate and joining back up with the squad for the last few days of training before the Preston game.

As things stand, there’s nothing in his recent form that suggests he could start and should start against Preston. And without him being on the training pitch during this international break to impress Scott Parker, he’s not going to be able to catch the manager’s eye.

In a recent development, edvin Austbø has certainly given Parker something to think about on the left wing. Indeed, Austbø’s recent performances have highlighted the competition for Solomon’s place, and I suspect the Norwegian is at the moment ahead of him in the pecking order.

In a recent development, but I don’t want to write off Solomon. We know what he’s capable of producing in this division, and West Ham will need every bit of attacking quality available if we’re serious about getting back into the Premier League.

In a recent development, hopefully, Israel will make the sensible decision and only involve him against Austria if he is genuinely fit enough to play. We cannot afford another international break to leave us with a player who returns to east London carrying another injury.

Latest Update: Former Rangers striker Peter van Vossen on THAT Old Firm miss 30 years ago today... 'I wasn't paying attention and the ball hit my shin, but I still blame Jorg Albertz!'

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail
