📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 09:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:44 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • In a career spanning almost 20 years, Peter van Vossen won the Champions League, made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup with his country and won league titles in both the Netherlands and Scotland.
  • Point being, it’s reductive to define his time in football by one excruciating miss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 09:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:44 EST, 14 November 2026.

In a career spanning almost 20 years, Peter van Vossen won the Champions League, made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup with his country and won league titles in both the Netherlands and Scotland.

Point being, it’s reductive to define his time in football by one excruciating miss. But here we are.

It’s 30 years to the day since Van Vossen missed an open goal for Rangers during a crucial Old Firm clash at Celtic Park. Leading 1-0 and with less than seven minutes remaining, the Dutch forward had a chance to seal all three points for the nine-in-a-row-chasing Light Blues. Instead, he blazed over with the goal at his mercy.

In the decades since, the spurned chance has become the benchmark by which all other misses have been measured. ‘Sure, it was bad — but was it “Van Vossen” bad?’.

Recent findings suggest that the man himself has seldom spoken about the events of that powder keg of a night. Until now. Living the quiet life in rural Holland, Van Vossen has given Daily Mail Sport a full account of his professional nadir.

Sources indicate that ‘I mostly remember being mad at Jorg [Albertz],’ he indicates. ‘I was seriously p***** off with him. Paul Gascoigne played a pass inside to me and I clipped a first-time ball in behind the Celtic defence, who were pressing high. If Jorg had just left it, I was one-on-one with the goalie and I would have fancied my chances.

Rangers striker Peter van Vossen sends the ball skywards in a crucial Old Firm clash in 1996.

‘I also thought there was a chance he might have been offside, so when you see me running through and stretching out my arms, that’s not me telling him that we’re through; that’s me telling him to leave it and get out of the way!

Sources indicate that ‘Anyway, he didn’t, I continued my run, he passed it to me and, because I was still livid when the ball arrived at me, I wasn’t paying enough attention. It took a bit of a bobble, I ended up basically hitting it with my shin and, yeah, it unfortunately flew over the bar.’.

To his relief, Rangers held on for a 1-0 win to leapfrog their bitter rivals at the top of the table, albeit only after Andy Goram saved a Pierre van Hooijdonk penalty awarded moments after Van Vossen’s horror miss.

‘Walter Smith came up to me in the dressing room afterwards and noted, “It’s just as well The Goalie saved that penalty otherwise I’d have f****** killed you!”’ smiles Van Vossen.

In a recent development, ‘It was horrible but I can laugh about it now because we won the game. I wish I had scored but I didn’t, so there’s nothing I can do except try to find the humour in it.’.

In a recent development, van Vossen signed for Rangers in January 1996 in a swap deal that saw Oleg Salenko join Istanbulspor. He came with some pedigree, too, having won the Champions League with Ajax in 1995, a year after featuring for the Netherlands on their run to the last eight of the World Cup in the US.

Recent findings suggest that at that time, Rangers, bankrolled by David Murray, were in the throes of a project designed to deliver European glory, while maintaining their dominance of Scottish football. Those two objectives, says Van Vossen, were misaligned.

In a recent development, ‘We had a quality group of players that was far better than anything else in Scotland at the time,’ he says. ‘That made us incredibly difficult to beat in the league. But when we went into European games, we were exposed. The lack of competition in the league along with the lifestyles of some of our players was not compatible with taking on champions from other countries.

‘I always felt like we were technically a little behind. Our training usually consisted of a warm-up, a game of football, and a warm-down. That was a major adjustment for me. At Ajax, we played in a system and we worked hard on making sure everybody knew their role. In Scotland, it seemed like there was no real system. You could run anywhere you wanted. I don’t really think I learned anything in my time there.’.

Industry observers note that that’s not to say he didn’t enjoy his two-and-a-half years in Glasgow. Quite the opposite.

‘I loved playing for Rangers,’ he notes. ‘Particularly that second season [1996/97]. I started really well and scored seven or eight goals in the first handful of games. I remember people being quite surprised because I had taken some time to settle. They would joke, “Who are you, Van Vossen’s better twin brother?” But I loved it.’.

A dejected Van Vossen can't believe he's missed in a moment that would follow him forever.

Recent findings suggest that he reserves particular affection for Walter Smith. ‘He was a fantastic manager and a true gentleman,’ he nods. ‘He helped me through a difficult time in my personal life. When I wasn’t in his team on the weekend, for example, I would ask him if I could go back to the Netherlands to see my children. He always said yes on the condition that I was back in time for training at 10am on Monday.

It has been revealed that ‘He genuinely cared about his players. I remember Vitesse being interested in bringing me back to Holland and their coach Leo Beenhakker coming to watch me at Ibrox.

‘After the game, he found Walter and said, “We want to sign Peter, but we think £300,000 is too much”. Walter said to him, “Listen to me carefully. We don’t do business like this. First, you and I will go for a lunch, have a respectful chat and only when we’ve got to know each other, that’s when we’ll talk about money”.

It has been revealed that ‘Walter came to me afterwards and stated, “Look, I know you’re not playing as much as you would like but I won’t let you sign for him. This isn’t a good manager and I can’t allow it. You’re one of my players and I care about getting you the right move, not just any move”. I really respected that.’.

Van Vossen endured a much more difficult relationship with Smith’s assistant Archie Knox, a man he describes as ‘manipulative’.

In a recent development, ‘I didn’t get on with him,’ he says. ‘People talk a lot nowadays about creating a safe space and the right culture in workplaces. To me, Archie didn’t do that. He was always shouting, always right on top of you, in your face, kicking bottles. He behaved like a madman.

Van Vossen scored nine goals in 31 caps for the Netherlands between 1992 and 2000.

In a recent development, ‘At Ajax, the coaches wanted to know how you were feeling. They understood that being well mentally was as crucial as being physically fit. Archie wasn’t interested in that. He was always aggressive, but only with the players he didn’t like. He had his favourites. If you weren’t one of them, he made sure you knew all about it.’.

Background tensions aside, Van Vossen’s first full season at Ibrox, 1996/97, has assumed a special place in Rangers’ folklore. They finished five points clear of Celtic to equal their rivals’ record of nine consecutive league titles, having laid the foundations with four league wins out of four over Tommy Burns’ side.

Despite his famous miss being the closest he ever came to scoring in an Old Firm clash, Van Vossen insists he relished those occasions.

‘I loved those games,’ he indicates. ‘The atmosphere, home and away, was unbelievable and the quality of the players on the pitch was outstanding. To be honest, there wasn’t a whole lot of football played. There were lots of mistakes, fights and loads of running. I remember feeling tired after just ten minutes. I wasn’t built for that kind of pace! But they were great to be part of.

In a recent development, ‘The week of Old Firm matches, you could feel the pressure building. I remember being in Glasgow city centre one day and I needed a taxi. I waved one down but when it pulled up, the driver must have been a Celtic fan because he raised his middle finger and swore at me before driving away. Whereas, with Rangers taxi drivers, it was the opposite. I honestly think they would have driven me around Scotland for free.

Van Vossen had a spell in charge of Fortuna Sittard but now labels himself a 'house husband'.

‘That’s just what football is like in Glasgow. It’s on a whole other level to anything else. I’ve played in massive derbies in the Netherlands and Turkey. Believe me, nothing comes close to the Old Firm.’.

After finding his playing time limited as Rangers pursued ten-in-a-row, Van Vossen was relieved to learn that his old international manager, Dick Advocaat, would take over from Smith in time for the 1998/99 season. His joy, however, was short-lived when Murray used him as a makeweight in a transfer for Feyenoord midfielder Giovanni van Bronckhorst.

Recent findings suggest that ‘David Murray was a brilliant guy, but he made a huge mistake when he tried to sell me to Feyenoord behind the back of Dick Advocaat,’ says Van Vossen. ‘Dick was taking over and he was keen for me to be part of his prepares.

Sources indicate that ‘I remember he was flying from Amsterdam to Glasgow when he phoned me to talk about some of his ideas. I said, “Dick, I’m sorry, but I think I’m joining Feyenoord. The deal is almost done”. He told me to stay put and said that when he got to Glasgow, he and I were going to go and see Murray.

‘I remember Dick mentioned to him, “How can you sell players behind my back? I need to be involved in these conversations”. Murray said, “You’re absolutely right, I apologise”. He handed me a blank cheque and said, “Peter, write down whatever number you want to stay. It’s not a problem”.

According to recent reports, ‘But I couldn’t do it. I respected him for apologising to Dick, but I had lost confidence in him. I couldn’t play for somebody who would do something like that.

Van Vossen scored 11 goals in his 36 appearances for Rangers between 1996 and 1998.

‘I took a 60 per cent drop in wages to join Feyenoord but they were the team I had supported as a boy and I needed to be somewhere I was wanted and where I was being treated with respect.’.

Although his spell at Ibrox ended on a slightly sour note, Van Vossen recalls it fondly. ‘It was a family,’ he notes. ‘Everybody had a part to play, from the players on the pitch to the ladies in the kitchen. I mean, they were incredible. I remember being on a ferry one time and I got chatting to a truck driver who told me he sold flowers. We had a good conversation and exchanged numbers.

‘When I got back to Glasgow, I got in touch with him and said, “Can you do me a favour? Can you deliver ten bouquets of flowers to Ibrox?” Sure enough, this huge truck pulled up outside the ground one day, with something like ten thousand flowers in the back. They pulled out ten bouquets and delivered them to the ladies in the kitchen. They were delighted, but it was the least I could do. They treated you like one of their own. Like I say, we were one significant family.’.

These days, the head of that family is one of Van Vossen’s old teammates, Derek McInnes, and he’s backing him to deliver silverware.

Despite carving out a successful career, Van Vossen is remembered primarily for THAT miss.

Industry observers note that ‘I remember Derek well,’ he says. ‘Like me, he didn’t play every game, but he always gave 100 per cent and I expect he’ll be the same as a manager. He’s a people person and I imagine he is a fantastic man-manager. I have no doubt he’ll do a great job.’.

Having dabbled in management and punditry since hanging up his boots, Van Vossen now describes himself as a ‘house husband’ who dotes on wife Jojanneke and his stepchildren Sem, Lilly, Madée and Eva. He’s also right now writing his autobiography. The simple pleasures, he insists, are what matter most to him.

It has been revealed that ‘I don’t need to have lots of expensive things and a certain kind of lifestyle to be a rich man,’ he adds. ‘I’m a rich man because of the memories I have and the good times I enjoyed as a footballer.

‘If I close my eyes, I can still remember what it was like to run onto the pitch at Ibrox in front of 50,000 supporters, and it gives me goosebumps. I am very fortunate to have had that opportunity.’.

It has been revealed that hincapie initially missed Ecuador’s September squad because of a groin problem. He had been named among the substitutes for Arsenal’s final match before that break, against Brighton.

Recent findings suggest that after recovering, the 24-year-old returned to action in the 2-1 Premier League win over Leeds United on October 10. However, he suffered another setback during the warm-down after the match.

According to recent reports, he has now given a much more positive update on his injury whilst on international duty. He is now “100% fit” and does not have any niggles.

Hincapie has also expressed his optimism for his initial discussions with Gallardo. The player is excited to work under the former River Plate manager and help the national team.

Industry observers note that he should prove to be a valuable asset in the squad, considering he can play in both roles. He is a natural centre back but can also play as a left back.

Hincapie has shown that he is happy to play anywhere in the team his manager requires. This can be an important factor for Arsenal as the fixture list gets tougher.

He has only featured three times in all competitions this season and has yet to play in the Premier League. Consistent playing time will be key if he is to become a regular in Arteta’s intends.

However, his latest update shows that he is no longer struggling with the physical problems. If he can stay fit over the international break, he will provide another key defensive option for Arsenal in the coming weeks.

#2379. The best Newcastle United number 10 for the Matthias Jaissle system

The best Newcastle United number 10 for the Matthias Jaissle system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across the season so far, Matthias Jaissle has consistently set up in a 4-2-3-1 formation, predominately using a distinct number 10 in that system.
  • The number 10 role is one of the most challenging roles in modern football – the best #10s in the modern game bring a mix of technique, creativity, off-the-ball running, pressing, goalscoring and defensive contributions.
  • They can find little pockets of space, receive the ball on the turn and find teammates in behind, or create goalscoring opportunities for themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the season so far, Matthias Jaissle has consistently set up in a 4-2-3-1 formation, predominately using a distinct number 10 in that system.

The number 10 role is one of the most challenging roles in modern football – the best #10s in the modern game bring a mix of technique, creativity, off-the-ball running, pressing, goalscoring and defensive contributions.

They can find little pockets of space, receive the ball on the turn and find teammates in behind, or create goalscoring opportunities for themselves.

They know when to drop into midfield, to help the team control the tempo or progress the ball forwards, and they can also threaten the opponents goal with clever movements, off-the-ball runs and late runs into the box.

It’s fair to say that no one has made this number 10 position their own so far for Newcastle United this season.

If Jaissle is to persist with that system, then he needs to find the right player to play as the #10 in his system.

Here, I’m going to rank the number 10 options available to Matthias Jaissle, as it stands right now.

Wissa started the season brightly and showed promise but has since dropped off in the last 6-7 matches.

He has something to offer, particularly in home games in the #10 role, but certainly doesn’t possess the creative ability to link play between defence, midfield and attack like a good #10 can.

In a recent development, he’s decent on the turn, and can dribble effectively through midfield, but the technical and creative side of the role is not his strength. We’ve seen him spurn multiple chances through poor decision making and his vision and weight of pass means he doesn’t effectively utilise the space he can create through his dribbling and turn it into goal scoring opportunities for him or his team mates.

Another player who has shown flashes this season but never fully grasped the opportunity.

Joe Willock relishes space – he doesn’t have the technique or tactical nous to show for and receive the ball in tight spaces, turn and play forwards. He offers Newcastle a ‘running’ # 10 – he can test the opponents defence with runs in behind, and he can be effective when drifting into space on the left or on the counter attack. But he doesn’t help us play through the lines because he doesn’t often show for the ball from the centre backs or from our two holding midfielders. He doesn’t help connect defence and midfield with our three attackers and doesn’t help control games in the middle of the park.

When he’s fit, massive Joe offers a better mix of attributes in the #10 role than Wissa and Willock.

According to recent reports, he’s played similar roles before, and has obviously played as a centre-forward for both Newcastle and in Germany, so (yes, despite his record) he does have some of the attacking attributes and instincts to score goals from the #10. He has shown he can chip in and score goals from midfield by bursting into the box or arriving to meet crosses. He’s strong in the air and strong on the ball, so offers us an outlet in the middle of the pitch aerially and his strength allows him to receive the ball to feet in tight spaces.

While he’s not particularly creative, he can find a pass and is pretty good at finding pockets of space to receive the ball. He offers the ability to drop into midfield and help progress the ball, and obviously brings tactical understanding and a strong defensive contribution. Opposition defensive midfielders would hate having him breathing down their neck every time they get the ball.

Recent findings suggest that he’s by no means the perfect fit but offers a better skill set than Willock and Wissa in the #10. With two of Nico, Steur and Miley behind him, big Joe could be an effective option in the #10 in the short-term.

In my opinion, Ramsey is the best fit for Jaissle’s #10 role from the current squad, and I’m bewildered as to why he hasn’t been given time there. Ramsey himself noted a few weeks ago that he had been training in that role, so hopefully that’s a sign that he might get a chance there… and not blow it by getting sent off.

Jacob Ramsey has far and away the best array of skills in our squad to play the #10 role. He has a high level of technical quality, is adept at finding pockets of space and is great at receiving the ball on the half turn to play forwards. He has the best eye for a pass of our current options and has the passing range and technique to find players to feet or running in behind.

He is very two-footed and can score goals with right and left, and possesses the ability to make well-timed runs in behind and into the box to meet crosses. He’s shown in previous seasons (with Villa) that he can be a strong contributor of goals and assists from an attacking midfield position in the premier league.

His technique and tactical awareness mean he can drop into midfield to help the team progress the ball, or can sit in the pocket and try and find space to connect the midfield with our front three.

Defensively, he has a great engine, is strong in the tackle and can track back or press as well as any other option we have.

Matthias Jaissle has much more depth in the deep roles now (Nico, Steur, Miley etc) so there is no need to use Ramsey there. When he got a run of 10-15 games in the middle of last season, Ramsey was brilliant and very consistent for us. He put in a 7-8/10 performance across most of those games and helped knit things together in midfield. I’d like to see him given that same opportunity now.

#1 – Change the system or buy a #10 in January.

It’s worth acknowledging that none of these options are the perfect fit.

In my opinion, Ramsey is the only player we have who could actually be a good option in the #10 for the medium term. He’s the best of a bad bunch really. Given this fact and the emergence of Steur and availability of Miley, Ramsey and (ahem) Bamba, then it makes sense for Jaissle to revert to a midfield three.

It has been revealed that if Jaissle wants to persist with this current system, and a #10 were available in January and we can spend the required cash (both doubtful) then I think we have to invest in that position as a priority. It’s the key position to unlock the rest of our attack, and requires a technical leader who can create and score goals. That’s a rare skillset and something we’ll need to work hard to find the right fit.

#2378. Tech Report: Arsenal receive mixed verdict after Liverpool penalty review

Tech Report: Arsenal receive mixed verdict after Liverpool penalty review

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readarsenal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve an key revision on the Arsenal Liverpool penalty decision.
  • The panel were unanimous in their decision that Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty after Jurrien Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt.
  • The panel also cleared the officials on the incident involving Noni Madueke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we’ve an key revision on the Arsenal Liverpool penalty decision. Arsenal received a mixed reaction from the Premier League’s independent panel after their controversial win at Anfield.

The panel were unanimous in their decision that Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty after Jurrien Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt. However, they were divided on whether it should have been reviewed by VAR.

The panel also cleared the officials on the incident involving Noni Madueke. This means that Arsenal were justified in their win due to the wrong decision being made on the penalty.

The incident happened during the 1-0 win for Arsenal at Anfield on November 1. Isak was trying to run onto a cross from Bradley Barcola after Kai Havertz had given the Gunners the lead.

As Timber pulled him back, he was unable to cleanly head the ball. The referee Andy Madley allowed play to continue. The decision was then made by VAR Stuart Attwell that there was not enough evidence to suggest a review.

The five-man Key Match Incidents panel has now ruled that this was the wrong decision. Four of the panel voted that Liverpool should have been awarded the spot kick after Timber’s handball.

However, there was a tight vote on whether VAR should have intervened. Three panellists felt that Attwell should have shown Madley to the pitchside monitor, whilst two felt it did not reach the threshold.

Recent findings suggest that one panellist felt the length of the hold was not long enough to affect the movement of Isak. The other two members who felt that VAR should not have intervened also mentioned that it is subjective as to how much the hold would affect the striker.

It has been revealed that this is an important point to note. Whilst they agreed that the penalty was deserved, there was less agreement on whether it was VAR’s responsibility to overturn the decision.

There was also good news for Arsenal in the panel’s decision regarding Madueke’s late altercation with Alexis MacAllister.

The Liverpool midfielder fell to the floor following a headbutt from the Arsenal winger. The incident was reviewed by the VAR, but Madueke was spared a red card. Mac Allister received a yellow.

All five panel members agreed that Madueke should not have been sent off. They felt that there had not been any contact, and Mac Allister’s reaction was certainly excessive.

It certainly gives us an alternative standpoint into the situation. Whilst Arsenal benefited from the incorrect decision regarding the penalty, the officials were backed up with the disciplinary incident.

This won’t have any impact on the result of the Anfield game, as Havertz’s goal was the winning goal and gave Arsenal their first league victory at the stadium in 14 years.

However, it does show how risky Timber was to make the challenge and how close the panel were with whether they should have intervened with VAR.

Breaking: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 48 min read (9673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~48 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Materials, at their essence, are networks defined by homogeneity: uniform bonds, fixed thicknesses and discrete length scales.
  • Sources indicate that at their core, materials are networks: in crystalline solids, atoms form regular lattices defined by uniform bonds, and in mechanical metamaterials, a distinct graph encodes the interactions among structural components.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, as network science has revealed in the past two decades, real-world networks rarely exhibit the homogeneity of crystalline or amorphous solids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Materials, at their essence, are networks defined by homogeneity: uniform bonds, fixed thicknesses and discrete length scales. Mechanical metamaterials, while representing structurally more diverse microstructures, remain defined by the homogeneity of their unit cells, pore sizes or repeating features1,2. In contrast, as network science has revealed, real-world and biological systems—from the Internet to the brain—derive their function from broad, multiscale variability in connectivity and link length3,4,5,6. Here we introduce scale-rich metamaterials, a design framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials, achieving orders-of-magnitude heterogeneity in ligament lengths, thicknesses and connectivity. Governed by only two parameters, scale-rich networks span orders of magnitude in structural features, overcoming previous constraints in metamaterial design. Translating these network models into physically realizable materials, we use simulations and experiments to show that scale-rich metamaterials exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems, including highly tunable elastic anisotropy, delocalized nonlinear deformation with high energy absorption, enhanced energy dissipation under dynamic loading and programmable elastic-wave control. This network-based framework establishes a minimal and universal model for engineering multifunctional materials whose mechanical behaviour emerges directly from scale diversity, and also opens avenues of enquiry for network science itself.

Sources indicate that at their core, materials are networks: in crystalline solids, atoms form regular lattices defined by uniform bonds, and in mechanical metamaterials, a distinct graph encodes the interactions among structural components. These graphs share a critical feature—an exceptional homogeneity of their local properties. Crystalline lattices are defined by unique bond lengths and interaction strengths, and even disordered systems such as amorphous microstructures show narrow distributions of connectivity and bond strength. Mechanical metamaterials, or architected materials, inherit this homogeneity: despite their structural diversity, they are typically governed by one or a few discrete length scales7, even in the presence of hierarchy2,8 or disorder9. Unit-cell design further enforces uniform connectivity10 and geometric compatibility constraints11,12, while plate- and shell-based architectures also rely on fixed thicknesses and uniform pore sizes13,14.

Recent findings suggest that however, as network science has revealed in the past two decades, real-world networks rarely exhibit the homogeneity of crystalline or amorphous solids. Instead, systems as diverse as protein–protein interaction networks, social networks and global infrastructures such as the Internet show remarkable structural variability: node degrees span orders of magnitude and interaction strengths cover broad ranges3,4,5,6. This heterogeneity underlies their robustness15,16,17 and resilience18, facilitates dynamical processes19, and enables control through a small subset of nodes20. Even physical networks21,22,23, such as neuronal and vascular networks, whose nodes and links have material presence, are highly heterogeneous, with degrees, link lengths and strengths spanning several orders of magnitude24.

Elements of multiscale organization are also a hallmark of biological systems, defining their mechanical and transport properties. Dragonfly wings, for example, display vein lengths spanning more than three orders of magnitude, from ℓmin = 0.1 mm to ℓmax ≈ 50 mm (ref. 25). Leaves exhibit equally complex venation patterns, with length scales ranging from ℓ ≈ 10−1 mm to ℓ ≈ 103 mm and connectivity spanning roughly 3 decades26. Spider webs are made of string whose lengths extend from ℓ ≈ 1 mm to ℓ ≈ 103 mm (ref. 27), and bones represent hierarchical architectures built from rod- and plate-like elements, whose lengths range from ℓ ≈ 100 μm to ℓ ≈ 1,500 μm and thicknesses from λ ≈ 40 μm to λ ≈ 400 μm (ref. 28).

Over the past two decades, network models have provided a powerful language for describing systems whose structure spans many scales29,30,31,32. Graph-theoretic descriptions increasingly link such structural organization to mechanics in natural and engineered materials, collagen and other biopolymers33, paper34, self-assembled nanoparticles35, and composite fibre networks36. These studies show that disorder and network topology can be used to tune mechanical response37, for example, through the selective pruning of elastic networks38. Yet no generative framework exists for architected materials in which length, thickness and connectivity simultaneously span orders of magnitude, nor one predicting how this structural heterogeneity shapes mechanical performance.

To address this gap, here we introduce a design paradigm for mechanical metamaterials that leverages a network-science-based approach to generate architectures with a controlled, yet broadly varying, span of connectivities, length scales and interaction strengths. We refer to these materials as scale-rich (SR) networks, as they allow the simultaneous coexistence of lengths, thicknesses and connectivities that span orders of magnitude within the same system. Using both computational modelling and experiments, we show that SR metamaterials, governed by only two parameters, enable properties unattainable in single-scale systems: a 190-fold tunable range of elastic anisotropy across densities, stable and delocalized nonlinear deformation with high energy absorption, enhanced energy dissipation under dynamic loading, and programmable elastic-wave responses. Finally, we derive an analytical model that connects the total stored energy to geometrical features such as ligament length, thickness and degree, unveiling the mechanical role of the multiple length scales present in the system. Taken together, these results establish SR materials as a versatile platform for engineering multifunctional systems with programmable, multiscale performance. They also provide a minimal yet powerful framework for inverse design and open avenues of enquiry for network science.

It has been revealed that to construct an SR metamaterial, we start with a unit square domain (L = 1) and iteratively add ligaments whose thickness λ decreases with time t as λt = λ0t−α, where λ0 is the initial thickness and α is the decay exponent. The generation process consists of two steps (Fig. 1a): (1) choose a random nucleation point (xt, yt) within the L2 domain and a random angle θt; (2) grow a ligament of thickness λt from the nucleation point in both directions, defined by θt, until it intersects other ligaments or the boundary. We repeat steps 1 and 2 until a predefined time t = T or until we are unable to add new ligaments, leading to a state of jamming22,39 (see Supplementary Information, section 1.5 for more examples and Supplementary Information, section 1.8 for the implementation). Each new ligament stops at its first intersection, being fused together, resulting in a planar network without overlaps.

a, Generation process of an SR metamaterial, starting at time step t = 1 where an initial ligament of thickness λ0 is generated from a randomized coordinate (x0, y0) in a randomized orientation θ0. Additional ligaments are then generated at each time step t (nucleated with randomized coordinates and orientations) with thickness λt = λ0t−α, terminating at the intersection with another ligament or the domain boundary. \({X}_{i}=({x}_{i},{y}_{i},{\theta }_{i},{\lambda }_{i})\) denotes the position, orientation and thickness of the ith ligament. b, The network behind the SR metamaterial, inspired by road networks45, represents ligaments as nodes and intersections as links. The panels show the growth of the network corresponding to the configurations shown in a. c, The analytically derived (α, λ0) phase diagram (two-parameter design space) of SR metamaterials. For small α the system gets jammed, that is, it does not allow the introduction of new ligaments. For large α, the system can indefinitely accommodate additional ligaments, reaching a phase where the density of the system is tunable (Supplementary Information, section 1.1). Experimentally realized SR metamaterials with T = 500 and relative density \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \), via two types of 3D-printing technique, are depicted with white symbols. d, Images of 3D-printed SR metamaterial specimens, at centimetre (vat photopolymerization) and micrometre (two-photon lithography) scales, corresponding to the white symbols in c. e–g, Distributions of ligament thickness P(λ) (e), ligament length P(ℓ) (f) and ligament degrees (number of connections per ligament) P(k) (g), for λ0 = 0.1; all exhibit a power-law tail. h, Relative density modulation as a function of α for λ0 = 1, averaged over 20 runs for T = 30,000. i–k, Thickness (i), length (j) and degree distribution (k) of SR metamaterials (T = 500, α = 0.5, λ0 = 0.06, averaged over 10 runs) compared with reference systems: hexagonal lattice, square lattice and Voronoi tessellation (all at \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \)).

In the model, the length of newly added ligaments decreases with time as \({{\ell }}_{t}\approx {((1-{\sum }_{j=0}^{t-1}{{\ell }}_{j}{\lambda }_{j})/t)}^{1/2}\), as the remaining undivided area follows the recursive relation \({A}_{t}={A}_{t-1}-{\lambda }_{0}{A}_{t-1}^{1/2}{(t-1)}^{-(\alpha +1/2)}\) (Supplementary Information, section 1.1). This reduction is governed by the convergence of the sum \({A}_{t}^{\mathrm{total}}=1-{\sum }_{j=0}^{t-1}{{\ell }}_{j}{\lambda }_{j}\approx 1-{\lambda }_{0}{\sum }_{j=0}^{t-1}{A}_{j-1}^{1/2}{(j-1)}^{-(\alpha +1/2)}\), whose asymptotic behaviour defines two distinct phases (Fig. 1c): jammed and tunable-density states. If α < 1/2, or if α > 1/2 and \({\lambda }_{0} > {({{\ell }}_{0}\zeta (2\alpha ))}^{-1}\), where \(\zeta \) is the Riemann zeta function and ℓ0 ≈ 0.946 (ref. 40), the sum diverges, hence \({A}_{\infty }^{\mathrm{total}}\to 0\), resulting in complete coverage and jamming (Fig. 1c, orange area). For other parameters, the sum converges, and the system reaches a finite tunable relative density (that is, fill fraction) \(\bar{\rho }\approx {{\ell }}_{0}{\lambda }_{0}\zeta (\alpha +\beta )\), where β is the ligament length decay rate (Fig. 1c, yellow area), a phase of particular interest for lightweight materials41. As we show in Fig. 1d, systems with small α are physically realizable across length scales via additive manufacturing processes such as vat photopolymerization, whereas higher α designs require submicrometre resolution offered by two-photon lithography (Supplementary Information, section 2.2).

Both regular and irregular architectures have unique characteristic length scales, determined by either a unique or narrowly varying coordination number (degree, k), length (ℓ) and ligament thickness (λ)14,42. The distinguishing feature of an SR network is its lack of characteristic scale for any of these three defining dimensions. Indeed, as the ligament thickness follows λt = λ0t−α, the overall thickness distribution P(λ) follows the power-law distribution P(λ) ≈ λ−(1+1/α) (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Information, section 1.2).

To determine the ligament length distribution, we must consider that the ligament lengths decay as ℓt = ℓ0t−β, where β = 0.5, except at the boundary, where β = α (Supplementary Information, section 1.1.1). As we derive in Supplementary Information, section 1.3, the resulting ligament lengths follow an Erlang distribution: for high ℓ (\({\ell }\approx \sqrt{2}\)) the distribution decays as a power-law tail P(ℓ) ≈ ℓ−μ with μ = 1 + 1/β, whereas for low ℓ it increases with exponent μ = −1 (Fig. 1f).

A fundamental network characteristic is the degree (or coordination number) distribution3,4,29. It is tempting to consider each ligament intersection a node and each connecting segment a link, an approach often adopted in physical networks43,44. However, in the SR model, ligament thickness spans multiple orders of magnitude, prompting us to adopt a representation frequently used in transportation networks23,45, where each ligament (or road) is conceptualized as a single node, and intersections are represented as edges (Fig. 1b). In this representation, the degree distribution P(k) follows the power law P(k) ≈ k−γ with γ = 3 (Fig. 1g, Supplementary Fig. 11 and Supplementary Information, section 1.4). The power law emerges owing to a spatial preferential attachment29: longer ligaments have linearly more opportunities to intersect with newly added ligaments (Supplementary Fig. 11).

Taken together, we find that in SR networks, all three salient features of the system’s architecture—coordination number (degree, k), length (ℓ) and ligament thickness (λ)—follow power-law distributions. In other words, whereas in conventional material systems k, ℓ and λ are constant or vary in a very narrow range, in SR materials they span several orders of magnitude within the same sample, encoding the coexistence of many different length scales. The unique heterogeneity of the SR network raises an notable question of whether SR metamaterials possess physical properties distinct from those of single-scale natural and architected materials.

We begin by determining the mechanical characteristics of SR microstructures, comparing them against three single-scale microstructures frequently used in engineering applications: the square lattice, the hexagonal lattice and the irregular Voronoi tessellation. By generating finite domains of each microstructure with a sufficiently large number of characteristic features, we confirm that the P(λ), P(ℓ) and P(k) for square and hexagonal lattices result in delta functions, whereas the Voronoi tessellation is characterized by narrow distributions (Fig. 1i–k).

Industry observers note that to extend the comparison beyond theoretical differences between architectures, we experimentally and numerically determined the mechanical properties of these metamaterial microstructures, using vat photopolymerization 3D-printing (Methods) to fabricate centimetre-scale specimens out of elastic–plastic polymer resin (Fig. 1d, left), with a feature resolution of approximately 100 μm. We focused on SR systems with T = 500—a point where the homogenized mechanical properties show convergence and boundary effects are minimized (Supplementary Information, section 2.3). Given this feature resolution and the 500-ligament constraint, the relative densities achievable with vat photopolymerization 3D-printing ranged between \(20 \% \le \bar{\rho }\le 75 \% \) (Supplementary Information, section 2.5); we can also demonstrate lower fill fractions within the tunable-density phase (\(\bar{\rho } < 20 \% \); Fig. 1c) through the use of two-photon lithography (Fig. 1d, right) with submicrometre minimum feature sizes. Next, we characterized the linear and nonlinear mechanical responses in the quasi-static and dynamic regimes of these SR microstructures.

To determine the linear-elastic response of SR metamaterials, we performed computational homogenization using the finite-element method. Imposing affine boundary conditions, we extracted a directional modulus Ed in each direction ed and calculated a non-dimensional modulus \(\bar{E}\equiv {E}_{{\rm{d}}}/{E}_{{\rm{s}}}\), where Es is Young’s modulus of the constituent material (Methods).

It has been revealed that at a relative density of \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \), we performed this analysis on the three single-scale systems (square, hexagonal and Voronoi) and SR geometries, demonstrated by the representative realizations in Fig. 2a, via polar representations of \(\overline{E}\) as a function of the probing direction. While the hexagonal and Voronoi structures show a near-constant \(\overline{E}\) in all orientations (that is, an isotropic stiffness response, as expected46; Fig. 2a(i),(ii)), the square lattice is highly anisotropic, displaying high stiffness parallel to its struts and minimal stiffness in any other direction (Fig. 2a(iii)). In contrast to these near extremes, we find the behaviour of the SR structures to be modulated by α: for α ≈ 0, the stiffness is nearly isotropic (Fig. 2a(iv)); and as α → 1, a principal orientation of maximum stiffness emerges (Fig. 2a(v),(vi)). Altogether, the full set of SR architectures exhibited highly tunable (an)isotropy exceeding that of the three conventional geometries combined.

The right panels show the experimentally measured directional stiffness for SR materials with α = 0 (vii),  α = 0.1 (viii) and α = 0.3 (ix), validating the theoretically predicted stiffness anisotropy. The black filled circles (vii)–(ix) show the experimentally measured anisotropy. c, As the decay parameter α increases, anisotropy arises because the maximum specific directional stiffness increases, whereas the minimum specific directional stiffness is constant. The solid lines represent the mean across all samples, and the shaded regions correspond to a ±1 standard deviation from the mean value. d, Phase diagram in (α, λ0) space of the anisotropy, which functions as a design map for a tunable anisotropic response across relative densities \(0.2\le \bar{\rho }\le 0.75\). e, Temporal evolution of ligament strain energy during the SR generation process. f, Snapshots at fixed time t are shown for two example ligaments in an SR network, corresponding to the markers in e. g, Universal scaling of the ligament energy Ui as a function of the degree, ki, thickness, λi and angle, θi. In a recent development, to quantify the mechanical implications of this observed range in anisotropy across the full space of SR architectures, we plot the elastic anisotropy ratio \({\eta }_{{\rm{E}}}\equiv {E}_{\min }/{E}_{\max }\in (0,1]\), where \({E}_{\text{min}}\equiv \text{min}(\bar{E})\) and \({E}_{\text{max}}\equiv \text{max}(\bar{E})\), as a function of relative density for the reference geometries and 2,600 distinct SR microstructures with different α and λ0 (Fig. 2b). We confirm that the hexagonal lattice (0.87 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.94) and the Voronoi tessellation (0.88 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.97) remain nearly isotropic across a wide range of relative densities. For the square lattice, the anisotropy decreases from ηE = 0.03 at \(\bar{\rho }=20 \% \) to ηE = 0.55 at \(\bar{\rho }=70 \% \). By contrast, we find that the SR materials cover 77% of the available area on the density–anisotropy plot (Fig. 2b), reaching values not accessible to the reference systems. Indeed, by changing α and λ0, we can attain highly anisotropic systems (ηE ≤ 0.2) across a wide range of densities (\(17 \% \le \bar{\rho }\le 64 \% \)) as well as nearly isotropic systems (ηE ≥ 0.85) in the range \(33 \% \le \bar{\rho }\le 72 \% \). Simultaneously, we can generate systems of widely varying anisotropies at any fixed relative density: at \(\bar{\rho }=20 \% \), we span 0.04 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.78; at \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \), we span 0.12 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.88; and at \(\bar{\rho }=70 \% \), we span 0.26 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.93. Directed growth approaches (Supplementary Information, section 2.15) further extend the achievable coverage to more than 96% of the density–anisotropy space.

Sources indicate that to elucidate the origin of this tunable anisotropy, we plot the mass-normalized (that is, specific) minimum and maximum stiffness values (\({E}_{\min }/\bar{\rho },{E}_{\max }/\bar{\rho }\)) as a function of the decay parameter α across the entire sample set (Fig. 2c). Although the minimum specific stiffness is largely independent of α, increasing α while keeping density constant enables an increase in the maximum achievable specific stiffness, leading to robust tunability in the architecture space. This tunable anisotropy is best captured by the (α, λ0) configuration space (Fig. 2d), which demonstrates that anisotropy increases with α and decreases with λ0. To validate our finite-element model predictions and confirm the isotropic and anisotropic responses, we performed uniaxial compression experiments across various SR geometries and orientations, confirming that at constant density increasing α directly leads to greater anisotropy (Fig. 2a(vii)–(ix), Fig. 2b, filled black circles, and Supplementary Information, section 2.7).

Industry observers note that next, we characterized the nonlinear response of SR metamaterials by conducting large-deformation uniaxial compression experiments (Methods) on the 3 reference geometries and SR systems of α = 0, chosen to minimize the impact of elastic anisotropy and emphasize the effects of the heterogeneity of ligament lengths (Fig. 3a; 3 specimens each, all at nominal \(\bar{\rho }=42 \% \); experimental results for SR systems with α > 0 are discussed in Supplementary Information, section 2.11.). It has been revealed that from each stress–strain response, we computed the toughness, measured as the integral under the stress–strain curve to an engineering strain of 40%—before the onset of complete densification. These toughness metrics, when plotted against relative density (Fig. 3b), showcase the ability of SR architectures to match or surpass the mechanical resilience of the three reference architectures.

In a recent development, to understand the deformation mechanisms that lead to these benefits, we extracted still frames from the experiments and computed the areal Jacobian Ji ≡ Ai/Ai,0 of each ith cell (the relative change in void area; Fig. 3c) where Ai,0 and Ai denote the undeformed and deformed cell areas, respectively47. The square lattice was prone to buckling of vertically aligned ligaments, resulting in the observed local maxima in its stress–strain response (Fig. 3a, blue curve). Buckling events began at a single ligament, followed by a horizontal cascade of buckling events that spanned the whole length of the specimen (Fig. 3c(i)), leading to a sudden drop in its load capacity. This process repeated in a layer-by-layer fashion until the entire specimen buckled. Similarly, the hexagonal lattice (teal; Fig. 3c(ii)) also developed wide compaction bands that spanned the width of the lattice. Although the Voronoi tessellation did not succumb to well-defined shear or compaction bands owing to its lacking periodicity, consistent with previous experimental findings48, it exhibited localized compaction near the bottom, ultimately forming a domain of compacted cells that spanned the width of the specimen (purple; Fig. 3c(iii)), whereas unit cells near the top remained largely undeformed.

In contrast, SR architectures lack compaction or shear bands, which can be attributed to the local coexistence of ligaments of different lengths and thicknesses; hence, the failure of the weakest ligament in one domain will not trigger the propagation of contiguous failure pathways (Fig. 3c(iv)). To understand the origin of this diffuse damage, we computationally evaluated the susceptibility of each unsupported ligament section to buckling under a macroscopic deformation (Supplementary Information, section 2.13). We find that the network consists of ligaments characterized by a broad distribution of critical buckling loads, and hence a local buckling event does not trigger a global cascade of instability, explaining the stable macroscopic response. Moreover, selectively removing a range of length scales degrades the load-bearing capacity of the network (Supplementary Information, section 2.14), suggesting that length-scale heterogeneity underlies the robustness of the system.

To further understand this delocalization, we introduce a localization parameter.

Recent findings suggest that where \({\mu }_{i}\equiv \frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{j\in {{\mathcal{B}}}_{r}(i)}{J}_{j}\) is the local average Jacobian of cell i, defined over a neighbourhood \({{\mathcal{B}}}_{r}(i)\) of i containing M cells (Supplementary Information, section 2.10), and N is the total number of cells. As a result, \({\mathcal{L}}\in [0,1]\), where \({\mathcal{L}}=0\) implies that the deformation in every neighbourhood is identical—the ideal case—and \({\mathcal{L}}=1\) indicates that the deformation variation between neighbourhoods is comparable to the deformation variation among all individual cells, corresponding to extreme localization.

In a recent development, for all samples, \({\mathcal{L}}\) initially increases with increasing strain (Fig. 3d); the square and hexagonal lattices exhibit rapidly increasing and high asymptotic \({\mathcal{L}}\) owing to the presence of compaction bands, whereas the disordered Voronoi lattice has lower \({\mathcal{L}}\). Consistently, the SR samples show the lowest value of \({\mathcal{L}}\)—with the localization within \({\mathcal{L}}\le 0.2\) through 25% macroscopic strain, which is 37% lower than the Voronoi geometry—confirming the material’s ability to uniformly distribute damage and offer a macroscopically stable load-bearing capacity. We can further reduce \({\mathcal{L}}\) by selectively nucleating the ligaments in an SR network (Supplementary Information, section 2.12) using a ‘checkerboarding’ approach, allowing us to constrain \({\mathcal{L}}\le 0.08\) through 25% strain, representing a 74% reduction over the Voronoi value.

Looking beyond the quasi-static regime, an ideal impact-absorbing material maximizes the energy dissipated during the impact event while minimizing the peak force49. We performed impact experiments on SR and reference architectures at relative density \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \), using a rigid impactor released with controlled initial energy corresponding to an instantaneous strain rate of \(\mathop{\varepsilon }\limits^{\cdot }=100\,{{\rm{s}}}^{-1}\) at impact.

Using a high-speed camera, we analysed frames during the impact event (Fig. 4a), finding that similar to the quasi-static experiments, the square lattice fails in a layer-by-layer fashion with fractured ligaments localized within sequentially forming horizontal crushing bands. The square lattice revealed a sharp initial peak force that dropped to nearly zero followed by subsequent peaks corresponding to local compactions (Fig. 4b, blue curve). The hexagonal lattice also exhibited extreme localization owing to the fracture of diagonally oriented planes in as little as 2 ms post-impact. Although the Voronoi tessellation diffused damage more effectively, it also showed clear localized crush bands, leading to a high maximum force (Fig. 4b, purple curve). The SR geometry, by contrast, lacks not only well-defined crushing bands but also diffused damage through the structure, leading to the most stable force–time behaviour (Fig. 4b, orange curve), with low initial peak force and a lower compaction force than the Voronoi geometry.

a, The SR system efficiently distributes damage under dynamic impact loading, captured by high-speed photography. Scale bars, 10 mm. b, Force–time data reveal a flat, plateau-like force–time response in the SR materials, compared with the reference architectures (square, hexagonal, triangle, sea-sponge53, and Kagome lattices; Gilbert55, Voronoi, and E-Voronoi48 tessellations; and isotropic (stretch h = 1) k-nearest foams54). c, This corresponds to simultaneous minimization of peak force and maximization of specific energy dissipation during impact. d, Anisotropy and localization under quasi-static loading. All systems have relative density \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \). Localization corresponds to the experimentally observed value at 25% macroscopic strain and anisotropy is computed from finite-element simulations.

We extracted the overall peak force, Fmax, and the change in kinetic energy of the impactor before and after the event, representing the energy dissipated by the architecture, allowing us to measure the specific energy dissipation as.

Recent findings suggest that where mimpactor is the mass of the impactor, mspecimen is the mass of the specimen, and vi and vf represent the impactor velocities before and after the impact event, respectively. In Fig. 4c, we plot Wsp against Fmax, finding that the SR system occupies the optimal space with maximum specific energy dissipation Wsp and minimum peak force Fmax among all reference geometries considered in this work, indicating that the advantageous quasi-static properties of SR materials offer clear benefits under dynamic loading as well.

Recent findings suggest that SR metamaterials also support programmable elastic-wave propagation, owing to their widely tunable elastic anisotropy, fully parameterized with only two parameters (α, λ0). To quantify direction-dependent wave propagation in SR metamaterials, we performed Bloch wave analysis on SR microstructures across the (α, λ0) design space—here reinterpreted as representative volume elements in an infinite tiling (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Information, section 2.16). Leveraging the tunability of SR metamaterials, we designed acoustic metamaterials out of quasi-isotropic SR architectures. Using the effective refractive index concept from optics neff = c0/vs, which compares the wave velocity in the constituent material c0 to the velocity vs of a wave travelling through an SR metamaterial made of the same constituent material, we find that for SR metamaterials, neff spans 1.5 ≤ neff ≤ 8.3 in the (α, λ0) configuration space, demonstrating a substantial range in achievable refractive indices compared with the hexagonal and square lattices, which span 1.0 ≤ neff ≤ 1.9 within the same relative-density limits (\(20 \% \le \bar{\rho }\le 75 \% \); Supplementary Information, section 2.17).

Recent findings suggest that a, SR samples with their corresponding directional velocity polar plots, demonstrating a wide range of achievable space of wave velocities and anisotropy. Curves, matching the colour of their respective geometries, denote the quasi-longitudinal wave velocities, and the green curve represents the wave velocity of the monolithic material. Samples in the grey–black colour scale show the breadth of wave anisotropy achieved and the samples in the rainbow scale demonstrate isotropic SR unit cells used to construct the elastic lens in b. We use each sample as a unit cell, adding a frame with small gaps to provide boundary conditions for building the superstructure. The effective refractive index, neff, is defined as the ratio of the green to blue curves along the x direction. b, One-quarter of a Luneburg-inspired lens constructed from SR samples with varying refractive indices, highlighted by colour (blue, high refractive index; orange, low refractive index). c, Schematic illustrations of the target ray-focusing behaviour of an ideal Luneburg lens (top) and the designed refractive index profile of the full pixelated lens (bottom). d, Steady-state wavefield of the SR elastic Luneburg-like lens showing the elastic perturbation plane source (white) and focal point (red). The elastic wave is focused on the side opposite the source, as evidenced by the radial wave pattern emanating from the focal point. e, The normalized displacement intensity along the y-axis cross-section through the lens focal point (white dashed line in d). The Luneburg-like lens (solid blue curve) exhibits a sharp focal peak, whereas the randomized lens (inset, green dashed curve) demonstrates no noticeable focusing. The residual intensity peak in the randomized lens—three orders of magnitude smaller—arises from weak energy trapping at the elastic circular boundary. A suitable excitation frequency was found in the range f ≈ 646.7 Hz, well within the long-wavelength regime of each pixel in the lens, where the refractive indices are still valid.

It has been revealed that the refractive index tunability of SR microstructures enables multiple elastodynamic functionalities such as wave guiding or lensing, with applications in subwavelength imaging and energy harvesting50,51. We designed a Luneburg-like cylindrical lens of diameter d in a pixelated gradient-index (GRIN) approach52 (Fig. 5b and in Methods), and validated it via steady-state dynamic finite-element method, focusing elastic perturbations from an incident plane wave (Fig. 5c). Displacement fields reveal that waves traversing the lens focus on the opposite side, producing semi-circular wave fronts at the focal point and indicating that SR lenses qualitatively follow Luneburg patterns50. The displacement intensity (squared displacement magnitude) contour along the vertical line through the focal point reveals a peak that is an order of magnitude larger than the side peaks, indicating energy concentration into a region approximately 0.1d wide (Fig. 5d). For comparison, a randomized reference lens constructed by randomly selecting SR cells at each radius produced a focal intensity roughly three orders of magnitude weaker, with a broader peak and side lobes of comparable magnitude, confirming that focusing arises from the GRIN arrangement of the SR pixels. Spanning such a breadth of neff enables the generation of graded materials with smoothly changing acoustic properties over a much larger range than any individual lattice family, achieved by tuning (α, λ0).

Deviating from the single-scale restriction inherent to unit-cell-based architected materials, we drew on advances in network science to introduce and experimentally characterize SR network-based metamaterials. These architectures accommodate orders-of-magnitude variation in ligament thickness, length and connectivity while retaining control over global properties such as density and anisotropy, offering unique mechanical features inaccessible to single-scale systems: highly tunable anisotropy across densities (Fig. 2), delocalized deformation that mitigates catastrophic failure without sacrificing energy absorption (Fig. 3), and the highest specific energy dissipation at the lowest peak force among all considered periodic and disordered reference architectures under dynamic loading (Fig. 4c). Although these remarkable linear and nonlinear properties are not independently unique to SR materials, the framework’s ability to combine both sets it apart from previous architected material designs. Plotting elastic anisotropy against measured localization at \(\bar{\rho }=40 \% \) (Fig. 4d), we find that the ordered Kagome and sea-sponge53 lattices and the disordered Voronoi, E-Voronoi48, k-nearest54 and Gilbert55 systems all delocalize deformation but only near the isotropic limit (Emin/Emax ≈ 1), the triangle and hexagonal lattices remain isotropic yet localize severely (high \({\mathcal{L}}\)), and the square lattice is both anisotropic and highly localized. The SR system is thus the only family spanning the full anisotropy range (0.2 ≤ ηE ≤ 0.9) while staying delocalized, occupying a distinct performance frontier (Fig. 4c,d) well suited to adaptive load-bearing structures, protective gear (for example, helmets), packaging and armour.

Beyond these properties, SR metamaterials offer broad design flexibility (Fig. 6a) through independent control of orientation, seed density and dimensionality, enabling tailored heterogeneity that expands beyond unit-cell constraints—from filling arbitrary non-convex domains (Fig. 6b) to selectively nucleating ligaments in a manner that further minimizes localization (Supplementary Information, section 2.12) or produces extreme anisotropy (Supplementary Information, section 2.9). As a demonstration, we programmed the ligament orientation (θi = f(xi, yi)) and, inspired by the microstructure of Citrus maxima56, the radial seed-density gradient ((xi, yi) ~ ri, where ri is the radial distance of ligament i from the centre) of an SR system to divert load-transfer pathways around a fragile poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) payload (Fig. 6c,d). Photoelastic imaging reveals stress fringes nucleating within the payload for square and hexagonal lattices of equal density, whereas the SR system suppresses them (Fig. 6e(i)–(iii)); nonlinear finite-element simulations confirm that at identical macroscopic strain, the SR-protected payload stress is reduced by up to 4.9-fold (Fig. 6e(iv)–(vii)).

Recent findings suggest that a, The SR framework enables precise control over ligament orientation, allowing the generation of random configurations where angles are selected from a uniform distribution (i), aligned networks using random selections from a prescribed set of angles (ii) and polarized patterns by sampling angles based on a predefined vector field (iii). Nucleation point positions can also be controlled to vary density across the domain, enabling gradient patterns (iv). The model further generalizes to three dimensions through the growth of plates (v) and beams (vi), where two angles specify the orientation of each plate or beam (for more examples, see Supplementary Information, section 1.5). b, SR microstructure generated within a non-convex domain Ω by combining three distinct orientation patterns—random, aligned and polarized—each applied on a different region of the domain. c, Functional design using the SR framework: a microstructure is chosen to fill a given domain under a relative-density constraint in an effort to protect a ‘payload’. d, The SR framework allows simultaneous variation of both the ligament density and orientation. A circular design inspired by the natural microstructure of C. maxima56 is shown, with a linear density gradient in the radial direction combined with a polarized orientation applied to 20% of the initial lines. e, Stress reduction in SR-protected payloads. (i)–(iii) Disk-shaped payloads made of PMMA were characterized using photoelasticity to visualize stresses under nonlinear deformation. Square and hexagonal lattices generate multiple fringes, indicating high internal stress, whereas the SR architecture demonstrates markedly fewer fringes. (v)–(vii) Nonlinear simulations confirm these findings: the SR design reduces the average von Mises stress, \(\bar{\sigma }\), here normalized by the Young’s modulus, Es, on the embedded payload by a factor of up to 4.91 compared with the reference geometries (iv). Scale bars, 10 mm (a,e).

Sources indicate that the sequential generation strategy of the SR system extends naturally to three dimensions by iteratively adding non-crossing plates or beams (Fig. 6a(v),(vi), yielding an analytically defined phase diagram, power-law area and degree distributions, and the same anisotropy trends as in two dimensions—anisotropy increasing with α (Supplementary Information, sections 1.6, 1.7 and 2.18), broadening the SR framework towards lightweight, robust and directionally tunable 3D metamaterials.

Finally, SR materials open opportunities for network science by revealing features inaccessible to networks without a material instantiation. Here link length and thickness—undefined or inconsequential in abstract networks—are fundamental, giving rise to phenomena, from anisotropy to stress propagation, beyond the reach of traditional network models. Taken together, these results suggest that architected network materials could open a rich domain of enquiry for network science.

In a recent development, we evaluated the directional stiffness of the SR and reference geometries in the linear-elastic regime by applying computational homogenization using the finite-element method implemented with the commercial software package ABAQUS/Standard. Owing to the aperiodicity of SR geometries, classical homogenization methods relying on periodic boundary conditions do not apply. Previous approaches to extracting effective elastic properties of aperiodic materials include prescribing a displacement-controlled uniaxial strain to estimate Young’s modulus along a given direction, provided the representative volume is sufficiently large57, or applying a set of mutually orthogonal affine boundary conditions to estimate the full stiffness tensor C, which provides an approximation of effective stiffness58. Assuming that the base material is isotropic and linear elastic (with material parameters Es and νs), we adopted the latter approach to characterize the complete elastic response of the SR system. Samples were discretized using six-node, quadratic plane-strain continuum elements (CPE6) with a mesh size obtained via a mesh convergence study (Supplementary Information, section 2.4). For SR geometries, meshing was performed using an adaptive strategy where the seed size for each strut was computed based on its width. Thus, the total number of degrees of freedom and the minimum element size varied across geometries.

Sources indicate that samples were fabricated using vat photopolymerization using a desktop 3D-printer (Phrozen Sonic Mini 8K). Geometries generated using the model were converted into three-dimensional solid bodies by adding a prescribed, uniform thickness that yielded a plane-strain response (that is, avoiding out-of-plane deformation). To aid in experimental repeatability, the specimens were printed with monolithic top and bottom plates with a thickness equal to 5% of the height of the architecture. For the nonlinear and impact experiments, we used a commercially available resin (Anycubic Tough Resin 2.0) with a high elongation to break (for representative stress–strain curves of monolithic specimens, see Supplementary Information, section 2.1). For the experiments within the linear regime, we selected a stiffer but more brittle resin (Formlabs Clear v4) so that linear-elastic properties could be more readily extracted. In each case, we printed using the manufacturer’s recommended settings for exposure parameters at a layer height of 0.025 mm. After printing, samples were washed in isopropanol and dried in air. The dried samples were then kept in storage away from ambient ultraviolet exposure and tested 72 hours after printing.

According to recent reports, quasi-static compression experiments were performed on an Instron 5500 series load frame under displacement control. The lower compression platen was held fixed and the upper platen was given a prescribed downwards velocity corresponding to a (quasi-static) strain rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1. To perform the areal Jacobian calculations, greyscale photographs were taken at regular intervals during loading. These photographs were thresholded to separate the printed beams from void spaces. A custom image tracking script using the Python library OpenCV was used to track the areas of each void as deformation progressed.

Drop weight impact experiments were conducted using an Instron Dynatup drop tower. We used an impactor mass of 6.2 kg and a constant initial height, set to 0.8020 m above the sample, to ensure a velocity at impact of approximately 4 m s−1 (equivalently, an instantaneous strain rate of 100 s−1 at impact). We used a high-speed camera to record snapshots at 9,000 Hz during the experiment.

We assembled a pixelated GRIN lens from SR unit cells to create a Luneburg-like cylindrical lens, which focuses a plane wave to a point image on the far side. The lens is constructed from quasi-isotropic SR representative volume elements tessellated in space to achieve a circular footprint with neff changing radially, selected from an SR library (Supplementary Fig. 42) to match the required refractive indices for each lens region. The Luneburg lens refractive index profile follows \(n=\sqrt{2-{(r/R)}^{2}}\), where r is a radial position in the lens and R is the radius of the lens; hence, the refractive index spans \(1.0\le n\le \sqrt{2}\). The circular lens footprint with R = d/2 = 2.5 is discretized into smaller pixels of side length l = 0.25, so that l/d = 0.05—this choice was made to strike a balance between lens profile accuracy and simulation complexity. We discretized the theoretical profile curve to seven distinct concentric regions equally radially spaced, whose refractive index value was calculated at the central radial location of its pixel. We constructed the lens out of quasi-isotropic SR unit cells—with minimum to maximum directional velocity ratio of vmin/vmax > 0.85—to suppress lens aberration as much as possible. Because the SR unit-cell refractive index library does not include some of the lower values of n required for the Luneburg lens, we offset the lens n profile and prioritize maintaining its absolute shape when choosing SR unit cells to fill the seven regions; this offset introduces a slight aberration but the focal point is maintained. Rigorously, we use an optimization algorithm to find the profile offset that minimizes the sum of the squared differences between the n values of the chosen unit cells and the ideal Luneburg lens with the added offset—that is, \(\min {\sum }_{i=1}^{7}{({n}_{\mathrm{pixel},i}-{n}_{\mathrm{ideal}}(r))}^{2}\) where npixel,i and nideal(r) are the refractive indices of the pixelated lens at region i and the theoretical refractive index of a Luneburg lens evaluated at that region, respectively. When assembling the lens, we add a thin disconnected border to each unit cell to ensure assembly compatibility and energy propagation between adjacent pixels. The lens was simulated in ABAQUS/Standard using a linear-elastic constituent material model. The final assembled lens was inserted into a background medium composed of the same constituent isotropic linear-elastic material, and the background was surrounded by a moderately dissipative medium which reduces reflections from its edges. The lens is excited by a plane wave of width d placed at a distance d/2 away.

To numerically evaluate the nonlinear behaviour of the architecture-payload system in Fig. 6, we used the finite-element method implemented with the commercial software package ABAQUS/Explicit. As in the elastic case, both the architecture and payload domains were discretized using modified six-node, quadratic plane-strain elements (CPE6M) with the same mesh density in the architecture. The architecture was modelled as elastic–plastic with hardening and the material properties were taken from experimental data (Supplementary Information, section 2.1). The rigid payload was modelled as isotropic and linear elastic with an elastic modulus 106 times that of the architecture. The compression platens were modelled as analytical rigid surfaces, with the bottom surface encastred and the top surface given a prescribed downwards velocity consistent with the experimental strain rate \(\mathop{\varepsilon }\limits^{\cdot }=5\times 1{0}^{-3}\,{{\rm{s}}}^{-1}\). We used the built-in general contact algorithm between all surfaces (including self-contact within the architecture), with a friction coefficient of 0.2 defining the tangential behaviour and a ‘hard’ pressure-overclosure condition defining the normal behaviour.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As reports grow suggesting West Ham will be back in the market place for another striker this winter, names are thrown into the ether  as suitable ‘targets’ and one in particular is the subject of a report today which, in the face of it, looks like good business.
  • There’s a massive catch however and West Ham will surely steer well clear after their experiences of blowing £27 million on a crocked Niclas Fullkrug who then spent a season and a half on the sick list.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As reports grow suggesting West Ham will be back in the market place for another striker this winter, names are thrown into the ether  as suitable ‘targets’ and one in particular is the subject of a report today which, in the face of it, looks like good business.

There’s a massive catch however and West Ham will surely steer well clear after their experiences of blowing £27 million on a crocked Niclas Fullkrug who then spent a season and a half on the sick list.

Hence when EFL specialist web site the72.co.uk repeats the suggestion that ‘West Ham should look at Leeds United’s Mateo Joseph ‘ there’s a very loud warning bell ringing.

Mateo Joseph – likely a long road ahead to regain match fitness.

According to recent reports, on the face of it the forward who can play as an out-and-out striker or a right winger – could be useful as a Bowen back up – seems a decent shout but one look at his injury record should see West Ham run ing for cover. Joseph is still recovering from a huge ACL injury suffered whilst on loan at La Liga side Mallorca last season.

In a recent development, which makes him a non-starter for me. And hopefully Nils Koppen will have the Niclas Fullkrug story at the front of his mind as cautionary tale to ensure West Ham don’t keep on making the same mistakes with crocked strikers.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been looking into how many England caps have been picked up by Newcastle United and Sunderland players.
  • So this is England Caps picked up by the players of Newcastle United and Sunderland whilst the individuals were at these clubs.
  • Last night England delivered a superb 3-2 away victory against Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been looking into how many England caps have been picked up by Newcastle United and Sunderland players.

So this is England Caps picked up by the players of Newcastle United and Sunderland whilst the individuals were at these clubs. Not England Caps picked up before or after their times playing on Tyneside and Wearside.

Last night England delivered a superb 3-2 away victory against Spain.

The World Cup winners very lucky that they only lost by one, England roaring into a 3-0 lead and then a trio of individual errors threatening to undermine a brilliant team performance.

In that match Lewis Hall started and was his usual brilliant self, picking up his 9th cap.

Dan Burn coming off the bench late on to win his 12th cap and help see England over the line.

Those two international appearances for the United pair in Madrid now make it 347 England Caps picked up by 44 different Newcastle United players (whilst they were also playing for NUFC).

Having a look at the Sunderland players and their stats, in the entire SAFC history only 101 England Caps have been won by 29 Mackem players..

Recent findings suggest that eight different Newcastle United players played for England during the four and a half years Eddie Howe was in charge at NUFC, with seven of them signed by him. Under Eddie Howe there was almost 70 England caps won by Newcastle United players whilst also playing for NUFC. Now Lewis Hall and Dan Burn picking up what will hopefully the the first of many under Matthias Jaissle.

Jermain Defoe picked up two England Caps nine years ago and he is the only Sunderland player to appear for England since 2012.

Indeed, only nine England Caps have been won by Sunderland players since 1999. Only 21 England Caps for the Mackems in the last 50 years and eight of those 21 were picked up by Kevin Phillips.

The entire Sunderland history of 101 England Caps could be exceeded by their old mate Jordan Pickford in the near future, he has 94 England Caps whilst playing for Everton.

Intriguingly, Sunderland are a distant third when it comes to the north east clubs, as when it comes to England Caps it is now Newcastle United 347, Middlesbrough players 167 and then Sunderland on that total of 101.
