📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 11:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 12:52 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Carlo Ancelotti hit out at an 'inexperienced' referee after the Brazil boss and captain Raphinha were sent off in the closing stages of their shock 3-2 defeat by Japan.
  • Security staff were required to enter the pitch at full time to separate players from the officials, with Brazil having been left furious over the nature of Japan's stoppage time winner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 11:31 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 12:52 EST, 14 November 2026.

Carlo Ancelotti hit out at an 'inexperienced' referee after the Brazil boss and captain Raphinha were sent off in the closing stages of their shock 3-2 defeat by Japan.

Security staff were required to enter the pitch at full time to separate players from the officials, with Brazil having been left furious over the nature of Japan's stoppage time winner.

Ancelotti and Raphinha, who had been substituted, were among those to furiously protest following Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's late strike.

Singaporean referee Jansen Foo Chuan Hui had allowed play to continue after Takumi Minamino had made multiple challenges on Brazil midfielder Joao Gomes, before eventually coming away with the ball.

Amid Brazilian appeals for a foul, Japan launched a late attack with Sakamoto ultimately lifting the ball over goalkeeper Pedro Morisco.

Brazilian protests continued despite Japan's winner being confirmed by VAR, with Ancelotti and Raphinha being shown red cards by the referee for their reactions.

Security staff intervened after Brazil stars confronted the referee after their 3-2 defeat by Japan.

Carlo Ancelotti was sent off as Brazil were beaten in stoppage time in their friendly in Singapore.

Ancelotti criticised the 'inexperienced' referee following the match and revealed he had been told he had been sent off for failing to control his bench.

🚨🚨| Raphinha and Carlo Ancelotti have been SENT OFF for Protesting. 🟥😳 pic.twitter.com/YoXrZW9N0U.

'He gave me the red card because he said I was not able to control the bench, and that all the players were on the field, that is the reason,' Ancelotti said.

Ancelotti added: 'A pity the result, because we don't like to lose the game, but we have to look at what we did well. There are many things. Some players who played for the first time, who showed good quality. For 70 minutes, the team was good.

'The result, obviously, is conditioned by the attitude of the referee, who did not blow the whistle.

'But it's not his fault; it was a high-level match, and I think he didn't have the experience to manage this type of match.'.

Barcelona star Raphinha claimed post-match that Brazil had also been angered over a potential handball in the build-up to Japan's opening goal, as well as seeing a penalty appeal waved away.

'First of all, I'd like to take this opportunity to apologise for my behaviour and for being sent off,' Raphinha told Globo.

'Sometimes it's hard to keep calm, especially after what I felt were so many refereeing errors during the match. I tried to speak to him several times, and not once did I feel he was open to discussion. I believe that he made many errors throughout the game, and that is unacceptable.

'In my view, their first goal involved a foul where the opponent took the ball off me with his hand. I think it's a foul, but I can understand why it wasn't given based on the current law.

Brazil captain Raphinha was also dismissed amid their protests over Japan's winning goal.

Brazil had been convinced there had been a foul in the build-up to Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's winner.

In a recent development, 'Then there was the penalty in the first half, in my opinion it was a penalty, but he said no. Then, for their third goal, there was a clear foul on Joao Gomes. With the help of VAR, he eventually allowed the goal. It's very difficult not to talk about the refereeing.'.

Brazil had fallen 2-0 down in the friendly with Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura scoring in the opening 20 minutes at Singapore's National Stadium.

Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr scored twice to level the match before Sakamoto's controversial late winner.

It is the second time Japan have beaten Brazil 3-2 in the past 18 months, but the five-time world champions did win 2-1 in their last-32 meeting at this summer's World Cup.

#2348. Writing’s on the wall for West Ham stalwart’s international career

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (289 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Claretandhugh ↗ Open Full Page

Writing’s on the wall for West Ham stalwart’s international career

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (289 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that time catches up with all of us, footballers just the same.
  • That, sadly, is likely to be the outcome for Czech stalwart and former captain Tomas Soucek who found himself an unused substitute last night after appearing for just five minutes in his countries’ previous game – during which Tornado Tom’s mistake in added time gifted Spain the injury time second goal in their 2 – 0 defeat of the Czechs.
  • A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer shows his fighting spirit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that time catches up with all of us, footballers just the same. Few are given much indication that the writing is on the wall, until suddenly that place which was automatically theirs is going to a younger, fitter, faster team mate – and then, suddenly, without a fanfare, almost always without even a ‘thank you’ –  it is over.

That, sadly, is likely to be the outcome for Czech stalwart and former captain Tomas Soucek who found himself an unused substitute last night after appearing for just five minutes in his countries’ previous game – during which Tornado Tom’s mistake in added time gifted Spain the injury time second goal in their 2 – 0 defeat of the Czechs.

A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer shows his fighting spirit.

You’d think it unlikely that Soucek will make the squad in the March window, after being virtually discarded for the two Nations League games just gone – both of which his Czech Republic side lost.

Hopefully it’ll give the veteran a little more gusto to complete the job and see his West Ham side over the line and promoted back to the Premier League – which would be a fitting swan song for Soucek who’d be 32 next season and probably a bit-part player if the Hammers make it back to the top tier.

Industry observers note that at least it’d mean domestically, he could go out at the top. Which he thoroughly deserves after more than 250 West Ham caps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s been a season of major renewals so far for Milan, and they’re not yet done. In fact, there are a few core players who they are looking to tie down to longer-term deals and Rabiot is among them.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Newcastle United defence has been the subject of much focus this season.
  • So has the criticism that’s come the way of the Newcastle United defence been fair?
  • In the ten Premier League matches so far, this has been the story of the Newcastle United defence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Newcastle United defence has been the subject of much focus this season.

Not a lot of the debate on it has been positive.

So has the criticism that’s come the way of the Newcastle United defence been fair?

In the ten Premier League matches so far, this has been the story of the Newcastle United defence.

The back four in each of the games:.

Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Liverpool 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Spurs 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Bournemouth 2 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Leeds 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 2 Hull 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Coventry 4 Newcastle 1 Lewis Miley, Malick Thiaw, Sven Botman, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Aston Villa 1 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Crystal Palace 0 Newcastle 2 Amar Dedić, Fabian Schar, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Newcastle 0 Everton 1 Amar Dedić, Malick Thiaw, Dan Burn, Lewis Hall – Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

It has been revealed that what I think should be acknowledged first of all, is that we have lacked a settled Newcastle United defence. Injuries playing havoc.

Secondly, there has been undeniable improvement. The Newcastle United defence leaked 13 goals in the opening six Premier League matches, only three goals conceded in the last four. In the last six and half hours (including added time) of Premier League action, United conceding just those three goals, an average of around a goal conceded each 130 minutes following the defeat at Coventry.

This is not to say the United defence were almost faultless, more a case of they are improving.

Industry observers note that when you look at those three goals that were conceded most recently in the Premier League, it gives added information. The Villa goal came when a cross from the right eluded Lewis Miley, a midfielder playing out of position at right-back. The Everton one was pure and simply a poor error from Lukas Hornicek who allowed a low standard cross to squirm under. Then the one at Fulham came via deflections off both Thiaw (in the build up) and Burn (to turn it beyond Hornicek.

Yes the opposition had other chances in these games but not loads.

Reality is as well that if Newcastle United had managed at the other end to score a couple of goals in each of these last four matches then it would have been 12 points out of 12 in the last quartet of Premier League games.

That is very different to the opening half dozen EPL matches, where Newcastle United scored six goals in the four games against Liverpool, Coventry, Leeds and Bournemouth but that only brought two points from a possible 12. The Newcastle United defending a lot better against Tottenham and Hull for the two victories early on, with only a single goal conceded in more than three hours of football against that pair.

Now though I think things could go to another level again with this Newcastle United defence, if a bit of fair luck starts going our way on the injury and fitness front.

An international level Newcastle United defence.

In a recent development, lewis Hall is brilliant, for England and Newcastle United. Surely no doubters amongst you on that one.

Dan Burn has been a huge miss in the opening seven Premier League matches this season. No coincidence only two goals conceded in the three EPL matches he has started on his return after a length injury spell. He has now backed that up with how he has performed for England in recent days.

We saw last season how good Malick Thiaw can be and I think the Fulham match definitely suggested than alongside Dan Burn we could at last have the best available partnership in place finally, of the current NUFC squad. Thiaw has started the last three Germany matches under Jurgen Klopp and they have only conceded one goal.

Industry observers note that tino Livramento was back in the Premier League matchday squad at Fulham and these couple of weeks should have brought him along further. For me there is no doubt about Tino’s quality, the problem has been getting him injury free and back to full fitness on a consistent basis.

Lukas Hornicek has had an up and down start with Newcastle United but taking everything into consideration, I think he has shown plenty to suggest he can do well, especially if he has a regular back four in front of him who have the capacity to give him decent protection week in week out.

Having the three England internationals and our German international making up a Newcastle United back four has huge potential to build the kind of solid platform NUFC need this season.

If Tino Livramento continues to have injury and fitness issues, I believe Amar Dedić is capable of doing a very good job in his absence. I think the Bosnian defender has done okay overall so far, having made the huge step up to the Premier League and walking into what was a chaotic NUFC situation.

If we can have the Newcastle United defence performing consistently well, that then gives us far more chance of improving things further up the pitch, helping United to have far more control of matches and giving a much more positive platform for midfielders and attacking players to prosper.

England goals coming from Kane (pen), Konsa and White, though it could have been five or six up if Thomas Tuchel’s side had turned their superiority into the goals it deserved.

‘Because of Quansah’s lack of concentration.’.

‘It was Quansah who got caught in possession, even if it was a foul.

‘Why is everyone calling out Quansah and not Gordon?’.

‘Not only him, why did Gordon after a perfect performance try showboating in the middle? He had passes on and declined them to look good. He’s a brilliant player, no need.’.

‘Hopefully one day when five nil down someone will put him in the stand.’.

‘He’s been bigged up on the strength of a handful of early performances.

Overrated. And goes down in ‘agony’ if an opposition player gets closer than a yard to him.’.

‘Lewis Hall played well against him – so much belief.’.

‘What a game against the world champions and arguably the best England performance in many years.

‘They look like a club side now – he’s built something.’.

Frank then stabilised Brentford in the top-flight, with league finishes of 13th, 9th and 16th across the following three seasons.’.

The official release going on to say: ‘In 2024/25, Frank once again secured a top-half finish at the Gtech Community Stadium, and guided the Bees to a run of just one defeat in their final eight league games. Frank won plaudits for his final season in West London, when only four other teams scored more goals than Brentford, and was subsequently nominated for the Premier League Manager of the Year award, before moving across London to join Tottenham Hotspur. Prior to his time in England, Frank managed his country at various youth levels, as well as Brøndby in his native Denmark, leading them to consecutive top-four finishes and qualification for the UEFA Europa League.’.

In a recent development, however, after playing the full game as Germany won 3-1 away against Serbia on Friday, Monday sees Jurgen Klopp dropping to the bench/resting Malick Thiaw for Monday night’s home game against the Netherlands. With Schlotterbeck and Tah starting at the heart of defence.

Earlier on Monday, another full match and international victory for Newcastle United’s Ousmane Diabate, the exciting midfield prospect played the full match as the 19-year-old helped Guinea to a 3-1 AFCON qualifying group win over Eritrea.

Ousmane Diabaté was still only 18 but already a full international for Guinea and first choice in the Turkey top tier for Gençlerbirliği playing as a defensive midfielder, when it was announced officially by the club in early September that Newcastle United had signed him.

In a recent development, the progress of the transfer of Ousmane Diabaté to Newcastle United was covered extensively in the Turkish media across August, eventually reported that a £3m deal had been agreed, with a guaranteed £2.7m plus another £300,000 in future add-ons. It was also stated that Ousmane Diabaté would be staying on loan with the Turkish club but Newcastle United able to recall him in January if they decided to.

Gençlerbirliği manager Metin Diyadin had this to say at the end of August about Ousmane Diabaté and his move to Newcastle United.

Recent findings suggest that “Ousmane Diabaté was playing in the youth team. We brought him into the team and because he came from Africa, there was a contract process involved. He has very high potential. We finalised his sale to Newcastle United. He is at the moment playing for us on loan. He is a very mature player for his age. He has good game vision and technical ability. I think he will reach different levels as he plays more. I’m really curious how our teams [in Turkey] didn’t see this in him. We transferred him to England.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Steven Gerrard has offered a theory as to why Alexis Mac Allister has looked so resurgent this season compared to last.

The midfielder was one of the Reds’ most disappinting players of a dreadful 2025/26 campaign, especially having been such a key component in the preceding Premier League title triumph, but he’s been playing near to his best since Andoni Iraola took charge in the summer.

Speaking on The Overlap Daily (via Liverpool Echo), our former captain claimed that the 27-year-old subconsciously let his performance levels drop last season as he was privately consumed by trying to retain the World Cup with Argentina.

According to recent reports, gerrard said of Mac Allister: “I’ve loved him this season. I think last year, like a lot of the Argentinian players, they had a bit of a distraction with the World Cup coming up.

“It’s the way they are. The World Cup takes over everything in their lives, and I lived that with Emiliano Martínez when I was at Aston Villa. I just think it becomes a priority.

“I think it becomes a bit of a distraction. It becomes the most crucial thing in their lives, to be ready and not injured and make sure that the national team is the priority.

“I think with a lot of the Argentina players, I’m sure a lot of managers, if they watch this, will say: ‘Yeah, I’ve experienced that.’”.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

It’s an interesting theory that Gerrard has put forward to explain why Mac Allister’s performances from last season to this have been so chalk and cheese.

Many footballers consider the World Cup as the pinnacle of their careers, and the Liverpool midfielder represents a nation where the sport is nothing short of an obsession.

Only the 27-year-old could truthfully answer whether or not he let his levels dip in 2025/26 because he was prioritising the global tournament in North America, but from a Reds perspective we’d hope that isn’t the case.

As a player employed by LFC, Mac Allister has a duty to give full commitment to representing the club. As disappointing as his performances were last season, though, we wouldn’t go as far as accusing him of not giving less than 100%, which’d be a serious indictment of an elite footballer.

Thankfully, the Argentine has looked much more like his usual self since August, to the point where Troy Deeney suggested that he would even inspire Liverpool to nudge their way into the Premier League title race if he maintains or improves further upon his current standards.

The 27-year-old has been vocal about his contract situation at Anfield, but if he keeps playing the way that he has been, securing a newly introduced deal for him should become a matter of priority for sporting director Richard Hughes.

In this, the second week of the second international break of the season, there’s an understandable eagerness amongst fans to get back to the serious business of league football again this coming weekend.

However there is still a crucial fixture tonight, before the autumn internationals are concluded, in which West Ham supporters should take an interest.

Greece against Serbia in the UEFA Nations League Group A hardly sets the pulse racing as a neutral: It’s normally a game I could happily ignore but it takes on a special meaning after West Ham’s Dinos Mavropanos performed so poorly in the crushing 7 – 0 defeat by the Netherlands last time out.

Consequently I will be taking a bit of an interest in this somewhat obscure game to see how West Ham’s number 15 is looking after such a demoralising result three days ago,.

West Ham need Mavropanos to return having put the 7 – 0 thrashing firmly behind him.

West Ham’s main man took a bit of a pasting in the Greek media after the game, in what was described as the ‘blackest night‘ for Greek football.

West Ham, already without Maximilian Kilman, remember, banned for the upcoming Saturday tie against Preston North End, will be keeping everything crossed that their one remaining senior centre-back has a solid evening facing up to the likes of Mitrovic, Jovic and co.

Scott Parker already has a selection dilemma over bringing in teenager Airidas Golambeckis or loanee Morato to replace Kilman.

The last thing he or West Ham need is another shaky Mavropanos performance tonight and a return to the ‘Mavropanic’ days of the past – which another heavy defeat could usher back in.

Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis1. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function2,3, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities4,5,6,7,8. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

So much pace and potential, not enough positive impact... surely Scotland must now redefine the role of Ben Gannon-Doak?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 12:41 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 13:14 EST, 14 November 2026.

In an age where much of the football on show in the English Premier League is so robotic as to be almost unwatchable, flashes of individual brilliance are increasingly becoming things to be cherished.

Across his time at Liverpool and Bournemouth, Ben Gannon-Doak has sporadically distinguished himself as someone who can light up a game by doing something out of the blue and out of the ordinary.

As many a defender will testify, that electric burst of pace across a short distance makes him unplayable at times. He has an X-factor which sets him apart from the crowd.

According to recent reports, what a shame that injuries have restricted his number of appearances to this point. Since moving south from Celtic in 2022, including a loan spell with Middlesbrough, Gannon-Doak has played fewer than 50 times.

At the very time in his career when he could have done with smoothing off the rough edges, he’s spent far too long rehabilitating from one setback or another.

In the build-up to Friday’s match with North Macedonia, Sebastien Pocognoli spoke about how encouraged he was that the player was finally seeing more game time on the south coast, partly as a result of the team’s maiden voyage in Europe.

Ben Gannon-Doak started in a right wing-back role and had an energetic yet frustrating night.

Recent findings suggest that the hope of all concerned was that the recent run of matches which the winger had so evidently needed would translate into a more accomplished display in a Scotland jersey. Alas, this proved to be wishful thinking.

Even against very ordinary opposition, Gannon-Doak’s display proved to be another frustrating watch for the Tartan Army.

In a recent development, time and time again, he brought them to the edge of their seats by facing up a white jersey and seemingly disappearing in a puff of smoke towards the line. Rarely, however, did the end product materialise.

For a winger with such blinding speed to continually struggle with the all-notable final ball is a difficult thing to repeatedly witness.

We shall never know, of course, if the player’s crossing ability would be better by this stage if he hadn’t endured such wretched luck with injuries. But you suspect it’s now just about as good as it’s ever going to be.

The trouble for Pocognoli is that the quality of the delivery from wing-backs into the penalty box is arguably the most vital facet of his preferred 3-4-3 system.

When it breaks down, as it did so often against the group outsiders, the whole thing threatens to grind to a halt.

Gannon-Doak's crossing remains an area of concern for Scotland given his wide position.

In a recent development, on his record-equalling 102nd cap, Andy Robertson was also guilty of being wasteful on the other flank. Given we know what the skipper has delivered down the years, though, we can write that off as merely a bad night at the office.

The difference with Gannon-Doak is that we’ve rarely seen him tear it up on the flank in a Scotland jersey. So much pace and potential. Not enough positive outcomes when it comes to delivering crosses. In 21 matches, he has three assists and one goal. Those aren’t great numbers.

Just how long do you persevere with a player who doesn’t look to have the requisite skill set for such a specialised and vital position?

Aaron Hickey clearly doesn’t have the pace of the man who he replaced late on, yet he’s hardly a slouch. He is, though, more switched on defensively. And he does know how to cross a football.

It was telling that Gannon-Doak’s most positive contribution of the night against the group outsiders came when he left his station to move infield and take Oli McBurnie’s pass in his stride with the score standing at one-apiece.

According to recent reports, his surge towards the goal initially looked like it had been hampered by a heavy touch only for VAR to correctly identify that he’d been impeded by the goalkeeper. He earned his corn in that moment.

John McGinn’s conversion from 12 yards, his second goal of the night, spared Pocognoli’s blushes after a display which didn’t exactly inspire.

That sequence of play certainly raised the possibility that Gannon-Doak could be utilised to better effect in another role.

Gannon-Doak's forward burst led to the award of a penalty and hinted at an alternative role.

In a recent development, if played more centrally, his crossing – undoubtedly his weak spot – would not be such an problem. But the acceleration and driving runs would still be there to cause chaos in and around the penalty box. That will always be his strong suit.

To get the best out of him, maybe the manager needs to redefine him.

Recent findings suggest that any redeployment would, obviously, create another glitch. If Pocognoli remains wedded to the current system, it seems likely that Billy Gilmour and Lewis Ferguson will occupy the two holding berths.

Ahead of them, and behind the main striker, McGinn and Scott McTominay are virtually undroppable. It might be the case then, that Gannon-Doak is eventually utilised as an impact sub. Yet, it would not be a strategy without its merits.

It has been revealed that he’s got a part to play in this set-up. Probably just not where he’s presently being positioned.

Industry observers note that you’d be surprised, frankly, if he started in St Gallen on Monday. Switzerland are a far superior side to North Macedonia, already assured of promotion to League A by topping the section and looking to end this campaign with a flourish against a Scotland side they beat comfortably at Hampden.

They’ll ask far more questions of Pocognoli’s side. It feels like a task more suited to Hickey.

Scotland, collectively, will need to buck up their ideas if they are to stand any chance of emerging with a positive outcome or, at the least, some credit.

Scotland fans are desperate to see Gannon-Doak succeed but a little change might be needed.

There was a flatness to Friday’s performance, especially in a first half in which the much-vaunted high-press was conspicuous by its absence.

The passing was too safe and predictable. The tempo was low and the play was unimaginative. By half-time, the visitors had fashioned the better chance when Enis Bardhi smashed the ball into the side net.

Scotland were markedly better after the turnaround. After Billy Gilmour’s scarcely believable miss, they were deserving of the opener which came when McGinn burst into the box and lashed home after fine work from Che Adams.

Stemming straight from a corner, North Macedonia’s equaliser – which ended their eight-game goal drought – asked a serious question of Pocognoli’s players.

To their credit, they stepped up with Gannon-Doak’s foray into the box causing the moment of indecision on which the game swung.

According to recent reports, the manner of a first Hampden win for Pocognoli won’t live long in the memory. The fervent hope is that it proves to be the start of something.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool, it’s fair to say, have a pretty active recruiting department.

A necessarily active recruiting department, it should be emphasised, given the squad-building challenges Andoni Iraola has already faced early on in his tenure as head coach.

Recent findings suggest that the Merseysiders navigated a potential centre-back crisis expertly in the summer with the arrival of loan signing Ronald Araujo from Barcelona. But questions remain as to the long-term viability of the centre-back department post the summer 2027 transfer window.

A recent report from Christian Falk with CF Bayern Insider asserted that Liverpool, among Europe’s elite, have scouted VfB Stuttgart centre-back Finn Jeltsch.

“It is TRUE: Liverpool have scouted VfB Stuttgart centre-back Finn Jeltsch. All the top clubs, including Bayern Munich, are scouting him,” the head of football at Bild said.

Industry observers note that “He was in the squad for Klopp first as a backup for the right-back. Then one of the central defenders became injured, and now he’s also the backup at centre-back. This shows he can play many positions, and everyone can see the 20-year-old’s potential.

“Such players really are a present to everyone. Jeltsch is young, talented and can play many positions, and he’s not so expensive! Bayern Munich has an eye on him.”.

If that name seems vaguely familiar, it might be because Bundesliga giants Bayern Munich are already significant fans of the footballer and are keeping a very close eye on matters close to home.

Liverpool’s interest is understandable. Come the summer transfer window, they could be two centre-halves down should Joe Gomez and Virgil van Dijk call time on their Anfield careers once their contracts run out. Ronald Araujo, though enjoying an impeccable campaign with the Reds, may not become a permanent addition to the squad, despite Liverpool possessing a buy option. Much here may depend on what Barcelona’s stance on the Uruguayan international looks like in May.

According to recent reports, that’s three centre-backs Liverpool could be short come the opening of the summer transfer window, so it’s very plausible that Julian Ward and Co. will be keeping a close eye on the centre-back market between now and the end of the 2026/27 season.

As James Pearce rightly notes on X (formerly Twitter), of course, Liverpool do have several high-potential, highly exciting young centre-backs in their stable.

Ifeanyi Ndukwe, by all accounts, is impressing on loan at Levante after an eye-catching pre-season; Giovanni Leoni remains an appetising option, and then there’s hope for young Mor Talla Ndiaye also.

According to recent reports, centre-back not a priority for Liverpool so highly unlikely they will invest heavily in that area either in Jan or next summer. Jacquet has made a huge impact and substantial hopes for fellow young CBs Leoni, Ndukwe and Ndiaye.

— James Pearce (@JamesPearceLFC) November 13, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that but these are three very young, very inexperienced centre-backs you’d be pairing with the also youthful, but extremely impressive, Jeremy Jacquet for the foreseeable future. The Frenchman will, however, have a season of Premier League football under his belt – but is that enough to help guide the next generation of Liverpool centre-backs?

Unless you’re planning to extend Van Dijk’s contract or activate Araujo’s buy option, Liverpool are looking incredibly short on options with experience and genuine leadership credentials at L4.

That might be worth considering if the blueprint isn’t to invest in Finn Jeltsch this summer.

By Ben Knapton | 14 Nov 2026 20:11, Last updated: 14 Nov 2026 20:11.

Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice has publicly confirmed that he is set to sign a upcoming contract with the Premier League champions.

The former West Ham United captain remains on the same terms he penned upon his arrival in 2023, and he is at the moment due to become a free agent in the summer of 2028.

However, the Gunners have made tying their engine room lynchpin down to an improved contract a priority, and Mikel Arteta hinted earlier this month that Rice was close to extending.

Fabrizio Romano also reported in October that Arsenal and Rice had made progress in talks over a renewal offer, and it is seemingly just a matter of time before the announcement is made.

Speaking to reporters ahead of Sunday's UEFA Nations League fixture between Spain and England, Rice dropped a major eight-word update, saying: "A upcoming contract will hopefully be arriving soon.".

Rice is at the moment on a £260,000 weekly salary at the Emirates, according to Capology, but his upcoming deal is expected to bump his pay up to a record £350,000 per week.

The England international would therefore become the highest-paid player in the Arsenal squad, ahead of Bukayo Saka, who is believed to be earning £300,000 per week.

Rice's bumper renewal will be just reward for the 27-year-old's seismic impact since joining in a £105m transfer, having registered 58 goal involvements in 173 Arsenal appearances.

Rice has scored 22 goals of his own while setting up 36 more in a red and white kit, and he started 35 Premier League matches during Arsenal's run to title glory last season.

The Englishman has scored one goal and set up five more in 15 matches in all tournaments this season, and he is set to make his 82nd England appearance in Sunday's clash with Spain, where a win will see the Three Lions through to the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners.

Rice is one of nine Arsenal players whose contracts expire at the end of the 2027-28 season, but not every member of that list will be in line for a renewal.

The long-term futures of Kepa Arrizabalaga, Illan Meslier and Mikel Merino are clouded in some uncertainty, and the same goes for the injury-plagued Ben White and Kai Havertz.

However, defensive stalwart Jurrien Timber - who recently delivered a Netherlands "masterclass" - is expected to be a top priority for a newly introduced deal in due course, in addition to number one David Raya.

Captain Martin Odegaard could also leave for nothing in 2028, and he recently delivered an update on his Arsenal contract situation.

#2325. Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 125m • 📚 Deep Dive (24915 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 125 min read (24915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~125 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism.
  • It has been revealed that the physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions.
  • According to recent reports, during the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nuclei in early mammalian embryos undergo epigenetic reprogramming that enables the zygote to develop into a complete organism. Whereas changes in chromatin state during this critical transition period have been extensively studied1,2,3, changes in the nucleus that houses chromatin remain poorly understood. Here, using direct organelle capture and biophysical manipulation methods, we find that nuclei attain profound softness and plasticity during the two-cell embryonic stage in mice, facilitating major zygotic gene activation. The prominent nuclear deformability is attributable to the rapid clearance of lamin B1 from the nuclear envelope by the autophagy factor LC3. Nuclear stiffening by lamin B1 retention or its overloading results in incomplete activation of zygotic genes and impaired development. However, embryos that maintain nuclear deformability escape from this transcriptional interference. High-resolution microscopy and sequential three-dimensional fluorescence in situ hybridization analyses revealed an accumulation of active RNA polymerase II and coordinated positioning of key genomic loci near the deformable nuclear envelope. An engineered molecular tether that stiffens the nuclei restricts these nuclear activities and suppresses expression of key zygotic gene activation genes. Together, our study identifies a distinct physical nuclear state that embryos acquire at the beginning of life that supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

It has been revealed that the physical characteristics of the cell nucleus are extraordinarily diverse, exhibiting distinct shape and mechanical phenotypes across tissue types, physiological states and disease conditions. Fragile or misshapen nuclei are hallmarks of cancer, cardiomyopathy and premature ageing4,5. Nuclei in stem cells gradually stiffen during differentiation4,5,6,7. While these changes are widely recognized as consequences of altered nuclear composition and chromatin dynamics, they also influence genome organization and transcription8,9,10. Despite the importance, the physical state of the nucleus at the earliest stages of mammalian development, when life begins, remains unclear.

According to recent reports, during the first few cleavages, nuclei undergo extensive epigenetic reprogramming, enabling the zygote to initiate a new developmental program. In mice, this transition occurs within the first approximately 48 h after fertilization and is associated with a surge in new transcript production, known as major zygotic gene activation (ZGA)11,12,13. Major ZGA occurs during the mid-to-late two-cell stage, and embryos that impair ZGA fail in subsequent development. Around the time of ZGA, chromatin exhibits distinct structural and biochemical changes accompanied by histone modifiers and transcription factors14,15. By contrast, whether the nucleus organizing chromatin undergoes any crucial changes that drive ZGA is not known. In somatic cells, nuclear shape and mechanics depend on lamins, which line the inner nuclear membrane16,17. Lamins are long-lived, enriched in eggs and are crucial for mammalian development18,19,20. Previous studies have documented that, of the two major types, A-type lamins exhibit cell-lineage-specific differential expression patterns, whereas B-type lamins are constitutively expressed throughout development16. However, their dynamics and transiency, as well as the underlying core regulatory mechanism, during the earliest embryonic stages are poorly understood. Likewise, how the nuclear lamina, which forms a structural meshwork, controls nuclear mechanics and genome dynamics during this critical transition is unknown. Investigating physical nuclear characteristics necessitates direct quantification and manipulation of their mechanical properties. However, achieving this without compromising cell viability poses a challenge.

To investigate physical nuclear properties, we first performed high-resolution confocal scanning of fertilized mouse eggs during early cleavages (Fig. 1a). Our three-dimensional (3D) images of nuclei with H2B–mCherry, expressed without perturbing development (Extended Data Fig. 1a), revealed their distinct shape features, showing uneven local deformation at the two-cell stage in contrast to their predominantly spherical appearance at the one-cell and four-cell stages (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1b). Timelapse imaging revealed that one-cell nuclei remained spherical during the cell cycle (Fig. 1d). Two-cell nuclei underwent slow, incremental deformation, which started at around 21 h post-insemination (h.p.i.), peaked at 24–26 h.p.i. and then gradually regressed by 32–36 h.p.i. (Fig. 1e). At the four-cell stage, nuclei were again spherical (Fig. 1f) (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Videos 1−3). Before the onset of deformation, two-cell nuclei had fully swollen and reached steady sizes; once deformed, the altered nuclear shapes persisted for hours (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Similar deformation was observed using emerin–eGFP for the nuclear envelope (Fig. 1g) or mCherry–NLS for the nuclear interior (Extended Data Fig. 1g).

a, Schematic of early-stage mouse embryos. b,c, Representative 3D images of nuclei visualized using H2B–mCherry (b) and quantification of nuclear sphericity (c). F, female; M, male. d–f, Time courses of 2D nuclear deformation during the one-cell (d), two-cell (e) and four-cell stages (f). Live imaging was performed at 1 h intervals over around 52 h for n = 9 embryos; the mean (orange) and s.d. (shaded area) of nuclear deformation, calculated as shown in the inset in d, are plotted. g, Nuclear membranes were imaged using emerin–eGFP (green) and analysed for 2D nuclear deformation. The arrowheads indicate prominent deformation sites. h, Schematic of nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement. An embryo is held with a holding pipette, while a pressure-controlled nanocapillary captures and stretches the nucleus to measure nuclear elasticity and stiffness. i, Snapshots of nuclei subjected to the nanocapillary-based measurement (red, H2B–mCherry; overlay with bright field). Representative from four (8 and 24 h.p.i.) and two (48 h.p.i.) independent experiments. j–l, Maximal nuclear deformation (j), nuclear stiffness (k) and the degree of elasticity (l) analysed from experiments as in i. S0, Smax and Sr are as in i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For c, g and j–l, statistical analysis was performed using Kruskal–Wallis tests followed by Dunn’s-multiple comparisons test; the thick horizontal bars represent the mean values (red or black). Scale bars, 10 μm (b, g and i).

According to recent reports, this finding prompted us to develop a biophysical setup that quantitatively characterizes the mechanical properties of early embryonic nuclei in situ (Fig. 1h). The setup equipped a pressure-controlled nanocapillary, of which the tip was inserted into a fertilized embryo to capture the nuclear surface. A weak, constant suction pressure (2.1 × 101 kPa) pinched the surface, which was then stretched through axial translocation of the nanocapillary. The nuclei could be gradually strained, resulting in tension, and the strain reached a maximum just before the detachment (Fig. 1i). The analysis could be performed from the one-cell to four-cell stages, over which the predominantly fluid-like cytoplasm minimally influenced the measured mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 2a–f). Measurements were also insensitive to nuclear markers and were comparable to label-free imaging results (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h).

Industry observers note that our analysis revealed that two-cell nuclei were significantly more deformable than one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1j). The deformable nature persisted throughout the cell cycle (from 21 to 32 h.p.i.) even as DNA doubled at about 24 h.p.i. Nuclear stiffness, as estimated based on the nanocapillary pressure and the extent of nuclear deformation, transiently lowered at the two-cell stage (one-cell, 5.0 ± 1.3 nN µm−1; two-cell, 2.0 ± 0.5 nN µm−1; four-cell, 4.6 ± 1.9 nN µm−1; n = 18, 38 and 13 embryos, respectively) (Fig. 1k). The stiffness values varied between male and female pronuclei (30.7 ± 21.3%, n = 8 pairs) and between blastomeres of each two-cell embryo (23.5 ± 14.5%, n = 16 pairs), while the differences were pronounced among the developmental stages (Extended Data Fig. 2i). Two-cell nuclei also exhibited significant plasticity, in contrast to more elastic one-cell and four-cell nuclei (Fig. 1l) (shape recovery, 91.0 ± 4.3% for one-cell; 66.9 ± 8.0% for two-cell; and 87.9 ± 4.6% for four-cell). The deformable two-cell nuclear stiffness was consistent when embryos were examined using lower nanocapillary pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). An alternative capillary-based approach, using an incremental suction pressure that aspirated nuclei, yielded consistent results (n ≥ 12 embryos per stage) (Extended Data Fig. 2l–n). These corroborate the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus.

Our nanocapillary-based assay at 1.2 × 101 kPa minimally perturbed development, enabling us to relate two-cell nuclear stiffness with embryos’ developmental competence (Fig. 2a). We found that all fertilized embryos that timely reached the blastocyst stage had soft nuclei (2.0 ± 0.6 nN µm−1; n = 66 of 66 embryos), while nearly half of the embryos that impaired development had stiff nuclei (n = 7 of 15 embryos; defined as more than twice the mean nuclear stiffness of the normal development) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Detecting embryos with stiff nuclei was infrequent (8.6%; n = 7 out of 81 embryos). The outcome was regardless of the fluorescent tag type and marker expression levels (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). A similar mechanical feature was observed for cloned embryos created through somatic cell nuclear transfer (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3a,d,e) (n = 46 embryos). Thus, deformable two-cell nuclei are a signature of normal preimplantation development.

a, Schematic of the assay. Embryos prepared through in vitro fertilization or through somatic cell nuclear transfer were subjected to the nanocapillary-based mechanical measurement during the two-cell stage using a pressure that minimally perturbed development (1.2 × 101 kPa; Extended Data Fig. 2j,k), after which the embryos resumed standard culture. b, The relationship between two-cell nuclear stiffness and the frequency of development to the blastocyst stage at 96 h.p.i. n values represent the numbers of embryos analysed. For b, statistical analysis was performed using Mann–Whitney U-tests (two-sided); the thick horizontal bars (red) represent the mean values.

In a recent development, we next explored the molecular mechanism underlying the distinct physical state of the two-cell nucleus. Using immunofluorescence, we first examined four major lamins, A/C, B1 and B2, and found that lamin B1 transiently cleared from the two-cell nuclear envelope, nearly paralleling nuclear softening (Fig. 3a,b). The clearance was rapid and substantial, with an approximately 70% decrease in peripheral signal during the early-to-mid two-cell stage (21 to 24 h.p.i.; Fig. 3b). Lamin A/C and B2 levels also changed, but their trends were gradual and monotonic, with only a minor decline, if any, during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Another nuclear envelope protein, Lap2β, also changed little (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Live-embryo imaging confirmed the clearance of lamin B1 from the two-cell nuclear envelope with a decay time constant of 86 ± 44 min (n = 5 embryos; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 4c). An immunoblotting assay revealed a reduction in lamin B1 during the two-cell stage (Fig. 3d), suggesting degradation.

Industry observers note that our pilot assay using wortmannin implicated that autophagy promotes lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Autophagy is active in early embryos and is essential for preimplantation development21. In live-embryo imaging, the autophagy factor LC322 was diffusive at the one-cell stage and accumulated in the two-cell nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Our antibody microinjection targeting LC3 suppressed lamin B1 clearance (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Cell cycle progression as monitored by EdU was normal (Extended Data Fig. 4g). We therefore designed a construct that interferes with the endogenous interaction between lamin B1 and LC3, using a short fragment of lamin B1 carrying LC3-binding domains and an intrinsic nuclear localization signal23 (hereafter, sfLB1; Fig. 3e). When expressed in embryos, this fragment was predominantly nucleoplasmic (Extended Data Fig. 4h), while a major autophagy substrate p62 maintained stable protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Our analysis revealed that the clearance of lamin B1 was suppressed by sfLB1, whereas lamin A/C and B2 remained largely unperturbed (Fig. 3f,g). An accumulation of lamin B1 was detectable in western blot analysis of lysates (Extended Data Fig. 4j). A sfLB1 variant (sfLB1Δ), which was nucleoplasmic but with abrogated LC3 binding23 (Extended Data Fig. 4h,k), had little influence on lamin B1 clearance (Fig. 3f,g). The development of embryos was impaired by sfLB1, but not by sfLB1Δ (Fig. 3h).

According to recent reports, to understand the mechanistic basis of lamin B1 clearance, we constructed fluorescent reporters based on full-length lamin B1 fused to mCherry. Consistent with the results shown in Fig. 3a–c, the wild-type (WT) construct (flLB1wt; Fig. 3e) localized to the nuclear envelope and exhibited rapid lamin B1 clearance (T1/2 = 83 ± 44 min, n = 18) (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 5a). The other three constructs carried mutations near or at an LC3-interacting region core motif (flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A)) or at the major N-terminal CDK1 phosphorylation site for nuclear-envelope breakdown24 (flLB1(S24A)) (Fig. 3e). These constructs also localized to the two-cell nuclear envelope (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Notably, the mutations that abrogated LC3 interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5b) suppressed the lamin B1 clearance, whereas the mutation at the CDK1 site did not prevent the clearance (Fig. 3i). The mutations in flLB1(5A) were at the site targeted for autophagic degradation of lamin B1 during oncogene-induced cell senescence23. The selectivity of lamin B1 over lamin A/C and B2 was also consistent with the phenomenon reported in senescent cells23.

Our assay further suggested that lamin B1 is degraded through an autophagy–lysosome pathway. This was confirmed by tracking the fate of flLB1wt and identifying its predominant lysosomal localization and formation of foci (n = 18 embryos; Fig. 3j,k). flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) localized much less to lysosomes (n = 12 and 14 embryos; Fig. 3j,k), while the numbers of lysosomes remained comparable (Fig. 3l). We did not observe prominent lamin-B1-positive structures bulging from the outer nuclear membrane23 nor an accumulation of lysosomes on the nuclear surface25 within the timescale examined. Collectively, our mechanistic view of lamin B1 clearance is shown in Fig. 3m.

Industry observers note that we next examined the effect of lamin B1 on two-cell nuclear stiffness. Nanocapillaries indicated that two-cell nuclei of which the envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1 were stiffer and less plastic than controls (4.2 ± 1.3 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (sfLB1; Fig. 4a–d). These nuclei were as stiff as normal one-cell and four-cell nuclei (~5 nN µm−1, Fig. 1k). We next overexpressed lamin B1. As WT lamin B1 rapidly dissociated from the nuclear envelope, we used flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A) to compensate for the clearance. Whereas excess loading of these lamins resulted in collapsed nuclei, titrating expression levels preserved the overall nuclear shape, with lamin B1 loaded to the nuclear envelope at a level comparable to that using sfLB1 (Fig. 4a,b). We found that flLB1(F454A/L457A) profoundly increased nuclear elasticity and stiffness (4.0 ± 1.1 nN µm−1, n = 17 embryos) (Fig. 4c,d), while overall autophagic activity as assessed by LC3 signal26 was maintained (Extended Data Fig. 5c). The phenotype quantitatively mirrored the embryos perturbed through sfLB1. By contrast, flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, which lacked the carboxy-terminal CaaX motif for farnesylation16 and remained nucleoplasmic, did not significantly alter nuclear shape and mechanics (Extended Data Fig. 5d). These data indicate that two-cell nuclear stiffness depends on the nuclear envelope localization of lamin B1.

Sources indicate that notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) showed nuclei of which the shape remained largely deformed as in normal two-cell embryos (Fig. 4a). These nuclei were soft and plastic (1.6 ± 0.4 nN µm−1, n = 10 embryos), despite their comparable level of nuclear envelope loading to sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4b–d). The minimal mechanical impact of flLB1(5A) was probably due to its poor assembly competency at the nuclear envelope for the following reasons: first, our nuclear isolation assay indicated that flLB1(5A) was more soluble than flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4e). Second, sfLB1(5A) showed comparably slightly higher affinity for LC3 than sfLB1(F454A/L457A) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Finally, our expansion microscopy (ExM) analysis revealed a less-uniform peripheral localization of flLB1(5A) in comparison to endogenous lamin B1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A)27 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–g). The difference in peripheral DNA signals appeared less pronounced between perturbed embryo groups (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Our nanocapillary-based assay further suggested an early reduction in nuclear stiffness before lamin B1 clearance (Figs. 1k and 3a,b). Collectively, our data suggest that lamin B1 controls two-cell nuclear stiffness depending on their assembly stability at the nuclear envelope and that the stability depends on the site to which LC3 binds.

According to recent reports, we next examined whether the observed nuclear changes impact the two-cell transcriptional reprogramming. We analysed the above embryos using RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 1). The first cleavage and following cell cycle progression were normal in those embryos; the overexpressed protein levels were stable and comparable among conditions (Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Our analysis indicated that the transcriptomes of flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos were distinct from those of the flLB1(5A) and non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified more than 3,000 downregulated genes in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos compared with the non-injected controls (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). The downregulation was evident even when compared with flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4g), whereas very few DEGs were detected between flLB1(5A) embryos and the non-injected controls (Fig. 4h). Importantly, the genes downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) overlapped more with major ZGA and two-cell-activated genes than with minor ZGA and one-cell-activated genes28 (972 out of 3,763 (25.8%) versus 251 out of 3,763 (6.7%); P < 0.01, Fisher’s exact test) (Fig. 4i). The overlap was even greater when compared with another major ZGA gene list29 (1,338 out of 2,508, 53.3%) (Fig. 4i,j). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC embryos did not show an appreciably altered transcriptome at comparable expression levels (Extended Data Figs. 5g and 7e). Our analysis also indicated perturbed expression of key transcriptional regulators Obox15 in flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos but it was not prominent in flLB1(5A) embryos (Fig. 4k). The profiles of maternal and zygotic Obox genes suggested a failure in minor-to-major ZGA transition15.

We next analysed how ZGA is altered when the nuclear envelope was enriched with endogenous lamin B1. Analysing embryos overexpressing sfLB1 or sfLB1Δ, along with the non-injected controls, we found that thousands of genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated through sfLB1 (Extended Data Fig. 7f–l and Supplementary Table 3). Many downregulated genes identified as DEGs were shared between sfLB1 and flLB1(F454A/L457A) embryos (71.1%; Fig. 4i (bottom right)). Developmentally essential genes were enriched among the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7m). Analysing published chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) datasets further indicated sharp H3K4me3 signals around the transcription start sites of the downregulated genes (Extended Data Fig. 7n). We therefore performed genome-wide profiling of H3K4me3 through an optimized cleavage under targets and tagmentation (Cut&Tag) analysis. By establishing a condition that maintained the nuclear structure, reproducible signals were obtained that agreed with previously published ChIP–seq data14,30 (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e). Our analysis indicated that H3K4me3 is more abundant at transcription start sites in sfLB1 embryos than in the non-injected control embryos (Extended Data Fig. 8f). It has been demonstrated that broadly spread noncanonical H3K4me3 is removed by histone demethylation for major ZGA14. Indeed, H3K4me3 remained accumulated in broad-domain H3K4me3 (bdH3K4me3) in sfLB1 embryos, whereas H3K4me3 enrichment in lamina-associated domains unchanged (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 8g). Analysing the expression levels of histone methylation-related enzymes, key lysine demethylase (KDM) genes, which are needed to eliminate bdH3K4me314, were downregulated through flLB1(F454A/L457A) and sfLB1, but the changes were not significant through flLB1(5A) and sfLB1Δ (Fig. 4m). These data suggest that the establishment of histone methylation status2 failed in embryos when lamin B1 stiffened the two-cell nuclear envelope.

It has been revealed that there was a marked difference in nuclear stiffness between the embryo groups that failed in major ZGA and those that were transcriptionally less perturbed. To test whether nuclear stiffness per se was inhibitory to ZGA, we developed a molecular tether–anchor system that targets the nuclear envelope and stiffens nuclei (Fig. 4n and Extended Data Fig. 9a). The tether comprised an elastic I27 module of titin31 of which the ends were fused to a pair of GFP nanobodies. The anchor was made based on a minimal KASH domain fused to mEGFP for outer-nuclear-envelope localization32. When co-expressed, the tether was recruited to the anchor-coated nuclear envelope and increased nuclear stiffness by around twofold (4.3 ± 1.5 nN µm−1, n = 20 embryos; Fig. 4n,o and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Nuclear plasticity and deformation decreased accordingly (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Importantly, in the tether-stiffened nuclei, lamin B1 levels were as low as in normal mid two-cell embryos (Fig. 4p). Lamin A/C and B2 also remained largely unperturbed (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Our mRNA microinjection into late zygotes minimally affected pronuclear stiffness, first cleavage and cell cycle progression (Extended Data Fig. 9f–i). Moreover, our two mutant tether derivatives, one that weakened its affinity to the anchor (tether LaG16(5A)) and one that impaired its elastic force-generating property (tether titin(W34E)), revealed no appreciable impact on nuclear shape and mechanics (Fig. 4o and Extended Data Fig. 9b–d,j). In contrast to the WT, neither of the two mutants significantly impaired development (Extended Data Fig. 9k). Thus, our tether–anchor system increases two-cell nuclear stiffness and perturbs embryonic development when it binds to the nuclear envelope and exerts force.

Our RNA-seq analysis revealed that embryos in which the nuclei were stiffened by the tether WT (tWT) exhibited distinct transcriptomes compared with those expressing the LaG16(5A) tether mutant and the non-injected controls (Extended Data Fig. 10a). A total of 634 genes, including major ZGA genes, were downregulated in the tWT embryos, while much fewer DEGs were identified in tether-mutant embryos (Fig. 4q and Extended Data Fig. 10b–e; versus the non-injected controls). Furthermore, the expression of the Obox cluster and other major ZGA genes was dampened (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Downregulation of key ZGA genes and transcriptional repression were detectable in quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) and 5-ethynyl-uridine (EU) incorporation analyses (Extended Data Fig. 10g,h). Whereas the impact on ZGA was broader and less variable for flLB1(F454A/L457A) than for tWT (972 versus 168 genes; Fig. 4i versus Extended Data Fig. 10e; Fig. 4j versus Fig. 4q), 82.2% of the downregulated genes in tWT embryos were shared with those perturbed through sfLB1 or flLB1(F454A/L457A) (Fig. 4r). Together, we conclude that deformable two-cell nuclei are integral to the execution of proper ZGA.

In a recent development, we next examined the effect of lamin B1 persistence on early development. As a result, approximately 50% of the embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) did not progress beyond the two-cell stage (Extended Data Fig. 5h), comparable to those perturbed through sfLB1 (Fig. 3h). flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC did not significantly affect development, indicating that the effective site of lamin B1 is at the nuclear envelope. Notably, embryos overexpressing flLB1(5A) also showed impaired development, despite their nearly normal transcriptome (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Our analysis indicated that those embryos accumulated DNA damage as detected through phosphorylated H2A.X (γH2A.X) foci (Extended Data Fig. 5i), a developmental impediment33. By contrast, DNA damage levels in embryos perturbed through flLB1(F454A/L457A) were as low as those of non-injection control. Our results do not exclude the possibility that the suppressed ZGA and basal DNA damage combinatorially impaired development. Nonetheless, our data indicate that embryos with stiff two-cell nuclei are unable to facilitate proper ZGA and early development. Embryos with tether-stiffened nuclei also exhibited a two-cell arrest (Extended Data Fig. 9k), supporting the necessity of nuclear softness for development.

Given the impact of nuclear stiffness on ZGA, we examined chromatin dynamics in deformable and non-deformable nuclei. Our ExM images at 24 h.p.i. revealed peripheral layers of DNA and lamins, with the overlap comparable to those analysed using electron microscopy34 (~150 nm; Extended Data Fig. 6i). Our imaging further revealed a preferential localization of DNA near concave regions of the two-cell nuclear envelope (Fig. 5a–c and Extended Data Fig. 6j). Lamin B1 signals also exhibited a weak negative correlation with nuclear deformation35 (Fig. 5b,c). However, the biased DNA localization was shared among deformable nuclei regardless of lamin B1 enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), suggesting that nuclear deformation is associated with peripheral DNA organization.

Sources indicate that we next examined how deformable nuclei are linked to gene expression regulation during ZGA. In 3D images, large fluorescent foci positive for elongating RNA polymerase II (Pol II Ser2P) shifted their distribution towards the nuclear periphery, as nuclear deformation increased from 21 to 24 h.p.i. (Fig. 5d,e). Notably, the majority of the Pol II foci became more frequently associated with nuclear concavity (Fig. 5f). The focus sizes increased over time, and their growth was suppressed by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5g). Concomitantly, DNA mass volume decreased by 14.7 ± 6.5% (Fig. 5h). We next performed sequential 3D fluorescence in situ hybridization (3D FISH) analysis36 to examine the link between peripheral transcriptional activity and ZGA (Fig. 5i–l). We analysed the genomic loci of Kdm5b and Obox6, along with Gabarapl1 as a non-ZGA control and found that their distributions were broad and changed from the early to the mid-to-late two-cell stage, but the average distance remained 2–3 µm from the nuclear periphery around the time of major ZGA (2.7 ± 2.0, 2.0 ± 1.6 and 2.1 ± 1.3 µm, respectively; 28 h.p.i.) (Fig. 5i–k). Pol II Ser2P intensities were greater when the Obox6 and Kdm5b loci were positioned >1 µm from the nuclear periphery, while DAPI signals remained unchanged, suggesting that the increased local transcriptional activity was not merely a consequence of higher chromatin density (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j). This trend was not observed in Gabarapl1 (Extended Data Fig. 10i). Our sequential FISH further enabled us to determine the locations of multiple gene loci within the same nucleus (Fig. 5l). Our data indicated a widespread positioning of Obox6 and Kdm5b loci at 21 h.p.i. and a change in the localization of gene loci at 28 h.p.i., with a frequent incidence of their concomitant presence near the nuclear periphery. This locus distribution was disrupted by tether-based nuclear stiffening (Fig. 5l). Notably, Pol II Ser2P intensities at Obox6 loci depended on the nuclear stiffening, while their changes at Kdm5b loci appeared less pronounced (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We therefore performed sequential 3D DNA–RNA FISH analysis to detect nascent Kdm5b transcripts and found a surge in the production around 2–4 µm from the nuclear envelope, and it depended on peripheral nuclear stiffness (Extended Data Fig. 10l–n). In summary, our data suggest that soft and plastic two-cell nuclei ensure the formation of active transcription sites a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope and enable the coordinated positioning of key ZGA gene loci around the sites for expression.

Industry observers note that our study reveals physical characteristics of early embryonic nuclei and their distinct changes that facilitate ZGA. Our data show that the autophagy factor LC3 and lamin B1 clearance confer nuclear plasticity and softness, and that deformable nuclei are key to robust zygotic transcription. Extensive studies have profiled epigenetic states of chromatin and provided a genome-centred view of this critical developmental transition. Our study highlights the importance of physical nuclear state for this transition and underscores the need for integration of diverse embryonic parameters, including their subcellular material properties.

In a recent development, our work identifies a transient phase of nuclear deformability that manifests as cells transition through a totipotent state (Fig. 1). Notably, this nuclear change marks normal preimplantation development and contributes to transcription and gene locus movement (Figs. 2, 4 and 5). Notably, the sites of active DNA transactions appear a few μm beneath the nuclear envelope, often associated with local negative curvature, suggesting the generation of inward forces around these sites (Fig. 5d–h). During ZGA, chromatin undergoes dynamic remodelling and compaction37,38,39, while maintaining contact with the nuclear lamina40. A flexible nuclear envelope may accommodate these internal and peripheral chromatin activities, mediating a mechanical conflict for the consolidation of functional genome architectures. Our analysis also suggests that intense transcriptional activity near the deformable nuclear envelope enables the full activation of key ZGA genes that shape the two-cell epigenome14 (Fig. 4l,m). Such mechanical control may also operate in naive embryonic stem cells, in which soft nuclei are linked to pluripotency and priming for differentiation41.

We find that the embryonic mechanism governing lamin B1 clearance shares similarities with nuclear autophagy activated during oncogene-induced cell senescence23 (Fig. 3). As autophagy is accompanied by an increase in intracellular calcium levels and is independent of mTORC1 in early embryos21,42, the clearance is most likely developmentally programmed. Our data suggest a role of nuclear translocation of LC3 and its distinct effect on nuclear shape and mechanics. Further analysis of its regulated nuclear-cytoplasmic shuttling43 should reveal the mechanistic basis behind the physiological and pathological nuclear remodelling.

Industry observers note that our findings also raise several interesting questions for future studies. First, our imaging assay detected diluted lamin B1 at convex regions of the nuclear envelope35 (Fig. 5b,c). It remains to be explored whether the clearance of lamin B1 merely contributes to nuclear softening or controls DNA organization by sensing local nuclear curvature. Second, as lamins influence transcription44,45 and the chromatin–lamina contacts change during development40, understanding the interplay between mechanical cues and biochemical factors that ensures robust transcriptional control will be an essential next step. Third, soft and transcriptionally active nuclei, yet enriched with lamin B1 at the nuclear envelope, were prone to DNA damage (Extended Data Fig. 5i). As excess lamin B1 can cause persistent DNA damage46, autophagic clearance of lamin B1 may be necessary to protect against such damage. It would be interesting to dissect nuclear actin in two-cell nuclei47, as per its involvement in DNA damage repair48.

Physical nuclear stability is likely important for early embryos, given the potential mechanical challenges they face during passage through the uterine tube49. Yet this period coincides with a transient state in which nuclei become less mechanically resilient. Early mammalian embryos are also prone to DNA lesions and chromosome missegregation50,51,52. Understanding how embryos navigate the vulnerable state may reveal principles underlying developmental robustness.

Sources indicate that mice (ICR and B6C3F1/Jc1 or slc (BCF1)) aged 5–15 weeks53 were purchased from CLEA Japan, Japan SLC or Kiwa Laboratory Animals, maintained in light-controlled (light: 08:00 to 20:00; dark: 20:00 to 08:00), air-conditioned rooms (ambient temperature: 23 °C ± 1.5 °C, humidity: 50 ± 10%) at each facility and used for experiments. All mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation and all efforts were made to minimize suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

In a recent development, to obtain oocytes, female mice were superovulated by intraperitoneal injections of 7.5 IU of pregnant mare serum gonadotropin (PMSG; ASKA Animal Health), followed by 7.5 IU of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG; ASKA Animal Health) at 48 h after PMSG injection. After the female mice were euthanized at 15–16 h after hCG injection, oocytes were collected from the oviducts by an abdominal operation and transferred to a pre-heated medium of Human Tubal Fluid (HTF; ARK Resource). Sperm were collected from the caudal epididymis of male mice for in vitro fertilization (IVF). For fertilization, freshly prepared or cryopreserved sperm were incubated in HTF medium for 1–1.5 h at 37 °C and 5% CO2 to allow for capacitation. Subsequently, the sperm suspension was mixed with the medium containing the oocytes, and fertilized eggs were collected 1–2 h after insemination followed by removal of cumulus cells with 0.1% hyaluronidase. The eggs were then transferred to drops of preheated KSOM medium (ARK Resource) and cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2.

Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) was performed as described previously54. In brief, enucleation of cumulus-free MII oocytes was performed in drops of CZB medium including 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B. One donor cumulus cell in CZB medium with 6% deionized-BSA was transferred to the perivitelline space of an enucleated oocyte together with a small amount of HVJ-E (GenomeONE-CF; Ishihara Sangyo) by tightly attaching the donor cell to the enucleated oocyte. The oocyte was then cultured in KSOM medium for 1 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 for the cell fusion. The reconstructed oocytes were activated in KSOM medium containing 5 mM SrCl2, 2 mM EGTA and 5 μg ml−1 cytochalasin B (Sigma-Aldrich) for 6 h at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. The activated SCNT embryos were cultured at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2 in KSOM medium.

Sources indicate that pharmacological inhibition experiments were performed by treating embryos with the following chemicals in KSOM medium containing 0.5% (v/v) DMSO: 10 µM wortmannin (19545-26-7, AdipoGen); and 200 nM bafilomycin A1 (SML1661, Sigma-Aldrich). Wortmannin treatment was started at 12 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 32 h.p.i. Bafilomycin treatment was started at 15 h.p.i. and terminated before fixation at 28 h.p.i. The mock control also contained 0.5% (v/v) DMSO throughout assays.

After insemination, fertilized embryos were collected at 12–14 h.p.i. and subjected to mRNA injection unless otherwise noted. Cumulus-free embryos were transferred to drops of M2 medium (ARK Resource) and mRNAs were injected using a piezo manipulator (Prime Tech). The final concentrations of injected mRNA were as follows: 500 ng μl−1 of sfLB1, 500 ng μl−1 of sfLB1Δ, 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(5A), 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(F454A/L457A), 350 ng μl−1 of flLB1(F454A/L457A)ΔC, 20 ng µl−1 of mCherry-NLS, 100 ng µl−1 of eGFP-LC3 or eGFP, 300 ng μl−1 of mEGFP-KASH-TM, 125 ng μl−1 of LaG16-titin-LaG16-mCherry (WT, LaG16(5A) and titin(W34E), respectively). In some experiments, mRNA of eGFP (25 ng μl−1) or histone H2B-eGFP (20 ng μl−1) were co-injected to confirm successful injection or to visualize nuclei. After mRNA injection, embryos were cultured in KSOM medium at 37 °C in air containing 5% CO2. For assays with flLB1, flLB1(5A) and flLB1(F454A/L457A), post-injected embryos were inspected at 24 h.p.i. using a fluorescence microscope and those displaying collapsed nuclei were excluded from analyses. mRNAs synthesis was performed using mMESSAGE mMACHINE T7 Transcription Kit (AM1344, Thermo Fisher Scientific) after linearization of plasmid vectors by restriction enzyme digestion. The synthesized mRNAs were purified using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (74034, Qiagen) and subjected to agarose gel electrophoresis and spectrophotometry to verify the purity (criteria: optical density at 260 nm/280 nm ratio of >2.0). The purified mRNAs were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, stored at –80 °C and used within 6 months.

Sources indicate that live-embryo imaging was performed using an inverted fluorescence microscope (Ti-U, Nikon) equipped with a motorized sample stage (MS-2000, Applied Scientific Instruments), a piezo-driven objective scanner (PIFOC, Physics Instruments) with a piezo controller (E-665, Physics Instruments), a stage-top incubator (TIZ, Tokai Hit), a spinning-disk confocal unit (CSU-X1, Yokogawa) with two excitation lasers (488 nm and 561 nm; OBIS LS, Coherent), a silicone-immersion objective lens (UPlanSApo ×60/1.30 NA, Olympus) and a sCMOS camera (Neo4.1, Andor).
