📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominik Szoboszlai has given an patch on his knee injury after Hungary’s win over Georgia on Saturday, and his comments could be quite concerning for Liverpool fans.

The midfielder’s involvement for his country during this international window was placed in doubt after the knock that he incurred in the Reds’ victory at Crystal Palace last weekend, although he still linked up with Marco Rossi’s squad for their UEFA Nations League fixtures.

The Hungarian FA had deferred any decision on whether the 26-year-old would play until the last minute, but he featured for the entirety of his nation’s 2-0 triumph in Tbilisi and claimed the assist for Barnabas Varga’s clinching goal.

Szoboszlai revealed after the match that he nearly pulled out of playing after he felt a twinge during the warm-up prior to kick-off, but his determination to feature would eventually prevail.

In quotes relayed by Nemzeti Sport, the Hungary captain said: “I was always 100% sure that I would be able to play, but the doctors were less sure. I progressed day by day, focused on myself, received treatment.

“I played with my leg for a training session and a half, and in the warm-up I was close to cancelling it because I felt my leg on one of the shots, but if I’ve come this far, I won’t let the team down. Now the treatment starts all over again. I have to be ready again by Tuesday.”.

According to recent reports, want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Szoboszlai’s comments may well come as a worry to Liverpool fans, with the midfielder admitting that he played through the pain barrier and seemingly defied the assessment of medical professionals.

His remark about getting ready for Hungary’s match against Northern Ireland on Tuesday night will also have Andoni Iraola sweating, with the 26-year-old set to push himself for a tight turnaround even though he seems nowhere near full fitness.

It’s natural that, as captain of his country, the Reds’ number 8 will stop at nothing to try and be available for them, but his club will be left praying that he comes through the Magyars’ next game unscathed.

Szoboszlai will return from international duty into a hectic run of 11 Liverpool fixtures before the end of December, and we’ll need him and his teammates to be operating at their best throughout that busy period.

For everyone at Anfield, Hungary’s match on Tuesday will be monitored with frayed nerves to see if the midfielder comes through without any further complications in his knee.

By Ben Sully | 14 Nov 2026 20:23, Last updated: 14 Nov 2026 21:11.

On Sunday, England will wrap up the 2026-27 UEFA Nations League league phase with an almighty test against the reigning world and European champions Spain.

The Three Lions are sitting in second spot in Group A3, while La Roja are in top spot with a perfect record after five games.

Here, Sports Mole covers all the information you need about how to tune into Sunday's highly anticipated contest.

The game will get underway at 8:45pm local time, which makes it a 7:45pm start for UK viewers.

The game will be played at Atletico Madrid's Metropolitano, which can hold over 70,000 supporters.

This will be Spain's first match at the venue since playing out a goalless draw in a friendly with Portugal in June 2021.

The UEFA Nations League fixture will be free to watch on ITV1 and STV for viewers in the UK.

Alternatively, you can stream the match on the ITVX website and app, the latter of which is available on a number of devices, including phones, tablets and game consoles.

Meanwhile, those watching from Scotland can tune into the game via the STV Player.

There will be match highlights available on the ITV Sport and England official YouTube channels.

The @itvfootball will share key moments of the game, including goals and any red cards.

After winning the World Cup in July, Spain have continued their remarkable form with five consecutive Nations League victories, extending their overall winning run to 12 matches.

As a result, Luis de la Fuente's side enjoy a three-point lead at the top of Group A3, knowing they simply need to avoid defeat against England to seal first spot.

Like Spain, England have already clinched a quarter-final berth after bouncing back from a 3-2 defeat against La Roja with four consecutive victories in their home and away games against the Czech Republic and Croatia.

Thomas Tuchel's side will snatch top spot if they are able to take three points from Sunday's fixture, but that will be easier stated than done as Spain have not lost a competitive game since falling to a 2-0 defeat to Scotland in European Championship qualifying in March 2023.

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

According to recent reports, sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage noted when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old remarked. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”.

The Frenchman noted that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

Recent findings suggest that “I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he noted. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

Industry observers note that “Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”.

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

Sources indicate that “The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”.

It has been revealed that for all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage mentioned. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”.

It has been revealed that sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really key to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”.

Sources indicate that with only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Industry observers note that diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

Sources indicate that all Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

Industry observers note that but the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Instead, his scanning of the pitch before receiving the ball had revealed that goalkeeper Walter Benítez was off his line and Brighton’s attacking players were being tightly guarded by defenders. And so, just as he entered the centre circle in the opposition half, Gómez attempted the absurd.

Recent findings suggest that "Would you look at that!" DIEGO GOMEZ SCORES FROM THE HALFWAY LINE! 🤯 https://t.co/qmagVbGEb4.

“I’m not training with Diego Gómez shooting from 50 metres in training,” head coach Fabian Hürzeler said while breaking into a smile. “It’s just about making the players quick in their minds.

“In these moments it’s about being very precise with his long kick. The perception to recognise the keeper and being quick to go to the action was impressive.”.

The presence of mind to attempt something outlandish was one thing; the execution was quite another. With Benítez vulnerable, Gómez took just one touch with his right foot before taking his shot, not giving the keeper enough time to scramble back to cover his line. As he looked up to confirm the opportunity, the 23-year-old struck the ball over Benítez with such venom that it did not even bounce until it reached the goal.

Industry observers note that all that remained was for the Paraguayan international to hurtle towards the corner flag, engulfed by his ecstatic team-mates. For the Brighton fans, soaked by showers at the Amex, rain can never have felt so sweet.

Gómez’s goal will earn comparisons with David Beckham’s lob from the halfway line at Wimbledon. The advancements in pressing and conditioning in the 30 years since, with space ever more congested, makes such a strike even harder today. Not since Wayne Rooney in 2017 has a player scored a Premier League goal from further out than Gómez’s 56 yards.

Gómez may well attempt an encore. He shot from even further out at the Stadium of Light a week ago. When October ends, three of the last four Premier League goal-of-the-month winners will be Brighton players. Alongside his meticulous emphasis on set-pieces, Hürzeler empowers flair in open play.

After he was pushed down the pecking order at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, leading to questions about his long-term role in Moyes' side, doubts have emerged over his future.

"That's exactly what he wants from his players, that willingness, that commitment and that desire to play a role for the team rather than just for the individual.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.
  • Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.
  • The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.

The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.

Speaking to reporters whilst on international duty with Sweden, Isak was asked if he felt that he should’ve had a penalty.

He replied (Aftonbladet, via Liverpool Echo): “Yeah, looking back I suppose it does look that way, but when you’re in the moment, you don’t always perceive exactly what’s happening.

Recent findings suggest that “I could feel myself being pulled a bit, but not to the extent that it appears later on. I was focused on scoring. It’s hard to try to score and then fall down at the same time. I was so locked in on the goal that I didn’t really register it.”.

According to recent reports, on whether he should’ve gone to ground to try and sway the referee, Isak remarked: “I don’t think there’s any need to embellish or go down on purpose. Sure, if I’d had a better read on the situation, I might have made sure the referee noticed it, that’s about all you can do, but I don’t believe you need to dive or exaggerate in situations like this.

“Perhaps it shouldn’t even matter that much, given that we have VAR and systems in place to make the decisive calls in these kinds of moments.”.

Isak is absolutely right in saying that a penalty should’ve been awarded, and that he shouldn’t have to act unnaturally to convince the referee to give the decision in his team’s favour.

Andoni Iraola remarked after the game that a spot kick probably would’ve been given if the Liverpool striker had gone to ground, but the onus isn’t on players to sway the officials – it’s on the latter to get these massive calls right, especially with recourse to VAR.

It feels as though the debate about officiating in the Premier League will continue indefinitely, with no discernible sign of an improvement in standards from Pro Ref figurehead Howard Webb.

It’s to Isak’s great credit that he’s given such a calm and measured verdict on the penalty incident when he and his team were so blatantly wronged. He’d have had every right to complain profusely about what happened; we’d suspect that many other players would’ve done so if they were in that situation.

He certainly hasn’t let it bother him in terms of his contributions on the pitch, with the 27-year-old scoring in Liverpool’s subsequent games against Fenerbahce and Crystal Palace to take his tally for the season to eight goals in 14 matches across all competitions.

That is, in fact, the best response to the injustice which was done against him Anfield two weeks ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 14 Nov 2026 20:34.

England manager Thomas Tuchel has confirmed that James Trafford will start in goal for Sunday's UEFA Nations League group-stage finale against Spain.

The Three Lions take on the world champions at the Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid, knowing that only a win will do if they are to progress to the quarter-finals as group winners.

Tuchel's side have already sealed a last-eight spot with 12 points on the board, but La Roja boast a perfect total of 15, having bested England 3-2 at Wembley back in September.

England confirmed a top-two finish by edging out Croatia 2-1 on Thursday, on an evening when Jordan Pickford was selected to make his 94th senior international appearance.

However, the Everton shot-stopper will now make way for Leeds United's Trafford, as confirmed by Tuchel in his pre-game press conference on Saturday evening.

"James Trafford will play tomorrow. We want to see how far Traff is," Tuchel told the media, as Trafford gears up to win just his fifth cap for England since making his debut in March.

An unused substitute throughout the World Cup, Trafford started both of England's first two Nations League games in the current cycle, shipping three to Spain before keeping a clean sheet in a 2-0 win over the Czech Republic.

Both Trafford and Pickford have played every minute of the 2026-27 Premier League season so far, and both have four clean sheets to their name from their 10 appearances.

Pickford has conceded 10 goals to Trafford's eight, though, and the Leeds number one also boasts the best save percentage in the league, stopping 82.2% of the shots on target he has faced.

Arsenal's David Raya is second on the list with 80%, while Pickford lies sixth with a 73.7% save percentage, and the Everton man has also made fewer saves in total; 28 to Trafford's 37.

In addition, the former Manchester City goalkeeper has prevented 4.4 goals in the 2026-27 Premier League - the joint-most with Bart Verbruggen and Lukas Hornicek - strengthening his case to oust Pickford as England's number one.

As well as confirming that Trafford will start in between the sticks, Tuchel also revealed that Ezri Konsa and Djed Spence are both fit to play on Sunday.

The Arsenal centre-back and Inter Milan full-back were absent from Thursday's win over Croatia, having been restricted to individual training during the week as a precautionary measure.

However, Konsa and Spence's returns means that Tuchel will be blessed with a triple boost on Sunday, as Myles Lewis-Skelly is also back from a yellow-card suspension.

He’s right now on £35,000 per week from the deal that he agreed in September 2025, which puts him among the Reds’ lower first-team earners (Capology), but we’d suspect that’d increase to six figures with the next extension that he signs in L4.

Since breaking into the senior setup just over a year ago, the winger has never looked back, taking to the elite level with a swagger and a confidence which is rare for players as young as him and even winning a handful of England caps.

Liverpool have other major contract situations to resolve over the next few months – Alisson Becker and Virgil van Dijk are nearing the end of their deals, and speculation continues to abound over Alexis Mac Allister – but keeping Ngumoha at the club for the long-term would be, to use his phrasing, a no-brainer.

It might take another little while yet for full confirmation to arrive, but we share O’Rourke’s optimism that the teenage forward will pen a fresh long-term contract at Anfield in the near future.

Declan Rice has laughed off criticism from Graeme Souness by claiming his numbers 'aren't bad for a centre back', after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' and 'cheating' by dropping into defence.

Souness has long believed the Arsenal and England star does not do enough for a midfielder and stated recently he might as well play centre back, adding that he would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona.

Rice is aware of what Souness has remarked but believes his return of 22 goals and 33 assists since joining the Gunners in 2023 disproves the former Liverpool midfielder's opinion.

Recent findings suggest that ‘My numbers since I joined Arsenal speak for themselves,’ said Rice. ‘For a “centre back”, I think that’s not bad numbers. I’ve had a lot of assists, a lot of goals. To be a top-class centre back getting those numbers, I’m delighted with that!’.

It has been revealed that rice, who will start as an advanced midfielder when England take on Spain here in Madrid on Sunday night, added: ‘Look, Graeme’s got his opinion. I think he’s had his opinion since my West Ham days. I’ve seen his views. I can’t change his opinion. I can only do what I do, which is go on the pitch, perform, play well and block out the noise.’.

Rice also believes Souness, 73, may not understand how the game has evolved.

England and Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice has laughed off Graeme Souness' criticism after he was accused of playing 'old man's football' 'cheating' by dropping into defence.

Pundit Souness believes Rice would not get a game for the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona.

‘If you speak about the positioning, the “old man's football”, look at Harry Kane, for instance,’ began Rice. 'We played him the other week and he dropped next to the centre backs 20-30 times to pick up the ball. The game is different now. It's what the game demands, to get away from your man, to go into different areas to create overloads, to create two v ones, to progress the ball up the pitch. Football is way different. It's changed a lot, and you're always trying to look for tactical advantages.

‘In terms of me as a midfielder, I'm constantly watching clips with Mikel (Arteta). He's constantly coaching me on the pitch. How I can progress the ball from deep, drop next to the goalkeeper, go to full back to get on the ball, to take the ball up the pitch.

It has been revealed that ‘So, I feel like we're now seeing something totally different to what he would see, but in his time football was different. He was a top-class midfielder who won lots of stuff. There's no argument against him. As a pundit, as a person, his career, you have to respect what he's done.

It has been revealed that ‘I didn't get to see him play, but obviously his accolades were top, and I've never got to meet him in person. If I did, there would be no disrespect. I’d shake his hand. I’d chat with him. It’s an opinion at the end of the day. It’s football.’.

Fabrizio Romano has warned that the future of one player at Liverpool is ‘becoming increasingly complicated’.

Long-serving goalkeeper Alisson Becker is into the final year of his contract at Anfield, but he recently expressed his desire to extend his stay at the club, and his agent has reportedly entered ‘preliminary talks’ with LFC chiefs over a prospective new deal.

With the Brazilian’s status as number 1 firmly intact, it leaves Giorgi Mamardashvili playing a backup role and having to be patient for opportunities, a situation that he might feel a compulsion to change in the foreseeable future.

In a video on his eponymous YouTube channel, Romano outlined that the Georgian mightn’t be prepared to wait for his chance for much longer if Alisson were to extend his contract.

The transfer reporter remarked: “Liverpool are no longer masters of Alisson’s destiny, let’s put it that way. Last summer they were able to say, ‘Stay with us, we’ll extend for another year, we’ll activate the option.’ Now that option has expired, so Alisson can decide his future.

Recent findings suggest that “There is certainly a possibility that Alisson will remain at Liverpool. However, the situation involving him and Giorgi Mamardashvili is becoming increasingly complicated.

“This is because Mamardashvili is not a player who wants to remain a backup goalkeeper indefinitely. He is playing second fiddle while waiting for the door to open for a starting spot at Liverpool and at some point, a decision will have to be made.”.

According to recent reports, want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Romano’s information echoes that of James Pearce a few weeks ago when the latter indicated that, if Alisson were to stay put, his understudy wouldn’t accept a third season of playing backup to the Brazil veteran.

The role of a second-choice goalkeeper is a peculiar one. They’re only one twist of fate away from getting what could be their substantial break, but they could be left waiting months (if not years) for that sliding doors moment.

Mamardashvili hasn’t yet managed to seriously challenge our number 1 for a place in the starting XI, but the Georgian has produced some strong performances in the Carabao Cup this season, including one world-class save against Tottenham in the third round in September.

Even his status as Alisson’s immediate deputy could come under threat from next year once Lucca Brughmans arrives from Genk, although that chain of command would be contingent on the Brazilian’s future at Liverpool.

We can see it from Mamardashvili’s perspective – he’s 26 now and won’t want to fritter away too much of his career warming the bench – but it’s essential for the Reds to have a solid succession plan in place for life after their long-serving number 1, whose world-class presence will be extremely difficult to replace.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 14 Nov 2026 21:52, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 11:43.

Namibia will be looking to revive their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations when they host Cameroon in Gaborone on Monday afternoon, four days after losing the first leg of their Group G double-header.

The Indomitable Lions claimed a 2-0 victory when the sides met on Thursday, leaving them three points clear at the top of the section, and another win would secure their place at the finals.

Cameroon are now one win away from reaching the AFCON finals for the 23rd time and a seventh consecutive tournament, with their resilient form playing a key role in their qualification campaign.

After recording a victory in the second match of March's biennial FIFA Series, the Indomitable Lions have collected seven points from their opening three qualifying games, including a first-round win over Comoros and a draw with Congo.

Thursday's first-leg triumph over Namibia came courtesy of first-half strikes from Saidou Alioum and Bil Nsongo, meaning David Pagou's side have scored at least twice in three of their last five outings.

Cameroon have also kept clean sheets in three matches during that period, including a 1-0 friendly victory over Ivory Coast on October 3, 2026, and the West-Central African nation, currently 42nd in the FIFA World Rankings, will look to maintain that form on Monday.

The Indomitable Lions have also been solid on the road, losing just one of their last eight matches outside their own country while winning five, and they have avoided defeat in each of their most recent three outings in that run.

Namibia, meanwhile, have seen their bid to reach the AFCON finals for only the fifth time and a second in the last three editions become more difficult, with Thursday's defeat leaving the Brave Warriors one point behind second place after Comoros drew with Congo.

The result also means Collin Benjamin's side have now lost each of their last three outings across all competitions, failing to score in any of them since their 1-0 victory over Congo in the opening round of the qualifiers.

The Brave Warriors have also been shaky defensively during that period, conceding nine goals across those three matches, including six in a friendly defeat to Russia after losing 1-0 to Comoros.

There is, however, some encouragement in the fact that Namibia have lost just one of their last five competitive matches as the designated hosts, winning the most recent two such outings.

Namibia have struggled in this fixture, though, losing four of their previous seven meetings (W1, D2) across all competitions, although their most recent home encounter with the Indomitable Lions ended in a goalless draw.

Namibia are expected to be without midfielder Peter Shitembi, who withdrew from the squad through injury, while no further injury concerns or suspensions were confirmed following the first leg.

Experienced figures Deon Hotto, Riaan Hanamub and Peter Shalulile are expected to feature again as Benjamin looks for a response from his side.

Cameroon remain without Carlos Baleba and Christian Kofane, who both withdrew before the first leg due to injuries sustained at their respective clubs.

Meanwhile, Mahamadou Nagida is available again after serving his suspension in the first leg, while Bryan Mbeumo could retain his place on the left side of attack after providing an assist last time out.

Ndisiro; Kamberipa, Eib, Katua, Hanamub; Rudath, Shidolo, Petrus, Hotto; Shalulile, Tjiueza.

Namibia will be desperate to produce a stronger performance after their subdued display in Douala, but their recent scoring record offers little encouragement ahead of another meeting with Cameroon, who should have enough quality and current form to secure a narrow victory.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Daniele De Rossi has looked back at Genoa’s defeat to AC Milan and how he wasn’t frustrated with his team afterwards.

According to recent reports, milan entered the international break with a much-needed victory against Genoa, but it wasn’t the easiest result of the season. After a disappointing defeat to Ferencvaros – which extended the midweek run of defeats – they couldn’t afford to drop points, and they succeeded, even if it wasn’t without flaw.

With two goals inside 20 minutes, you’d be forgiven for expecting Milan to win by more than a couple. However, that was the end of their goalscoring for the afternoon and although Genoa pulled one back, they didn’t grab more than a consolation goal.

Speaking to Sky Sport – in the new series ‘Radici’ – De Rossi looked back on the defeat to the Rossoneri, as well as a comment that stuck with him from Diego Moreira, as MilanPress have relayed today.

Recent findings suggest that we indeed lost against Milan, but we lost ‘well.’ We didn’t deserve it. Three or four weeks ago, the latest results seemed like a pipe dream. I thank the players, staff, and my club for giving me faith and patience at a time when other clubs wouldn’t have had it.

Recent findings suggest that “They remembered how good we did last year. I’m happy to have emerged from a difficult period and to be Genoa’s coach; I’m really happy there.”.

It has been revealed that “I’m passionate about the fans and the supporters. I’m part of a club that, in terms of fan base, is among the best in Europe. I’m passionate; I don’t punch a clock. I spend two hours with the stockman or the waitress with the same enthusiasm I spend time with the team captain. Experiencing it like that, you realise that Genoa is a great team.

Recent findings suggest that “Genoa is full of Genoese fans who remind you every second how much they love their club, the pride of being the top club in Italy. The architecture of the stadium and the warmth of the fans… I’m not saying this to be a sycophant, but on Sunday Moreira came to me and said, ‘I’ve never seen anything like this here in Italy.’ It’s a reality that even our opponents notice.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, plastic pollution is a defining feature of the Anthropocene1, and microplastics are dispersed by air and water into even remote terrestrial habitats2,3,4,5,6,7, yet the ecological and landscape-level processes that shape microplastic accumulation in terrestrial ecosystems remain poorly understood. Human land-use change is rapidly transforming landscapes worldwide, but the influence of this expanding human footprint on the microplastic burdens in wildlife remains largely unknown. This knowledge gap is particularly pressing in regions that are facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil. Here we pair in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution tracking data from lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil and show that the microplastic burdens carried by free-ranging mammals increase with both the magnitude of their human footprint exposure and their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in the blood of individuals occupying seemingly pristine habitats far from development, suggesting that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. In a period of accelerating global land-use change, these findings reveal how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics and suggest that managing animals’ proximity to development and waste management infrastructure may reduce the microplastic burdens carried by terrestrial wildlife.

Plastic pollution, once thought to be a predominantly aquatic matter, is increasingly being recognized as a threat to terrestrial ecosystems1. Microplastics (synthetic polymer particles with diameter less than 5 mm) are a particularly problematic form of plastic pollution, as these small particles are easily dispersed through pathways that include atmospheric deposition, precipitation, river transport and groundwater flow2,3,4,5,6,7. The high environmental mobility of microplastics has allowed them to infiltrate even the most pristine habitats8 where they can persist for centuries9,10. For wildlife exposed to microplastics, the small size and diverse chemistry of these particles facilitate ingestion11 and the penetration of biological membranes12,13. Once internalized, microplastics can bioaccumulate, biomagnify through food webs and pose severe health risks14,15,16,17,18.

Although much work has been done on detecting microplastics in different biological compartments (reviewed in ref. 19), studies in terrestrial ecosystems have largely been limited to descriptive surveys that document the presence of microplastics without investigating how these pollutants accumulate within wildlife20,21,22. Although such studies have proven informative for identifying the scope and scale of plastic pollution, this approach has left the bioaccumulation dynamics of microplastics in terrestrial environments poorly understood. As a result of this knowledge gap, even high-profile studies on plastic ingestion risk in wildlife have had to rely on assumptions about the relationship between individual habitat use and the uptake of microplastics rather than empirically grounded associations23. Because both sources and dispersal pathways for microplastics are amplified by land-use change24,25,26, the intensity of human landscape modification should have a key role in shaping the internal microplastic burdens of terrestrial wildlife. Whether this is the case, however, is still largely unknown. With the continuing expansion of human-modified landscapes into wild spaces27 and the concomitant increase in global plastic production28, there is an urgent need to move beyond presence/absence studies and towards understanding the ecological and landscape-level factors that shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial species29.

Here we integrate movement ecology, land-use data and in vivo contaminant measurements within the same individuals to investigate how the intensity and proximity of anthropogenic land-use change shape systemic microplastic burdens in terrestrial mammals. The role of anthropogenic disturbance in shaping internal plastic burdens is particularly pressing in regions facing escalating environmental pressures, such as Brazil, where the extent of anthropogenic land-use change since the turn of the century has substantially outpaced the global average30,31 and deforestation, resource extraction, urbanization, agricultural intensification and an expanding road network are rapidly transforming the country’s landscapes30,32. By pairing in vivo microplastic measurements with high-resolution Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking data, we provide quantitative evidence that links individual-level habitat use and human landscape modification to systemic microplastic burdens in free-ranging terrestrial wildlife.

Recent findings suggest that between February 2021 and November 2022, we collected blood samples and high-resolution GPS-based movement data from lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris; n = 26) and giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla; n = 21) sampled at the Arc of Deforestation in the Amazon, an agricultural mosaic in the Cerrado, and a relatively undisturbed cattle ranch in the Pantanal (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Table 1). For each individual, we quantified blood microplastic concentrations and polymer profiles using confocal Raman spectroscopy, detecting particles larger than 1 μm. We then paired these data on in vivo microplastic burdens with the GPS tracking data to understand how inter-individual differences in habitat use and disturbance exposure shaped internal microplastic burdens. In particular, we quantified each individual’s exposure to human disturbance through the Human Footprint Index (HFI), a globally standardized measure of cumulative anthropogenic pressure ranging from 0 (undisturbed) to 50 (most heavily modified)33. We also examined local-scale effects through each animal’s proximity to the nearest human development (that is, the built environment including urban areas, mining infrastructure and power plants)34 and waste management facilities34.

Recent findings suggest that a, Locations of the monitored lowland tapirs (blue, n = 26 animals) and giant anteaters (green, n = 21 animals) throughout Brazil, overlaid on top of the HFI. The numbers depict the sample sizes within each study area. b, Heat map depicting the concentration of the analysed microplastic polymers for lowland tapirs (blue) and giant anteaters (green). Each row in the heat map corresponds to an individual animal. Polymers categorized as ‘other’ were those that occurred at low abundance, and included polyvinyl butyralolyethyleneimine, poly(butylene terephthalate), polyvinylformal, polyacetal, polymethylpentene, polyurethane and polyethylene glycol. Industry observers note that across all samples, we identified a total of 17,165 particles with a hit quality index (HQI) > 75, of which 2,815 (16.4%) were identified as microplastic. Microplastics were near-ubiquitous and found in the blood of all but four animals (three giant anteaters and one tapir), but systemic concentrations varied markedly across individuals (mean: 73.8 particles per ml; range 0 to 1,211.3 particles per ml). Lowland tapirs had the highest microplastic burdens (98.9 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 52.0–188.0 particles per ml), followed by giant anteaters (42.8 particles per ml; 95% confidence interval 26.7–68.6 particles per ml); however, concentrations did not differ significantly between species (β = 0.84, t = 1.88, P = 0.067). Tapirs and giant anteaters did differ in polymer composition (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Information), with additional inter-individual variation detailed in the Supplementary Discussion and Extended Data Fig. 2. Although comparable data on systemic microplastic burdens are not presently available for other species of terrestrial wildlife, the mean concentration of 73.8 particles per ml found in these animals is within the range reported in human blood using spectroscopic methods35 (1.9 to 108 particles per ml).

Across species and sampling sites, individual differences in blood microplastic burdens were consistently associated with anthropogenic disturbance. Of the 47 animals from which blood samples were collected, 40 had sufficient GPS tracking data for inclusion in the habitat use analyses. These animals spanned a wide gradient of human pressure (Fig. 2a), with the maximum HFI individuals experienced ranging from as low as 2.6 to 40.5. The home ranges of these animals were 12.6 km from the nearest human development on average, ranging from 95 m to 67.4 km. There was a significant positive relationship between blood microplastic concentrations and the maximum HFI within an animal’s home range (β = 0.07, t = 2.66, P = 0.011; Fig. 2b), although weighted mean HFI exposure was non-significant (β = 0.061, t = 1.73, P = 0.092; Extended Data Fig. 3).

Lines in b,c show the fitted population-level trend from a hierarchical generalized linear model (Tweedie distribution; log link) with species-specific random intercepts and slopes; shaded bands are 95% confidence intervals. P values are based on two-sided tests, with no correction for multiple comparisons; coefficients are on the link scale. Giant anteater image credit: Steven Traver via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0); tapir image credit: Christophe Mallet via PhyloPic (CC0 1.0).

According to recent reports, although these results highlight how direct exposure to human-modified landscapes shapes internal microplastic burdens, plastic pollution is a transboundary matter with complex dispersal pathways36. Atmospheric deposition and waterborne transport are likely contributors, as airborne microplastics from urban, industrial and agricultural sources can travel long distances before settling in remote ecosystems, and rainfall runoff, river discharge and seasonal flooding redistribute particles across landscapes to habitats far from their original sources2,3,4,5,7,37. Focusing on direct HFI exposure alone can obscure such effects. Indeed, we found that the local-scale effects of human land use were particularly important in shaping the systemic microplastic concentrations of the monitored animals, with significant effects of distance to development (β = −0.032, t = −2.94, P = 0.0057) and distance to the nearest waste management facility (β = −0.026, t = −2.73, P = 0.0096) (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3). Additional data on giant armadillos (Priodontes maximus) living in the Pantanal corroborate this trend (see Supplementary Discussion). These relationships were all robust to sensitivity analyses (Extended Data Tables 2 and 3 and Supplementary Discussion) and highlight the role of anthropogenic land use in driving species’ exposure to plastic pollution. The polymer profiles also varied across sampling sites in patterns that were broadly consistent with the dominant human activities at each site (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 and Supplementary Discussion).

Industry observers note that recent estimates38 reveal that the mean global HFI increased from 5.26 in 2001 to 6.63 in 2020, representing a 26% increase. This trend in land-use change was even more pronounced in Brazil, where the HFI rose by 42% over the same period, from 4.17 to 5.92. Problematically, anthropogenic land-use expansion often outpaces the development of waste management infrastructure39,40. This infrastructural gap leaves regions experiencing the most rapid change the least equipped to contain plastic waste. Across large parts of rural and interior Brazil, for example, solid waste collection remains inadequate and wastewater treatment is limited or absent altogether41,42,43. The plastic materials tied to the expanding human footprint thus have few barriers preventing them from becoming highly mobile environmental pollutants42. The relationship between human disturbance and blood microplastic concentrations identified here suggests that microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife will continue to rise as land-use change intensifies. Notably, even at an HFI of zero the model predicted blood microplastic concentrations of 10.5 particles per ml (95% confidence interval 4.6–24.2 particles per ml; intercept: β = 2.36, t = 5.58, P < 0.001). While we can not discount the potential that this non-zero intercept was the result of an unmodelled non-linear relationship at low HFI exposure, it does provide support that direct exposure to human-modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic microplastic burdens. The seemingly pervasive reach of microplastic pollution is most strikingly illustrated by our findings from the animals in the Pantanal. The Pantanal is the world’s largest and most pristine wetland, supporting an extraordinary diversity of wildlife within a relatively undisturbed landscape44. Unlike other biomes in Brazil, much of the Pantanal has remained ecologically intact owing to its remote location, limited infrastructure and seasonal flooding, which naturally regulate many human activities. Yet, we found microplastics in the blood of all of the individuals we sampled in the Pantanal, despite these animals living more than 65 km from the nearest development and more than 112 km from the nearest waste management facility. This finding is corroborated by several recent studies that reported substantial concentrations of microplastics in both aquatic environments and sediments throughout the Pantanal45,46,47, with the highest levels of microplastics (up to 1,174.2 items per m2) found near rivers flowing from urban areas46. The presence of microplastics in the blood of animals living many tens of kilometres from the nearest development or waste facility highlights how microplastics are a threat not only to wildlife with direct exposure to human-modified landscapes, but also to species across even the most remote and ecologically intact environments8. Developing a mechanistic understanding of the pathways through which microplastics reach remote terrestrial ecosystems will be essential for protecting wildlife from this highly mobile pollutant. Although environmental sampling across these sites would strengthen the causal inference of these relationships by directly linking environmental polymer profiles to those detected in blood, isolation protocols for chemically diverse samples such as blood and soil complicate spectroscopy-based comparisons48,49. Paired blood–environment sampling designs thus represent a productive, albeit challenging path forward.

By combining in vivo microplastic measurements with fine-scale movement data and high-resolution landscape disturbance indices, our study moves terrestrial microplastic research beyond detection surveys towards a spatially informed quantitative framework for predicting wildlife burdens from landscape context. This approach revealed how individual habitat use and anthropogenic land-use change interact to shape wildlife exposure to microplastics, and is readily transferable to other species and regions, offering a scalable tool for identifying vulnerable populations and informing targeted conservation responses. While no ecosystem is likely to be entirely free of microplastics50, we did find that animals in less disturbed habitats carried substantially lower burdens than those in close proximity to human infrastructure. These findings suggest that management efforts aimed at limiting animals’ exposure to human-modified environments and reducing their proximity to development and waste management infrastructure can serve to reduce the microplastic burdens carried by wildlife.

Lowland tapir (T. terrestris) samples were collected across three sites in Brazil. The agricultural mosaic site in the Cerrado was located between the municipalities of Nova Alvorada do Sul and Nova Andradina, in Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−21.99° N, −53.83° E). It features a mosaic of natural habitats, including Cerradão fragments, gallery forests and marshlands, which constitute approximately 12% of the study area. The remainder is heavily influenced by human activities, including agriculture (for example, sugarcane, soybean and corn), cattle ranching, eucalyptus plantations, highways and rural settlements. Precipitation exhibits marked seasonality, with approximately 70% of the total annual rainfall occurring between November and March51.

It has been revealed that the field site in the Pantanal was situated on Baía das Pedras Ranch, in the Nhecolândia Sub-Region of the Southern Pantanal, Municipality of Aquidauana, Mato Grosso do Sul State, Brazil (−19.33° N, −55.72° E). This private property spans 145 km² and comprises a mosaic of seasonally inundated grasslands, lakes, gallery forests, scrub, and deciduous forests. The Pantanal is a nearly pristine biome with a low human footprint, and is far removed from areas experiencing deforestation and other anthropogenic pressures. The ranch supports abundant wildlife and extensive cattle grazing on native grasses. The average annual temperature is 25 °C, and the annual rainfall is 1,185 mm.

According to recent reports, the site in the Amazon was located at Tanguro Farm, a privately owned 103,000 ha property in Querência, Mato Grosso state, that sits at the transition between the Cerrado savanna and the Amazon rainforest along the southern Arc of Deforestation. Owned by AMAGGI, a major actor in Brazil’s soybean industry, the farm comprises 59,000 ha (57%) of croplands (soybean, corn, and cotton) and 44,000 ha (43%) of legally protected forest reserves. This region is the driest portion of the Amazon basin and experiences a prolonged dry season (May–September) with annual rainfall of 1,700–2,200 mm. Forests in this region are shorter (~20 m) than the moist Amazon rainforest (~30 m). About 40% of the farm was cleared for pasture (1976–1992) and later converted to soy cultivation (2003–2010), leaving riparian forests surrounded by croplands.

Industry observers note that the giant anteater (M. tridactyla) data collection was conducted in the Cerrado savanna of Mato Grosso do Sul state, Brazil, as part of the Anteaters and Highways Project (ICAS, www.icasconservation.org.br), which investigates wildlife-vehicle collisions and their impacts on wildlife populations. Sampling areas were located near two federal roads: BR-267 (−21.64° N, −53.51° E) and BR-262 (−20.86° N, −52.04° E). As described above, the study region is a mosaic landscape dominated by open areas, including grasslands, pastures, and croplands, interspersed with small remnants of native savanna and forest vegetation, as well as eucalyptus plantations52.

In a recent development, in addition to the tapir and giant anteater data, we also obtained a smaller amount of data from three giant armadillos (P. maximus). The giant armadillo data collection was also conducted at the Baía das Pedras Lodge and Ranch in the Pantanal, which served as the base of operations for the Giant Armadillo Conservation Program (GACP).

All animal capture, handling, and blood sampling procedures were approved by the Brazilian Ministry of the Environment (MMA) and the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio) under license numbers 14603-25 (lowland tapirs), 53798-18 (giant anteaters) and 27587-1 (giant armadillos). All procedures were performed in accordance with the terms of these licenses and with relevant national and institutional animal welfare guidelines. Chemical immobilization was performed under veterinary oversight, and all animals were released at their capture sites following full recovery.

Lowland tapirs were captured using a combination of methods, including darting, following physical restraint in box-traps or pitfall traps, or darting from a distance. Box traps and pitfall traps were deployed in areas frequently visited by tapirs. Tapirs captured by these methods were anaesthetized intramuscularly with a combination of butorphanol (0.17 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.012 mg kg−1) and ketamine (0.7 mg kg−1). Reversal agents, including atipamezole (0.04 mg kg−1) and naltrexone (0.35 mg kg−1), were administered at the conclusion of procedures. For tapirs darted from a distance, anaesthetics included tiletamine-zolazepam (1.25 mg kg−1), medetomidine (0.006 mg kg−1), ketamine (0.6 mg kg−1) and atropine (0.03 mg kg−1). Darts (3 ml or 5 ml) were used to deliver anaesthetics. Midazolam (0.03 mg kg−1) was administered 30 min later to maintain anaesthesia. Captured tapirs underwent a range of procedures, including subcutaneous microchip insertion, morphometric measurements, sex and age determination, physical examinations, blood sample collection and telemetry collar placement for adults.

Tapirs were equipped with GPS collars (Telonics TGW SOB and GPS IRIDIUM models) programmed to obtain hourly location fixes, with a median operational life of 15.4 months. Additional location data were collected from stationary tags placed in the Pantanal (n = 883) and Cerrado (n = 174) to calibrate the measurement error in the GPS datasets.

Sources indicate that giant anteaters were captured between February 2021 and November 2022 using motorized active searches between 15:00 and 17:00, when they exhibit higher diurnal activity due to colder temperatures53,54. Searches were conducted along dirt roads in open areas, with two team members stationed in the back of a truck to improve detectability. Upon spotting an individual, technicians approached the animal on foot and captures were performed using two long-handled dip nets (1.5 m handles, 0.7 m diameter hoops). Physical capture typically lasted around 1 min.

Sources indicate that captured giant anteaters were chemically immobilized, equipped with GPS radiotelemetry harnesses (Telonics) as previously described55 and blood samples were collected. In brief, animals were anaesthetized using a protocol of butorphanol tartrate (Zoetis Indústria de Produtos Veterinários; 0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (Agener-União; 0.1 mg kg−1) and midazolam hydrochloride (Cristália; 0.2 mg kg−1), adapted from ref. 55. The induction period averaged 8.27 ± 4.78 min.

Industry observers note that giant armadillos were captured between February 2021 and November 2022, using a method tailored to their natural behaviour56. Researchers tracked footprints and signs of recent predation, such as termite mounds, to locate burrows. When a burrow was identified and confirmed to contain an armadillo (indicated by the entrance being sealed with sand), an iron funnel trap (jequi-type) was placed at the entrance. Once captured, animals were transported in iron-reinforced wooden crates and held overnight for nocturnal species, with procedures beginning the following morning at the capture site.

Sources indicate that captured giant armadillos were anaesthetized for the collection of blood samples and surgical implantation of intra-abdominal transmitters. Anaesthetic protocols included an intramuscular injection of butorphanol tartrate (0.1 mg kg−1), detomidine hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1), and midazolam hydrochloride (0.1 mg kg−1) into the hind limbs. Before surgery, intradermal local anaesthesia with lidocaine hydrochloride (2 mg kg−1, Eurofarma) was infiltrated into the infra-umbilical region. Ketamine hydrochloride (10 mg kg−1) was administered intramuscularly as a supplementary anaesthetic immediately after the animals were completely washed. Transmitters (IMP 310 model, Telonics; 9.4 × 2.3 cm, 42 g, 36-month operational life) were surgically implanted within the abdominal cavity under sterile conditions. Following surgery, anaesthesia was reversed using a combination of naloxone hydrochloride (0.02 mg kg−1), yohimbine hydrochloride (0.125 mg kg−1), and flumazenil (0.01 mg kg−1). Armadillos were released at their capture sites upon recovery, typically remaining in their burrows for 24 to 120 h (average of 48 h) before emerging. Daily monitoring was conducted for 12–22 days post-release using telemetry receivers (model TR-4, Telonics) and VHF antennas (model RA-23K). After the initial monitoring period, armadillos were monitored monthly until the end of the transmitter’s operational life.

In a recent development, approximately 10 ml of blood was collected within 20 min of immobilization via venipuncture of the medial saphenous or cephalic veins using a sterile glass vacutainer system (BD Vacutainer). Tapir captures were conducted in remote forest sites without access to field refrigeration. Blood samples were therefore stored in pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept shaded at ambient temperature, and transferred to a −20 °C freezer on return to the base camp within 5–6 h.

According to recent reports, blood samples (~5 ml) were collected approximately 20 min after induction from the cephalic or saphenous veins using a sterile vacutainer system with 23G or 25G needles (BD Vacutainer). Samples were transferred to pre-cleaned glass collection tubes with no preservatives, sealed with clean aluminium foil and a metal cap to prevent contamination during storage, kept refrigerated at 4 °C on site, and frozen at −20 °C within 12–24 h for subsequent processing. We note that blood samples were obtained from three individual giant armadillos, however we obtained repeat samples at two time points for two of these animals. Although these blood samples were processed individually, they were pooled (that is, averaged) in our statistical analyses.

Cold storage under the above-mentioned conditions is standard practice in microplastic analyses and does not affect particle abundance or polymer identity. Microplastics are chemically stable over these timescales, and method reviews emphasize that environmental samples containing microplastics are routinely stored at 4 °C for days to weeks prior to processing, or frozen at −20 °C for longer periods, without alteration of polymer composition (reviewed in ref. 57).

In a recent development, blood microplastic isolation was performed following a protocol previously developed by our team58,59,60. Depending on the sampling date, blood samples were stored at −20 °C for ~1–22 months between collection (Feb 2021–Nov 2022) and digestion (Dec 2022). On the first day of isolation, 1 ml of each blood sample was placed in an Erlenmeyer flask along with 50 ml of 10% KOH solution (sample ratio of 1:50). The mixture was incubated on a shaker at 60 °C and 250 rpm for 24 h. After the initial 24-h incubation, 10 ml of 47% NaClO were added to each sample to achieve a final concentration of 7.7%. The samples were then incubated under the same conditions (60 °C and 250 rpm) for an additional 24 h.

In a recent development, following the second day of digestion, all samples were filtered through a 47 mm polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size (Merck Omnipore) and rinsed 3 times with filtered ultrapure water. The membranes containing the particles were then submerged in 50 ml of 20% HNO3 and placed in an ultrasonic bath with sweep function at 100% power and 45 kHz frequency for 15 min to transfer the particles from the membrane to the solution. The samples were further incubated for 30 min at 40 °C and 250 rpm.

After removing the membranes, the samples underwent a 24-h incubation at 40 °C and 250 rpm. On the final day, the samples were filtered through a 13 mm PTFE membrane with a 0.45 μm pore size, rinsed three times with filtered ultrapure water, and mounted on glass slides for microscopy and spectroscopy analysis. The resulting filter membranes were then stored in pre-cleaned glass Petri dishes and analysed by Raman spectroscopy over the subsequent ~12 months (Jan–Dec 2023). After digestion, a proportion of non-plastic particulates remained on the membrane, such that microplastics accounted for an average of 16.4% of imaged particles with HQI > 75 (range 0–89.9%).

Quality assurance and quality control methods used throughout the process are detailed in the Supplementary Methods (see also Extended Data Figs. 6 and 7).

Recent findings suggest that microplastic identification and characterization were conducted using a confocal Raman microscope (alpha300 R, WITec) equipped with a UHTS 300 spectrometer (WITec) and a 532-nm laser. The microscope was operated using Control Five software, and the acquired data were processed with Project Five software to compensate for background noise and cosmic radiation signals.

Industry observers note that as an initial step, a whole membrane image was captured using a 10× NA 0.25 Zeiss objective with the Area Stitching option. From this image, a specific field was selected for detailed imaging with a 50× NA 0.75 Zeiss objective, employing both the Area Stitching option and Z-stack autofocus. Particle identification was facilitated by the Particle Scout software, which enabled the acquisition of Raman spectra for all identified particles across the entire membrane. Raman spectra were then obtained using a 100× DIC NA 0.9 Zeiss objective, with a laser power of 10 mW, an accumulation of 4, and an integration time of 0.45 s. Spectra autofocus was used throughout the measurements. The acquired spectra were then compared against the S.T. Japan database (S.T. Japan Europe GmbH) and the SLoPP MPs Raman library61 using the True Match-Integrated Raman Spectra Database Management software. Microplastic characterization was based on an automated, 3-step process that was optimized for spectra acquisition rather than image sharpness. This precluded the manual assessment of particle shape (for example, fibres or fragments) or colour. Only matches with an HQI greater than 75% were considered for further analysis.

Recent findings suggest that to assess changes in the HFI over time, we obtained and processed global HFI rasters at a 300 m resolution for the years 2001 and 2020 from the Wildlife Conservation Society Human Footprint dataset (https://wcshumanfootprint.org/). After ensuring projections and resolutions were consistent between the HFI rasters, a difference raster was generated by subtracting the 2001 HFI from the 2020 HFI to visualize areas of increasing and decreasing human influence. We cropped and masked the HFI rasters to remove areas outside of Brazil and then computed the mean HFI for 2001 and 2020, as well as the absolute differences. These analyses were conducted in R using the terra (v1.8-54)62, sf (v1.0-21)63,64, tmap (v4.0.0.9000)65, fields (v16.3)66, rnaturalearth (v1.0.1)67, and geobr (v1.9.1)68 packages.

Before analysis, we pre-processed the GPS location data in order to calibrate the measurement error and filter outliers. Pre-processing was done via the methods implemented in the R package ctmm (v1.2.1)69. For each location estimate, the GPS trackers recorded a unitless Horizontal Dilution of Precision (HDOP), a value which is a measure of the accuracy of each positional fix. We converted the HDOP values into calibrated errors by specifying 20-m error at an HDOP of 1 for 2D fixes, and 10-m error at an HDOP of 1 for the 3D fixes70. For each individual dataset, we then removed outliers based on error-informed distance from the median location, and the minimum speed required to explain each location’s displacement. Through this process we identified a total of 16,656 outliers, which represented ca. 3.55% of the total 469,410 locations. After filtering outliers, the final dataset consisted of 343,913 GPS locations across 20 individual giant anteaters, 6,072 GPS locations across 2 individual giant armadillos, and 102,769 GPS locations across 20 individual lowland tapirs.

Recent findings suggest that for each of the tracked animals, we used a continuous-time approach to estimate their movement rates and home ranges, enabling robust comparisons across individuals71. We first fitted a series of continuous-time stochastic process movement models to the location data. Parameters were estimated using perturbative-hybrid residual maximum likelihood (pHREML)72, and identified the best model via small-sample-sized-corrected Akaike’s information criterion (AICc). From both visual inspections of the semi-variograms, and the parameters of the fitted movement models, all animals occupied stable home ranges throughout the monitoring period with no indication of range shifts or large-scale dispersal events.

According to recent reports, from the selected models, we estimated each animal’s diffusion rate (in km2 day−1) as a measure of their movement rate. We next estimated each animal’s home range, using autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE)73. AKDE home range estimates were conditioned on the autocorrelation structure of the fitted movement model, and we implemented the small-sample-size bias correction of Fleming & Calabrese (2017)74, as well as the optimal weighting of Fleming et al. (2018)75 to correct for uneven sampling. Home range areas (in km2) were estimated as the area contained within the polygon delimited by the 95% isopleth of the probability density.

Industry observers note that we estimated the mean and maximum HFI within each individual’s home range. HFI is an aggregate measure of human disturbance that ranges from 0 in natural habitats to 50 in the most anthropogenically modified habitats33. A raster of HFI data with a spatial resolution of 100 m was obtained from Gassert et al.38. The weighted mean HFI within an individual’s home range was estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean of HFI values:.

with weights (wu) determined by the probability density at each location u. Maximum HFI exposure was estimated by identifying the maximum value of HFI within each animal’s home range. We also estimated more nuanced patterns of habitat use via the MapBiomas database34, which details land use throughout Brazil at a spatial resolution of 10 m. We focused on habitats classified as water, development, agriculture, pasture, and native forest, which represented the majority of the land classes within the monitored animals’ home ranges. The proportions of each of these land classes within each animal’s home range were again estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean. Lastly, we used the MapBiomas land classification data, the Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI), and the Waste Methane Assessment Platform 1.5.0, 2025 (https://wastemap.earth) to generate spatial rasters of distance to development, and distance to the nearest waste management facility (both in m). Development was a compound measure that captured the built environment, and was composed of the MapBiomas collection 10 classes: urban areas (24), mining (30), photovoltaic power plants (75), and other non-vegetated areas (25). From these spatial data, we estimated each animal’s mean distance to development and to the nearest waste management facility, estimated by calculating the weighted arithmetic mean.

To study how human land-use change shaped blood microplastic concentrations, we fit hierarchical generalized linear regression models using the methods implemented in the mgcv package (v1.9-1)76. Because the microplastic concentrations scaled between [0,∞], we used a Tweedie distribution with a log link for the error distribution77, with parameters estimated via restricted maximum likelihood (REML). The regression models testing for correlations between individual habitat use and microplastic concentrations included a population-level effect, as well as random intercepts and slopes for each of the species, with the following general form.

where β0 represents the population-level intercept, β is the population-level slope, us[i] is the species-specific random intercept, vs[i] is the species-specific random slope, and s[i] indexes the species of individual i. This structure was used for all of the habitat covariates xi. From these models, inference was then made on the population-level trend.

All analyses were conducted in R (v4.3.3). Weighted means and proportions of land-use exposure were computed with the weights package (v1.0.4). Figures were produced with ggplot2 (v3.5.2), ggspatial (v1.1.9), tidyterra (v0.7.0), rphylopic (v1.5.0; animal silhouettes), fmsb (v0.7.6) and gridExtra (v2.3).

No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Sample sizes were determined by the number of animals that could be safely captured during the study period (February 2021 to November 2022) given the logistical constraints of live-capturing large, threatened, free-ranging mammals under national permits, and all animals captured during this period were sampled. This was an observational field study, so randomization was not applicable; animals were not allocated to experimental groups, and exposure to human land use was determined by each individual’s own space use. The investigators were not blinded to species or sampling site during laboratory processing or analysis; however, particle detection and polymer identification were automated (Particle Scout and True Match software) and based on a fixed spectral-match threshold (HQI > 75%), which limits observer bias. Each animal contributed one blood sample, with the exception of two giant armadillos sampled at two time points, whose values were averaged before analysis. Seven animals lacked sufficient GPS tracking data and were excluded from the habitat use models but retained in descriptive analyses. Samples were processed in two batches, each with a procedural blank (Supplementary Methods); all lowland tapir samples were processed in the same batch. The polymer-integrity test shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 was repeated three times independently with similar results.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

According to recent reports, the blood microplastics data (particle-level measurements, polymer identifications and per-individual summaries underlying Figs. 1 and 2, Extended Data Figs. 1, 2 and 4–7 and Extended Data Tables 1–3), raw GPS tracking data, and the per-individual movement and land-use summaries (underlying Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 3) are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34001445 (ref. 78) and on GitHub (https://github.com/QuantitativeEcologyLab/microplastics_brazil). This study also used the following publicly available datasets: the 100 m HFI79 (https://source.coop/repositories/vizzuality/hfp-100/description); the Wildlife Conservation Society 300 m Human Footprint rasters for 2001 and 2020 (https://wcshumanfootprint.org/data-access); MapBiomas Brazil Collection 10 land use and land cover maps (https://brasil.mapbiomas.org/, downloads at https://brasil.mapbiomas.org/en/downloads/); waste management facility locations from the Waste Methane Assessment Platform (WasteMAP) v1.5.0, developed by RMI and Clean Air Task Force (https://wastemap.earth); and Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com) and geobr68 basemap data. Raman spectra were matched against the SLoPP library61 (openly available) and the S.T. Japan commercial spectral database (S.T. Japan Europe GmbH), which is available under licence from the vendor. Source data are provided with this paper.

Brighton centre-back Luka Vuskovic is proving there is more to his game than simply defending.

The Croatian has been a standout star for manager Fabian Hurzeler since arriving in the summer window from Tottenham.

His performances have been a large part of the Seagull's strong start to the campaign which has them sitting in second place.

And he continued to impress on his latest international outing for Croatia.

In Croatia's game against Czechia, Vuskovic has showcased another side of his abilities, with some unusual data for a centre-back.

As he topped plenty of creative stats despite being in the backline.

It was only a narrow win for the Croats, defeating their fellow European opposition 2-1, with Vuskovic right at the heart of it.

As per FotMob, despite playing at centre-back, the 19-year-old defender managed to create the most chances of the game between Croatia and Czechia.

He created four in total, with two of those coming as significant chances for his nation.

The Brighton ace was also influential, as one of those chances did result in a goal, handing him an assist.

Vuskovic also completed the most passes into the final third (nine), while maintaining a total passing accuracy of 94 per cent.

Defensively, he also performed well, winning six out of his nine duels - a 66 per cent success rate.

But nonetheless, seeing a centre-back dominate those creative stats is a rare sight, and perhaps a quality that could be honed back in England.

A Brighton centre-back being capable on the ball is no surprise and his qualities there are likely part of why he was signed in the first place.

However, his ability to produce chances from centre-back and put the ball into the final third is a rare sight.

This season in the Premier League, over his 10 appearances, Vuskovic has only managed to create one chance for Brighton.

While, in terms of getting the ball up the pitch, he ranks mid-range for line-breaking passes with 10.95 per 90. This places him in the 58th percentile.

If this latest performance for Croatia gives him more confidence to try for those final passes, that would add another edge to an already exciting Brighton side.

Whether or not this was just a one-off good day at the office remains to be seen, but he showcase a new possible weapon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool are reportedly keen for Ifeanyi Ndukwe to continue his development on loan with Levante in Spain, despite the player now being eligible for a UK work permit.

The 18-year-old was a revelation for the Reds in pre-season but, at the time, he didn’t meet the criteria to play competitively in England and was subsequently dispatched to the LaLiga outfit for this season.

He’s continued to perform impressively for Los Azulgranas, and there were reports last month of his agents arranging to discuss the possibility of a January recall to Anfield.

According to Graeme Bailey for TEAMtalk, Liverpool are convinced that Ndukwe could break into their first-team setup next year and view him as ‘hugely key’ for their long-term intends.

Although he could theoretically be recalled in January, the Reds’ preference is for him to remain with Levante for the rest of his season and proceed with his development there.

That hasn’t stopped some Premier League clubs from enquiring about his availability for a loan move for the second half of the campaign to give him a first taste of English top-flight football.

According to recent reports, want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

Having had to wait until October for his first start for Levante, Ndukwe was then included from the first whistle in all six of their LaLiga games since the extended international break earlier in the autumn (Transfermarkt).

Luis Castro demonstrably has faith in the Austrian teenager, whose performances on loan have earned praise from the Spanish media, although the occasional error has served as a reminder that he’s still developing and will have off-days as part of that.

While Premier League exposure would be a quite informative barometer of the youngster’s readiness for the Liverpool first team, we’d be in favour of him continuing with Levante if he’s enjoying regular game-time there.

At the moment Ndukwe is featuring regularly in one of Europe’s foremost domestic leagues, and doing so with a club where media attention and scrutiny is comparatively sparse, thus keeping him away from the harshest of exposure.

He must be doing plenty right to have English top-flight clubs asking about taking him on loan in the winter. If that’s the case, then the current strategy seems to be working, and we see no reason to deviate from that any time soon.
