Igli Tare has spoken without holding anything back about his time at AC Milan, explaining his frustration with several things.

When Tare arrived, many Milan fans were happy to see someone with Serie A experience oversee the project and whilst his first season didn’t end how anyone had hoped, he wasn’t seen as a major glitch.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

So, when it was unveiled that he was part of a complete overturning of the management, there was a bit of a surprise, even if it did feel inevitable at one point.

In a recent development, with the overhaul of changes in the summer, one does wonder what Tare would have done differently, especially with suggestions that his hands were tied in the mercato last season. Nevertheless,.

Speaking on Sky Sport’s ‘Calcio Unplugged’, Igli Tare revealed all to Gianluca Di Marzio and Stefano Borghi in an in-depth interview about his time with the Diavolo, as Radio Rossonera has relayed.

Industry observers note that “Today is the first time I’ve spoken out after all these months. The wound of not having reached the Champions League is still enormous, and since I arrived at Milan – also questioning myself with the type of contract I signed – the objective couldn’t be only the Champions League; otherwise I wouldn’t have understood where I was.”.

“It was great because he was the one who convinced me. He had such a huge desire to join Milan. I wanted to video chat before going to see him because I couldn’t believe it. But after five minutes, I knew in my head that he was the player Milan really lacked.

According to recent reports, “Not just because of his qualities, but as a man and as a figure that that team didn’t have. He never said no. A photo with a child, an autograph, a meeting, talking to someone… He never said no. These are the things that humility is key to in life.

“I’m proud to have brought a great champion to Milan. In my opinion, if he wants, he can play another two seasons without any problem. He never missed a training session. Sometimes we were the ones to stop him because he was always there, ready. Loving football at that age is truly an honour.”.

Is it a characteristic of the champion or is it a generational concern? Today’s champions seem to have a different mentality:.

According to recent reports, “Today we live in the age of social media. At 16, you’re already a footballer who can earn millions of euros. Living this way, you have the problem of not only managing a player, who is still a child, but you have to manage the business they bring with them: family, agents, girlfriends….

In a recent development, “These are obstacles that didn’t exist back then. We were a generation that played in the streets. Back then, our parents beat us to get us to come home. Today, however, it’s to get them out of the house because they spend all day in front of computers.

“This aspect has been lost a bit, but it’s our fault. Education and discipline are the key to success.”.

In a recent development, fullkrug. He performed poorly in Milan, but in the Bundesliga he’s scoring a lot and is the top scorer. How do you explain that?

It has been revealed that “It’s simple. He came to us after a tough time in England, with a lot of scepticism. And then, right away, he broke his toe. No one ever noted he’d been having injections on the bone for two months just to train, let alone to play.

Industry observers note that “I knew he was a centre forward that the team was missing; given his characteristics and his interpretation of the game, his qualities were unquestionable. Just two years before coming to Milan, he’d played in the Champions League final, playing a key role in a competition with Borussia Dortmund.

“There are situations where, for a player, even a very key one, it matters how you feel. If you feel appreciated, valued, taken into consideration… When you play for a club like Milan, the weight of the shirt is completely different than when you play for other clubs.

“You feel it from the first day you join. I had no doubt that he could be what he’s demonstrating now.”.

Sources indicate that “We tried to sign him back in June. We made a first attempt. In the final days of the transfer window, another important name we tried to sign was Akanji. The Champions League was crucial for both of them. They turned him down, not because of the club’s importance, but because he wasn’t playing in the Champions League.

“Then the opportunity arose again at the end of August for Rabiot. Defeat against Cremonese? No, we had already decided to bring him. It was just a matter of contract details.”.

In a recent development, “It was difficult for us because we decided to change the formation five days before the transfer window closed. Switching from a 4-3-3 to a three-man defense meant we were having a really hard time finding a quality player in the last five days.

Sources indicate that “We were a bit unlucky, first with the Akanji story and then with Liverpool’s Joe Gomez… Guehi’s move from Crystal Palace to Liverpool fell through, and at the last minute they—we already had the deal ready, we were just waiting for this to happen—made a step back. And to avoid being left without a central defender at the last minute, we signed Odogu as a promising player.”.

On not being able to reach the Champions League and not being able to continue his work at Milan….

“This is the first time today, after all these months, that I’ve spoken about this… The wound of not reaching the Champions League is still enormous. I think that from the first day I arrived at Milan, even in the way I signed—I questioned myself with the type of contract.

Recent findings suggest that “I noted, ‘If I have to come only for the Champions League objective, then I don’t understand where I’ve come from.’ Milan has a different story. I had to go through a trial. The disappointment is that those who run the club didn’t understand how much time people needed, which is now being done, rightly so.

“That is to say, it takes several transfer sessions to get a competitive team ready to win. At the beginning, I felt the responsibility to put the pieces together immediately, because after the defeat in the Coppa Italia final the year before, there were some key signs.

“I didn’t know where to start. But I think we did an important job last summer, we sold for a lot and also signed 10 latest players. Then you need time to integrate, learn new philosophies and create a cohesive group, hungry to win.

“Until March-April, we were a group with difficulties, but we were at the top of the table. Then in the last 10 matchdays, we had a mental breakdown, also due to other external dynamics, which I don’t want to discuss here, which had a significant impact.

Industry observers note that “Internal or external dynamics? External to the team. But we also have some blame: myself first and foremost, along with Max [Allegri].

“We had to be a little more attentive to certain dynamics. We needed to be more present with the team to ultimately lead them to the final result. Isolation is the wrong word; I don’t believe in these things. I believe in teamwork; I believe in cohesion: from the club to the team.

“When this happens, you transmit it to the team. When these situations become possible, you could also see it in the team’s results, because the players are very attentive. Sometimes we think they have other interests, but they pay attention to everything that comes out. They follow everything very carefully and transmit it.

“Instilling serenity… How can you convey serenity? When, in difficult moments, you show that you believe in the project more than before. Sometimes I missed this feeling, a lack of something that could give us the final push.”.

But despite this, did you think you could continue? Does this farewell after only a year feel like a stab in the back?

“Look, I would have asked for a round table where we could all sit down together and analyze everything. Then they could have just said ‘no, thanks’… But I respect the decision they made. I accept it with great regret, but I’ve never questioned it because there’s someone above me who has to decide, including for the fate of the club.

“And when they decide to take a different path, you have to accept it. I know things could have gone differently, even much better. I’ll always be a Milan fan, even after an experience like that.”.

Was AC Milan a team that needed the constant presence of a manager or coach to avoid letting itself go as it later did?

According to recent reports, “The feeling I had at the beginning was that this leadership was a bit lacking. The arrival of Modric—and another of our goals was also Granit Xhaka, Leverkusen’s captain—was precisely to bring real players into the group, with important characteristics and capable of leading others.

In a recent development, “Granit didn’t arrive; Luka arrived, who has a different way of being a leader: he does it in silence and with his attitude on the pitch. I had the opportunity to meet Mike Maignan: an extraordinary guy, a soul who cares deeply about the AC Milan shirt.

“Gabbia is another extraordinary guy; he lives for this club. Rabiot too… His experience spoke for itself. The great disappointment is that I expected something more in terms of responsibility and leadership from Pulisic: he’s a top-class player with unquestionable qualities. But in terms of performance, things happened that I had never experienced in my career….

“Like Gimenez: an extraordinary guy with numbers that spoke for themselves; for a year he failed to score a goal. Then it happened that Pulisic didn’t score for six months. He scored a goal. Then Leao didn’t score for four months.

“Situations that are hard to come by in football have happened… It can happen that you don’t score for a month, two months, but that long a period of time also affected the team’s final performance.

In a recent development, “Losing a match against Cagliari the way we did, 2-1, I think was the worst match of my life. The feeling and the disappointment I felt towards the fans in the stadium that night is something I will never forget for the rest of my life.”.

If Cardinale had been the Cardinale he is today, the one who is also physically present, would you still be AC ​​Milan’s DS?

“I can’t answer that question; he has to answer it. I can say that I remember when the Jashari negotiations were going on… I had just landed in Rome and I was very pleased when he called me because he wanted to understand what was happening in that negotiation.

“I explained all the dynamics to him and I really liked that he said, ‘Anything you need, if you have to spend a little more, let me know because I’m here.’ Then during that process I never had the chance to talk to him, even intentionally.

In a recent development, “There were other people above me who I never wanted to bypass. I never had a direct relationship with him, and the possibility of a discussion would have helped everyone. Not me, but everyone. By putting all the problems and dynamics on the table, we could have resolved things much sooner. But I think it’s a new experience for Cardinale.

“He’s had experience in other sports in America. Now he’s done something important, taking responsibility and putting his face on the line. I would have preferred to have had that presence even when I was there because it would have been very useful. But for the Milan, better late than never.

It has been revealed that “Now, for better or worse, he will make his own decisions and responsibilities. I think that for him, too, the best interests of Milan come first.”.

Was Leao a problem or a resource in your mind?

According to recent reports, “I knew him from the outside. When I had the chance to meet him in person, I thought he was an extraordinary guy. I truly loved him as a person, like everyone else. But he was the player from whom we all expected something more. I think football was no longer a priority for him. That’s the key to understanding him.”.

“I think a bit about his life outside of football. Music, fashion, things… But I never doubted the sense of belonging he had towards Milan. You could sense that he loved playing for Milan and was suffering from not performing.

It has been revealed that “He had many physical problems… First a calf, then a bit of pubalgia… He always played with his hands under control. I always tried to have individual conversations with him more than with any other Milan player.

In a recent development, “Every time I spoke to him, I left with a positive feeling. I sensed that he wanted to. But sometimes wanting isn’t enough.”.

Was there a chance that Leao would leave during your summer too?

Industry observers note that “A concrete offer never came for him. Regarding the other transfers, it’s not just Tare’s job. When I arrived – even at Lazio – I was a bit alone, but I tried to involve all the members of the club to give him the importance he needed to build a sense of belonging and responsibility. I think I did a very good job, together with Furlani, Ibra, and Moncada.

It has been revealed that “We achieved significant sales figures, in a year when we weren’t even in the Champions League. Thanks to the work we did last summer, investments were made this year, with the money we had at the time. I really believe in teamwork.

“I noted it even before the Coppa Italia match against Bari; I asked to speak to convey the importance of the work of the people within the club because it was right that way. Then afterwards, it’s human….

“They were coming off a bad year, when two cumbersome figures like Tare and Allegri arrive, and everyone was talking about Tare and Allegri, some disappointment was understandable. I understood the feeling they had, but I could… There was little to do about it.

“For me, it was a new path, a new opportunity. It was essential to work as a team and present ourselves as a real manufacturer.”.

By Lewis Nolan | 14 Nov 2026 23:43, Last updated: 15 Nov 2026 01:33.

Liverpool are keen on Lens centre-back Pierre Ismaelo Ganiou despite interest from a number of other clubs, the latest report has claimed.

The Premier League is now on pause for the November international break, and that has given Reds supporters the chance to assess the squad.

Andoni Iraola has made a positive start to life at Anfield, with the team's defence having notably improved, led by the likes of Virgil van Dijk and Ronald Araujo.

However, Van Djik has entered the final year of his contract, while Araujo is only on loan from Barcelona and could return to the Spanish side at the end of the season.

Amid uncertainty regarding the future of their defence, Football Insider report that the Reds are one of several clubs keen on signing Lens defender Ganiou, who is valued by Transfermarkt at just over £25m.

Ganiou does not have an extensive history of top-flight football considering he has played just 28 games in Ligue 1 in his entire career, though he has been impressive for Lens.

In five league matches for the French side this season, the 21-year-old has won 69% of his duels, including 73% of his ground duels.

Liverpool have typically looked to sign aerially dominant defenders, so while the Frenchman boasts an impressive 64% duel success rate in the air, he only averages 1.8 aerial duels won per game.

Van Dijk has won an average of 3.8 duels in the air in the league so far, while Jeremy Jacquet has won 2.6 aerial duels in the Premier League, and the Reds would almost certainly aim to get Ganiou closer to those figures.

While Van Dijk is 35 and is into the final year of his contract, he has shown no signs of physical decline, and he has expressed a desire to remain at Anfield.

If he was to extend his stay on Merseyside, the Reds may not need to delve into the market for another centre-back.

Joe Gomez is expected to leave, and he could be replaced in the squad by Araujo, which would then leave the club in need of a right-back.

Jacquet and Giovanni Leoni will be part of the squad for the coming seasons, while many believe that Ifeanyi Ndukwe could play a role for the team once his loan at Levante ends.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fighting for a place in the UEFA Nations League quarter-finals, Germany are set to host League A's Group A2 leaders, the Netherlands, at Olympiastadion Berlin on Monday.
  • Die Mannschaft know that they likely need to win to progress, while Oranje are through barring an unprecedented swing in goal-difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Anthony Nolan | 14 Nov 2026 23:59, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 10:15.

Fighting for a place in the UEFA Nations League quarter-finals, Germany are set to host League A's Group A2 leaders, the Netherlands, at Olympiastadion Berlin on Monday.

Die Mannschaft know that they likely need to win to progress, while Oranje are through barring an unprecedented swing in goal-difference.

Jurgen Klopp's Germany are pushing to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals for just the second time, but they face a tough test to reach the last eight.

Die Mannschaft are at the moment third in Group A2, level on eight points with Greece and three behind the Netherlands, and their chance to go through leans on the fact UEFA prioritises head-to-head points between tied teams.

Klopp's side were beaten 1-0 by the Azure and White on September 27 before drawing 0-0 with them on matchday four.

However, Ivan Jovanovic's men were hammered 7-0 by the Dutch on Friday, meaning that a German victory over the Netherlands on Monday would see them progress ahead of Greece regardless of their result against Serbia.

Die Mannschaft were held to a 1-1 stalemate by Oranje on matchday one, with Cody Gakpo equalising in second-half stoppage time to deny his former Liverpool manager maximum points.

Klopp's team have remained undefeated in the group since their loss to Greece, most recently beating Serbia 3-1 on Friday, when they raced into a 2-0 lead within the first 14 minutes thanks to an own-goal from Srdjan Babic and a follow-up by Florian Wirtz.

Meanwhile, Xavi's Netherlands have yet to taste defeat in the Nations League this term, and are in a commanding position at the top of their group going into the final matchday.

Leading with 11 points, Oranje's 7-0 demolition of Greece last time out - following a 2-2 draw on October 1 - means the only possibility of them finishing below the top two is if there is a dramatic 14-goal swing in the Azure and White's favour.

Xavi is without talismanic centre-back Virgil van Dijk this month, but his team were still able to keep their first clean sheet in the competition on Friday, while Tijani Reijnders's first-half hat-trick set the tone at the opposite end of the pitch.

However, it remains to be seen whether the Netherlands can repeat that attacking showcase in Germany, considering that they have won just one of their last six away clashes against Die Mannschaft.

On the other hand, Oranje are unbeaten in their past seven matches on the road, and last suffered a travelling defeat in a penalty shootout against Spain during the Nations League quarter-finals in March 2025, following a 5-5 aggregate draw.

Netherlands Nations League form:.

Germany have no latest injury challenges to contend with, though they are missing Bayern Munich stars Jamal Musiala and Serge Gnabry due to respective muscle problems.

In their absence, Klopp could continue with Brajan Gruda, Florian Wirtz and Derry Scherhant behind Arsenal man Kai Havertz up top.

As for the Netherlands, they were forced to take off Frenkie De Jong at half time against Greece after he suffered back pain, and he has now left the national squad to return to Barcelona.

Teun Koopmeiners looks set to step in and fill the gap alongside Joey Veerman at the base of Xavi's midfield, while Tijani Reijnders operates in the number 10 role.

Further forward, Donyell Malen has been a standout for Roma this season with 12 goals across all competitions, and he will be keen to add to his goal against Greece while Cody Gakpo and Crysencio Summerville provide width.

Captain Virgil van Dijk has sat out this international break with complaints of physical discomfort, so expect to see Tottenham Hotspur's Micky van de Ven and Jan Paul van Hecke start at centre-back.

Germany possible starting lineup:.

Ter Stegen; Treu, Thiaw, Tah, Mittelstadt; Kimmich, Pavlovic; Gruda, Wirtz, Scherhant; Havertz.

Netherlands possible starting lineup:.

Verbruggen; Dumfries, Van Hecke, Van de Ven, Timber; Veerman, Koopmeiners; Summerville, Reijnders, Gakpo; Malen.

The maths of the table may be complex, but Germany know that a simple victory will see them through to the quarter-finals.

Oranje have yet to lose in the Nations League this season, though with the stakes lowered, they could be caught off guard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cody Gakpo has heaped praise on one of his Liverpool teammates who boasts ‘incredible football intelligence’ and is an ‘extraordinary player’.

The 27-year-old will come up against fellow Reds star Florian Wirtz tonight when Netherlands face Germany in the UEFA Nations League. The Dutchman is also set for a reunion with his former Anfield boss Jurgen Klopp, who takes charge of the home side in Berlin.

LFC’s number 7 has faced some stinging criticism among the British media since his £100m move from Bayer Leverkusen in June 2025, but he went into the international window off the back of scoring one goal and setting up another in the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace eight days ago.

Speaking to the media ahead of tonight’s match, Gakpo was keen to highlight the standout traits of his Liverpool teammate.

In a recent development, the Dutch forward mentioned of Wirtz (via GOAL): “Regarding his situation at the club, I think in his last match he played amazingly. He scored a goal, provided an assist, and was very important for us.

It has been revealed that “As a team, we know the quality he possesses; he shows it in every match and training session. He is an extraordinary player.

“Coming to Liverpool with an expensive transfer fee certainly makes the adaptation process in this league not easy for anyone, even for players who have had a 10-year career here.

“However, he has incredible football intelligence. The way he reads and dictates the pace of the game is very important to our style of play. We are very happy to have him.”.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

With nine goals and 15 assists in 64 games for the Reds so far, it’d be fair to expect a higher return from Wirtz considering his position on the pitch and the transfer fee that the club paid for him.

However, the German is scintillating to watch when he’s at his best, and the win over Palace showed that he’s capable of bending matches to his will when he’s on song.

There have been other standout displays in recent weeks, including the game at Brentford when he created nine chances, and a terrific outing against Villarreal that he marked with a well-taken goal.

There are signs that Wirtz is now properly hitting his stride at Liverpool and primed to consistently turn in impactful performances, something he didn’t do often enough in his first season at Anfield.

Industry observers note that gakpo sees the 23-year-old at close quarters on a daily basis and is perfectly placed to speak about the German’s main qualities. On current form, our number 7 will be pivotal to our chances of success in the 2026/27 campaign.

#2272. Latest Update: Luke Graham seizes his chance to shine in Scotland back-line... now Stoke defender aims to make himself a fixture for years to come

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1116 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Luke Graham seizes his chance to shine in Scotland back-line... now Stoke defender aims to make himself a fixture for years to come

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026.
  • Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 18:01 EST, 14 November 2026.

Whatever concerns there may legitimately be about the limited progress seen in Sebastien Pocognoli’s brief time in charge of Scotland, the Belgian has hardly been blessed with good fortune.

According to recent reports, in five matches to date in the Nations League, the manager has not yet been able to select the same back-three in two consecutive outings. Injuries and suspensions have seen to that.

For all that, you sense that even if he’d had a full quota of players to choose from, Pocognoli would still be figuring out his preferred defensive grouping.

According to recent reports, this does feel like a time of opportunity for those who are fresh on the scene. Catch the eye and there’s a real chance to become established as a mainstay of the team moving forward.

Luke Graham did his chances of doing just that no harm at all in his first start and second cap for his country on Friday.

Playing in between Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney, the Stoke City man made a compelling case to stay there with a strong and diligent display.

Luke Graham enjoyed a composed debut for Scotland as they recorded a much-needed win.

On the back of a summer move from Dundee to the English Championship, Graham appears to have taken the step-up to international level in his stride.

‘It’s something I’ve always wanted to do since I was growing up, so I have to be ready for the moment and take it when it comes,’ he noted.

‘I think there’s good competition. We have a lot of good centre-halves. Obviously, it was unfortunate for Welshy (Stephen Welsh) and Binksy (Luis Binks) to go out with injury, but that opens up a space for me to come in and try to cement a place.

‘When you’re out on that pitch, you have to do everything you can to try and stay in the team. I gave my all and I’ll just need to wait and see what happens going forward.’.

In a recent development, timing can be vital in football. And it’s conceivable that Graham’s might just propel him to become a Scotland regular.

While playing at Dens Park saw him mentioned in dispatches with regards to a call-up, his move to England, coming just before Pocognoli was declared as Steve Clarke’s successor, has seen his dream promptly become reality.

‘I’ve always said that one thing I wanted to do in my career was play for Scotland, so to get it over the line was pretty special,’ he reflected.

Former Dundee defender Graham proudly belts out the national anthem ahead of kick-off.

‘Not much is going wrong for me at the moment, so it’s just about maintaining that and keeping it going every week.

‘I wouldn’t say I merited a start as we have a lot of good players in the camp. It’s up to the manager to pick the team and, luckily, he gave me the chance.

‘He just said to go out and enjoy it and do what you’re doing every week at Stoke. I think I did all right.’.

Notwithstanding how limited the North Macedonians were on the night, Pocognoli was entitled to take encouragement from the way the back three acquitted themselves.

Sources indicate that playing closer to each other than we’d seen in the previous matches, they were rarely unpicked by balls through the middle. Angus Gunn was not overworked in goal. Tellingly, the only concession of the night came when Scott McTominay lost his man at a corner.

‘I think a lot of it is just being brave,’ Graham reflected. ‘It’s about bravery in going man-to-man with the striker, being brave on the ball, trying to break the lines and keeping possession.

‘So, I think bravery is the main thing and concentration as well.’.

Graham keeps a close eye on North Macedonian danger man Elmin Rastoder at Hampden.

In a recent development, with the defence solid enough, Pocognoli had a platform for a much-needed win. While the narrow scoreline made the final moments more anxious than they should have been, on balance, Scotland were deserved winners.

Recent findings suggest that ‘It’s just about winning games at this stage of the competition, so that was good,’ noted Graham. ‘I think, if I’m being harsh, we should have killed the game off before it got to 1-1. We had a few good chances to put them to bed.

Industry observers note that ‘Then we kinda shot ourselves in the foot by conceding from a set piece. But Ben Gannon-Doak does well for the penalty and for us to go 2-1 up and see it out was good.’.

No one would dispute that the display was a long way from perfect. There’s significant room for improvement ahead of the concluding group match with Switzerland on Monday.

Industry observers note that ‘We’re going through a bit of a transitional spell at the minute, so it’s not going to be all smooth sailing from the get-go,’ Graham mentioned. ‘It’s about adjusting and trying to build on performances in every game. I think it’s going to take time.

‘It’s a different style, a different manager and we just have to keep being patient. You look at the squad now and there’s a lot of upcoming, young players coming through. It’s just about encouraging us young boys and showing we can get a place in the squad.

‘It is going to take time but, once we get there, we’re going to do really well and compete right at the top of the game.’.

Graham has been a huge success in Stoke's flying start to the Championship season.

Graham does look like he’s moving in the right direction. From watching Scotland compete at the World Cup on licensed premises five months ago, he hopes he too can be the toast of the nation one day.

‘I didn’t go. It was too expensive for me,’ he explained. ‘I think I was just like everyone else, watching in the pub with their mates. It was pretty amazing and hopefully I can be part of something like that one day.

‘I wasn’t too far away (previously), I think. Steve Clarke, the former manager, told me that. It’s just about trusting myself now and hopefully getting there one day.

According to recent reports, ‘There’s been a lot of hard work and dedication which has led me to this point. I’m very grateful to a lot of people who have helped me in my career so far and just to get this chance is amazing.’.

Recent findings suggest that it has been a difficult season for Milan, at least where injuries are concerned. In defence, they have had concerns reminiscent of the 2023/24 season, where Gabbia had to be brought back from his loan spell at Villarreal.

This season, though, it seems Gerry Cardinale is going to go down a different route and spend to help Ruben Amorim with his defensive options. Indeed, there have been plenty of rumours about recruitments at the back.

However, Gabbia could again be a key returnee in January, with him hoping to return from injury early in the upcoming year.

Speaking to Sky Sport (via MilanNews) – at an event organised by the Milan Foundation at Milan’s “Arturo Toscanini” secondary school, where they met with several children with disabilities – Gabbia discussed the importance of the event, as well as his recovery.

What were the emotions of this meeting?

Sources indicate that “It’s wonderful, very enjoyable to spend hours with them. It’s also beautiful to see how they manage to create a group, something that really shows the importance of teamwork, the importance of friendship, even among themselves.

“We’re happy; we thank Fondazione Milan for the project, which is always beautiful and important: we’re happy to be a part of it and we’re enjoying the afternoon.”.

Are you able to rejoin the group in January?

Recent findings suggest that “Yes, that could be the time: we’re trying to work hard and do everything as best we can. I obviously have to thank the physiotherapists and the doctor because we’re really doing everything we can every day to try to heal the injury and get back on the pitch feeling good.

“It’s definitely been an unlucky season for me so far: I don’t want it to happen again or for any recurrences, so it’s also notable to take the right time, get back in shape, and support the team right now.”.

“Although it’s bad for the team that there are so many injured players, we’re together right now, supporting each other and trying to encourage each other through therapy, gym work, and the entire recovery process. Therefore, we’re trying to work as a team this week too, to overcome all the players’ injuries.

“From a personal standpoint, I’m trying to take this time calmly, in the sense that these things are part of sport, part of life, and not all moments are the same.

According to recent reports, “This is certainly a difficult time, but it still allows me to stay close to the team, to try to lend my support, even in the good and bad times. That’s what I’m doing, in addition to obviously doing what I can to try to return as soon as possible and make my contribution on the pitch.”.

How do you explain the team’s ups and downs?

“I think it’s something we need to get our heads around; we need to understand the importance of every game.

“The other day I heard our coach give an interview in which he mentioned something important: we need to understand that every game, when you don’t win, is taken as a defeat, a heavy defeat. We need to truly understand the importance of every game and approach training to prepare 100%, as best as possible, for every match.

“Therefore, I think this is room for improvement, but I see a group that is really eager to improve, to work, and as a result, I’m sure we’ll be able to fix this flaw as well.

“Although we’ve had a good start to the year in the league and less so in the Europa League, we have plenty of time to improve and have a strong year.”.

#2268. Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read (7289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~36 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1.
  • Sources indicate that the global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies.
  • It has been revealed that despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an notable barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

Sources indicate that the global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

It has been revealed that despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an notable barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

To address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

According to recent reports, an alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

It has been revealed that this study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a fresh pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

The structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 reveals the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

In a recent development, the key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as important for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

a–c, Time-averaged coefficients of power (a), thrust (b) and root bending moment (c) as a function of the tip-speed ratio for rigid and flexible blades at different flow speeds.

Industry observers note that to quantify the practical benefits of the passive load mitigation of the chordwise-flexible blade in realistic inflow, we simulate the performance over a representative tidal cycle and compare it against a rigid blade turbine with the same control strategy and a state-of-the-art, actively pitch-controlled turbine (see Supplementary Note 2 for modelling of the active pitch-and-speed control turbine). The sinusoidal inflow velocity represents the flow seen by a tidal turbine during a tidal cycle is shown in Fig. 2a, which is.

Sources indicate that a–d, Time history over a simulated tidal period of the freestream speed (a), the quasi-steady power (b), the tip-speed ratio (c) and the quasi-steady thrust (d). Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

The cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

According to recent reports, an effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 highlights a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

In a recent development, a–c, Standard deviation of power (a), thrust (b) and root-bending moment (c) of flexible and rigid blades, for the optimum tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5). All quantities are divided by those of the rigid blade at rated velocity.

In a recent development, to illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 shows the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

In a recent development, phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

Recent findings suggest that the measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

According to recent reports, DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

The observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

To further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

According to recent reports, the fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

According to recent reports, to demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

According to recent reports, finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Sources indicate that overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

This experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

According to recent reports, the main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Recent findings suggest that therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

In a recent development, the mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up fresh pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

According to recent reports, all experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,.

In a recent development, from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

FloWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

According to recent reports, A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

Sources indicate that the results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

It has been revealed that the main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

The thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

Industry observers note that the principal measured quantities were torque (Q), thrust (T), flapwise root-bending moment (M) and angular velocity (ω). Measured loads and power are non-dimensionalized using standard turbine coefficients:.

The tip-speed ratio is defined as.

where ω is the turbine angular velocity in radians per second.

Sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

According to recent reports, blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

It has been revealed that images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a upcoming deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to patch the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

According to recent reports, this code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. In the full-scale simulations (Extended Data Fig. 5), the stiffness of both the spar and the rubber is 10.6 times higher than at model scale to ensure that the model and full-scale Cauchy number for both the spar and the rubber is the same, where.

where ρ is the fluid mass density and E is the Young’s modulus.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Nsidibe Akpan | 14 Nov 2026 23:59.
  • Central African Republic host Benin at the Japoma Stadium in Douala, Cameroon, on Monday in the fourth round of Group F in 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying.
  • Benin won the first leg 4-1 in Abidjan on Thursday and lead Group F on goal difference, level on seven points with Burkina Faso, while Central African Republic remain bottom with no points and a goal difference of -6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nsidibe Akpan | 14 Nov 2026 23:59.

Central African Republic host Benin at the Japoma Stadium in Douala, Cameroon, on Monday in the fourth round of Group F in 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying.

Benin won the first leg 4-1 in Abidjan on Thursday and lead Group F on goal difference, level on seven points with Burkina Faso, while Central African Republic remain bottom with no points and a goal difference of -6.

Central African Republic, known as Les Fauves, have lost all three qualifiers, scoring two goals and conceding eight, and have not won any match since October last year.

Mauritania won 3-1 in their opener on September 24, and Burkina Faso followed with a 1-0 victory over them on September 28.

Head coach Abdelaziz Kerkache, a Moroccan who has previously worked at Mouloudia d’Oujda, was appointed on November 6 to replace Eloge Enza Yamissi, only six days before the first leg.

Kerkache recalled Geoffrey Kondogbia of Olympique de Marseille and Le Mans forward Louis Mafouta, who both missed the opening two qualifiers, and Mafouta responded by equalising in the first leg.

Les Fauves had more of the ball in Abidjan, with 56% possession and eight corners to Benin’s five, yet goalkeeper Dominique Youfeigane faced eight shots on target and conceded four.

Central African Republic are still chasing a first Africa Cup of Nations finals appearance after narrowly missing out in 2021 and 2023, and their home leg is being staged in Douala rather than in Bangui.

Benin, nicknamed Les Guepards, have taken seven points from three Group F games under Gernot Rohr, beginning with a 1-1 draw at Burkina Faso on September 25.

A 2-1 win over Mauritania in Abidjan on September 29 followed, with Rodolfo Aloko scoring either side of half time, as Benin again used an Ivory Coast venue because the Stade de l’Amitie in Cotonou is not yet approved for qualifiers.

Hassane Imourane opened the scoring in the seventh minute of the first leg, Louis Mafouta equalised in the 19th, and Benin were 3-1 up at half time after Aloko struck in the 31st minute and Aiyegun Tosin in the 36th.

Tosin completed his brace in the 56th minute, and he and Aloko have now scored six of Benin’s seven goals in qualifying.

Benin won despite having only 44% of the possession, turning 18 shots into four goals, with eight efforts on target against Central African Republic’s 14 shots and five on target.

Rohr said afterwards that the scoreline flattered his side because Central African Republic attacked a great deal, and he expects a reaction in a rematch only four days later.

Central African Republic Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

Central African Republic form (all competitions):.

Benin Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:.

For the Central African Republic, Edwin Quarshie, booked in the 1-0 defeat by Burkina Faso, missed the first leg through suspension for accumulated yellow cards and should be available again on Monday.

Venuste Baboula, who has an ankle sprain, was left out of the starting lineup on Thursday, and he could be saved for the return match.

Kondogbia, Mafouta and Goduine Koyalipou all started in Abidjan, and Kerkache has had only one match to work with that group.

For Benin, captain and striker Steve Mounie remains out injured, so Rohr again leans on Aloko, Tosin and Junior Olaitan, who has three goals and seven assists for Besiktas this season.

Parfait Faton, a 16-year-old midfielder from AAS Sarcelles, received his first senior call-up in a 25-player squad that also includes Sessi D’Almeida and Jodel Dossou.

Central African Republic possible starting lineup:.

Youfeigane; Yangao, Kouadio, Gambor, Yapende; Solet, Kondogbia, Diomande; Yawenendji, Koyalipou, Mafouta.

Benin possible starting lineup:.

Sources indicate that dandjinou; T. Ouorou, Roche, Tijani, Azongnitode; D’Almeida, Imourane; Aloko, Olaitan, Y. Ouorou; Tosin.

Benin were far more efficient than their numbers suggest, putting eight of 18 shots on target with only 44% of the ball, and they did it without Mounie.

Central African Republic have conceded eight goals in three qualifiers, and a second game in four days under Kerkache is unlikely to repair a defence that let in three before half time on Thursday.

Benin cannot afford to slip either, because Burkina Faso are also on seven points after an added-time winner from Elohim Kabore against Mauritania, and the Cheetahs lead the table only on goal difference.

A clean sheet is less certain, because Mafouta equalised in the first leg and Kondogbia gives Les Fauves a better platform than they had in September, so we expect Central African Republic to score but not to take anything from the game.

One Liverpool player has been criticised for making a ‘stupid’ decision while representing his country during the international window.

Andoni Iraola was unsure whether Dominik Szoboszlai would partake in Hungary’s UEFA Nations League fixtures against Georgia and Northern Ireland after the midfielder sprained his knee in the Reds’ 3-1 win at Crystal Palace the weekend before last.

The 26-year-old did end up playing the entirety of his country’s 2-0 victory in Tbilisi on Saturday, although he admitted post-match that he felt a twinge during the warm-up and was close to pulling out before opting to play.

Liverpool-focused journalist David Lynch was critical of the midfielder for playing through the pain barrier to the potential detriment of his club, albeit with an acknowledgement that the Reds’ number 8 would feel duty-bound to represent his nation.

The reporter said on Anfield Index’s Media Matters podcast: “I think there’s no other way to describe this than stupid, really. He could have been a little bit smarter in terms of either not playing the game or, if you’re going to play through the pain in that way, maybe don’t talk about it.

“I don’t think Liverpool supporters are going to like it that you’re prioritising to such a degree. Playing for your country is a massive honour, and particularly when you are the captain, I absolutely understand that. I don’t want to play that down at all.”.

This is a classic case of multiple parties having their own vested interests at heart. Hungary were obviously pushing for Szoboszlai to play, and he understandably wanted to come through for his country, whereas anyone of an LFC persuasion would much rather he sat it out.

If the midfielder comes through the match against Northern Ireland tomorrow night and is operating at (or close to) 100% for the Reds’ showdown against Manchester United next Sunday, then he’ll feel vindicated in his stance to continue playing.

However, by admitting that he wasn’t fully fit on Saturday, he’s left himself open to condemnation from Liverpool fans (and reporters, in Lynch’s case) who are justifiably asking why he took the risk of potentially aggravating an existing injury and curtailing his involvement for the club which employs him.

That sense of concern is heightened by Iraola’s team entering a frantic period of 11 matches in 40 days to end this calendar year, plus two more in the first five days of 2027. We can’t afford for Szoboszlai to be out of action amid that thankless fixture schedule.

We get that he didn’t want to let his country down unless he was completely unable to play, but he’s now placed added pressure on himself to be available over the coming weeks for Liverpool, and to deliver the kind of consistently top-class performances that he produced last season.
